entries.title: Aaron
entries.summary: Named once, to establish Elizabeth's priestly pedigree before John is even born (1:5) — 'a daughter of Aaron.' Josephus gives the office itself its own origin story: Moses publicly vouching for his brother's character before the people accept him.
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Micah, Luke, Acts, Hebrews
entries.dictNote: Aaron was the first high priest of Israel and the elder brother of Moses and Miriam, born to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi. When Moses balked at speaking for himself before Pharaoh, God sent Aaron to act as his mouthpiece, and the two brothers together led the exodus out of Egypt. Aaron married Elisheba and fathered four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, whose descendants carried the priesthood after him. He is named 333 times across the Old and New Testaments, most often at Moses's side, though the golden calf at Sinai remains the one moment he acted alone.

witness.excerpt: God appeared to Moses, and enjoined him to bestow the High Priesthood upon Aaron his brother: as upon him that best of them all deserved to obtain that honour, on account of his virtue.

entries.title: Abaddon
entries.dictNote: The Hebrew name, meaning "destruction" and rendered in Greek as Apollyon ("destroyer"), given to the angel ruling the demonic locusts released from the abyss in Revelation 9:11. Elsewhere in the Old Testament the same word simply personifies ruin or the realm of the dead rather than naming an individual being (Job 26:6, 28:22; Proverbs 15:11).

entries.title: Abarim
entries.dictNote: Abarim was a mountain range east of the Dead Sea in Moab, overlooking Jericho and the Jordan Valley; Mount Nebo, its best-known peak, was where Moses viewed the promised land before his death (Deuteronomy 32:49-50; 34:1-5). Israel camped in these mountains after crossing the Arnon during the final stage of the wilderness journey (Numbers 33:47-48).

entries.title: Abel
entries.dictNote: Abel was Adam and Eve's second son, a shepherd whose offering of the firstborn of his flock God accepted while rejecting the offering of his farmer brother Cain, and Cain's resulting jealousy led to history's first murder. Jesus refers to Abel's blood as the first in a long line of righteous blood shed by Israel, and Hebrews credits Abel's faith, not just his offering, as the reason his sacrifice pleased God, adding that his blood still speaks even though he is dead.

entries.title: Abel
entries.summary: The first name in Jesus's list of murdered prophets, 'from the blood of Abel' (11:51) — echoing Genesis 4:10's blood that cries out. 1 Enoch's own vision of the afterlife has Abel's spirit still literally pleading his case in the world of the dead, generations later.
entries.dictNote: (Heb. Hebhel), a breath, or vanity, the second son of Adam and Eve. He was put to death by his brother Cain (Gen. 4:1-16). Guided by the instruction of their father, the two brothers were trained in the duty of worshipping God. “And in process of time” (marg. “at the end of days”, i.e., on the Sabbath) each of them offered up to God of the first-fruits of his labours. Cain, as a husbandman, offered the fruits of the field; Abel, as a shepherd, of the firstlings of his flock. “The Lord had respect unto Abel and his offering; but unto Cain and his offering he had not respect” (Gen. 4:3-5). On this account Cain was angry with his brother, and formed the design of putting him to death; a design which he at length found an opportunity of carrying into effect (Gen. 4:8, 9. Comp. 1 John 3:12). There are several references to Abel in the New Testament. Our Saviour speaks of him as “righteous” (Matt. 23:35). “The blood of sprinkling” is said to speak “better things than that of Abel” (Heb. 12:24); i.e., the blood of Jesus is the reality of which the blood of the offering made by Abel was only the type. The comparison here is between the sacrifice offered by Christ and that offered by Abel, and not between the blood of Christ calling for mercy and the blood of the murdered Abel calling for vengeance, as has sometimes been supposed. It is also said (Heb. 11:4) that “Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain.” This sacrifice was made “by faith;” this faith rested in God, not only as the Creator and the God of providence, but especially in God as the great Redeemer, whose sacrifice was typified by the sacrifices which, no doubt by the divine institution, were offered from the days of Adam downward. On account of that “faith” which looked forward to the great atoning sacrifice, Abel’s offering was accepted of God. Cain’s offering had no such reference, and therefore was rejected. Abel was the first martyr, as he was the first of our race to die. Abel (Heb. ‘abhel), lamentation (1 Sam. 6:18), the name given to the great stone in Joshua’s field whereon the ark was “set down.” The Revised Version, however, following the Targum and the LXX., reads in the Hebrew text ’ebhen (= a stone), and accordingly translates “unto the great stone, whereon they set down the ark.” This reading is to be preferred. entries.title: Abel-beth-maachah
entries.summary: Abel of Beth-maakah, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Abel-beth-maachah was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, near Dan, called a mother in Israel, a way of naming it a leading city of the region (2 Samuel 20:19). Joab besieged it there to root out the rebel Sheba (2 Samuel 20:14-15), and it was later captured first by the Aramean king Ben-hadad at Asa's instigation (1 Kings 15:20) and then by Assyria's Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:29). Tiglath-pileser's own summary inscriptions list the conquest of this same region's towns, including Abel-beth-maacah, independently corroborating the biblical account.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Abel-maim
entries.dictNote: An alternate name, "Abel on the waters," for the northern Israelite town of Abel-beth-maachah, used in the account of King Asa of Judah hiring Ben-hadad of Syria to attack Israel's northern towns (2 Chronicles 16:4). The same city was captured more than a century later by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, an episode corroborated by Tiglath-pileser's own annals recording his campaign against the towns of Galilee and the north.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abel-meholah
entries.dictNote: Abel-meholah was a town in the Jordan Valley, near Issachar's territory, along the route the defeated Midianites fled after Gideon's night attack (Judges 7:22). It was the birthplace and home of the prophet Elisha, whom Elijah found there plowing with oxen before calling him into his service (1 Kings 19:16, 19). It lay near where the Wadi el-Maleh opens into the Jordan Valley, south of Beth-shean.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Abel-mizraim
entries.dictNote: The name the Canaanites gave to the threshing floor of Atad, west of the Jordan, where Joseph and his brothers held a seven-day mourning ceremony for Jacob on their way to bury him in Canaan (Genesis 50:11). The name means "mourning of Egypt," and its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abelshittim
entries.summary: Abel hash-Shittim, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Abel-shittim, "the meadow of acacias," was Israel's last encampment on the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan into Canaan (Numbers 33:49). Usually called simply Shittim elsewhere in the Old Testament, it was the setting for Balak's hire of Balaam, Israel's apostasy with Baal-peor, and Moses' final instructions before his death. It lay east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, though its exact site in the valley remains disputed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Abez
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar in the Jezreel Valley region (Josh. 19:20). Its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Abi
entries.dictNote: Abi was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah and wife of King Ahaz, identified as the daughter of a Zechariah (2 Kings 18:2). The parallel record in 2 Chronicles 29:1 calls her Abijah.

entries.dictNote: Abia is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Abijah. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus uses it for Abijah, king of Judah and son of Rehoboam (Matthew 1:7). Luke uses it differently, naming the eighth of the twenty-four priestly divisions David established, the division to which Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, belonged (Luke 1:5; 1 Chronicles 24:10).

entries.title: Abiasaph
entries.dictNote: The youngest of the three sons of Korah the Levite and head of one of the Korahite family divisions (Exodus 6:24). The parallel genealogies in Chronicles call him Ebiasaph. His descendants later included lines of temple gatekeepers and singers, a striking legacy given that Korah himself led a rebellion against Moses and was destroyed for it.

Abiathar backed the wrong side in the succession struggle at David's death, supporting Adonijah over Solomon, and Solomon exiled him from the priesthood rather than execute him, ending his family's long hold on the office.

entries.title: Abilene
entries.dictNote: Abilene was a small tetrarchy in the eastern foothills of the Anti-Lebanon range, between Damascus and Baalbek, named for its chief town Abila. Luke names it as the domain of the tetrarch Lysanias when dating the start of John the Baptist's ministry (Luke 3:1). An inscription found near the site of Abila, dated to the reign of Tiberius, names a ruler called Lysanias the tetrarch, which answered a long-standing objection that Luke had confused this figure with an earlier, better known Lysanias of Chalcis who had died decades before; it points instead to a second ruler by that name and title governing the region exactly when Luke says he did.

entries.title: Abraham
entries.summary: Luke's most-cited Old Testament figure outside the genealogy — ‘father Abraham’ anchors the whole parable of the rich man and Lazarus (16:22-31). Josephus, writing for a Roman audience a generation after Luke, makes the same figure into the first monotheist philosopher — a very different rhetorical job, same man. Philo also gave him his own dedicated treatise, reading his whole life as one long act of obedience — a third independent voice (with Luke and Josephus) on the same figure.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter
entries.dictNote: Abraham was called by God out of Ur to become the father of a new nation, leaving his home at seventy-five with his wife Sarah and a promise that had no visible way of coming true, since Sarah was childless and both of them were old. He eventually fathered Ishmael through Sarah's servant Hagar and then Isaac through Sarah herself after God renamed him from Abram, and Genesis traces the rest of his life through Canaan in altars, wells, and one wrenching test on Mount Moriah. Clay tablets from Nuzi, written centuries after Abraham but preserving the same Hurrian legal customs, explain a strange line in his own story: his fear that a servant named Eliezer would inherit everything reflects a real adoption practice for childless couples, not an invented plot device.

entries.title: Accad
entries.dictNote: Akkad was one of the founding cities of Nimrod's kingdom in the Table of Nations, paired with Babel, Erech, and Calneh in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:10). It was the capital of Sargon of Akkad's empire around 2300 BC, the first empire to unite Mesopotamia's city-states under one ruler, and the Akkadian language it gave its name to became the region's dominant tongue for the next two thousand years. Despite more than a century of searching, archaeologists have never located the city itself; its site, somewhere along the Euphrates near Babylon, remains one of the most sought-after unsolved locations in Near Eastern archaeology.

It appears in Egyptian sources and the Amarna letters centuries before Israel's conquest, and was later rebuilt and renamed Ptolemais under the Greeks, the city where Paul landed near the end of his final journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7).

entries.title: Achmetha
entries.summary: Achmetha (i.e. Ecbatana), the summer capital of Persia
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the Aramaic name in Ezra 6:2 for Ecbatana, the ancient capital of Media and summer residence of the Persian kings, located near modern Hamadan, Iran. The decree of Cyrus authorizing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple was found archived there, since Cyrus had held court at Ecbatana before later Persian kings shifted their main residence to Susa. Excavations at Hamadan have confirmed continuous occupation from the Median period onward, though the ancient Achaemenid palace itself has not been conclusively located beneath the modern city.

entries.title: Achor
entries.summary: Akor, the name of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Achor lay near Jericho, on the border of Judah and Benjamin, and takes its name from the trouble Achan brought on Israel when he stole devoted plunder from Jericho and was executed there (Joshua 7:24-26). Centuries later the prophets turned that memory of judgment into a promise of restoration: Hosea pictures the valley becoming "a door of hope," and Isaiah pictures it as pastureland for flocks, God's judgment transformed into blessing (Hosea 2:15; Isaiah 65:10). It is usually identified with the Buqei'a plain or the Wadi Qelt southwest of Jericho.

entries.title: Achsah
entries.dictNote: Achsah was Caleb's daughter, given in marriage to Othniel after he captured a Canaanite city, and she boldly asked her father for springs of water to go with the dry land he'd given her, a request he granted in full.

entries.title: Achshaph
entries.dictNote: Achshaph was a Canaanite royal city whose king joined the northern coalition that Joshua defeated near the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1; 12:20). It fell within the territory allotted to Asher (Joshua 19:25). The city appears independently in Pharaoh Thutmose III's fifteenth-century BC topographical list of conquered Canaanite towns at Karnak, confirming it as a real Late Bronze Age settlement centuries before Joshua's campaign.

entries.summary: Akzib, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Achzib was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah, and also the name of a Phoenician coastal town within Asher's territory that Israel never fully conquered.

entries.title: Adadah
entries.dictNote: A town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed with Dimonah and Kedesh (Joshua 15:22). Its exact site is unknown.

entries.dictNote: Adah was one of Lamech's two wives in Cain's genealogical line, and a different Adah was one of Esau's wives, a daughter of the Hittite Elon.

entries.title: Adam
entries.summary: Luke's genealogy runs all the way back to him — 'the son of Adam, the son of God' (3:38), the only name in the whole list with no human father. Josephus opens his entire 20-book history on the same page of Genesis, in Whiston's own 18th-century English.
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Hosea, Luke, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, Jude
entries.dictNote: Red, a Babylonian word, the generic name for man, having the same meaning in the Hebrew and the Assyrian languages. It was the name given to the first man, whose creation, fall, and subsequent history and that of his descendants are detailed in the first book of Moses (Gen. 1:27-ch. 5). “God created man [Heb., Adam] in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” Adam was absolutely the first man whom God created. He was formed out of the dust of the earth (and hence his name), and God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and gave him dominion over all the lower creatures (Gen. 1:26; 2:7). He was placed after his creation in the Garden of Eden, to cultivate it, and to enjoy its fruits under this one prohibition: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” The first recorded act of Adam was his giving names to the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, which God brought to him for this end. Thereafter the Lord caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, and while in an unconscious state took one of his ribs, and closed up his flesh again; and of this rib he made a woman, whom he presented to him when he awoke. Adam received her as his wife, and said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.” He called her Eve, because she was the mother of all living. Being induced by the tempter in the form of a serpent to eat the forbidden fruit, Eve persuaded Adam, and he also did eat. Thus man fell, and brought upon himself and his posterity all the sad consequences of his transgression. The narrative of the Fall comprehends in it the great promise of a Deliverer (Gen. 3:15), the “first gospel” message to man. They were expelled from Eden, and at the east of the garden God placed a flame, which turned every way, to prevent access to the tree of life (Gen. 3). How long they were in Paradise is matter of mere conjecture. Shortly after their expulsion Eve brought forth her first-born, and called him Cain. Although we have the names of only three of Adam’s sons, viz., Cain, Abel, and Seth, yet it is obvious that he had several sons and daughters (Gen. 5:4). He died aged 930 years. Adam and Eve were the progenitors of the whole human race. Evidences of varied kinds are abundant in proving the unity of the human race. The investigations of science, altogether independent of historical evidence, lead to the conclusion that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26. Comp. Rom. 5:12-12; 1 Cor. 15:22-49).

entries.title: Adbeel
entries.dictNote: Adbeel was the third of Ishmael's twelve sons, each of whom became head of an Arabian tribal confederation (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). Some scholars connect his descendants with the “Idibi'ilu” named in the eighth-century BC annals of the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III as a tribe controlling Egypt's desert border. Nothing further is recorded of Adbeel himself.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Addan
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a place name, one of several Babylonian localities named in Ezra 2:59 (called Addon in the parallel list of Nehemiah 7:61) from which a group of exiles returned to Judah after the exile but could not prove their genealogical descent from Israel. Its exact location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Addar
entries.summary: Addar, a place in Palestine; also an Israelite
entries.dictNote: This entry actually names a person, not a place: Addar is the form of the name given in 1 Chronicles 8:3 for a son of Bela, grandson of Benjamin, called Ard in Genesis 46:21 and Numbers 26:40. It is a duplicate record of that same individual rather than a separate location.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Addi
entries.dictNote: Addi appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Cosam and father of Melchi, one link in the ancestral chain traced through Joseph back to David (Luke 3:28).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Addon
entries.dictNote: Addon is named among a group of returning exiles who could not produce genealogical proof of their Israelite descent when the community's family records were checked after the return from Babylon (Neh. 7:61; called Addan in the parallel list at Ezra 2:59). The episode reflects how carefully priestly and tribal lineage was guarded in the postexilic community.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ader
entries.dictNote: A Benjaminite leader, son of Beriah, listed among the family heads settled in Aijalon; some manuscripts give the name as Eder (1 Chronicles 8:15).

entries.title: Adiel
entries.summary: Adiel, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Adiel was a common name, borne by a Simeonite clan leader, a priest in the genealogies of Chronicles, and the father of one of David's treasury officials.

entries.title: Adin
entries.summary: Adin, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Adin was the head of a family among the returning exiles, large enough to be listed by household count in both Ezra and Nehemiah.

entries.title: Adina
entries.dictNote: Adina was a Reubenite who led thirty men and served among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:42).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adithaim
entries.dictNote: Adithaim, a lowland town of Judah named between Sharaim and Gederah in the Shephelah district list of Joshua 15:36. It occurs only here and its site remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adlai
entries.dictNote: Adlai was the father of Shaphat, who oversaw King David's cattle grazing in the valleys as one of the officials managing the royal estates (1 Chronicles 27:29). He is mentioned only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Admah
entries.summary: Admah, a place near the Dead Sea
entries.dictNote: Admah was one of the five "cities of the plain" in the Jordan Valley, paired throughout Scripture with its neighbor Zeboiim, destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah for their wickedness (Genesis 10:19; 19:24-25; Deuteronomy 29:23). Hosea later cites Admah and Zeboiim's total destruction as a measure of the mercy God chose instead to show Israel (Hosea 11:8).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Admatha
entries.dictNote: Admatha was one of seven princes of Persia and Media who had access to the king and sat first in the kingdom, consulted by Ahasuerus after Queen Vashti's refusal to appear before him (Esther 1:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adna
entries.summary: Adna, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men bear this name. One was among the Israelites listed by Ezra who had married foreign wives during the exile and agreed to separate from them (Ezra 10:30). The other was a priest, head of the family of Harim, in the generation after the return from exile (Nehemiah 12:15).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Adnah
entries.summary: Adnah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Adnah refers to two distinct men in Chronicles who share this name. The first was a chief of the tribe of Manasseh who defected to David's side just before the battle of Gilboa, one of several Manassite commanders who joined him at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:20). The second, evidently unrelated, was the senior commander in King Jehoshaphat's army, leading a force of 300,000 men, the largest single division named in Jehoshaphat's military reorganization (2 Chronicles 17:14).

entries.title: Adonibezek
entries.dictNote: Adonibezek was a Canaanite king ruling at Bezek who had subdued seventy rival chiefs, mutilating each by cutting off his thumbs and big toes and forcing them to scavenge scraps under his table. The tribes of Judah and Simeon defeated him during the conquest and inflicted the same mutilation on him before bringing him to Jerusalem, where he died (Judges 1:4-7). He is recorded acknowledging the punishment as just retribution for his own cruelty, one of the few conquest-era accounts that quotes a defeated Canaanite ruler's own words.

Nathan and Bathsheba intervened, and David ordered Solomon anointed king immediately, collapsing Adonijah's attempted coup. Adonijah survived that failure only to be executed soon after for requesting marriage to one of David's former attendants, a request Solomon read as a renewed claim on the throne.

entries.title: Adonikam
entries.summary: Adonikam, the name of one or two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Adonikam was the ancestor of a family of 666 men who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, according to the census list in Ezra 2:13; a slightly different number, 660, appears in the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:18. A further group of his descendants came up later under Ezra (Ezra 8:13).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Adoniram
entries.dictNote: Adoniram, also called Adoram, was the son of Abda and served as the official in charge of forced labor levies under David, Solomon, and briefly Rehoboam (2 Samuel 20:24; 1 Kings 4:6; 1 Kings 12:18). When Rehoboam sent him to enforce the labor tax on the northern tribes after Solomon's death, the people stoned him to death, an act that helped trigger the kingdom's split into Israel and Judah (1 Kings 12:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adonizedec
entries.dictNote: Adonizedec was the Amorite king of Jerusalem who organized a coalition of five Canaanite kings to attack Gibeon after it made peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's forces to march to Gibeon's defense in the battle where the sun and moon reportedly stood still (Joshua 10:1-13). His coalition was defeated and the five kings were captured, humiliated, and executed (Joshua 10:16-27). His name, meaning “lord of righteousness,” echoes the earlier Melchizedek, priest-king of the same city centuries before (Genesis 14:18), and the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters independently show Jerusalem ruled by its own king corresponding with Egypt around this period, confirming the city's status as an established Canaanite city-state.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adoraim
entries.dictNote: A fortified city built by Rehoboam as part of Judah's southern defensive line after the kingdom split (2 Chronicles 11:9). Its name survives in Dura, a village southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adoram
entries.dictNote: Adoram, also called Adoniram, was the official in charge of forced labor under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:6). Years later, King Rehoboam sent him to collect tribute from the northern tribes during the crisis that split the kingdom, and the people stoned him to death, a killing that confirmed the revolt against the house of David (1 Kings 12:18).

entries.title: Adria
entries.dictNote: Adria, or the sea of Adria, refers to the central Mediterranean waters between Crete, Sicily, and Malta through which Paul's ship drifted during the storm before his shipwreck (Acts 27:27). In the first century the term covered this broader stretch of sea rather than only the modern Adriatic between Italy and the Balkans.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Adriel
entries.dictNote: Adriel, son of Barzillai the Meholathite, married Merab, Saul's elder daughter, after Saul withdrew her from his earlier promise to give her to David (1 Samuel 18:19). Their five sons were later handed over to the Gibeonites and executed as part of the reparations for Saul's earlier massacre of Gibeonite lives (2 Samuel 21:8-9); a textual difficulty in that passage names Michal rather than Merab as the mother, which most interpreters resolve either as scribal confusion between the two sisters or as Michal having raised her sister's sons.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Adronicus
entries.summary: man of victory; Andronicos, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: This entry's name reflects a likely data spelling of Andronicus, a Jewish Christian and relative or fellow countryman of Paul whom Paul greets in Romans 16:7 along with Junia, calling the pair "outstanding among the apostles" and noting that they had been believers in Christ before Paul's own conversion.

entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Micah
entries.dictNote: Adullam was a Canaanite royal city in the Shephelah near the valley of Elah, where David killed Goliath. After fleeing Saul, David took refuge in a cave near Adullam, where he was joined by family members and by everyone in distress, debt, or discontent, roughly four hundred men who became the core of his fighting force. Rehoboam later fortified Adullam against Egyptian invasion, and Micah calls it "the glory of Israel."

entries.title: Adummim
entries.dictNote: Adummim, meaning "the red ones," was a pass on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho, on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:7; 18:17). The rugged, blood-colored rock of the ascent made it a natural setting for banditry, and the location is traditionally associated with the road pictured in Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37).

entries.title: Aenon
entries.dictNote: A place "near Salim" with abundant water where John the Baptist carried out baptisms (John 3:23). Its precise location is debated, with proposals ranging from a site near Salim east of Shechem to another closer to the Jordan Valley further south, but its description as a well-watered spot fits either region.

entries.title: Agabus
entries.dictNote: Agabus was a Christian prophet in the early church who, at Antioch, predicted a severe famine that later occurred during the reign of Claudius, prompting the church to send relief to believers in Judea (Acts 11:27-30). Years later he met Paul at Caesarea and dramatically bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to warn that Paul would be arrested and handed over to the Gentiles if he went to Jerusalem, a warning Paul heeded as a caution but not a command to turn back (Acts 21:10-14). His famine prediction is one of the clearer instances in Acts of a specific, later-verified prophecy.

entries.title: Agag
entries.summary: Agag, a title of Amalekitish kings
entries.dictNote: Agag was a king of the Amalekites whom King Saul was ordered to destroy completely along with his people and livestock, but Saul spared Agag and the best animals instead, a direct act of disobedience that cost Saul God's favor and the kingdom. The prophet Samuel personally executed Agag afterward to finish what Saul had refused to do. Agag also appears to function as a dynastic title for Amalekite kings generally, since a much later Amalekite figure, Haman in the book of Esther, is identified as an Agagite.

entries.title: Agagite
entries.summary: an Agagite or descendent (subject) of Agag
entries.dictNote: Agagite is the title given to Haman in the book of Esther, most likely marking him as a descendant of Agag, the Amalekite king Saul had spared against God's command and whom Samuel then killed. entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Aharah
entries.dictNote: Aharah was the third son of Benjamin, listed in the tribal genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:1). He is likely the same figure called Ahiram in Numbers 26:38 and Aher in 1 Chronicles 7:12, since the lists of Benjamin's sons vary somewhat between Genesis, Numbers, and Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aharhel
entries.dictNote: Aharhel is named as a descendant of Harum's clan in a terse and difficult fragment of Judah's genealogy (1 Chr. 4:8). Little else can be reconstructed about his family from the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahasai
entries.dictNote: Ahasai was a priest listed as an ancestor of Maasiai among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:13). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 9:12 gives the same figure's name as Jahzerah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahasbai
entries.dictNote: Father of Eliphelet, one of David's mighty men listed in the roster of 2 Samuel 23:34; the parallel roster in 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives a garbled form of the same family line as Ur and Eliphal.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahasuerus
entries.summary: Achashverosh (i.e. Ahasuerus or Artaxerxes, but in this case Xerxes), the title (rather than name) of a Persian king
entries.dictNote: Ahasuerus is the Persian king who made Esther his queen after deposing Vashti, usually identified with Xerxes the First, whose reign is independently documented in Greek and Persian sources and whose famously lavish, extended banquets match the opening scene of the book of Esther closely. A different Ahasuerus appears briefly in the book of Daniel as the father of Darius the Mede.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ahava
entries.dictNote: Ahava was a river or canal in Babylonia where Ezra gathered the exiles who would return with him to Jerusalem, and where he proclaimed a fast to seek God's protection for the journey since he was ashamed to ask the king for a military escort (Ezra 8:15, 21-23). Its precise location is unknown, though it likely lay along one of the canals feeding the Euphrates near ancient Babylon.

entries.title: Ahaz

entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Hosea, Micah
entries.dictNote: Ahaz was a king of Judah who abandoned the reforms of his predecessors, sacrificing his own son in the fire and closing the temple to set up pagan altars instead, and rather than trust God's promise of protection through the prophet Isaiah, he paid the Assyrian empire for protection against a coalition of enemies, a decision that made Judah an Assyrian vassal for a generation. It was during Ahaz's crisis that Isaiah delivered the famous prophecy of a child to be called Immanuel, God with us.

entries.dictNote: Ahiam, son of Sharar (also called Sacar) the Hararite, was one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:33; 1 Chronicles 11:35). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ahian
entries.dictNote: Ahian was a Manassite descendant of Shemida, listed in the tribal genealogy of Manasseh east of the Jordan (1 Chr. 7:19). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Ahiezer
entries.summary: Achiezer, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ahiezer was the tribal leader of Dan during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahihud
entries.dictNote: A leader of the tribe of Asher chosen by Moses to help Eleazar the priest and Joshua divide the land of Canaan among the tribes west of the Jordan (Numbers 34:16-27). He represented Asher on the twelve-man commission, one leader from each tribe. He is a different man from the Ahihud, son of Bela, listed in Benjamin's genealogy (1 Chronicles 8:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahihud
entries.dictNote: A son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, listed as head of a family group that was deported from Geba to Manahath, likely during an early population shift within Benjamin's territory (1 Chronicles 8:6-7). He is a different man from the Ahihud of Asher who helped divide the land under Moses (Numbers 34:27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahikam
entries.dictNote: Ahikam was a court official under King Josiah who supported the prophetess Huldah's warnings and later protected the prophet Jeremiah from a mob that wanted him killed for his prophecies of judgment. His son Gedaliah was later appointed governor of Judah after Jerusalem's fall.

entries.summary: Achimaats, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ahimaaz was Zadok's son, and during Absalom's rebellion he served as a courier relaying intelligence to David, later racing another messenger to be first to bring David news of the battle's outcome, though he couldn't bring himself to tell David directly that his son Absalom was dead.

witness.excerpt: But now Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok the high priest, went to Joab, and desired he would permit him to go and tell David of this victory, and to bring him the good news that God had afforded his assistance and his providence to him.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ahiman
entries.summary: Achiman, the name of an Anakite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ahiman was one of the descendants of Anak, the giant clan whose size terrified the Israelite spies, and Caleb personally drove Ahiman and his brothers out of Hebron decades later when he finally claimed the land he'd been promised.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ahimelech
entries.summary: Achimelek, the name of an Israelite and of a Hittite
entries.dictNote: Ahimelech was the priest at Nob who unknowingly helped David while he was fleeing Saul, giving him consecrated bread and Goliath's sword, and Saul had him and the rest of the priestly community at Nob massacred for it once Doeg reported the assistance.

witness.excerpt: How David fled to Ahimelech ; and afterwards to the Kings of the Philistines and of the Moabites : and how Saul slew Ahimelech , and his family.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ahimoth
entries.dictNote: Ahimoth was a Kohathite Levite named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6. The same genealogy later gives the name as Mahath, reflecting the sort of variant spellings common in these priestly family records.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahinadab
entries.dictNote: One of Solomon's twelve district officers, assigned to Mahanaim east of the Jordan, responsible for supplying provisions to the royal household one month each year (1 Kings 4:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahinoam
entries.summary: Achinoam, the name of two Israelitesses
entries.dictNote: Ahinoam was the name of two women in David's life: Saul's wife, and a separate Ahinoam from Jezreel whom David married and who became the mother of his firstborn son Amnon.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ahio
entries.summary: Achio, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ahio was Uzzah's brother, and together they were guiding the cart carrying the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem when Uzzah reached out to steady it and was struck dead.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahira
entries.dictNote: Ahira was the tribal leader of Naphtali during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahiram
entries.dictNote: Ahiram was a son of Benjamin, ancestor of the Ahiramite clan counted in the wilderness census (Num. 26:38). He is probably the same figure called Ehi in Genesis 46:21, since the lists of Benjamin's sons differ somewhat across Genesis, Numbers, and Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahiramites
entries.summary: an Achiramite or descendant (collectively) of Achiram
entries.dictNote: Ahiramites were the clan descended from Ahiram, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same man is usually identified with Ehi in Genesis 46:21.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahisamach
entries.dictNote: Ahisamach was the father of Oholiab, the skilled craftsman from the tribe of Dan appointed alongside Bezalel to help construct the tabernacle.

witness.excerpt: Now their names are set down in writing in the sacred Books; and they were these: Besaleel , the son of Uri , of the tribe of Judah, the grandson of Miriam, the sister of their conductor; and Aholiab the son of Ahisamach , of the tribe of Dan.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahishar
entries.dictNote: An official "over the household" in Solomon's royal administration, part of the list of high officers who ran the kingdom's affairs (1 Kings 4:6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahishar
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the sons of Bilhan in the tribal genealogies, where the Hebrew text actually reads Ahishahar, "brother of dawn" (1 Chronicles 7:10). Despite the similar spelling, he is a different person from the Ahishar who served as steward of Solomon's household.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahithophel
entries.dictNote: Ahithophel was David's most trusted counselor, so respected that his advice was regarded as equal to consulting God directly, and his defection to Absalom's rebellion was one of the most devastating betrayals of David's reign. When Absalom rejected Ahithophel's sound military advice in favor of a rival counselor's plan, Ahithophel recognized the rebellion was doomed, went home, put his affairs in order, and hanged himself.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahitub
entries.summary: Achitub, the name of several priests
entries.dictNote: Ahitub was a common name among Israel's high priestly line, borne by at least two priests in that lineage, including Ahimelech's father and, generations later, Zadok's father.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Ahlab
entries.dictNote: Ahlab was a Phoenician town within Asher's allotted territory that the tribe failed to conquer, so its Canaanite inhabitants continued living there alongside the Israelites (Judges 1:31). It is generally identified with Khirbet el-Mahalib, a site on the Lebanese coast a few miles north of Tyre, matching "Mahalliba," a town among the Phoenician cities that submitted to the Assyrian king Sennacherib during his 701 BC campaign, recorded in his own annals. The identification rests on both geographic fit and the close sound of the two names.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahlai
entries.summary: Achlai, the name of an Israelitess and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ahlai is named in 1 Chronicles 2:31 as a child of Sheshan, who according to the surrounding genealogy had no sons, so Ahlai is usually taken to be a daughter through whom the family line continued by way of an Egyptian servant, Jarha. Zabad, one of David's mighty warriors, is called "son of Ahlai" in 1 Chronicles 11:41, likely as a descendant of this same line rather than a direct son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahoah
entries.dictNote: A son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, also called Ahiah in the same chapter and Iri elsewhere (1 Chronicles 8:4, 7; 7:7). His descendants, the Ahohites, included Dodo and his son Eleazar, one of David's three chief mighty men (2 Samuel 23:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahohite
entries.summary: an Achochite or descendant of Achoach
entries.dictNote: Ahohite marks descent from Ahoah, a Benjamite, and is applied to three men connected with David's military: Dodo, one of his officers; Dodo's son Eleazar, counted among the three mightiest of David's warriors; and Zalmon, one of the thirty.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aholah
entries.summary: Oholah, a symbolic name for Samaria
entries.dictNote: Oholah is a symbolic name Ezekiel uses for Samaria in an extended allegory alongside her sister Oholibah, representing Jerusalem, portraying both cities' political alliances with foreign powers as spiritual adultery.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aholiab
entries.dictNote: Oholiab was a skilled craftsman from the tribe of Dan whom God appointed alongside Bezalel to help design and construct the tabernacle and its furnishings.

witness.excerpt: Besaleel and Aholiab appeared to be the most skilful of the workmen: for they invented finer works than what others had done before them: and were of great abilities to gain notions of what they were formerly ignorant of.

Now their names are set down in writing in the sacred Books; and they were these: Besaleel , the son of Uri , of the tribe of Judah, the grandson of Miriam, the sister of their conductor; and Aholiab the son of Ahisamach , of the tribe of Dan.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aholibah
entries.summary: Oholibah, a symbolic name for Judah
entries.dictNote: Oholibah is a symbolic name Ezekiel uses for Jerusalem in an extended allegory alongside her sister Oholah, representing Samaria, portraying both cities' political alliances with foreign powers as spiritual adultery.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aholibamah
entries.dictNote: Oholibamah was one of Esau's wives, a daughter of a Hivite chief, and her sons became tribal leaders among the Edomites.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ahumai
entries.dictNote: Ahumai was a descendant of Judah through Shobal, listed as the head of one of the families of the Zorathites in 1 Chronicles 4:2. Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahuzam
entries.dictNote: Ahuzam was one of the sons of Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, born to his wife Naarah (1 Chronicles 4:6). He appears only in this genealogical listing alongside his brothers Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ahuzzath
entries.dictNote: A friend or advisor of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, who accompanied him when he came to make a treaty with Isaac after their earlier disputes over wells (Genesis 26:26).

witness.excerpt: And he called the name of that place the "Well of the Oath"; for there he had sworn to Abimelech and Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol the prefect of his host.  27.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ai
entries.summary: Ai, Aja or Ajath, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ai was a fortified Canaanite city near Bethel that first repelled an overconfident Israelite attack because of Achan's hidden sin, then fell to Joshua's ambush once the sin was dealt with, becoming the second Canaanite city Israel captured. It was later resettled by Benjaminites returning from exile. The site is usually identified with et-Tell, though excavations there have found little significant Late Bronze Age occupation matching the traditional conquest period, a discrepancy that continues to divide scholars over the city's exact location or the dating of the conquest. A separate, minor Ai in Ammonite territory is mentioned once by Jeremiah.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Aiah
entries.summary: Ajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Aiah was the father of Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, and also the name of a Horite chief listed among Edom's earlier inhabitants.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Aijalon
entries.summary: Ajalon, the name of five places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Aijalon was a valley and town where Joshua commanded the moon to stand still alongside the sun during the battle against the Amorite coalition, and it later marked the boundary of Danite and Benjamite territory.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ain
entries.summary: Ajin, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ain was a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory, later designated as one of the cities given to the Levites.

witness.excerpt: 21 Or Ain .

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Akan
entries.dictNote: Akan, called Jakan in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:42, was a son of Ezer and one of the Horite clan chiefs descended from Seir in the land of Edom before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Akkub
entries.summary: Akkub, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Akkub was a common name among Levites, gatekeepers, and temple servants listed among the returning exiles in Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Alameth
entries.summary: Alemeth, the name of a place in Palestine and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Alameth, elsewhere spelled Alemeth, names both a town and two different men in the Old Testament. The town was a Levitical city in Benjamin's territory, given to the priestly line of Aaron along with Geba and Anathoth (1 Chronicles 6:45); the parallel list in Joshua 21:18 calls the same town Almon. Among the men who share this name, one Alemeth was a son of Becher, a grandson of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 7:8), while a different Alemeth was one of the sons of Jehoadah, a descendant of Jonathan several generations removed who kept Saul's royal line alive after the northern kingdom had already fallen (1 Chronicles 8:36; 9:42).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alammelech
entries.dictNote: Alammelech, "king's oak," was a place within Asher's territory, named between Achshaph and Amad in Joshua's boundary description (Joshua 19:26). Nothing else is known of it, and its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alamoth
entries.summary: properly, girls, i.e. the soprano or female voice, perhaps falsetto
entries.dictNote: Alamoth is a musical term found in the record of temple worship and in the headings of the Psalms, most likely indicating a high pitch or treble voice, literally "maidens" or "young women" (1 Chronicles 15:20). It appears as the heading of Psalm 46, and probably describes how the psalm was meant to be sung or played rather than naming any person.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Aliah
entries.dictNote: Aliah is an alternate spelling of Alvah, one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau (Genesis 36:40; 1 Chronicles 1:51). The two Edomite king-lists in Genesis and Chronicles show minor spelling variation of this kind throughout. Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Alian
entries.dictNote: Alian, also called Alvan, was a son of Shobal and a Horite clan chief in the region of Seir, listed in the genealogy of Edom's earlier inhabitants (Genesis 36:23). Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Allon
entries.summary: Allon, an Israelite, also a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Easton's dictionary treats "Allon" as two unrelated items: an oak tree used as a boundary landmark on the border of Naphtali in Joshua 19:33, and a Simeonite named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:37, an ancestor of the clan that drove out the descendants of Ham from the valley of Gedor in the days of Hezekiah. The verse tied to this entry, 1 Chronicles 4:37, belongs to the second, genealogical sense, so despite the place tag here, the text actually names a person in a family line rather than a location.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Allon-bachuth
entries.dictNote: Allon-bachuth, meaning "oak of weeping," is not a person but the site near Bethel where Rebekah's nurse Deborah was buried (Genesis 35:8). It was likely the same landmark later called the palm tree of Deborah, near Bethel, where the judge and prophetess Deborah held court (Judges 4:5).

entries.title: Almighty
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Ruth, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Joel, 2 Corinthians, Revelation

entries.label: 11 books

entries.title: Almodad
entries.dictNote: Almodad was the first named of the sons of Joktan in the Table of Nations, understood as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). His descendants are usually placed somewhere in the Arabian peninsula, though the exact tribe has not been identified with certainty.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Almon
entries.dictNote: Almon was one of the towns assigned to the priestly Levites within the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18). It is called Alemeth in the parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6:60, and is generally located near the modern village of Almit, northeast of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Almondilathaim
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite in Moabite territory, better known as Almon-diblathaim, between Dibon-gad and the mountains of Abarim, one of the last stops before Israel reached the plains of Moab opposite Jericho (Num. 33:46-47).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Alpheus
entries.dictNote: Alphaeus was the father of James, one of the twelve apostles, distinguishing him as James the son of Alphaeus from James the son of Zebedee.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Alush
entries.summary: Alush, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite between Dophkah and Rephidim, one of the last stops before Israel reached Mount Sinai, likely along the western Sinai coastal route (Num. 33:13-14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amad
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Asher, named only once between Alammelech and Misheal (Joshua 19:26). Its site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amal
entries.dictNote: Amal was a son of Helem, listed among the descendants of Asher in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:35.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amalek
entries.summary: Amalek, a descendant of Esau; also his posterity and their country
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalm
entries.dictNote: Amalek was a grandson of Esau, and the Amalekites descended from him became one of Israel's oldest and most bitter enemies, attacking the vulnerable rear of Israel's column during the exodus wilderness journey. God declared perpetual war against Amalek for that attack, a mandate Saul's incomplete obedience against them later cost him his kingdom.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Amam
entries.dictNote: Amam was a town in the Negev district of Judah's territory, named together with Shema and Moladah in a single verse of Joshua's town lists (Josh. 15:26). No other information about it survives, and its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amana
entries.dictNote: Amana names two related things sharing one root. The Hebrew margin at 2 Kings 5:12 gives Amana as an alternate reading for the Abana, the river flowing through Damascus that Naaman preferred to the waters of Israel. In the Song of Solomon it names a mountain, likely the southern summit of the Anti-Lebanon range, from whose slopes the Abana's waters rise (Song 4:8).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amariah
entries.summary: Amarjah, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Amariah was a common name among Israel's priests, borne by several men in the high priestly genealogy as well as a chief priest appointed by King Jehoshaphat to oversee religious matters.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Amasai
entries.summary: Amasai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Amasai was a Levitical chief who defected to David with a group of armed men while David was still an outlaw, declaring his loyalty in a burst of prophetic assurance, and he later helped oversee temple duties under David's organization.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amashai
entries.dictNote: Amashai was a priest, son of Azareel, appointed to reside in Jerusalem after the exile and assist with the work of the temple (Nehemiah 11:13). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amasiah
entries.dictNote: A commander of thousands in the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed among the officers who volunteered themselves for the LORD's service in the military reorganization of 2 Chronicles 17:16. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amaziah
entries.summary: Amatsjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Amaziah became king of Judah after his father Joash was assassinated, and he executed the assassins but spared their children, citing the law that children shouldn't be punished for their parents' sins. After a costly victory over Edom, Amaziah brought Edomite idols home and began worshiping them, and he foolishly provoked a war with northern Israel that ended in his own capture and Jerusalem's walls being torn down. A different Amaziah was the priest of the golden calf shrine at Bethel who confronted the prophet Amos and ordered him to leave the kingdom.

entries.title: Ami
entries.dictNote: Listed among the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel; the parallel list in Nehemiah gives the name as Amon (Ezra 2:57; Nehemiah 7:59).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aminadab
entries.dictNote: Aminadab is the Greek form of Amminadab, an ancestor of David through the line of Judah, named in the genealogies of both Matthew and Luke (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:33). In Exodus, Amminadab's daughter Elisheba married Aaron, linking this family line to Israel's priesthood as well as to its future kings (Exodus 6:23).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amittai
entries.dictNote: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah, identified as a native of Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1). Nothing else is recorded of him beyond this identification.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ammah
entries.dictNote: Ammah was not a person but a hill east of Gibeon that Joab and Abishai reached at sunset while pursuing Abner's forces after the skirmish at the pool of Gibeon (2 Sam. 2:24). It was there that Abner called out to Joab and the two commanders agreed to a truce.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammiel
entries.summary: Ammiel, the name of three or four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ammiel was a common name, including one of the twelve spies representing the tribe of Dan and the father of Bathsheba according to 1 Chronicles, where she is called Bath-shua.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ammihud
entries.summary: Ammihud, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ammihud was a common Old Testament name, borne by the father of a tribal leader of Ephraim during the wilderness census and by the father of a king of Geshur whose daughter Maacah married David.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Amminadab
entries.summary: Amminadab, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Amminadab was an ancestor of both Aaron, through his daughter Elisheba whom Aaron married, and of David, through his son Nahshon, placing him in the genealogies of both the priestly and royal lines of Israel.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Amminadib
entries.dictNote: A name found only in the King James Version's translation of Song of Solomon 6:12, describing chariots compared to "the chariots of Amminadib." Most modern translations, following the Hebrew more closely, render the phrase differently, as "my noble people" or "the chariots of my people, a prince," treating it as a poetic description rather than a proper name. Whether it refers to an actual individual has long been disputed among translators.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammishaddai
entries.dictNote: Ammishaddai was the father of the tribal leader of Dan during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ammizabad
entries.dictNote: Son of Benaiah, David's commander over the third division of the army; Ammizabad appears to have overseen that division on his father's behalf (1 Chronicles 27:6).

entries.title: Amorite
entries.summary: an Emorite, one of the Canaanitish tribes
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Ezekiel, Amos
entries.dictNote: The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel's conquest, traditionally traced to a son of Canaan in Genesis 10, and the Old Testament sometimes uses their name loosely for the hill country's inhabitants in general. A specific Amorite kingdom east of the Jordan, ruled by Sihon and Og, fell to Israel under Moses and became the basis for Reuben and Gad's territory in Numbers 21. Outside the Bible, Amorites, called Amurru in Mesopotamian texts, were a real West Semitic people who migrated into Mesopotamia in the early second millennium BC and founded several dynasties there, including the one that produced Hammurabi of Babylon. Their language and personal names are well documented in cuneiform archives from Mari and elsewhere.

entries.title: Amos
entries.dictNote: Amos was a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah who was sent north to prophesy against Israel, insisting he was no professional prophet and had no prophetic family background, just a farmer God pulled off the job. His book condemns Israel's wealthy for exploiting the poor while performing empty religious rituals, and its most quoted line demands that justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. A different Amos is listed simply as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.

entries.title: Amoz
entries.dictNote: Amoz was the prophet Isaiah's father, distinct from the prophet Amos despite the similar English spelling, which come from different Hebrew names entirely.

entries.title: Amphipolis
entries.summary: a city surrounded by a river; Amphipolis, a place in Macedonia
entries.dictNote: Amphipolis, a major Macedonian city on the Strymon River and an important Roman administrative center on the Via Egnatia, through which Paul and Silas traveled on the road from Philippi to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). Extensive Greek and Roman remains, including a well known lion monument and a large basilica complex, have been excavated at the site.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amplias
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul greets warmly as "my beloved in the Lord" in the list of greetings that closes Romans (Romans 16:8). The fuller Greek form of the name, Ampliatus, was common among slaves and freedmen, and a decorated early Christian tomb in the Catacomb of Domitilla bears that name, though it cannot be proven to belong to the same man Paul greets.

entries.dictNote: Amram was Aaron, Moses, and Miriam's father, a Levite who married his father's sister Jochebed, and beyond that marriage and his children's roles, little else is recorded about him personally.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Amramite
entries.summary: an Amramite or descendant of Amram
entries.dictNote: Amramites were the descendants of Amram, son of Kohath and father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, one of four Levitical families descended from Kohath. Under David, men of this family served among the officials overseeing the treasuries of dedicated gifts for the temple.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Amran
entries.dictNote: Amran, called Hemdan in the parallel genealogy of Genesis 36:26, was a son of Dishon and a descendant of Seir the Horite, one of the clan chiefs of Edom recorded before Israel had a king (1 Chronicles 1:41).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amraphel
entries.dictNote: Amraphel was the king of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia, who joined Chedorlaomer of Elam and two other kings in a campaign against the cities of the plain, including Sodom, described in Genesis 14. Older scholarship once proposed identifying him with the famous Babylonian king Hammurabi, whose law code survives on a well-known stone stele, but most scholars today consider the equation linguistically and chronologically doubtful.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Amzi
entries.dictNote: Two men named Amzi appear in postexilic records. One was a Levite ancestor of Ethan, one of the temple musicians David appointed (1 Chronicles 6:31, 44-45). The other was a priest whose descendant resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:12).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Anab
entries.dictNote: Town in the Judean hill country from which Joshua drove out the Anakim, a people remembered in Israel's tradition for their unusual height (Josh. 11:21; 15:50). It still bears its ancient name today, preserved in the ruin Khirbet Anab southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anah
entries.summary: Anah, the name of two Edomites and one Edomitess
entries.dictNote: Anah was an Edomite figure, described in Genesis as discovering hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing his father's donkeys, and appears in the genealogies of Esau's descendants.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Anaharath
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar, listed alongside Shihon and Rabbith (Joshua 19:19). It is tentatively identified with a site near Mount Tabor in the Jezreel Valley, though the identification is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anaiah
entries.summary: Anajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Anaiah stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform built for the public reading of the law in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4) and is likely the same man who later signed Nehemiah's covenant of renewed obedience to the law (Nehemiah 10:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anak
entries.dictNote: Anak was the ancestor of the Anakim, a people of great stature who inhabited Hebron and struck fear into the Israelite spies sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:33). Joshua 15:13 identifies his father as Arba, for whom the city of Hebron was originally named Kirjath-arba. Caleb eventually drove the descendants of Anak out of Hebron and received the city as his inheritance (Joshua 15:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anakim
entries.summary: an Anakite or descendant of Anak
entries.dictNote: The Anakim were a race of unusually tall people living in Canaan before the conquest, and the fear they inspired in ten of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land was the direct cause of Israel's forty years of wilderness wandering; Caleb and Joshua alone were unafraid, trusting God to give victory regardless of the odds.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Anamim
entries.summary: Anamim, a son of Mizraim and his descendants, with their country
entries.dictNote: Anamim was not an individual but one of the tribal groups descended from Mizraim, the biblical name for Egypt, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). Like several names in this list, its exact historical people group has not been identified with confidence, though scholars have proposed connections to various Egyptian or Libyan populations.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Anammelech
entries.dictNote: Anammelech was a deity worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, a Mesopotamian population the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:31). The colonists reportedly burned their children in fire to Anammelech and its companion god Adrammelech, a practice associated in the ancient Near East with Molech worship. Assyrian resettlement policy of this kind is well attested in Assyrian royal inscriptions, including those of Sargon II, who claims credit for Samaria's conquest.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anan
entries.dictNote: Anan was one of the Jewish leaders who affixed his name to the sealed covenant by which the postexilic community bound itself to keep the law of Moses under Nehemiah (Neh. 10:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anani
entries.dictNote: The seventh of seven sons of Elioenai listed at the end of the royal genealogy of David's line in 1 Chronicles 3:24, several generations after the return from Babylonian exile. The list shows David's family continuing intact well into the postexilic period, a detail later Jewish and Christian readers drew on when tracing a "son of David" even centuries after the monarchy had ended.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ananiah
entries.summary: Ananjah, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin near Jerusalem, listed among the settlements Jews reoccupied after returning from exile (Neh. 11:32). It is commonly identified with the modern village of Beit Hanina, a few miles north of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book

A different Ananias was the disciple in Damascus who restored Paul's sight and baptized him after his conversion, despite his own fear of the man who had been persecuting Christians.

entries.title: Anath
entries.dictNote: Anath was the father of Shamgar, one of Israel's early judges who struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (Judges 3:31; 5:6). The name is shared with the Canaanite warrior goddess Anat, but in these verses it functions as a personal or place name for Shamgar's father.

entries.summary: Anathoth, the name of two Israelites, also of a place in Pal
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Anathoth was a priestly town in Benjamin, about three miles north of Jerusalem, best known as the hometown and lifelong home of the prophet Jeremiah, who bought a field there as a sign of hope even while announcing Jerusalem's coming fall. It also produced two of David's mighty men. The site is identified with the modern village of Anata.

entries.title: Andrew
entries.dictNote: Andrew was Peter's brother and, according to John's Gospel, a former disciple of John the Baptist before he followed Jesus and immediately brought Peter to meet him as well. Andrew appears at several practical moments in the Gospels, pointing Jesus to the boy with five loaves and two fish before the feeding of the five thousand and bringing a group of inquiring Greeks to Jesus in his final week. Tradition holds that he was crucified on an X-shaped cross, which became known afterward as Saint Andrew's cross.

entries.title: Anem
entries.dictNote: Anem was a Levitical town in the tribal territory of Issachar (1 Chronicles 6:73). It is generally identified with En-gannim in the earlier town list of Joshua 19:21, whose name survives in the modern city of Jenin.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aner
entries.summary: Aner, a Amorite, also a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Aner carries two distinct senses under one name. In Genesis it names an Amorite chief allied with Mamre and Eshcol who joined Abraham in pursuing the four kings who had captured Lot (Genesis 14:13, 24). Separately, 1 Chronicles lists Aner as a town in the territory of Manasseh set aside for the Levites of Kohath's clan, alongside Taanach in the fuller parallel list at Joshua 21:25.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aniam
entries.dictNote: A Manassite, son of Shemida, listed in the tribal genealogy of Manasseh (1 Chr. 7:19).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anim
entries.dictNote: Anim, a town in the hill country of Judah near Eshtemoa, in the district south of Hebron (Josh. 15:50). It is commonly identified with the ruin of el-Ghuwein, southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Anna
entries.dictNote: An elderly prophetess of the tribe of Asher who, widowed after only seven years of marriage, spent decades in the Jerusalem temple in prayer and fasting (Luke 2:36-37). She arrived at the temple the same day Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus for presentation, just after the aged Simeon had spoken his own prophecy over the child, and she went on to speak of Jesus to others looking for Jerusalem's redemption. Luke pairs her with Simeon as a second, independent witness confirming the child's significance at the very start of his account.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Annas
entries.summary: Luke names Annas and Caiaphas together as if there were two high priests at once (3:2) — which sounds like an error until Josephus explains why: Rome deposed and replaced high priests on its own schedule through this whole period, and Annas (Ananus), long out of office, still held the real influence as Caiaphas's father-in-law.
entries.dictNote: Was high priest A.D. 7-14. In A.D. 25 Caiaphas, who had married the daughter of Annas (John 18:13), was raised to that office, and probably Annas was now made president of the Sanhedrim, or deputy or coadjutor of the high priest, and thus was also called high priest along with Caiaphas (Luke 3:2). By the Mosaic law the high-priesthood was held for life (Num. 3:10); and although Annas had been deposed by the Roman procurator, the Jews may still have regarded him as legally the high priest. Our Lord was first brought before Annas, and after a brief questioning of him (John 18:19-23) was sent to Caiaphas, when some members of the Sanhedrim had met, and the first trial of Jesus took place (Matt. 26:57-68). This examination of our Lord before Annas is recorded only by John. Annas was president of the Sanhedrim before which Peter and John were brought (Acts 4:6).

entries.title: Antioch
entries.dictNote: Antioch on the Orontes, in Syria, was the third largest city of the Roman Empire and became the base from which the early church sent missionaries to the Gentile world; it was there that believers were first called Christians. Barnabas and Paul both taught there, and the church at Antioch commissioned Paul's missionary journeys, sending him first to a different Antioch, in Pisidia, where he preached with initial success before opposition from local Jewish leaders drove him out; he returned there later to strengthen the church he had founded. Antioch on the Orontes survives today as the Turkish city of Antakya.

entries.title: Apollos
entries.dictNote: Apollos was an eloquent Jewish preacher from Alexandria, well versed in the Scriptures, who taught accurately about Jesus but knew only the baptism of John until Priscilla and Aquila took him aside and explained the way of God more fully. He went on to become an effective teacher in Corinth, so much so that a faction in that fractious church began claiming him as their favorite leader over Paul, a rivalry Paul directly addressed in his letters.

entries.title: Appaim
entries.dictNote: Appaim was a son of Nadab in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's tribe, one of the family lines that helped establish Judah's prominence among the twelve tribes (1 Chronicles 2:30-31). His own line continued through his son Ishi. Nothing further is recorded of him.

Tradition, though not the text itself, identifies her as Philemon's wife, and her place in the greeting suggests she held some standing in the household church that met there.

entries.title: Apses (including the article)

entries.title: Arad
entries.summary: Arad, the name of a place near Palestine, also of a Canaanite and an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Arad was a Canaanite city about 20 miles south of Hebron whose king attacked Israel as they approached Canaan from the south, taking prisoners, before Israel destroyed the town under the ban (Numbers 21:1-3; 33:40); it was later subdued by Joshua's forces (Joshua 12:14). The name also belongs to a descendant of Benjamin through Beriah (1 Chronicles 8:15). Excavations at Tel Arad have uncovered both a Canaanite city and, on a nearby hill, a fortified Israelite citadel with its own small temple, among the few Israelite sanctuaries yet excavated outside Jerusalem.

entries.title: Aram-zobah
entries.dictNote: Aram-zobah was an Aramean kingdom David defeated in a series of campaigns under its king Hadadezer, expanding Israel's territory and bringing substantial tribute into David's kingdom.

entries.title: Aran
entries.dictNote: Aran was a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom in Genesis 36:28 and 1 Chronicles 1:42. The Horites were the indigenous cave-dwelling population of Mount Seir before the Edomites displaced them, and genealogies like this one preserve their tribal structure. Nothing else about him is recorded.

entries.dictNote: Archevites were people of Erech, the ancient Mesopotamian city better known as Uruk, among the foreign populations the Assyrians settled in Samaria who later wrote to the Persian king opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. Uruk was one of the world's earliest cities and the traditional setting of the Epic of Gilgamesh, and its extensive ruins have been excavated in modern Iraq.

entries.title: Arcturus
entries.summary: the constellation of the Great Bear (perhaps from its migration through the heavens)
entries.dictNote: Arcturus is not a person but the King James rendering of a Hebrew word in Job 9:9 and 38:32 that most likely designates the constellation now called Ursa Major, the Great Bear, rather than the star Arcturus itself; the verses point to God's authority over the fixed courses of the constellations.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ard
entries.summary: Ard, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ard was a grandson of Benjamin, son of Bela, and became the ancestor of the clan of the Ardites; he is called Addar in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:3 (Genesis 46:21; Numbers 26:40).

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ardites
entries.summary: an Ardite (collectively) or descendant of Ard
entries.dictNote: Ardites were the clan descended from Ard, a grandson of Benjamin through Bela, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same man is called Addar in 1 Chronicles 8:3.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ardon
entries.dictNote: The youngest of Caleb's three sons by his first wife Azubah, part of the Judahite genealogy in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 2:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Areli
entries.summary: Areli (or an Arelite, collectively), an Israelite and his descendants
entries.dictNote: Areli was a son of Gad and ancestor of the Arelite clan, listed among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob and later among the clans counted in the wilderness census (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:17).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Areopagite
entries.summary: an Areopagite or member of the court held on Mars' Hill
entries.dictNote: Areopagite marks Dionysius as a member of the Areopagus, the ancient council of Athens that met on the rock outcrop of that name near the Acropolis. He was among the few Athenians who believed after hearing Paul's speech there, and the Areopagus itself still stands today, overlooking the Athenian agora.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Areopagus
entries.summary: rock of Ares, a place in Athens
entries.dictNote: The Areopagus, Mars' Hill, was both a rocky outcrop below the Acropolis in Athens and the ancient council that met there, composed of the city's leading magistrates and former magistrates. Paul was brought before this body to explain his teaching about Jesus and the resurrection, and delivered there his address to the men of Athens about the unknown god (Acts 17:19-34).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aretas
entries.dictNote: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataean kingdom based at Petra, whose daughter married Herod Antipas until Antipas divorced her to marry Herodias, an insult that led to war between the two rulers, a conflict Antipas lost. After the death of Emperor Tiberius, an official under Aretas controlled Damascus and sought to arrest Paul, who escaped the city by being lowered over the wall in a basket (2 Cor. 11:32-33; Acts 9:24-25). Aretas IV is well attested in Nabataean inscriptions and coinage found throughout the former Nabataean kingdom.
