entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Argob
entries.dictNote: Argob was a region in Bashan known for its sixty fortified cities, conquered by Israel when they defeated King Og.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Aridai
entries.dictNote: One of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned, an event the book of Esther says gave rise to the feast of Purim (Esther 9:7-10). Nothing else is recorded of him individually.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aridatha
entries.dictNote: Aridatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews of the empire under King Ahasuerus. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction, and his body was later hanged (Esther 9:8-10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arieh
entries.dictNote: One of the men killed with King Pekahiah of Israel when his officer Pekah assassinated him in the citadel of the royal palace at Samaria (2 Kings 15:25). He and Argob are named only as fellow victims of the coup, otherwise unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ariel
entries.summary: Ariel, a symbolical name for Jerusalem, also the name of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ariel is a poetic name Isaiah uses for Jerusalem, likely meaning lion of God or altar hearth, used in a prophecy describing the city under siege and God's judgment on it.

witness.excerpt: These had with them, Gad seven - Saphoniah, Augis, Sunis, Azabon, Aerin, Erocd, Ariel.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Arimathaea
entries.summary: Arimathæa (or Ramah), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Arimathaea was the hometown of Joseph, the wealthy and secret disciple of Jesus who requested Jesus' body from Pilate after the crucifixion and buried it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57-60; John 19:38). All four Gospels identify Joseph by this town, though its precise location is uncertain; many scholars have proposed identifying it with Ramathaim-zophim, the hometown of the prophet Samuel a few miles northwest of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Arioch
entries.summary: Arjok, the name of two Babylonians
entries.dictNote: Arioch was a king of Elam who joined a coalition of eastern kings that raided Sodom and captured Lot, a raid Abraham personally reversed by rescuing Lot and recovering the stolen goods.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Arisai
entries.dictNote: One of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, killed by the Jews of Susa along with his brothers during the events of Esther 9. His name appears only in the list of Haman's sons impaled after Purim (Esther 9:6-10), with nothing else recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aristarchus
entries.dictNote: Aristarchus was a Macedonian companion of Paul who was swept up in a riot at Ephesus, later traveled with Paul to Rome, and shared imprisonment with him there, described by Paul as a fellow prisoner.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arkite
entries.summary: an Arkite or inhabitant of Erek
entries.dictNote: Arkites descended from Canaan and inhabited Arka, a city about twelve miles northeast of Tripoli in modern Lebanon, opposite the northern end of the Lebanon range. The site, known today as Tell Arqa, has been excavated and appears as Irqata in the Amarna letters and in earlier Egyptian execration texts, confirming it as a real Bronze Age city.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Armageddon
entries.dictNote: Armageddon appears only in Revelation 16:16, where it names the place where the kings of the earth are gathered for the final battle against God. The name derives from the Hebrew Har-Megiddo, "mount of Megiddo," recalling the strategic plain of Megiddo where Israel fought several of its most decisive battles, including Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera and Josiah's death in battle against Pharaoh Necho. Excavations at Tel Megiddo have uncovered more than twenty superimposed layers of settlement spanning millennia, confirming the site's long history as a military crossroads controlling the pass between the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Armoni
entries.dictNote: One of two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah, handed over by David to the Gibeonites and executed to atone for Saul's earlier slaughter of Gibeonites in violation of Israel's ancient treaty with them (2 Sam. 21:1-9). Rizpah's subsequent vigil guarding his exposed body, and that of his brother Mephibosheth, from scavenging animals became one of the Old Testament's most striking images of grief and finally moved David to give the dead a proper burial.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arnan
entries.dictNote: Listed in the genealogy of Zerubbabel's descendants in 1 Chronicles 3:21, continuing the royal line of Judah after the exile. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arnon
entries.summary: the Arnon, a river east of the Jordan, also its territory
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: The Arnon was a swift river flowing into the Dead Sea from the east, marking the boundary between Amorite, and later Moabite, territory and Israel's tribal lands beyond the Jordan. Its steep gorge, about seventy miles long from its source in Gilead's mountains, still carries water in the modern Wadi al-Mujib. The Moabite Stone, an inscription set up by King Mesha of Moab in the ninth century BC, describes building a highway across the Arnon valley, corroborating the river's role as a real strategic boundary rather than a merely symbolic one.

witness.excerpt: The people mourned for Aaron thirty days: and when this mourning was over, Moses removed the army from that place, and came to the river Arnon: which issuing out of the mountains of Arabia, and running through all that wilderness fell into the lake Asphaltitis; and became the limit between the land of the Moabites, and the land of the Amorites.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Arod
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad and ancestor of the Arodite clan, listed in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:17; he is called Arodi in the earlier genealogical list of Genesis 46:16.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arodi
entries.summary: an Arodite or descendant of Arod
entries.dictNote: Arodi, also called Arod, was a son of Gad and the founder of the Arodite clan, listed among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:17).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aroer
entries.summary: Aroër, the name of three places in or near Palestine
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Aroer was a border town on the edge of Moabite and Ammonite territory, marking the southern limit of the tribal lands Israel took east of the Jordan.
entries.label: 10 books

entries.title: Aroerite
entries.summary: an Aroerite or inhabitant of Aroer
entries.dictNote: Aroerite marks Hothan, father of two of David's mighty men, Shama and Jehiel, as a native of Aroer, most likely the town on the Arnon gorge in Transjordan rather than the similarly named site near Beersheba.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arpad
entries.dictNote: Arpad was a Syrian city near Hamath that Assyrian kings repeatedly cite as proof of their conquering power (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13; Isaiah 10:9; 36:19; 37:13); it fell to Tiglath-pileser III after a lengthy siege around 740 BC, an event confirmed in Assyrian royal annals. Jeremiah later pairs it with Damascus and Hamath in his oracle against Syria (Jeremiah 49:23), and its ruins are identified with Tell Rifaat north of Aleppo.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Arphaxad
entries.summary: Arpakshad, a son of Noah; also the region settled by him
entries.dictNote: Arphaxad was a son of Shem born two years after the flood, and Genesis traces his descendants forward through several generations to Abraham, making him a key link in the genealogy connecting Noah to the patriarchs.

witness.excerpt: Arphaxad named the Arphaxadites, who are now called Chaldeans.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Artaxerxes
entries.summary: Artachshasta (or Artaxerxes), a title (rather than name) of several Persian kings
entries.dictNote: Artaxerxes was a Persian king who authorized and funded both Ezra's return to Jerusalem with temple articles and instructions to teach the law, and later Nehemiah's mission to rebuild the city's walls, making him a decisive supporter of Judah's postexilic restoration despite being a foreign emperor.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Artemas
entries.summary: gift of Artemis; Artemas (or Artemidorus), a Christian
entries.dictNote: Artemas was a companion of Paul whom the apostle considered sending to Crete to relieve Titus (Titus 3:12). Later church tradition names him bishop of Lystra, though this cannot be confirmed from the New Testament itself.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aruboth
entries.dictNote: Aruboth was the district assigned to Ben-hesed, one of the twelve officials responsible for supplying provisions to Solomon's court one month each year (1 Kings 4:10). It included the town of Socoh and apparently lay in the fertile grain-growing lowlands of Judah's Shephelah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arvad
entries.dictNote: Arvad, modern Arwad, was a small fortified island city off the Syrian coast whose sailors and soldiers Tyre hired as mercenaries and mariners according to Ezekiel's oracle against that city (Ezekiel 27:8, 11). Founded by Phoenician settlers early in the second millennium BC, Arvad ran its own fleet and local dynasty and appears already in the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters, where its ships figure in the political struggles among the Levantine coastal cities.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Arvadite
entries.summary: an Arvadite or citizen of Arvad
entries.dictNote: Arvadites were descendants of Canaan associated with Arvad, a fortified island city off the Phoenician coast, known today as Arwad in Syria. Ezekiel names Arvad's men as skilled mariners and soldiers hired by Tyre, and Assyrian records from Tiglath-Pileser III and Sennacherib confirm Arvad as a real Phoenician city-state that paid tribute to Assyria.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Arza
entries.dictNote: The steward in charge of the royal palace at Tirzah under King Elah of Israel. Elah was assassinated in Arza's house during a drinking bout by his own officer Zimri, who then seized the throne (1 Kings 16:9).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asa
entries.summary: Asa, the name of a king and of a Levite
entries.dictNote: Asa was king of Judah for forty-one years and one of the kingdom's genuine reformers, removing his own grandmother from her position as queen mother for making an obscene idol and expelling male shrine prostitutes from the land. Early in his reign he trusted God for a decisive victory over a massive Cushite invasion, but late in life, facing a threat from northern Israel, he hired a foreign king to attack Israel instead of trusting God as he once had, and a prophet's rebuke of that decision made Asa angry enough to throw the prophet in prison.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Asahel
entries.summary: Asahel, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Asahel was Joab's younger brother and one of David's elite warriors, known for his speed, and he died chasing down Abner during a battle between David's and Saul's rival factions, a death Joab later avenged by murdering Abner, an act that haunted David's reign afterward.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Asaiah
entries.summary: Asajah, the name of three or four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Asaiah was a common name, borne by a royal official Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah and by a Levite involved in bringing the ark to Jerusalem under David.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Asaph
entries.summary: Asaph, the name of three Israelites, and of the family of the first
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah
entries.dictNote: Asaph was a Levite David appointed to lead one of the temple's choirs and musical guilds, and his name is attached to twelve psalms, including Psalm 50 and the run from Psalm 73 through 83, suggesting either his personal authorship or a musical guild that continued under his name for generations after him.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Asareel
entries.dictNote: Asareel was a son of Jehaleleel listed in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:16).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asarelah
entries.dictNote: Asarelah was one of the sons of Asaph whom David appointed to prophesy with the harp and cymbals in temple worship; he is called Jesharelah later in the same chapter (1 Chr. 25:2, 14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asenath
entries.dictNote: Asenath was an Egyptian woman, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), whom Pharaoh gave to Joseph as his wife (Genesis 41:45). She bore Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who became the ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes (Genesis 41:50-52; 46:20). Her marriage into an Egyptian priestly family reflects Joseph's full integration into Egyptian court life during his rise to power under Pharaoh.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aser
entries.dictNote: Aser is the Greek New Testament form of Asher, Jacob's eighth son and ancestor of the tribe of Asher. The name appears identifying the prophetess Anna's tribal descent (Luke 2:36) and among the twelve tribes listed as sealed in Revelation 7:6.

Gad and Aser were the sons of Zilpha, who was the handmaid of Lea.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ashan
entries.dictNote: Ashan was a small town in the lowlands of Judah that was later reassigned to Simeon, whose inheritance lay within Judah's larger territory (Joshua 15:42; 19:7). It was given to the Levites of Aaron's line as one of their priestly cities (1 Chronicles 6:59). Its exact site has not been identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Asharoth
entries.summary: Ashtaroth, the name of a Sidonian deity, and of a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: This entry's spelling appears to be a variant of Ashtaroth, the fortified capital of Og, king of Bashan, east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4; 13:12). It was assigned to the half-tribe of Manasseh and later given to the Levites of Gershon; its name comes from Ashtoreth, the Canaanite goddess whose worship was centered there, and archaeologists generally locate it at Tell Ashtarah in the Golan region of modern Syria.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ashbea
entries.dictNote: A name in the genealogy of Judah that Chronicles itself leaves ambiguous, "the house of Ashbea," identified only as the ancestor or founding location of a family of linen workers (1 Chr. 4:21). Whether Ashbea names an individual or the place his descendants settled is not clear from the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashbel
entries.dictNote: Ashbel was a son of Benjamin, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Benjamin's tribe.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ashbelites
entries.summary: an Ashbelite (collectively) or descendant of Ashbel
entries.dictNote: Ashbelites were the clan descended from Ashbel, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashdoth-pisgah
entries.summary: Ashdoth-Pisgah, a place east of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Ashdoth-pisgah, rendered "the slopes of Pisgah" in most modern translations, describes the descending ridges of Mount Pisgah on the eastern side of the Jordan, within territory taken from Sihon the Amorite (Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 12:3; 13:20). It is likely not a separate place name at all but a geographic description of Pisgah's terrain, the same ridge from which Moses viewed the promised land before his death (Deuteronomy 34:1). It has been associated with springs near Mount Nebo still known today as Ayun Musa, "the springs of Moses."
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Asher
entries.summary: Asher, a son of Jacob, and the tribe descended from him, with its territory; also a place in Palestine
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Asher was Jacob's eighth son, born to Leah's servant Zilpah, and the tribe descended from him received a fertile coastal strip in northern Canaan running toward Phoenicia, described in Joshua as containing some of the richest land in Israel. Little is recorded of the tribe's individual history beyond its territorial boundaries and city list, and along with Simeon it produced no judge or major hero in the biblical narrative. Anna the prophetess, who recognized the infant Jesus in the temple, is identified in Luke as being of the tribe of Asher.

entries.label: 10 books

entries.title: Asherites
entries.summary: an Asherite (collectively) or descendant of Asher
entries.dictNote: Asherites are the members of the tribe of Asher, descended from Jacob's eighth son by Zilpah. Judges 1:32 reports that Asher failed to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants of its allotted coastal territory and instead settled among them, a pattern of partial conquest repeated by several tribes in that chapter.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashima
entries.dictNote: Ashima is not a person but a deity, the god of the people of Hamath whom the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom's population (2 Kings 17:30). Little is known of the cult beyond this notice; some scholars connect the name to "Ashim-Bethel," a divine name that turns up centuries later among Aramaic-speaking Jews at Elephantine in Egypt.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashkelon
entries.books: Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Ashkelon was one of the five principal Philistine cities, a coastal port midway between Gaza and Joppa that Judah briefly captured after the conquest before the Philistines retook it. Samson killed thirty of its men there to pay off a wager, and the prophets repeatedly singled it out for judgment. Ashkelon appears by name in the Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian inscription from around 1208 BC boasting of its conquest, one of the earliest extrabiblical references to a place named in the Bible; the same inscription contains the earliest known mention of Israel.
entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Ashkenaz
entries.summary: Ashkenaz, a Japhethite, also his descendants
entries.dictNote: Ashkenaz was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, and Jeremiah calls on the kingdom of Ashkenaz, along with Ararat and Minni, to join in Babylon's coming destruction.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ashnah
entries.summary: Ashnah, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ashnah is the name of two towns in the lowland (Shephelah) territory of Judah, not a person. One is listed near Zorah and Eshtaol (Joshua 15:33), and the other appears later in the same tribal boundary list near Nezib and Keilah (Joshua 15:43). Their exact sites are uncertain today.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashpenaz
entries.dictNote: Chief official over Nebuchadnezzar's court eunuchs, responsible for selecting and training young Judean nobles, including Daniel and his three companions, for royal service in Babylon (Daniel 1:3).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashriel
entries.summary: Asriel, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Asriel was a descendant of Manasseh, and his family formed one of the clans counted among Manasseh's tribe in Israel's genealogies.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ashterathite
entries.summary: an Ashterathite or inhabitant of Ashtaroth
entries.dictNote: Ashterathite marks Uzzia, one of David's mighty men, as a native of Ashtaroth, the Bashan city east of the Jordan that had once been the capital of Og's Amorite kingdom before Israel's conquest.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashtoreth
entries.summary: Ashtoreth, the Phoenician goddess of love (and increase)
entries.dictNote: Ashtoreth was a Canaanite and Phoenician goddess of fertility and war, closely associated with Baal worship, and Solomon's construction of a shrine to her late in his reign, to please one of his foreign wives, is cited as a major reason for the kingdom's later division.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ashtoreth Karnaim
entries.summary: Ashteroth-Karnaim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: A city in Bashan, east of the Jordan, home to a branch of the Rephaim who were defeated by the coalition of eastern kings under Chedorlaomer in Genesis 14:5. The compound name, "Ashtoreth of the two horns," ties the town to the worship of the goddess Ashtoreth (Astarte), likely under a horned or crescent-moon symbol. It is generally identified with Tell Ashtarah in the Golan region of modern Syria.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashur
entries.dictNote: Ashur was a son of Hezron born after his father's death, remembered in Chronicles as the founder of Tekoa (1 Chronicles 2:24; 4:5), the town later home to the prophet Amos.

witness.excerpt: Ashur lived at the city Nineve; and named his subjects Assyrians: who became the most fortunate nation, beyond others.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ashvath
entries.dictNote: Son of Japhlet, of the tribe of Asher, included in the genealogical record of Asher's descendants (1 Chronicles 7:33).

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Asiel
entries.dictNote: Asiel was a Simeonite ancestor named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:35, appearing several generations back from Jehu, one of the tribal leaders listed there. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asnah
entries.dictNote: The ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43-50). The Nethinim were likely descended from war captives assigned to menial sanctuary duties, and their careful listing alongside priests and Levites shows how closely the returning community tracked lineage.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asnapper
entries.dictNote: Identified with Ashurbanipal, the last powerful king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, who resettled conquered peoples in Samaria after putting down rebellions in his territory. Opponents of the Jews cite him by this name in a letter urging the Persian king to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:10). Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, which held thousands of cuneiform tablets including the Epic of Gilgamesh, is now one of the richest surviving windows into the ancient Near East and is held largely in the British Museum.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aspatha
entries.dictNote: Aspatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the enemy of the Jews in the book of Esther, listed among those killed after Haman's plot against the Jewish people failed (Esther 9:7). Their deaths marked the reversal of Haman's plan and are still commemorated in the reading of Esther at Purim.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asrielites
entries.summary: an Asrielite (collectively) or descendant of Asriel
entries.dictNote: Asrielites were the clan descended from Asriel, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.dictNote: Asshur was a son of Shem whose name became attached to the land and empire of Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris in what is now northern Iraq. Its earliest capital, also called Asshur, later gave way to Nineveh and Calah as royal cities. Assyria grew into the dominant Near Eastern power of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, deporting Israel's northern tribes after Samaria's fall and repeatedly threatening Judah. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, which depicts Israelite king Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king, is one of several royal inscriptions that corroborate Assyria's dealings with Israel and Judah as the Bible records them.

entries.label: 17 books

entries.title: Asshurim
entries.summary: an Ashurite (collectively) or inhabitant of Ashur, a district in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Asshurim (also rendered Ashurites) names one of the regions over which Abner made Saul's son Ish-bosheth king after Saul's death, listed alongside Gilead, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin. Since Assyria itself lay far outside Israelite control at this date, most read the word as a scribal variant of Asherites, referring to territory belonging to the tribe of Asher, rather than to the distant Assyrian nation.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Assir
entries.summary: Assir, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Assir was a common Levitical name, borne by a descendant of Korah and by a son of Jeconiah listed in the royal genealogy after the exile.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Assos
entries.summary: Assus, a city of Asia MInor
entries.dictNote: Assos was a port city on the Aegean coast of the Roman province of Asia, in the district of Mysia, facing the island of Lesbos. Paul traveled to Assos on foot while his companions sailed around by ship, and he rejoined them there to continue toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:13-14). The city's well-preserved ruins, including a Doric temple of Athena on its acropolis, still stand above the modern Turkish village of Behramkale.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Asyncritos
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome greeted by Paul along with Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes and others (Romans 16:14). Nothing beyond his name and membership in this Roman house-church group is known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Atarah
entries.dictNote: Second wife of Jerahmeel and mother of Onam, named in the genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ataroth
entries.summary: Ataroth, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ataroth was a town name shared by several sites east of the Jordan, requested by the tribes of Reuben and Gad for their livestock because of its good pastureland.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ataroth the house of Joab
entries.dictNote: "Ataroth the house of Joab" is one of several place-clans listed as descendants of Salma in the genealogy of Judah, alongside Bethlehem and the Netophathites (1 Chronicles 2:54). The awkward phrasing likely reflects a compound name, Atroth-beth-Joab, distinguishing this Ataroth, meaning "crowns," a name shared by several unrelated biblical towns, from those other places. Its precise location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ataroth-adar(-addar)
entries.dictNote: Ataroth-addar was a town on the boundary between the territories of Ephraim and Benjamin, mentioned twice in the tribal boundary descriptions of Joshua (Josh. 16:5; 18:13). Its name combines a word for crowns with a term of uncertain meaning, and it should be distinguished from other towns simply called Ataroth elsewhere in the same region. No confident modern identification has been established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ater
entries.summary: Ater, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ater was the head of a family among the returning exiles, and also the name of a family of temple gatekeepers listed separately in Ezra's record.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Athach
entries.dictNote: Athach was one of the towns David sent spoil to after recovering the plunder Amalekite raiders had taken from Ziklag, a gift meant to reward the elders of Judah for tolerating his band's presence in their territory during his years as an outlaw (1 Samuel 30:26-30). Because the name occurs nowhere else in the Bible, some have suggested it is a copyist's error for Ether, a similarly spelled town in Judah's lowlands (Joshua 15:42). Its exact site, if distinct from Ether, is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Athaiah
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Pharez, of the tribe of Judah, listed among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Neh. 11:4). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:4 calls the same man, or his line, Uthai.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Athaliah
entries.summary: Athaljah, the name of an Israelitess and two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Athaliah was Ahab and Jezebel's daughter, married into Judah's royal line, and when her son King Ahaziah was killed she seized the throne for herself by murdering nearly the entire royal family, the only woman to ever rule Judah in her own name. She reigned six years worshiping Baal in Jerusalem until the priest Jehoiada revealed that one grandson, the infant Joash, had survived, and staged a coup that ended with Athaliah's execution.

entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Bebai who had married foreign women during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:28). He appears only in this list of names.

entries.title: Atroth
entries.dictNote: Short form of Atroth-shophan, one of the towns in Gilead that the tribe of Gad rebuilt and fortified after the conquest of the Transjordan (Numbers 32:35). Its precise site is unknown.

entries.title: Attai
entries.summary: Attai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Attai was a common name, borne by one of David's Gadite warriors and by a descendant of Judah through a marriage between an Israelite woman and her Egyptian servant.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Attalia
entries.dictNote: A port city of Pamphylia in Asia Minor, founded in the second century BC by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamon, and named after him. Paul and Barnabas sailed from here back to Antioch at the close of their first missionary journey (Acts 14:25); the city survives today as Antalya, Turkey, where sections of the ancient harbor and city wall are still standing.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Augustus
entries.summary: Named exactly once, for the census that puts Joseph and Mary on the road to Bethlehem (2:1). Josephus's Augustus (still Octavian here) is the same emperor deciding Herod's fate after Actium — the decree in Luke and the patronage in Josephus are two small views of the same distant, absolute power over Judea.
entries.dictNote: The cognomen of the first Roman emperor, C. Julius Caesar Octavianus, during whose reign Christ was born (Luke 2:1). His decree that “all the world should be taxed” was the divinely ordered occasion of Jesus’ being born, according to prophecy (Micah 5:2), in Bethlehem. This name being simply a title meaning “majesty” or “venerable,” first given to him by the senate (B.C. 27), was borne by succeeding emperors. Before his death (A.D. 14) he associated Tiberius with him in the empire (Luke 3:1), by whom he was succeeded.

entries.title: Ava
entries.summary: Ivvah or Avva, a region of Assyria
entries.dictNote: Ava, also called Ivah, was a city in Assyria's Mesopotamian heartland from which the Assyrians deported settlers to repopulate Samaria after Israel's exile in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24). Sennacherib's field commander later cited Ava's conquered gods, alongside those of Hamath and Sepharvaim, to taunt Hezekiah into surrendering Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13). It is commonly identified with Hit, an ancient town on the Euphrates known for its natural bitumen springs.

entries.title: Aven
entries.summary: Aven, the contemptuous synonym of three places, one in Coele-Syria, one in Egypt (On), and one in Palestine (Bethel)
entries.dictNote: Aven is not a person but a Hebrew word meaning nothingness or vanity, used in several places as a mocking wordplay on real place names. Hosea applies it to Bethel, calling it Beth-aven, 'house of vanity,' because of the golden calf Jeroboam had set up there (Hosea 4:15; 10:8). Ezekiel 30:17 uses it for the Egyptian city of On, better known as Heliopolis, and Amos 1:5 uses it for a Syrian city usually identified with Baalbec.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Avim
entries.summary: Avvim (as inhabited by Avvites), a place in Palestine (with the article prefix)
entries.dictNote: Avim was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among its territory's settlements (Josh. 18:23). It is a different Avim from the coastal people called the Avvites, who lived farther southwest near Gaza before being displaced by the Caphtorim (Deut. 2:23); this town's exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Avims
entries.summary: an Avvite or native of Avvah (only plural)
entries.dictNote: The Avvim, also spelled Avims, were a pre-Israelite people who lived in villages in the region of Gaza before being driven out and largely destroyed by the Caphtorim, migrants from Crete associated with the Philistines (Deuteronomy 2:23; Joshua 13:3). The same Hebrew name is applied in 2 Kings 17:31 to settlers from Avva whom the Assyrians relocated to Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom's population; those settlers brought their own gods, Nibhaz and Tartak, with them.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Avith
entries.summary: Avvith (or Avvoth), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Edomite city of Hadad son of Bedad, another of the early Edomite kings who ruled before Israel's monarchy began; he defeated the Midianites in the territory of Moab (Gen. 36:35; 1 Chr. 1:46).

witness.excerpt: And ’Asâm died, and ’Adâth,  the son of Barad,  who slew Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead, and the name of his city was Avith.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azal
entries.summary: Atsel, the name of an Israelite, and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Azal, also spelled Azel, is used in the Hebrew Bible for both a person and a place, though it is the same underlying name. Azel was a great-great-grandson of King Saul through Jonathan, a Benjamite listed with his six sons in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:37-38 and 9:43-44. Separately, the prophet Zechariah uses "Azal" as a place name near Jerusalem, saying that when the Mount of Olives splits in two, the resulting valley will reach "as far as Azal" (Zechariah 14:5), though its precise location is uncertain and some translators render the phrase simply as "very near."
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azaliah
entries.dictNote: Azaliah was the father of Shaphan, the royal scribe who read the newly discovered Book of the Law to King Josiah and helped spark Josiah's religious reforms (2 Kings 22:3; 2 Chronicles 34:8).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azaniah
entries.dictNote: Azaniah was a Levite, the father of Jeshua, one of the Levites who set their seal to the covenant renewed under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 10:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azarael
entries.summary: Azarel, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Azarel was a common name among Levitical musicians and military officers in David's organization, appearing in the lists of 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Azariah
entries.summary: Azarjah, the name of nineteen Israelites
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Daniel
entries.dictNote: Azariah was a common name shared by many Old Testament figures, most notably serving as an alternate name for King Uzziah of Judah, and also as the birth name of Abednego, one of Daniel's three friends thrown into the fiery furnace in Babylon for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image.

entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Azariah
entries.dictNote: Azariah was a common name shared by many Old Testament figures, most notably serving as an alternate name for King Uzziah of Judah, and also as the birth name of Abednego, one of Daniel's three friends thrown into the fiery furnace in Babylon for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azaz
entries.dictNote: Azaz was a Reubenite, father of Bela, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben settled east of the Jordan (1 Chr. 5:8). Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azaziah
entries.summary: Azazjah, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Azaziah was a common Levitical name, including a musician appointed under David and the father of one of Solomon's district governors.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azbuk
entries.dictNote: The father of a different Nehemiah than the book's main figure, this one identified as ruler of half the district of Beth-zur and credited with repairing a section of Jerusalem's wall (Neh. 3:16). He appears only to identify his son in this list of wall-builders.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azekah
entries.dictNote: Azekah was a fortified town in the Shephelah of Judah, the scene of Joshua's rout of five Amorite kings during a hailstorm (Joshua 10:10-11) and later resettled by returning exiles (Nehemiah 11:30). The Lachish ostraca, letters written by a Judean officer during Nebuchadnezzar's final campaign against Judah, report watching for signal fires from Lachish because "we cannot see Azekah," widely read as evidence the town had already fallen, which corroborates Jeremiah 34:7's note that Azekah and Lachish were the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out.

witness.excerpt: 1106] Now the Philistines gathered themselves together again, no very long time afterward; and having gotten together a great army, they made war against the Israelites: and having seized a place between Shochoh and Azekah, they there pitched their camp.

on, who, as we said before, was king of the two tribes, built strong and large cities, Bethlehem, and Etare, and Tekoa, and Bethzur, and Shoco, and Adullam, and Ipan, and Maresha, and Ziph, and Adorlam, and Lachlsh, and Azekah, and Zorah, and Aijalon, and Hebron; these he built first of all in the tribe of Judah.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Azem
entries.dictNote: Azem, also spelled Ezem, was a town in the extreme south of Judah's territory (Joshua 15:29) that was later assigned to Simeon, whose inheritance was carved out from within Judah's larger allotment (Joshua 19:3; 1 Chronicles 4:29). Its exact site in the Negev has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azgad
entries.dictNote: Azgad was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, listed by household in both Ezra and Nehemiah's records.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Aziel
entries.dictNote: Aziel was a Levite appointed by David to play a stringed instrument, the psaltery, when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr. 15:20). His name appears to be a shortened form of Jaaziel, named two verses earlier in the same list.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aziza
entries.dictNote: Aziza was a layman from the family of Zattu who had married a foreign wife after the return from Babylonian exile and was required to divorce her under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:27). He is one of over a hundred men named in this list who complied with the covenant to end intermarriage with surrounding peoples.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azmaveth
entries.summary: Azmaveth, the name of three Israelites and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Azmaveth was a town near Jerusalem, in the territory associated with Anathoth, whose residents are twice listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile. The name was also borne by several different men: one of David's thirty mighty warriors, a Benjamite archer who joined David at Ziklag, and an official who oversaw the royal storehouses under David and Solomon.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Azmon
entries.dictNote: A point on the southern boundary of the promised land, near the Wadi el-Arish, the Brook of Egypt that marked Israel's southwestern border (Num. 34:4-5; Josh. 15:4). Its exact location remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Aznoth-tabor
entries.dictNote: Aznoth-tabor, "the summits" or "ears of Tabor," marked one of the boundary points of the tribe of Naphtali's territory, near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:34). It may refer to a cluster of hills rather than a town proper. Its precise location is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azorigin
entries.dictNote: Azor appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Eliakim and the father of Zadok, one link in the postexilic chain connecting Zerubbabel to Joseph, husband of Mary (Matthew 1:13-14). He is not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture and has no independent narrative beyond this genealogical placement.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azotus
entries.summary: Azotus (i.e. Ashdod), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Greek name for Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities, used in the account of Philip the evangelist's ministry along the coastal road after he baptized the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:40). The city retained this Hellenized name throughout the Roman period.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Azriel
entries.summary: Azriel, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Azriel was a common name, borne by a tribal leader of Manasseh and by the father of an official King Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Azrikam
entries.summary: Azrikam, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Azrikam was a common name, including a palace official executed along with King Ahaz's son during an invasion, and a descendant of David listed in the royal genealogy.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Azubah
entries.summary: Azubah, the name of two Israelitesses
entries.dictNote: Azubah was King Jehoshaphat's mother, and also the name of a wife of Caleb listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.

witness.excerpt: He was born of Asa's wife Azubah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Azur
entries.summary: Azzur, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Azur (properly Azzur, meaning “he that assists”) is the name of at least three men in the Old Testament: a covenant-signer under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:17), the father of the false prophet Hananiah who broke Jeremiah's symbolic yoke and predicted a swift return from exile that never came (Jeremiah 28:1), and the father of Jaazaniah, one of the corrupt princes Ezekiel saw plotting evil counsel in a vision (Ezekiel 11:1).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Azzah
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Azzah is the more literal transliteration of the name usually rendered Gaza in English Bibles, the southernmost of the five chief Philistine cities on the coastal road between Egypt and Canaan.

entries.label: 11 books

entries.title: Azzan
entries.dictNote: Azzan was the father of Paltiel, the leader from the tribe of Issachar appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:26). He is mentioned only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal
entries.books: Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Hosea, Zephaniah, Romans
entries.dictNote: Baal was the chief storm and fertility god of the Canaanite pantheon, worshiped as the power behind rain, crops, and fertility, and the Old Testament treats Baal worship as Israel's most persistent and dangerous temptation, from the judges period through the divided monarchy. Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, where fire from heaven answered his prayer while Baal's prophets got no response from their own god, is the Bible's most direct confrontation between the two.

entries.label: 10 books

entries.title: Baal-berith
entries.summary: Baal-Berith, a special deity of the Shechemites
entries.dictNote: Baal-berith, meaning "lord of the covenant," was not a person but a Canaanite god worshipped at Shechem after Gideon's death, when Israel again fell into idolatry (Judges 8:33). The same shrine is later called simply the house of the god "El-berith" or "Berith," and it funded the violent bid for kingship by Gideon's son Abimelech (Judges 9:4, 46).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-gad
entries.dictNote: Baal-gad, named for the worship of Baal there, was a Canaanite town in the valley below Mount Hermon and marked the northernmost point Joshua's conquests reached (Joshua 11:17; 12:7). It lay near the sources of the Jordan River, in the same district later called Baal-hermon, and is often identified with the site later known as Panias or Banias, later renamed Caesarea Philippi.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-hamon
entries.dictNote: Baal-hamon, meaning lord of a multitude, was the site of an extensive vineyard belonging to Solomon, mentioned in a closing verse of the Song of Solomon that he leased out to tenants for a substantial rent (Song of Sol. 8:11). Its location is unknown, though some have proposed identifying it with Baal-gad near Mount Hermon or with a site near Dothan in central Israel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-hanan
entries.summary: Baal-Chanan, the name of an Edomite, also of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Baal-hanan was an early Edomite king, listed in Genesis among the rulers who governed before Israel had any king of its own.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baal-hazor
entries.dictNote: Baal-hazor, on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin, was where Absalom held a sheep-shearing feast and used the occasion to have his men murder his half-brother Amnon, in revenge for Amnon's rape of their sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13:23-29). The killing set off the chain of events that led to Absalom's exile and later revolt against David. The site is generally identified with modern Tell Asur, northeast of Bethel, the highest peak in the central hill country.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-hermon
entries.dictNote: Two references share this name. One is a town near Mount Hermon inhabited by the half-tribe of Manasseh, possibly the same as Baal-gad (1 Chr. 5:23). The other is the mountain itself, listed among the strongholds of Canaanite peoples that Israel failed to fully conquer during the period of the judges (Judges 3:3).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baal-meon
entries.summary: Baal-Meon, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Baal-meon was a town east of the Jordan rebuilt by the tribe of Reuben and known by several related names, including Beth-baal-meon and Beth-meon (Numbers 32:38; Ezekiel 25:9). It lay in territory that passed back and forth between Israel and Moab, and the Moabite king Mesha claims on his own inscription, the Moabite Stone, to have rebuilt Baal-meon and built a reservoir there, an extrabiblical confirmation of the town's existence. It is identified with the modern site of Ma'in, southeast of Heshbon.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Baal-peor
entries.dictNote: Baal of Peor was a Moabite deity Israel was seduced into worshiping through relationships with Moabite women shortly before entering the promised land, provoking a plague that Phinehas's zealous action finally stopped.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Baal-perazim
entries.dictNote: Baal-perazim, meaning roughly lord of breakthroughs, was the name David gave to the site where he defeated the Philistines early in his reign over all Israel, comparing the victory to a flood bursting through (2 Sam. 5:20; 1 Chr. 14:11). Isaiah later refers to the same event at Mount Perazim (Isa. 28:21). The location lay near the Valley of Rephaim southwest of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baal-shalisha
entries.summary: Baal of Shalishah, Baal-Shalishah, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Baal-shalisha lay in the district of Shalisha, apparently not far from Gilgal, and is remembered for the man who brought Elisha twenty barley loaves and fresh grain, which the prophet multiplied to feed a hundred people (2 Kings 4:42-44). The episode anticipates Jesus' feeding miracles in the Gospels. It is usually located near Sirisia, north of Lydda, though the identification is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-tamar
entries.dictNote: Baal-tamar, "lord of the palm tree," was a site near Gibeah in Benjamin's territory where the other Israelite tribes regrouped for their final assault against Benjamin during the civil war sparked by the outrage at Gibeah (Judges 20:33). The name likely refers to a Baal shrine marked by a notable palm tree, possibly the same palm associated with the judge Deborah a few chapters earlier (Judges 4:5). Its exact site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-zebub
entries.summary: Baal-Zebub, a special deity of the Ekronites
entries.dictNote: Baal-zebub, meaning lord of the flies, was the Philistine god of Ekron that King Ahaziah of Israel sent messengers to consult about his health, a decision Elijah confronted directly by asking whether Israel had no God of its own to ask instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baal-zephon
entries.dictNote: Baal-zephon was a site on the shore near where the Israelites camped before crossing the sea during the exodus, mentioned as a landmark in both the crossing narrative and the wilderness itinerary (Exodus 14:2, 9; Numbers 33:7). The name reflects the Canaanite storm god Baal-Zaphon, whose cult had spread into Egypt's eastern Delta, and Egyptian records of the period independently mention a place of that name near the frontier. Its exact location along the ancient shoreline is still debated.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Baalah
entries.summary: Baalah, the name of three places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Baalah was an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark of the covenant rested for twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baalath
entries.dictNote: Baalath was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:44) that Solomon later fortified along with other store cities as part of his building program (1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chronicles 8:6). Its name, meaning mistress or lady, reflects Canaanite goddess worship connected to the site before Israel's conquest. Its exact location is uncertain, though it lay somewhere in the Shephelah near Gezer.

witness.excerpt: Moreover, he built two other cities not far from it, Beth-horon was the name of one of them, and Baalath of the other.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Baalath-beer
entries.dictNote: Baalath-beer, meaning Baalah of the well, was a town assigned to the tribe of Simeon on the southern frontier of Judah's territory (Josh. 19:8). It is likely the same town called simply Baal in the parallel list of Simeonite towns in 1 Chronicles 4:33.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baale of Judah
entries.dictNote: Baale of Judah, an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark of the covenant rested for years before David brought it up to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:2; 1 Chr. 13:6). Excavations at Kiriath-jearim's traditional site, Tell Deir el-Azhar, have uncovered a massive stone platform that some archaeologists have proposed was built to support a sanctuary, consistent with the town's role as long-term keeper of the ark.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baalis
entries.dictNote: King of the Ammonites during the Babylonian conquest of Judah, Baalis incited Ishmael son of Nethaniah to assassinate Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had appointed over the remnant left in the land, an act that triggered further Jewish flight into Egypt (Jeremiah 40:14; 41:1-3).

witness.excerpt: Now there was of the royal family one Ishmael, a wicked man, and very crafty; who during the siege of Jerusalem fled to Baalis, the King of the Ammonites, and abode with him during that time.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baana
entries.summary: Baana, the name of four Israelite
entries.dictNote: Three men carry this name. Two were district officers who supplied provisions for Solomon's royal household, one stationed in the region of Megiddo and Taanach (1 Kings 4:12), the other a son of Hushai in a different district (1 Kings 4:16). A third Baana was the father of Zadok, one of those who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:4).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baanah

entries.summary: Babel (i.e. Babylon), including Babylonia and the Babylonian empire
entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Micah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Babel is the plain in Shinar where humanity, still speaking one language after the flood, attempted to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens to make a name for themselves, and God responded by confusing their language and scattering them across the earth. The name is closely tied to Babylon, built in the same region and remembered throughout Scripture as a symbol of human pride set against God.

entries.summary: Babylon, the capitol of Chaldæa (literally or figuratively (as a type of tyranny))
entries.books: Ezra, Daniel, Matthew, Acts, 1 Peter, Revelation
entries.dictNote: Babylon was the dominant Mesopotamian empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and deported Judah's population, and its name became prophetic shorthand throughout Scripture, including in Revelation, for worldly power arrayed against God. The Tower of Babel narrative is set in the same region, tying Babylon's later arrogance to humanity's earliest recorded act of collective pride.

entries.title: Babylonia
entries.dictNote: Babylonia was the ancient region and empire of lower Mesopotamia, centered on the Euphrates and Tigris valleys with Babylon as its capital. Its armies conquered the kingdom of Judah in 586 BC, destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple, and deported much of the population, an event corroborated by Babylonian ration tablets that name the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin among captives at Nebuchadnezzar's court. Babylonia's own dominance ended when it fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BC, an event the Cyrus Cylinder itself commemorates. In Ezra 4:9 the name refers to Babylonian officials and settlers who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile.

entries.dictNote: Baca, the "Valley of Baca," a dry valley pictured in Psalm 84:6 as turning into a place of springs for pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem in faith. The name likely plays on the balsam or mulberry trees mentioned elsewhere (2 Sam. 5:23-24) and probably describes any parched valley on the pilgrim road rather than one fixed, identifiable site.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bachrites
entries.summary: a Bakrite (collectively) or descendants of Beker
entries.dictNote: Bachrites were the clan descended from Becher, a son of Ephraim, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baharumite
entries.summary: a Bacharumite or inhabitant of Bachurim
entries.dictNote: Baharumite marks Azmaveth, one of David's mighty men, as a native of Bahurim, a Benjaminite village east of Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan. The same man appears in the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:31 under the spelling Barhumite, an alternate form of the same place name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bahurim
entries.dictNote: Bahurim was a village east of Jerusalem on the road down to the Jordan Valley, home to the Benjamite Shimei, who cursed David and pelted him with stones as he fled Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 16:5-13). It was also where Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well to avoid Absalom's search party while carrying intelligence back to David (2 Samuel 17:18-21).

witness.excerpt: When David was at Bahurim, a place so called, there came out a kinsman of Saul's, whose name was Shimei, and threw stones at him, and gave him reproachful words; and as his friends stood about the king and protected him, he persevered still more

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bakbakkar
entries.dictNote: Bakbakkar was a Levite, apparently descended from Asaph, listed among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (1 Chronicles 9:14-15). Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bakbuk
entries.dictNote: Bakbuk's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). The name means “bottle” or “flask,” possibly an occupational designation from an ancestor's trade. Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bakbukiah
entries.dictNote: Bakbukiah was a Levite who served among the temple musicians and gatekeepers in Jerusalem during the postexilic period.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Balaam
entries.summary: The prophet hired to curse Israel who blesses them instead, famous for the talking donkey (Numbers 22-24). Josephus gives him his own chapter title and treats him as a real, complicated figure — genuinely gifted, genuinely compromised — rather than a folk-tale villain.
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Micah, 2 Peter, Jude, Revelation
entries.dictNote: Balaam was a non-Israelite prophet hired by the Moabite king Balak to curse the invading Israelites, and God famously made Balaam's own donkey speak to rebuke him after the animal saw an angel blocking their path that Balaam himself couldn't see. Every time Balaam opened his mouth to curse Israel as instructed, blessing came out instead, and his oracles include a famous prophecy of a star that would rise out of Jacob. Later biblical writers remember Balaam as a corrupting influence who advised Balak on how to seduce Israel into idolatry through Moabite women, and he is killed in the resulting conflict.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Balaam the Prophet, and what kind of man he was.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Balac
entries.dictNote: Balac is the Greek form of Balak, the Moabite king who hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel in Numbers 22-24. The name appears in Revelation 2:14, where Christ rebukes the church at Pergamum for tolerating teaching that echoes Balaam's counsel to Balak, luring Israelites into idolatry and sexual immorality.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baladan
entries.summary: Baladan, the name of a Babylonian prince
entries.dictNote: Baladan appears only as the father of Merodach-baladan, the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah after his illness (2 Kings 20:12; Isaiah 39:1). Nothing else about him is recorded in the biblical text; his son's rebellions against Assyria are independently attested in Assyrian and Babylonian chronicle records of the period.

witness.excerpt: 709.] At this time it was that the dominion of the Assyrians was overthrown by the Medes.  But of these things I shall treat elsewhere.1 But the King of Babylon, whose name was Baladan, sent ambassadors to Hezekiah, with presents; and desired he would be his ally, and his friend.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Balah
entries.dictNote: A town assigned to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh. 19:3), called Bilhah in 1 Chronicles 4:29 and Baalah in Joshua 15:29, three spellings of the same place.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Balak
entries.dictNote: Balak was the Moabite king who hired the prophet Balaam to curse the invading Israelites, and his growing frustration as Balaam's oracles kept turning into blessings instead of curses is one of the more darkly comic threads in the Pentateuch.

witness.excerpt: When Balak, the King of the Moabites, who had from his ancestors a friendship and league with the Midianites, saw how greatly the Israelites were grown, he was much affrighted on account of his own and his kingdom’s danger.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bamah
entries.dictNote: A generic Hebrew term for a hilltop shrine, used by Ezekiel in a pointed wordplay against Israel's idolatry: the prophet asks what this high place is that the people keep going to, noting that it is called Bamah, high place, to this very day (Ezek. 20:29).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bamoth
entries.summary: Bamoth or Bamoth-Baal, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel in Moabite territory, its name meaning "heights" (Num. 21:19-20). It is likely connected to Bamoth-baal, a nearby Moabite high place to which Balak later took Balaam in hopes of cursing Israel (Num. 22:41).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bani
entries.summary: Bani, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bani was a common name in the postexilic period, borne by several Levites and returning exiles listed in Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Baptist
entries.summary: a baptizer, as an epithet of Christ's forerunner
entries.dictNote: John the Baptist was a wilderness preacher, the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, born to elderly parents after an angel announced his birth in the Jerusalem temple. He preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan River, and it was John who baptized Jesus and publicly identified him as the one Israel had been waiting for. Herod Antipas had John arrested and eventually beheaded after John condemned his marriage to his brother's wife, a death carried out, according to the Gospels, as a birthday party favor to Herod's stepdaughter.

witness.excerpt: As also concerning the death of John the Baptist.

The Recognitions assuring us that they began about the days of John the Baptist, I.54 .

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bar-jona
entries.summary: son of Jonas (or Jonah); Bar-jonas, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Bar-jona, meaning "son of Jonah," is the patronymic Jesus used to address Simon Peter after Peter's confession that Jesus was the Christ (Matthew 16:17). It identifies Peter's father as a man named Jonah or John (compare John 1:42; 21:15-17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Barabbas
entries.summary: son of Abba; Bar-abbas, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Barabbas was a prisoner held for insurrection and murder, and Pilate offered the crowd a choice between releasing him or Jesus as part of a Passover custom of pardoning one prisoner; the crowd chose Barabbas, and Jesus was crucified in his place.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Barachel
entries.summary: Barakel, the father of one of Job's friends
entries.dictNote: Barachel was a Buzite, the father of Elihu, the youngest of the friends who spoke to Job (Job 32:2, 6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Barachias
entries.dictNote: Barachias is named in Matthew 23:35 as the father of the Zacharias whom Jesus says was murdered between the temple and the altar. The wording most closely matches Zechariah the priest stoned in the temple court under King Joash, whose father was actually named Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20-22), so some see this as an added or confused patronymic, possibly conflating him with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1).

witness.excerpt: (10) Some commentators are ready to suppose, that this Zacharias the son of Baruch, here most unjustly slain by the Jews in the temple, was the very same person with Zacharias the son of Barachias, whom our Saviour says the Jews slew between the temple and the altar : Matt.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Barak
entries.dictNote: Barak was the military commander Deborah summoned to lead Israel's forces against the Canaanite general Sisera, and he refused to go into battle unless Deborah came with him, a hesitation that cost him the personal glory of the coming victory, since Deborah told him credit would go to a woman instead. That woman turned out to be Jael, who killed the fleeing Sisera in her own tent.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Barhumite
entries.summary: a Barchumite, or native of Bachurim
entries.dictNote: Barhumite marks Azmaveth, one of David's mighty men, as a native of Bahurim, a Benjaminite village near Jerusalem. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:33 gives the same man's home town as Baharumite, an alternate spelling of the same name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bariah
entries.dictNote: Bariah was one of five sons of Shemaiah, listed within the postexilic royal line of David in 1 Chronicles 3:22. Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Barjesus
entries.summary: son of Jesus (or Joshua); Bar-jesus, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Bar-Jesus was a Jewish false prophet and magician attached to the court of Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul of Cyprus (Acts 13:6). He is also called Elymas, sought to turn the proconsul away from the faith, and was struck blind by Paul for opposing the gospel, after which Sergius Paulus believed. His name means son of Jesus, an ironic title for a man Paul denounced as a son of the devil.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Barkos
entries.dictNote: Barkos was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile, listed among those unable to prove their Israelite lineage through genealogical records (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Barnabas
entries.summary: son of Nabas (i.e. prophecy); Barnabas, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus whose given name was Joseph, and the apostles nicknamed him Barnabas, meaning son of encouragement, after he sold a field and gave the money to the Jerusalem church. He was the one who vouched for the newly converted Saul when the other believers still feared him as a persecutor, and he later recruited Saul to help lead the church at Antioch and traveled with him on the first missionary journey. Barnabas and Paul eventually split over whether to bring Barnabas's cousin John Mark on a second journey, a sharp enough disagreement that they went separate ways afterward.

witness.excerpt: In the mean time, it is not to be doubted, but in their education they must have both learned more Jewish interpretations; such I mean as we meet with in the epistle of Barnabas , in that to the Hebrews, and elsewhere among the old Jews.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Barsabas
entries.summary: son of Sabas (or Tsaba); Bar-sabas, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Barsabas, meaning son of Sabas, was a surname carried by two different men in Acts. Joseph Barsabas, also called Justus, was one of the two candidates put forward to replace Judas among the twelve apostles (Acts 1:23). Judas Barsabas was a prophet in the Jerusalem church sent along with Paul and Silas to deliver the council's letter to the believers in Antioch (Acts 15:22, 32). The two are unrelated beyond sharing the same family name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bartholomeus
entries.summary: son of Tolmai; Bar-tholomæus, a Christian apostle
entries.dictNote: Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles, and many identify him with Nathanael, since the Synoptic Gospels never mention a Nathanael and John's Gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, and both names are consistently paired with Philip in their respective lists.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bartimaeus
entries.summary: son of Timæus (or the unclean); Bar-timæus, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Bartimaeus was a blind beggar at Jericho, son of a man named Timaeus, whose sight Jesus restored after Bartimaeus called out to him as Son of David (Mark 10:46-52). His persistence despite the crowd's attempts to silence him is presented as an example of faith. The parallel account in Matthew 20:30 mentions two unnamed blind men, while Luke 18:35 places the healing as Jesus approached rather than left the city.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Baruch
entries.summary: Baruk, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Baruch was Jeremiah's scribe and close companion, personally writing down Jeremiah's dictated prophecies onto a scroll that King Jehoiakim later cut up and burned, and Baruch rewrote it from Jeremiah's dictation with additional material added. He was forced into exile in Egypt along with Jeremiah after Judah's remaining leadership was assassinated. A clay seal impression bearing his name and title, found in Jerusalem, is widely believed to be his own.

entries.title: Barzillai
entries.summary: Barzillai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Barzillai was a wealthy and elderly Gileadite who supplied David and his men with provisions during Absalom's rebellion, and David later offered to reward him with a place at the royal court, an honor Barzillai declined due to his advanced age, asking David to take his son instead.

entries.title: Bashan
entries.summary: Bashan (often with the article), a region East of the Jordan
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah, Nahum, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Bashan was the fertile tableland east of the Jordan between Gilead and Mount Hermon, ruled by Og, the last of the Rephaim, until Israel defeated him and gave the territory to half the tribe of Manasseh. It was famous in the Bible for its oak forests, its rich pastures, and the strong cattle they produced, images the prophets used for pride and excess. After the exile the region was divided into the districts of Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Trachonitis, and Batanaea, names that carried into the New Testament era.

entries.label: 15 books

entries.title: Bashemath
entries.summary: Bosmath, the name of a wife of Esau, and of a daughter of Solomon
entries.dictNote: Basemath was the name of more than one wife of Esau in Genesis's genealogical lists, and also the name of one of Solomon's daughters.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bath-rabbim
entries.dictNote: A gate of the Ammonite-bordering city of Heshbon, near which lay pools of water; the Song of Solomon compares the eyes of the beloved to "the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim" (Song of Solomon 7:4). Its exact location within Heshbon is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bath-sheba
entries.dictNote: Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite until David saw her bathing, summoned her, and got her pregnant while Uriah was away at war under David's own command. David's cover-up ended with Uriah's engineered death in battle, a sin the prophet Nathan confronted directly with a parable that trapped David into condemning himself, and the child born from the affair died in infancy as part of the judgment. Bathsheba later became the mother of Solomon and intervened at a critical moment near David's death to make sure Solomon, not a rival half-brother, inherited the throne.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bath-shua
entries.dictNote: Bath-shua, meaning “daughter of Shua,” is used of two different women in Chronicles. It names the Canaanite wife of Judah, mother of Er, Onan, and Shelah, elsewhere called simply “the daughter of Shua” (1 Chronicles 2:3; compare Genesis 38:2). It is also used as a variant of Bathsheba, wife of David and mother of Solomon (1 Chronicles 3:5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bavai
entries.dictNote: Son of Henadad, Bavai ruled the district of Keilah and helped repair a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bazlith
entries.dictNote: Bazlith, also spelled Bazluth, headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:52; Nehemiah 7:54). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bealiah
entries.dictNote: Bealiah was a Benjamite among the skilled warriors, expert with bow and sling from both hands, who defected to David at Ziklag while he was still an outlaw fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:1-5). His name, meaning "the Lord is my lord," is notable for using the divine name Yahweh rather than Baal despite superficially resembling a Baal-compound name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bealoth
entries.dictNote: Town in the far south of Judah (Josh. 15:24), likely the same as Baalath-beer (Josh. 19:8). Solomon's list of administrative districts also names a region called Aloth or Bealoth under one of his twelve governors (1 Kings 4:16).

witness.excerpt: And he removed from thence and went towards the south,  and he came to Hebron, and Hebron was built at, that time, and he dwelt there two years, and he went (thence) into the land of the south, to Bealoth  and there was a famine in the land.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bebai
entries.dictNote: Bebai was the head of a family among the returning exiles, prominent enough to be listed among those who sealed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Becher
entries.summary: Beker, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Becher was a son of Benjamin, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Benjamin's tribe in Israel's genealogies.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bechorath
entries.dictNote: Bechorath was an ancestor of King Saul, named in the genealogy of 1 Samuel 9:1 as the son of Aphiah and an early forebear of Kish, Saul's father. The genealogy is given to establish Saul's Benjamite pedigree just before his introduction into the narrative. Nothing beyond this genealogical mention is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bedad
entries.dictNote: Bedad was the father of Hadad, one of the early kings of Edom who defeated the Midianites in the territory of Moab (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bedan
entries.summary: Bedan, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bedan is named among Israel's deliverers in Samuel's farewell speech, alongside Jerubbaal, Barak, and Jephthah, though his identity is uncertain since no judge by that name appears in the book of Judges; some identify him with Samson or Abdon, or take the name as a variant of Barak (1 Samuel 12:11). A different Bedan, of the tribe of Manasseh, appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:17.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bedeiah
entries.dictNote: Bedeiah was one of the sons of Bani who had married a foreign wife and agreed, under Ezra's reform after the Babylonian exile, to send her away, around 458 BC (Ezra 10:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beeliada
entries.dictNote: One of David's sons born in Jerusalem, listed in 1 Chronicles 14:7; the parallel lists in 2 Samuel 5:16 and 1 Chronicles 3:8 call him Eliada instead, Beeliada apparently being an earlier form of the name later avoided because it contained the element "Baal."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beelzebub
entries.summary: dung-god; Beelzebul, a name of Satan
entries.dictNote: Beelzebub, meaning lord of the flies, was a title for a Philistine deity that became a common New Testament name for the prince of demons, and Jesus's opponents accused him of casting out demons by Beelzebub's power, a charge Jesus rebutted by pointing out a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.
