entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Beer
entries.summary: Beer, a place in the Desert, also one in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Beer, simply meaning well, names two separate places. The first was a stopping point in the wilderness of Moab where Israel's leaders dug a well, commemorated by a short song recorded in the text (Num. 21:16-18). The second was a town in Judah's hill country where Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, fled after denouncing his brother Abimelech's kingship at Shechem (Judg. 9:21).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beer-elim
entries.summary: Beer-Elim, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Beer-elim, meaning well of the mighty ones, is named in Isaiah's oracle against Moab as a border point where news of Moab's downfall reached (Isa. 15:8). It is generally connected with the well called simply Beer in Numbers 21:16-18, dug by Israel's leaders during the wilderness journey and celebrated in a short victory song.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beer-lahai-roi
entries.summary: Beer-Lachai-Roi, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Well in the Negev, its name meaning "the well of the one who lives and sees me," where the angel of the Lord found the pregnant, fleeing Hagar and spoke to her (Gen. 16:7-14). Isaac later settled in the area and was there when Rebekah's caravan first arrived to meet him (Gen. 24:62), and he returned to it again after Abraham's death (Gen. 25:11). It is traditionally placed near Kadesh-barnea, though the precise site is unconfirmed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beer-shebah
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Amos
entries.dictNote: Beersheba marked the southern edge of Judah's territory, allotted first to Simeon before it came to define the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba," shorthand for the full length of Israel. Genesis gives two separate stories for how it got its name, one where Abraham and Abimelech swore an oath over seven ewe lambs, another where Isaac's servants struck water there a generation later. Tel Aviv University excavated the site from 1969 to 1975 and uncovered a fortified Iron Age city, giving the patriarchal stories a real settlement to sit against rather than just a name in the text.
entries.dictSource: Source: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915); Logos Factbook
entries.label: 11 books

entries.title: Beera
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Asher through Zophah, named among the heads of households in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:37.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beerah
entries.dictNote: A chief of the tribe of Reuben carried into exile by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, part of the same eighth-century deportation that emptied out Israel's Transjordan territories (1 Chronicles 5:6). Tiglath-pileser's own annals, recovered from Nimrud, record his campaigns against Israel and corroborate the biblical picture of Assyrian pressure on the region in this period.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beeri
entries.summary: Beeri, the name of a Hittite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Two Old Testament men bear this name. The first was a Hittite whose daughter Judith became one of Esau's wives, a marriage that grieved his parents Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 26:34-35). The second was the father of the prophet Hosea, known only from the opening verse of Hosea's book (Hosea 1:1).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beerites
entries.summary: a Beriite (collectively) or descendants of Beriah
entries.dictNote: Beerites were the clan descended from Beriah, a son of Asher, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beeroth
entries.dictNote: Beeroth was one of four Hivite cities, with Gibeon, Chephirah, and Kiriath-jearim, whose people tricked Joshua into a peace treaty by posing as distant travelers (Joshua 9:3-17). It was allotted to Benjamin, and two of its native sons, Baanah and Rechab, later murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's surviving heir, hoping to curry favor with David, who instead had them executed (2 Samuel 4:2-12). Its people are listed among those returning from Babylonian exile in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:25).
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Beeroth of the children of Jaakan
entries.summary: Beeroth-Bene-Jaakan, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, "wells of the Bene-jaakan," was a wilderness campsite from which the Israelites journeyed on to Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, according to Deuteronomy's itinerary (Deuteronomy 10:6). Numbers 33:31-32 records the same stop simply as Bene-jaakan, listing it among the stations between Sinai and the plains of Moab. Its location in the Sinai or Transjordan wilderness is not established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beerothite
entries.summary: a Beerothite or inhabitant of Beeroth
entries.dictNote: Beerothite marks someone from Beeroth, a town belonging to the Gibeonite league that Joshua had spared. Rechab and Baanah, the two Beerothite officers who assassinated Saul's son Ish-bosheth and were then executed by David for it, are the most notable examples.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beeshterah
entries.summary: Beeshterah, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beeshterah, a Levitical city given to the Gershonite clan out of the tribe of Manasseh's territory east of the Jordan (Josh. 21:27). It is likely the same as Ashtaroth, the old Amorite capital of King Og listed elsewhere (Josh. 12:4; 13:31).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Behemoth
entries.summary: a water-ox, i.e. the hippopotamus or Nile-horse
entries.dictNote: Behemoth is not a person but a massive land creature God describes to Job as proof of his own power over creation, most often identified with the hippopotamus given the description of its strength, its grass diet, and its habitat among the reeds of the river (Job 40:15-24). Some interpreters read it instead as a more general symbol of untamable animal power, or pair it with Leviathan as a primeval chaos-beast, but the hippopotamus identification best fits the physical details in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bel
entries.summary: Bel, the Baal of the Babylonians
entries.dictNote: Bel was the Babylonian title for the god Marduk, and Isaiah and Jeremiah both mock Bel directly as a powerless idol that will itself go into captivity when Babylon falls.

entries.title: Bela
entries.summary: Bela, the name of a place, also of an Edomite and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bela, also called Zoar, was the only one of the five cities of the plain spared destruction, preserved at Lot's plea so he would have somewhere nearby to flee. The same name belongs to Benjamin's firstborn son, to an early king of Edom listed in Genesis and Chronicles, and to a descendant of Reuben.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Belaites
entries.summary: a Belaite (collectively) or descendants of Bela
entries.dictNote: Belaites were the clan descended from Bela, the firstborn son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Belial
entries.summary: worthlessness; Belial, as an epithet of Satan
entries.dictNote: Belial is not the name of an individual but a Hebrew word meaning 'worthlessness' or 'wickedness,' used throughout the Old Testament in phrases like 'sons of Belial' for scoundrels and troublemakers (Judges 19:22; 1 Samuel 2:12). By the New Testament era it had become a proper name for Satan or a chief evil power, as reflected in Paul's rhetorical question in 2 Corinthians 6:15, 'what concord hath Christ with Belial?' The term appears often in this personified sense in Second Temple Jewish writings such as the Dead Sea Scrolls.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Belshazzar
entries.summary: Belshazzar ruled Babylon during the exile and appears in the Bible almost entirely in one scene: the night handwriting appeared on the wall of his banquet hall in Daniel 5. Scripture calls him Nebuchadnezzar's son, though cuneiform records identify his real father as Nabonidus, Babylon's last official king, who left Belshazzar running the city for over a decade while he campaigned in Arabia. That same inscription answered a long-standing objection to the book of Daniel: critics had assumed Daniel simply had the wrong king, since ancient king lists never named Belshazzar as ruler, until the Nabonidus Cylinder confirmed he was exactly what Daniel implies, the man actually in charge when the Persians took the city.

entries.title: Belteshazzar
entries.summary: Belteshatstsar, the Babylonian name of Daniel
entries.dictNote: Belteshazzar was the Babylonian court name given to Daniel by Ashpenaz, the official in charge of the king's court servants, likely honoring the god Bel, following the common Babylonian practice of renaming foreign officials taken into royal service (Daniel 1:3, 7). The name is used throughout the book, including at Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:12) and in Daniel's later visions (Daniel 10:1).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben
entries.dictNote: Ben was a Levite appointed by David as one of the porters, or gatekeepers, for the ark of the covenant, named in the list of temple musicians and doorkeepers in 1 Chronicles 15:18. He does not reappear in the parallel list a few verses later, leading some to think his name was duplicated by accident from a neighboring word in the Hebrew text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben-ammi
entries.dictNote: Ben-ammi, whose name means "son of my people," was the son born to Lot by his younger daughter after they fled the destruction of Sodom; he became the ancestor of the Ammonites (Genesis 19:38).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben-hail
entries.dictNote: One of the officials King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent, along with priests and Levites, to teach the Book of the Law in the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 17:7-9). This teaching mission is one of the few biblical accounts of organized religious instruction outside the temple.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben-hanan
entries.dictNote: Son of Shimon, named in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben-oni
entries.summary: Ben-Oni, the original name of Benjamin
entries.dictNote: Ben-oni, meaning "son of my sorrow," was the name Rachel gave her second son with her dying breath after a difficult childbirth near Bethlehem. Jacob renamed the boy Benjamin, "son of the right hand," and he became the ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin (Genesis 35:16-18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ben-zoketh
entries.dictNote: Ben-zoketh was a Judahite, one of the sons of Ishi listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:20. The verse groups him with Zoheth, Jezoah, and other descendants in a brief, otherwise unexplained genealogical note. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Benaiah
entries.summary: Benajah, the name of twelve Israelites
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Benaiah commanded David's personal bodyguard and was famous even before that role for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day and defeating an Egyptian giant by wrestling away the giant's own spear and killing him with it. He stayed loyal to Solomon during Adonijah's attempted coup and personally executed both Joab and Adonijah on Solomon's orders afterward, and Solomon rewarded him by making him commander of the entire army in Joab's place.

entries.dictNote: Bene-barak, a town allotted to the tribe of Dan in the coastal plain (Josh. 19:45). The King James Version spells it Beneberak, and it is identified with modern Bnei Brak near Tel Aviv-Jaffa, a name still in use today.

entries.title: Bene-jaakan
entries.summary: Bene-Jaakan, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Bene-jaakan, sons of Jaakan, was a wilderness station on Israel's route, also called Beeroth Bene-jaakan, wells of the sons of Jaakan (Num. 33:31-32; Deut. 10:6). The name likely derives from a clan descended from Jaakan, a Horite chief listed in Edom's genealogy (Gen. 36:27), whose territory the wells belonged to.

entries.dictNote: Berites appear only once, among the groups Joab passed through while chasing the rebel Sheba son of Bichri to Abel of Beth-maachah. The name's exact identity is uncertain; some take it as a corrupted form of Bichrites, followers of Sheba's own clan, rather than a separate people.

entries.title: Berith
entries.dictNote: Berith, meaning "covenant," is not a person but a Canaanite deity worshipped at Shechem; Judges 9:46 refers to "the house of El-berith," the god's temple stronghold where the citizens of Shechem took refuge before Abimelech burned it down. This deity appears to be the same one called Baal-berith earlier in the same narrative (Judges 8:33; 9:4).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Berodach-baladan
entries.dictNote: Berodach-baladan is a variant spelling of Merodach-baladan, the Chaldean king who twice seized the throne of Babylon from Assyrian control in the late eighth century BC. In 2 Kings 20:12 he sends envoys to Hezekiah, officially to congratulate him on recovering from illness but likely also to explore an alliance against their common enemy Assyria, a mission Hezekiah answered by foolishly showing off his treasuries (2 Kings 20:13-15). Merodach-baladan is well attested outside the Bible, named repeatedly in the inscriptions of Sargon II and Sennacherib as the rebellious Chaldean prince they fought to dislodge from Babylon.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Berothah
entries.summary: Berothah or Berothai, a place north of Palestine
entries.dictNote: Berothah, called Berothai in Samuel, was a town belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, from which David took a great quantity of bronze after defeating him (2 Sam. 8:8). Ezekiel later names it, alongside Hamath and Damascus, as a marker on the northern boundary of the land in his vision of Israel's restoration (Ezek. 47:16). It probably lay between Damascus and Hamath, and should not be confused with the coastal city of Beirut, which some have wrongly equated with it.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Berothite
entries.summary: a Berothite, or inhabitant of Berothai
entries.dictNote: Berothite identifies Naharai, Joab's armor-bearer and one of David's mighty men, as being from Beeroth, a Gibeonite city allotted to Benjamin. The parallel account in 2 Samuel spells the same epithet Beerothite.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Besai
entries.dictNote: Besai's descendants were among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:49; Nehemiah 7:52).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Besodeiah
entries.dictNote: Besodeiah was the father of one of the men who repaired the old gate of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Besor
entries.dictNote: The Besor was a brook in southern Judah where two hundred of David's exhausted men stayed behind while the rest pursued Amalekite raiders, and David's insistence afterward that those who stayed with the supplies share equally in the plunder became a standing rule in Israel.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Betah
entries.dictNote: Betah was a city belonging to Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, that David plundered for a large quantity of bronze after defeating Hadadezer's forces (2 Sam. 8:8). The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 18:8 calls the same city Tibhath, and its bronze reportedly went toward furnishings Solomon later made for the Temple.

witness.excerpt: Now as for the king of the Hebrews, he was assisted by God, who gave him great success in his wars, and he made all expedition against the best cities of Hadadezer, Betah and Machen; so he took them by force, and laid them waste.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beten
entries.dictNote: A town on the border of the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:25). Its location has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-anath
entries.dictNote: Beth-anath was a fortified town assigned to Naphtali whose Canaanite inhabitants the tribe failed to drive out, reducing them instead to forced labor (Joshua 19:38; Judges 1:33). Its name, house of Anath, honors the Canaanite goddess Anath, and the site is usually identified with a village west of Kedesh in Upper Galilee.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beth-anoth
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:59), generally identified with the modern village of Beit Ainun northeast of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-arabah
entries.dictNote: Beth-arabah, house of the desert plain, was a small town in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea, listed on the border between Judah and Benjamin. Joshua 15:61 places it among the towns of Judah in the wilderness district, while Joshua 18:22 lists it under Benjamin, suggesting it sat right on the tribal boundary. It is also called simply Arabah in Joshua 18:18.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-aram
entries.summary: Beth-ha-Ram, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beth-aram was a town of Gad east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, probably the same as Beth-haran in Numbers 32:36 (Joshua 13:27). Herod Antipas later rebuilt and renamed it Livias, in honor of the Roman empress Livia, wife of Augustus, a renaming recorded by the first-century historian Josephus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-Arbel
entries.dictNote: A town alluded to in Hosea 10:14 as the site of a brutal military destruction, "as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle," where mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children. "Shalman" is generally taken as a shortened form of Shalmaneser, likely the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V. Many identify the town with Arbela in Galilee, near cliffs riddled with caves that Josephus later described as a refuge and a site of violent conflict.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-aven
entries.dictNote: Beth-aven, "house of vanity," was a place in the hill country of Benjamin near Ai and Bethel, used as a boundary marker in the conquest narrative (Joshua 7:2; 18:12) and as the staging ground for Israelite forces before Jonathan's raid on the Philistine garrison at Michmash (1 Samuel 13:5; 14:23). Hosea later applies the name mockingly to Bethel itself, turning its old meaning, "house of God," into "house of idols" to condemn the golden calf shrine Jeroboam had set up there (Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Beth-baal-meon
entries.dictNote: Beth-baal-meon lay east of the Jordan on the tableland allotted to Reuben, and appears under several related forms in the text, Baal-meon and Beon among them (Josh. 13:17; Num. 32:38). It later passed into Moabite hands, and Jeremiah names it among the Moabite towns facing judgment (Jer. 48:23). The site is usually located at Ma'in, a ruin a few miles southwest of Madaba whose name still echoes the ancient one.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beth-barah
entries.dictNote: Beth-barah, "house of the crossing," marked a ford of the Jordan that Gideon's messengers seized ahead of the fleeing Midianites, cutting off their escape and allowing the men of Ephraim to capture and kill the Midianite commanders Oreb and Zeeb there (Judges 7:24-25). Because the name simply means "the crossing place," it may not be a proper town at all but a ford identified by its function. Its exact location along the river is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-car
entries.dictNote: Beth-car, a point west of Mizpah to which Israel pursued the fleeing Philistines after Samuel's victory, the same battle after which the stone Ebenezer was set up (1 Sam. 7:10-12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-dagon
entries.summary: Beth-Dagon, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Beth-dagon, meaning “house of Dagon,” names two separate towns rather than a person: one in the lowland plain of Judah near Philistine territory (Joshua 15:41), identified with modern Beit Dajan near Lydda, and another on the southeastern border of Asher (Joshua 19:27). Both names preserve the memory of shrines to Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines, whose worship is also recorded at Ashdod in the account of the captured ark of the covenant (1 Samuel 5:1-5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-diblathaim
entries.summary: Beth-Diblathajim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beth-diblathaim, a town of Moab condemned in Jeremiah's oracle against that nation (Jer. 48:22). It is called Almon-diblathaim among Israel's wilderness stations in Numbers 33:46 and Diblah in Ezekiel 6:14; its name, "house of the double fig cake," points to fertile farmland on Moab's tableland.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-eden
entries.dictNote: Beth-eden, "house of pleasure," appears in Amos's oracle against Damascus, where the prophet announces that the Lord will cut off the ruler holding its scepter (Amos 1:5). It is generally identified with Bit-Adini, an Aramean kingdom on the middle Euphrates that Assyrian records describe Shalmaneser III conquering in the ninth century BC, a campaign recorded in that king's own annals. Amos's oracle, written well after that conquest, uses the kingdom's fall as a byword for Damascus's own coming judgment.

photo.description: panorama of a plain in Beth-eden

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-el
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Bethel was a town about ten miles north of Jerusalem, originally the Canaanite city of Luz, where Abram built an altar and where Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, naming the place “house of God.” It served as a religious center through the period of the judges, housing the ark for a time, and later became one of two sites where Jeroboam I set up golden calves for the northern kingdom's worship, drawing Hosea's mocking renaming of it “Beth-aven,” house of idols. Josiah destroyed its altar during his reforms, and the site is generally identified with the ruins of Beitin. The same name is also applied to a nearby hill district and to a separate town in southern Judah.
entries.label: 14 books

entries.title: Beth-emek
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Asher, near the ravine of Jiphthah-el (Joshua 19:27). Its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-ezel
entries.dictNote: Beth-ezel, a town in the Shephelah of Judah named in Micah's lament over towns facing the Assyrian invasion of Sennacherib's campaign (Mic. 1:11). Its neighboring towns in the same oracle, Lachish and Moresheth-gath, confirm a location near the Philistine border, though the exact site of Beth-ezel is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-gader
entries.dictNote: Beth-gader ("house of the wall") appears in the genealogy of Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:51, listed as though it were a descendant of Hareph. As with several other names in this same list, it almost certainly denotes a town founded or settled by the clan rather than an individual person, a common feature of Chronicles' tribal genealogies. Its location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-gamul
entries.summary: Beth-Gamul, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beth-gamul, a town of Moab condemned in Jeremiah's oracle against that nation (Jer. 48:23), likely to be identified with a ruin east of Dibon on the Moabite plateau.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-gilgal
entries.dictNote: Beth-gilgal, house of Gilgal, is named as home to a group of singers who gathered for the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Neh. 12:29), probably referring to the same Gilgal near Jericho where Israel first camped after crossing the Jordan.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beth-haccerem
entries.dictNote: "House of the vineyard," a Judean town whose ruler, Malchiah, helped repair a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:14), and which Jeremiah names as a place to raise a signal fire warning of invasion from the north (Jeremiah 6:1). Many archaeologists identify it with Ramat Rahel, a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem where excavations have uncovered a substantial fortified Judean royal compound from the Iron Age, along with stamped storage-jar handles used in the kingdom's royal administration.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-haran
entries.summary: Beth-ha-Ran, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: A town east of the Jordan rebuilt and fortified by the tribe of Gad after the conquest, in the plains of Moab (Num. 32:36). It is generally identified with Beth-haram of Joshua 13:27, later refounded by Herod Antipas as Livias, named for the wife of Augustus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-hoglah
entries.dictNote: Beth-hoglah, house of the partridge, was a town on the border between Judah and Benjamin near the Jordan and the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:6; 18:19, 21). It is usually identified with Ain Hajlah, a spring a few miles southeast of Jericho where a similar name has survived into modern times.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-horon
entries.summary: Beth-Choron, the name of two adjoining places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Beth-horon was twin towns on a strategic pass connecting the coastal plain to the hill country, the route Joshua's army used chasing the defeated Canaanite coalition during the battle where the sun stood still.

Moreover, he built two other cities not far from it, Beth-horon was the name of one of them, and Baalath of the other.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Beth-jeshimoth
entries.summary: Beth-ha-Jeshimoth, a town East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beth-jeshimoth was a town on the plains of Moab where Israel camped before crossing the Jordan into the promised land.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Beth-lebaoth
entries.dictNote: A town in the territory allotted to Simeon within Judah, in the Negev (Joshua 19:6). It appears as simply Lebaoth in Joshua 15:32 and as Beth-birei in 1 Chronicles 4:31, three spellings for what is generally taken to be the same town.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-maachah
entries.dictNote: Beth-maachah appears in the account of Sheba's revolt against David, where the rebel fled north and was besieged inside the city until its residents threw his head over the wall to end the siege, on the advice of a wise woman from the town (2 Samuel 20:14-22). It was closely associated with, and possibly identical to, the small Aramean kingdom of Maachah on Israel's northern frontier, later absorbed along with Abel-beth-maachah into Assyrian territory under Tiglath-pileser III, an annexation recorded in that king's own inscriptions (2 Kings 15:29).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-Nimrah
entries.summary: Beth-Nimrah, a place east of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Fortified town east of the Jordan in the plain opposite Jericho, rebuilt by the tribe of Gad after they requested the well-watered lands of Gilead for their livestock (Num. 32:36; Josh. 13:27). Its name, meaning "house of clear water" or "house of leopards," survives in the nearby Wadi Nimrin.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beth-palet
entries.dictNote: Beth-palet, meaning house of flight, was a town in the extreme south of Judah's territory, in the district bordering Edom (Josh. 15:27). It reappears after the exile, spelled Beth-phelet, as one of the settlements resettled by the people of Judah when they returned to the land (Neh. 11:26). Its exact site has not been securely identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Beth-pazzez
entries.dictNote: Beth-pazzez was a town of the tribe of Issachar, listed alongside En-haddah in Joshua's territorial allotment (Joshua 19:21). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-rapha
entries.dictNote: A name in the genealogy of Judah, listed as a son of Eshton in the line descended from Chelub (1 Chronicles 4:12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-rehob
entries.dictNote: Beth-rehob was a small Aramean kingdom in the north of Israel's territory, near the valley where the Danites later resettled and renamed the conquered city of Laish as Dan (Judges 18:28). It also supplied mercenaries to the Ammonite coalition that fought David in 2 Samuel 10:6. It is often identified with the site of modern Hunin, in the hills north of the Huleh valley.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-shean
entries.summary: Beth-Shean or Beth-Shan, a place in Palestine
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Beth-shean was a Canaanite city belonging to Manasseh's territory at the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys; after Saul's death in battle on nearby Gilboa, the Philistines hung his body and his sons' bodies on its walls until the men of Jabesh-gilead recovered them by night. Excavations at Tel Beth-shean uncovered an Egyptian garrison town from the New Kingdom period, including monumental stelae of pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II describing campaigns to relieve the city, confirming Egypt's direct control over the site centuries before Saul's reign.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Beth-shemesh
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” was most notably a Levitical city on Judah's northern border where the ark rested and was welcomed with sacrifice after the Philistines returned it, following an incident in which curious residents were struck down for looking into it. It was later the site of a battle in which Judah's king Amaziah was captured by Israel's king Jehoash. Excavations at Tel Beth-Shemesh have uncovered a fortified Iron Age town with evidence of both Israelite and Philistine material culture, consistent with its position on the contested border between the two. Two smaller places bore the same name elsewhere in Israel, and a fourth, an Egyptian sun-temple city the Greeks called Heliopolis, appears in Jeremiah's prophecy against Egypt.
entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Beth-shittah
entries.dictNote: Beth-shittah, meaning house of the acacia, was one of the towns toward which the routed Midianite army fled after Gideon's night attack scattered their camp (Judg. 7:22). It lay somewhere in the Jordan valley near Beth-shean, on the flight route that continued toward Abel-meholah, though its exact site is not fixed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-tappuah
entries.dictNote: A hill-country town of Judah whose name means house of apples (Josh. 15:53). It survives as the Palestinian village of Taffuh, about five miles west of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Beth-zur
entries.dictNote: Beth-zur was a fortified town in the hill country of Judah, a few miles north of Hebron, that Rehoboam strengthened as part of a defensive network protecting his kingdom after the ten northern tribes seceded (2 Chronicles 11:7). It later became a key strategic site in the Maccabean wars against the Seleucids. Excavations at the site, Khirbet et-Tubeiqa, conducted by William Albright and Ovid Sellers in the 1930s, uncovered occupation layers running from the Middle Bronze Age through the Hellenistic period, confirming the town's long strategic importance guarding the road from Hebron to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bethany
entries.summary: date-house; Beth-any, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Gospels use this name for two different places. The better known is a village on the southeastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem, home to Lazarus, Mary, and Martha; Jesus stayed there in his final week, raised Lazarus from the dead nearby, and it was near here that he ascended into heaven. A separate Bethany "beyond the Jordan" was the location where John the Baptist was baptizing when he first pointed his disciples to Jesus as the Lamb of God.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bethaz-maveth
entries.summary: house of Azmaveth, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Beth-azmaveth, meaning house of Azmaveth, was a town near Jerusalem whose residents are counted among those returning from the Babylonian exile in Nehemiah's list (Neh. 7:28). The parallel list in Ezra 2:24 gives the shorter form Azmaveth for the same place, generally located near Anathoth just north of Jerusalem.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bethbirei
entries.dictNote: Beth-birei was a town of the tribe of Simeon in the far south of Judah's territory, appearing in the genealogical town-list of 1 Chronicles 4:31. The parallel list in Joshua 19:6 gives the same town as Beth-lebaoth, "house of lionesses," suggesting the name simply shifted between the two records. Its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bethelite
entries.summary: a Beth-elite, or inhabitant of Bethel
entries.dictNote: Bethelite marks Hiel, who rebuilt Jericho in the days of King Ahab, as a native of Bethel. He lost his firstborn and youngest sons in the process, fulfilling the curse Joshua had pronounced on anyone who rebuilt the city centuries earlier.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bether
entries.dictNote: The mountains of Bether appear in a poetic refrain in the Song of Solomon, most likely describing rugged, cleft hills rather than naming one specific location (Song of Sol. 2:17). Some associate the name with the village of Bittir west of Jerusalem, later the site of the fortress Betar where the Bar Kokhba revolt made its last stand against Rome in 135 AD, though given the poem's imagery that link is far from certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bethesda
entries.summary: house of kindness; Beth-esda, a pool in Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a pool in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate, surrounded by five covered porches, where John 5:2 sets the healing of a man who had been unable to walk for thirty-eight years. Archaeologists excavating near St. Anne's Church in Jerusalem uncovered a twin pool with five porticoes matching John's description, confirming the site's existence and location.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bethlehem
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Micah, Matthew, Luke, John
entries.dictNote: Bethlehem, “house of bread,” is a small town about five miles south of Jerusalem, earlier called Ephrath, where Rachel died and was buried and where Ruth gleaned in Boaz's fields. It was David's birthplace and the site of his anointing by Samuel, but it is remembered above all as the birthplace of Jesus, foretold in Micah and fulfilled under Herod, whose massacre of the town's young children followed. A church built by Constantine over the traditional birth cave still stands, among the oldest continuously used churches in the world. A separate, minor Bethlehem existed in the territory of Zebulun. A clay seal impression reading “Bethlehem” in ancient Hebrew script, found in Jerusalem's City of David excavations and dated to the seventh century BC, is the earliest known extra-biblical reference to the town.

entries.label: 15 books

entries.title: Bethlehemite
entries.summary: a Beth-lechemite, or native of Bethlechem
entries.dictNote: A Bethlehemite is simply someone from Bethlehem, the title Scripture gives Jesse and his son David before either man needed a longer introduction. The same word later marks Elhanan, the soldier credited in 2 Samuel 21 with killing a giant named Goliath, distinct from the more famous duel in 1 Samuel 17.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bethmarcaboth
entries.summary: Beth-ham-Markaboth or Beth-Markaboth, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Beth-marcaboth, house of the chariots, was a town of Simeon in the far south of Judah (Joshua 19:5; 1 Chronicles 4:31). In the parallel list of Judah's towns in Joshua 15:31, Madmannah appears in its place, suggesting the same site carried both names or that the two lists simply diverged.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bethpeor
entries.summary: Beth-Peor, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Beth-peor, "house of Peor," was a place across the Jordan from Jericho, in the territory of Reuben, near the sanctuary of the god Baal-peor for which it was named (Joshua 13:20). Moses gave his final address to Israel in the valley opposite Beth-peor before climbing Mount Nebo to view the promised land and die there, and he was buried in that same valley, though no one has ever known the exact location of his grave (Deuteronomy 3:29; 34:6).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bethphage
entries.summary: fig-house; Beth-phage, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Bethphage, meaning house of unripe figs, was a small village on the Mount of Olives near Bethany, on the road between Jericho and Jerusalem. It was there that Jesus sent two disciples ahead to fetch the donkey he rode into Jerusalem at the start of his triumphal entry (Matthew 21:1; Mark 11:1; Luke 19:29). Its exact site is uncertain, though tradition places it close to modern Bethany, now the West Bank town of al-Eizariya.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bethsaida
entries.summary: fishing-house; Bethsaida, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Bethsaida was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, home to Peter, Andrew, and Philip (John 1:44), and the target of Jesus's sharpest rebuke among the unrepentant Galilean towns (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13). Archaeologists have long debated its exact location between two mounds, et-Tell and el-Araj; recent excavations at el-Araj, closer to the ancient shoreline, have uncovered a Roman bathhouse, an early church, and first-century remains that many scholars now think settle the question in its favor.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bethshemite
entries.summary: a Beth-shimshite, or inhabitant of Bethshemesh
entries.dictNote: Bethshemite designates an inhabitant of Beth-shemesh, a town in Judah's territory near the Philistine border. After the Philistines returned the captured ark of the covenant on a cart, it came to rest in a Bethshemite's field, where the townspeople offered sacrifices before several of them were struck down for looking inside it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bethuel
entries.summary: Bethuel, the name of a nephew of Abraham, and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Bethuel was the son of Nahor and Milcah, Abraham's nephew, and father of Laban and Rebekah; he appears in person only once, giving his consent when Abraham's servant asked for Rebekah as a wife for Isaac. A separate town in the Negev called Bethuel, also known as Bethul or Bethel, was assigned to Simeon within Judah's territory.

entries.title: Bethuel
entries.summary: Bethul (i.e. Bethuel), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: This Bethuel was a town in the southern territory of Simeon, called Bethul in Joshua 19:4 and Bethel in 1 Samuel 30:27, not the more famous Bethel near Jerusalem. It shares its name with, but is unrelated to, the Aramean Bethuel who was the father of Rebekah and grandfather of Jacob and Esau.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Betonim
entries.dictNote: Betonim was a town on the northern boundary of Gad's territory east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:26). Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bezai
entries.summary: Betsai, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bezai was the head of a family among the returning exiles, listed among those who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bezaleel
entries.summary: Betsalel, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bezalel was the chief craftsman God specifically named and filled with his Spirit to design and build the tabernacle and its furnishings, including the ark of the covenant, the first person in the Bible described as being filled with the Spirit for a task of skilled craftsmanship.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Bezek
entries.dictNote: Two places share this name. The first, near Jerusalem in Judah's territory, was where Judah and Simeon defeated the Canaanite king Adoni-bezek and cut off his thumbs and big toes, the same mutilation he admitted inflicting on seventy captured kings before him (Judges 1:4-7). The second, farther north near the Jordan valley, is where Saul mustered Israel's forces before marching to relieve Jabesh-gilead from an Ammonite siege (1 Sam. 11:8).

witness.excerpt: But the affairs of the Canaanites were at this time in a flourishing condition; and they expected the Israelites with a great army at the city Bezek: having put the government into the hands of Adonibezek: which name denotes the Lord of Bezek : for Adoni in the Hebrew tongue is called Lord .
And the multitude were numbered at the city Bezek.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bezer
entries.summary: Betser, a place in Palestine; also an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Bezer was a city of refuge for the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan, one of three such cities on that side designated for anyone who killed a person accidentally, so they could flee there for protection (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). The name also belongs to a descendant of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:37); the city's exact site remains uncertain, with proposed locations on the plateau north of the Arnon.

witness.excerpt: Now the cities which were set apart for this flight were these: Bezer , at the borders of Arabia; Ramoth , of the land of Gilead; and Golan , in the land of Bashan.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bichri
entries.dictNote: Bichri was the father of Sheba, the Benjamite who led a brief rebellion against David shortly after Absalom's revolt was crushed.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bidkar
entries.dictNote: An officer of Jehu who had served alongside him as a chariot officer under Ahab. After Jehu killed King Jehoram of Israel, he ordered Bidkar to throw the body into the field that had belonged to Naboth, fulfilling the judgment Elijah had pronounced on Ahab's dynasty (2 Kings 9:25-26).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bigtha
entries.dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs of the Persian king Ahasuerus's court sent to summon Queen Vashti to his banquet, a command she refused (Esther 1:10-12). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bigthan
entries.summary: Bigthan or Bigthana, a eunuch of Xerxes
entries.dictNote: Bigthan, also spelled Bigthana, was one of two eunuchs who guarded the entrance to King Ahasuerus's chambers and conspired with a colleague, Teresh, to assassinate the king. Mordecai uncovered the plot and reported it, leading to the conspirators' execution by hanging, an act recorded in the palace chronicles that later proved crucial to Mordecai's own fortunes (Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).

witness.excerpt: Some time after this [two eunuchs] Bigthan and Teresh plotted against the King; and Barnabazus, the servant of one of the eunuchs, being by birth a Jew, was acquainted with their conspiracy, and discovered it to the Queen’s uncle.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bigvai
entries.dictNote: Bigvai was the head of a family among the returning exiles, listed among those who came back with Zerubbabel and later signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bildad
entries.dictNote: Bildad was the second of Job's three friends to speak, a Shuhite whose arguments, like his companions', insisted that Job's suffering must be the result of hidden sin, a position God later rebukes for not speaking rightly about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bilgah
entries.summary: Bilgah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bilgah was the head of one of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized for rotating temple service, and his family name reappears among the priests who returned from Babylonian exile.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bilgai
entries.dictNote: Bilgai is a variant of the name Bilgah, a priest who set his seal to the covenant renewed under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 10:8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bilhah
entries.summary: Bilhah, the name of one of Jacob's concubines; also of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Bilhah was Rachel's maidservant, given to her by her father Laban, whom Rachel in turn gave to Jacob as a wife when she herself remained childless. Bilhah bore Jacob two sons, Dan and Naphtali, who became tribal ancestors of Israel. Reuben's affair with Bilhah after Rachel's death cost him his birthright as firstborn, which passed instead to the sons of Joseph.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bilhan
entries.summary: Bilhan, the name of an Edomite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Bilhan was a Horite clan chief in Edom's genealogies, and also the name of a descendant of Benjamin listed separately in Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bilshan
entries.dictNote: Bilshan was one of the leaders who returned to Judah from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:2; Nehemiah 7:7). His name, meaning roughly “eloquent” or “man of the tongue,” suggests he may have served as a spokesman for the returning community, though nothing further is recorded of his role.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bimhal
entries.dictNote: Bimhal was one of the sons of Japhlet, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:33. He appears only in this genealogical record.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Binea
entries.dictNote: Binea was a descendant of King Saul through the line of Jonathan and Mephibosheth, preserved in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:37; 9:43).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Binnui
entries.dictNote: Binnui was a common Levitical name among those who helped rebuild Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah and among those confronted for foreign marriages under Ezra.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Birsha
entries.dictNote: King of Gomorrah at the time Chedorlaomer's coalition invaded the cities of the plain, named alongside Bera of Sodom in Genesis 14:2 as one of the five kings who rebelled against Chedorlaomer's overlordship and were defeated.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Birzavith (from the marg.)
entries.dictNote: Appears in the genealogy of Asher as a descendant of Malchiel; some translations treat the underlying Hebrew as a place name rather than a person's name, and the identification remains uncertain (1 Chronicles 7:31).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bishlam
entries.dictNote: A Persian official in Samaria named among those who wrote to King Artaxerxes opposing the Jews' rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7). Some scholars think the Aramaic word behind this name may not be a personal name at all but a phrase meaning "in peace," leaving his exact identity uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bithiah
entries.dictNote: Bithiah was the daughter of an unnamed Pharaoh who became the wife of Mered, a man of Judah, according to 1 Chronicles 4:18. Her name, meaning 'daughter of the LORD,' suggests she was regarded as a convert to Israel's faith. Jewish tradition sometimes identifies her with the Egyptian princess who rescued the infant Moses, though the Bible itself does not make that connection.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bithron
entries.summary: Bithron, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Bithron was a district or ravine in the Jordan Valley on the eastern side of the river, through which Abner and his men marched by night on their retreat to Mahanaim after Asahel was killed while pursuing Abner (2 Samuel 2:29). Its exact boundaries and location are unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bithynia
entries.dictNote: Bithynia was a Roman province on the southern shore of the Black Sea where Paul attempted to go but was prevented by the Spirit (Acts 16:7), and where a Christian community had taken root by the time Peter addressed his first letter to believers scattered across the region (1 Peter 1:1). Bithynia's Christian population is independently confirmed a generation or two later by the governor Pliny the Younger's letter to Trajan, in which he describes interrogating believers there and asks the emperor how to handle prosecutions for the name alone.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bizjothjah
entries.dictNote: A town in the Negev of Judah, listed near Beersheba among the towns allotted to Judah's tribe (Josh. 15:28).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Biztha
entries.dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs who served in the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, likely Xerxes I, sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's banquet, a summons she refused (Esther 1:10-12). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Blastus
entries.summary: Blastus, an officer of Herod Agrippa
entries.dictNote: Blastus was the personal chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa I, whom the people of Tyre and Sidon persuaded to help reconcile them with the angry king (Acts 12:20).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Boanerges
entries.summary: sons of commotion; Boanerges, an epithet of two of the apostles
entries.dictNote: Boanerges, meaning sons of thunder, is not an individual but a nickname Jesus gave jointly to the brothers James and John (Mark 3:17). The name reflects their fervent and sometimes impetuous temperament, seen when they wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that rejected Jesus (Luke 9:54).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Boaz
entries.summary: Boaz, the ancestor of David; also the name of a pillar in front of the temple
entries.dictNote: Boaz was a wealthy landowner in Bethlehem and a relative of Naomi's late husband Elimelech, and he first noticed the widowed Moabite Ruth gleaning grain behind his harvesters. He agreed to exercise the right of a kinsman-redeemer, marrying Ruth and buying back her deceased husband's property after a closer relative declined the responsibility, and their son Obed became the grandfather of David. Boaz also became the name given to one of the two bronze pillars Solomon set up at the entrance of the temple.

entries.summary: David's great-grandfather, one line in Luke's genealogy (3:32). Josephus retells the whole Book of Ruth as its own episode (spelling the name 'Booz'), explicitly naming the payoff Luke's genealogy is really built toward: the line running straight to David.

The name given (for what reason is unknown) to one of the two (the other was called Jachin) brazen pillars which Solomon erected in the court of the temple (1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chr. 3:17). These pillars were broken up and carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bocheru
entries.dictNote: Bocheru was a son of Azel, a descendant of King Saul through Jonathan's line, listed in the genealogies of Benjamin preserved in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:38; 9:44).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bochim
entries.dictNote: Unidentified site, likely near Bethel or Shiloh, where the angel of the Lord confronted Israel for making treaties with the Canaanites in defiance of God's command. The people wept bitterly at the rebuke, which gave the place its name, meaning "weepers," and offered sacrifices there (Judges 2:1-5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bohan
entries.dictNote: Bohan was a Reubenite whose name was given to a boundary stone, "the stone of Bohan," marking part of the border between the territories of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:6; 18:17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bosor
entries.dictNote: Bosor is the Greek transliteration of Beor, the father of the prophet Balaam, and appears only in 2 Peter 2:15, where Balaam is called the son of Bosor. Numbers 22:5 gives the more familiar Hebrew form of the same name, Beor. The variant spelling likely reflects a regional Aramaic pronunciation.

witness.excerpt: To this exhortation Judas hearkened, and returned to the wilderness; and in the first place fell upon the inhabitants of Bosor, and took the city, and beat the inhabitants, and destroyed all the males, and all that were able to fight, and burnt the city.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bozcath
entries.dictNote: Bozcath was a town in the Shephelah of Judah, listed among the cities near Lachish and Eglon (Josh. 15:39). It is remembered chiefly as the hometown of Adaiah, whose daughter Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah, noted in the record of Josiah's accession (2 Kings 22:1).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Bozez
entries.dictNote: Bozez was not a person but one of two rocky crags, the other named Seneh, that flanked the narrow pass through which Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed to surprise the Philistine garrison at Michmash (1 Sam. 14:4-5). The steep terrain around Michmash still matches the description in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bozrah
entries.dictNote: Bozrah was the capital of Edom, the city of the early Edomite king Jobab, and became a favorite target of prophetic oracles against Edom for its treatment of Israel and Judah. Isaiah pictures the Lord coming from Bozrah with garments stained red from judgment on Edom. Excavations at Buseirah in Jordan, which preserves the ancient name, have uncovered a fortified Iron Age citadel with monumental buildings, confirming its role as Edom's political center. A different town also called Bozrah lay in the plains of Moab.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Bozrah
entries.dictNote: In Micah's oracle of restoration, the remnant of Israel is pictured gathered together like sheep, and the text reads literally "as the sheep of Bozrah" (Micah 2:12). Interpreters differ over whether this points to the famous Edomite city of Bozrah and its pastures, described in the separate place record for Bozrah, or whether the Hebrew word functions here as a common noun for a sheepfold rather than a proper name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bukki
entries.summary: Bukki, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Bukki was a common name, borne by a leader from the tribe of Dan who helped divide the conquered land and by a priest in the high priestly genealogy connecting Aaron to Zadok.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Bukkiah
entries.dictNote: Bukkiah was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman, and headed one of the divisions of temple musicians organized under David (1 Chronicles 25:4, 13).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bul
entries.dictNote: Bul was not a person but the name of the eighth month of the ancient Israelite calendar, corresponding roughly to October-November, in which Solomon completed construction of the temple (1 Kings 6:38). The name reflects a Canaanite term tied to the rainy season, and it was later replaced in common use by the Babylonian-derived name Marcheshvan after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bunah
entries.dictNote: A son of Jerahmeel, listed in the genealogy of Judah through the line of Pharez (1 Chronicles 2:25). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Bunni
entries.dictNote: Bunni was a common Levitical name among those who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal and helped lead worship after the law was read publicly.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Buz
entries.summary: Buz, the name of a son of Nahor, and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Buz's name means “contempt” or “scorn.” The first Buz was the second son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and an ancestor of Elihu, one of Job's counselors (Genesis 22:21; Job 32:2). A second Buz was a leading man of the tribe of Gad (1 Chronicles 5:14). The name is also attached to a region in Arabia denounced alongside Dedan and Tema in Jeremiah's oracle against foreign nations (Jeremiah 25:23), likely named for the same family line.

witness.excerpt: Now Nahor had eight sons by Milcha; Uz, and Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Azau, Pheldas, Jadelph, and Bethuel.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Buzi
entries.dictNote: Buzi was the father of the prophet Ezekiel, who is introduced as "Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi" (Ezek. 1:3). Buzi himself was likely also a priest, since the office was hereditary in Israel, though the text does not say so directly.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Buzite
entries.summary: a Buzite or descendant of Buz
entries.dictNote: Buzite identifies Elihu, the younger man whose speeches close the dialogue in Job, as belonging to the family of Ram, of the kindred of Buz. Buz was a son of Nahor and brother of Uz, from whom Job's own homeland likely took its name, making Elihu a distant relation of Job.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cabbon
entries.dictNote: Cabbon, a lowland town of Judah in the district that included Lachish and Eglon (Josh. 15:40). It is not mentioned elsewhere and remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cabul
entries.summary: Cabul, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Cabul refers to two places, not a person. One was a town on the eastern border of Asher (Joshua 19:27). The other was the name given, apparently disparagingly, to a district of twenty towns in Galilee that Solomon ceded to King Hiram of Tyre in payment for building materials and labor; Hiram was displeased with them and called the land “Cabul,” meaning roughly “good for nothing” (1 Kings 9:10-13).

witness.excerpt: at lay not far from Tyre; which, when Hiram went to, and viewed, and did not like the gift, he sent word to Solomon that he did not want such cities as they were; and after that time these cities were called the land of Cabul; which name, if it be interpreted according to the language of the Phoenicians, denotes what does not please.

entries.title: Caesar
entries.summary: Cæsar, a title of the Roman emperor
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Philippians
entries.dictNote: Caesar is used throughout the New Testament as the standard title for the reigning Roman emperor rather than one specific man, covering at least Augustus, under whom Jesus was born, and Tiberius, during whose reign Jesus was crucified. Jesus's famous instruction to render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's was a direct response to a politically loaded question about paying imperial taxes.

entries.title: Caiaphas
entries.summary: The sitting high priest at 3:2, named in the same breath as Annas. Josephus's list of rapid Roman-appointed replacements just before him — three high priests in as many years — makes Caiaphas's own unusually long eighteen-year tenure (not stated in this excerpt, but well attested) look like the exception, not the rule.
entries.dictNote: Caiaphas was the Jewish high priest who presided over the council that condemned Jesus, arguing beforehand that it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to suffer, words John's Gospel treats as an unwitting prophecy of what Jesus's death would actually accomplish. He held the high priesthood for eighteen years under Roman oversight, an unusually long tenure that suggests he was skilled at managing the delicate relationship between Jewish religious life and Roman power. An ornate limestone ossuary discovered south of Jerusalem in 1990, inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas, is widely believed to be his family burial box.

entries.title: Calah
entries.dictNote: Calah was one of the ancient cities Nimrod is said to have built in Assyria, along with Nineveh and Resen (Genesis 10:11-12). It is identified with Nimrud, on the east bank of the Tigris south of Mosul, which Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt as his royal capital in the ninth century BC, complete with palaces, temples, and a garden watered by canal from the Great Zab. British and Iraqi excavations there since the 1840s, most extensively under Max Mallowan in the 1950s, uncovered colossal winged bulls, palace reliefs, and a rich hoard of carved ivories that now count among the finest surviving examples of Assyrian art.

entries.dictNote: Caleb was one of twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, and along with Joshua he was the only one who returned urging Israel to trust God and take the land, a minority report that cost the rest of that generation forty years of wandering as punishment for their fear. entries.summary: a Kenaanite or inhabitant of Kenaan; by implication, a pedlar (the Canaanites standing for their neighbors the Ishmaelites, who conducted mercantile caravans)
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Ezra, Nehemiah, Job, Proverbs, Ezekiel, Obadiah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Canaanites were the inhabitants of the land promised to Israel, descended in the biblical genealogy from Canaan, son of Ham, and the Old Testament repeatedly commands their displacement because of practices like idol worship and child sacrifice associated with them. The term also became attached to the apostle Simon, called "the Canaanite" in Matthew and Mark, though this actually transliterates an Aramaic word for "zealot" rather than marking Canaanite ancestry; Luke's Gospel calls him Simon the Zealot instead. Canaanite religion and culture are well documented outside the Bible through the Ugaritic tablets found at Ras Shamra in Syria, which describe the god Baal and the goddess Asherah, both named elsewhere in the Old Testament as objects of Israelite idolatry. The Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian inscription from about 1208 BC, is the earliest known text to mention Canaan by name.

entries.title: Canan
entries.summary: Chanan, the name of seven Israelites
entries.dictNote: This entry's Hebrew form is a variant rendering of Hanan, a common Old Testament name borne by several minor Levites and postexilic officials.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Candace
entries.dictNote: A hereditary title, not a personal name, carried by the ruling queens of the Kushite kingdom centered at Meroe in Nubia, comparable to "Pharaoh" for Egypt's kings. The treasury official of one such queen was converted and baptized by Philip on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:27). The power of these Kushite queens is corroborated outside the Bible: Roman sources describe a war between Rome and a Kushite army led by one of them around 24 BC, and archaeologists later recovered a bronze head of Augustus that Kushite forces had looted and buried beneath the steps of a Meroe temple as an act of triumph, now held in the British Museum.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Canneh
entries.dictNote: Canneh appears only once, in Ezekiel's list of Tyre's trading partners, grouped with Haran and Eden in the region of upper Mesopotamia and northern Syria (Ezek. 27:23). It is generally taken as the same place as Calno or Calneh, likely to be identified with Kullani, a north Syrian city named in Assyrian annals as conquered by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Capernaum
entries.summary: Capernaum (i.e. Caphanachum), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee that Jesus made his base of operations after leaving Nazareth, calling it “his own city.” Several of his best known miracles and teachings took place there, including the healing of a centurion's servant and the bread of life discourse in its synagogue, yet Jesus also pronounced judgment on the town for its unbelief. The site, Tell Hum, has been excavated to reveal a limestone synagogue built over the basalt foundations of an earlier first century structure, along with an octagonal Byzantine church built over a house identified by ancient graffiti as Peter's, matching the Gospels' description of Jesus staying at Peter's house there.

entries.title: Caphtor
entries.summary: Caphtor (i.e. a wreath-shaped island), the original seat of the Philistines
entries.dictNote: Caphtor is identified in the Old Testament as the original homeland of the Philistines before they migrated to Canaan's coastal plain, generally understood to be Crete or a nearby Aegean region.

entries.title: Cappadocia
entries.summary: Cappadocia, a region of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Cappadocia was a large province in eastern Asia Minor, home to Jewish pilgrims present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9) and later to one of the churches Peter addressed as scattered exiles (1 Peter 1:1). The region's connection to Mesopotamian trade networks goes back at least to the early second millennium BC, when Assyrian merchants from Ashur ran a trading colony at Kanesh, modern Kultepe, and left behind thousands of cuneiform tablets documenting their business. By the first century it was a Roman province with an active Jewish diaspora community.

entries.title: Carchemish
entries.dictNote: Major city on the west bank of the Euphrates, long a Hittite provincial capital and later the seat of an independent Neo-Hittite kingdom after the Hittite empire's collapse. Pharaoh Necho's army was crushed there by Nebuchadnezzar in 605 BC, a battle Jeremiah cites as the turning point that handed regional power to Babylon (Jer. 46:2; 2 Chr. 35:20), while Isaiah names the city among those already conquered by Assyria a century earlier (Isa. 10:9). Excavations begun in 1911 by David Hogarth and continued by Leonard Woolley, with T. E. Lawrence assisting, uncovered Hittite and Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions confirming the city's long history as recorded in the biblical text.

entries.title: Casiphia
entries.dictNote: Casiphia was a place in Babylonia, apparently a center of Jewish community life, where Ezra sent messengers to secure Levites and temple servants for the journey back to Jerusalem, since none had volunteered from among the returning exiles (Ezra 8:15-20). Its exact site is unknown, but its existence fits what cuneiform records from Babylonia itself have since confirmed: archives such as the so-called Al-Yahudu, or "Judah-town," tablets document real communities of Judean exiles and their descendants living under Persian rule, exactly the kind of Jewish settlement Ezra would have needed to draw Levites from.

entries.title: Casluhim
entries.summary: Casluchim, a people cognate to the Egyptians
entries.dictNote: Casluhim was not an individual but one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13-14; 1 Chronicles 1:11-12). Genesis names the Philistines as coming from this group, placing their origin somewhere along the eastern Nile delta or the Mediterranean coast near Egypt's border with Canaan.

John 18:1 records that Jesus crossed the Kidron with his disciples on the night of his arrest, on the way to the garden of Gethsemane. Excavations along the valley have uncovered tombs and monuments dating back to the First Temple period, confirming its long use as a boundary and burial ground for the city.

entries.label: 10 books

entries.title: Chanaan
entries.summary: Chanaan (i.e. Kenaan), the early name of Palestine
entries.dictNote: Chanaan is the King James Version's transliteration of “Canaan” as it appears in the Greek text of Acts, referring to the land promised to Abraham's descendants rather than to a person. Stephen's speech recalls God giving Israel no inheritance there before the conquest (Acts 7:11), while Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch recounts God destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan to give it to Israel (Acts 13:19).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Charran
entries.summary: Charrhan (i.e. Charan), a place in Mesopotamia
entries.dictNote: Charran is the Greek form of Haran used in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recounts that Abraham settled there with his father Terah after leaving Ur, before God called him onward to Canaan following Terah's death (Acts 7:2, 4). The city of Harran in northern Mesopotamia is well attested outside the Bible as a major trade and religious center devoted to the moon god Sin, important enough that Babylon's last king, Nabonidus, rebuilt its temple there some fifteen centuries after Abraham's time.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chebar
entries.dictNote: The Chebar was a river or canal in Babylonia, in the region where Jewish exiles including Ezekiel were settled after Jerusalem's fall. It was by the Chebar that Ezekiel received his inaugural vision of God's glory and the living creatures, and several of his later visions are likewise dated to this location. Some scholars identify it with a great irrigation canal branching off the Euphrates near Nippur, where cuneiform tablets have since documented a Jewish exile community.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chedorlaomer
entries.dictNote: Chedorlaomer was an Elamite king who led a coalition that raided Sodom and captured Lot along with the city's goods, a raid Abraham reversed with a surprise night attack that rescued Lot and recovered everything taken.

witness.excerpt: And in this year came Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and Amraphel, king of Shinar, and Arioch, king of Sêllâsar  and Têrgâl,  king of nations, and slew the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Sodom fled, and many fell through wounds in the vale of Siddim, by

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chefarhaamonai
entries.dictNote: Chefarhaamonai, one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, its name meaning "the villages of the Ammonites" (Josh. 18:24). It is listed alongside Ophni and Geba but is not mentioned again, and its site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chelal
entries.dictNote: Chelal was one of the sons of Pahath-moab who had married a foreign wife and agreed to divorce her under Ezra's reform after the return from exile (Ezra 10:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chelluh
entries.dictNote: Chelluh was one of the men of Bani who had married a foreign wife and agreed to divorce her as part of Ezra's covenant reform after the exile (Ezra 10:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chelub
entries.summary: Kelub, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Chelub is a name given to two different men in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. One was the brother of Shuhah and father of Mehir, in the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:11). The other was the father of Ezri, who oversaw the farm workers in David's administration (1 Chronicles 27:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chelubai
entries.dictNote: Son of Hezron and also called Caleb, this figure heads a branch of Judah's genealogy in Chronicles; he is a different man from the more famous Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy who entered Canaan with Joshua (1 Chronicles 2:9, 18, 42).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chemosh
entries.summary: Kemosh, the god of the Moabites
entries.dictNote: Chemosh was the national god of Moab, and Solomon's construction of a shrine to Chemosh to please one of his foreign wives is listed among the reasons God raised up adversaries against his kingdom late in his reign.

witness.excerpt: Woe unto thee, Moab, Chemosh is destroyed: their sons who had sought to escape have been given up, and their daughters have become captive to Sihon, king of the Amorites.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Chenaanah
entries.summary: Kenaanah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Chenaanah was the father of Zedekiah, a false prophet who confidently but wrongly predicted victory for King Ahab and mockingly struck the true prophet Micaiah for contradicting him.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Chenani
entries.dictNote: A Levite who stood on the stairs with several others and cried out to the LORD during the great public confession and covenant renewal described in Nehemiah 9, following the reading of the Law under Ezra. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chenaniah
entries.dictNote: Chenaniah was a Levite David placed in charge of music for the ark's procession into Jerusalem, chosen specifically for his skill.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chephirah
entries.dictNote: Chephirah was one of four Hivite towns, along with Gibeon, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim, whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a treaty of peace by disguising themselves as travelers from a distant country (Joshua 9:3-17). It fell within Benjamin's territory, and its people are later listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:25; Nehemiah 7:29). It is identified with Khirbet Kefireh, west of Jerusalem near Ajalon.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Cheran
entries.dictNote: Cheran was one of the sons of Dishon, a Horite chief listed among the clans of Seir before Edom's kings arose (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41). The Horites were the region's earlier inhabitants, later displaced or absorbed by Esau's descendants.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Cherethims
entries.books: 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezekiel, Zephaniah
entries.dictNote: The Cherethites were a group closely associated with the Philistines, likely originally from Crete, and along with the Pelethites they formed David's personal bodyguard under the command of Benaiah.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Cherith
entries.dictNote: Cherith was not a person but a ravine with a seasonal stream where the prophet Elijah hid and was fed by ravens during the early part of a three-year drought under King Ahab (1 Kings 17:2-6). Its exact location is uncertain; proposals range from the Wadi Qelt near Jericho to ravines further east in Gilead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cherub
entries.dictNote: This entry names a place in Babylonia, not the winged heavenly beings that share the same English spelling. Cherub, along with Tel-harsa and Addan, was one of the Babylonian settlements named among the returning exiles who could not prove their Israelite ancestry after the exile (Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61). Its exact location is unknown; it was apparently a community of Judean deportees living in southern Mesopotamia during the Babylonian captivity.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chesalon
entries.dictNote: Chesalon marked a point on the northern border of Judah's tribal territory, on the slope of Mount Jearim (Joshua 15:10). It is identified with the modern village of Kesla in the hill country west of Jerusalem, which preserves the ancient name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chesed
entries.dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor, listed among his descendants in Genesis 22:22. Some scholars connect his name to the Hebrew term for the Chaldeans (Kasdim), suggesting later tradition saw him as an ancestor of that people, though the text itself states only his place in Nahor's family.

witness.excerpt: Now Nahor had eight sons by Milcha; Uz, and Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Azau, Pheldas, Jadelph, and Bethuel.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chesil
entries.dictNote: A town in the Negev of Judah (Josh. 15:30), likely the same place called Bethul in Joshua 19:4 and Bethuel in 1 Chronicles 4:30, all apparently variant spellings of one settlement.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chesulloth
entries.dictNote: Chesulloth was a town of Issachar on the slopes between Jezreel and Shunem (Joshua 19:18). It is usually equated with Chisloth-tabor, named a few verses earlier on Zebulun's boundary, and identified with modern Iksal near Mount Tabor. The overlap suggests the two tribal boundaries met close to the same town.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chezib
entries.dictNote: Chezib was the town where Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife, Shelah, was born (Genesis 38:5). It is generally taken as another name for, or an early form of, Achzib, a town later listed among the Shephelah towns of Judah (Joshua 15:44) that the prophet Micah plays on for its meaning "deceitful" (Micah 1:14). Its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chidon
entries.dictNote: Chidon, the threshing floor where Uzzah touched the ark of the covenant and died as it was being carried toward Jerusalem (1 Chr. 13:9). The parallel account in 2 Samuel 6:6 calls it Nachon's threshing floor; it stood along the route from Kiriath-jearim, northwest of Jerusalem.

witness.excerpt: But as they were come to the threshing-floor of Chidon, a place so called, Uzzah was slain by the anger of God; for as the oxen shook the ark, he stretched out his hand, and would needs take hold of it.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chileab
entries.dictNote: Chileab was David's second son, born to Abigail after David married her following the death of her first husband Nabal (2 Samuel 3:3). He is called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1. He is never mentioned again after his birth notice and is generally thought to have died young, since he plays no role in the succession disputes among David's other sons.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chilion
entries.dictNote: Chilion was Naomi's son and one of Ruth's brothers-in-law, who died in Moab along with his father and brother, leaving both Israelite widows before Ruth's eventual return to Bethlehem with Naomi.

witness.excerpt: d with a famine, Elimelech of Bethlehem, which is a city of the tribe of Judah, being not able to support his family under so sore a distress, took with him Naomi his wife, and the children that were born to him by her, Chilion and Mahlon; and removed his habitation into the land of Moab: and upon the happy prosperity of his affairs there, he took for his sons wives of the Moabites, Orpah for Chilion and Ruth for Mahlon.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chilmad
entries.summary: Kilmad, a place apparently in the Assyrian empire
entries.dictNote: Chilmad appears once, among the trading partners of Tyre listed in Ezekiel's lament over the city's commercial empire, grouped with Sheba and Asshur (Ezekiel 27:23). Its identity is uncertain; some read it as a place near Assyria, while others take it not as a place name at all but as a Hebrew phrase meaning something like "as a pupil," referring to Tyre's trading apprenticeship. No location has been established with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chimham
entries.dictNote: Chimham was the son of Barzillai, the elderly Gileadite who supported David during Absalom's rebellion, and David brought Chimham back with him to Jerusalem as a reward, apparently granting him property near Bethlehem that carried his name for generations.
