entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chinnereth
entries.summary: Kinneroth or Kinnereth, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Chinnereth was a fortified Canaanite city near the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee that gave the lake its earliest biblical name, "the Sea of Chinnereth" (Numbers 34:11; Joshua 13:27), later known by its Greco-Roman names Gennesaret and Tiberias. It marked part of Naphtali's territory (Joshua 19:35), and in its plural form, Chinneroth, it named the surrounding district raided by Ben-hadad of Syria in the reign of Baasha (1 Kings 15:20).
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Chios
entries.summary: Chios, an island in the Mediterranean
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a large island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Asia Minor, past which Paul's ship sailed on his return from the third missionary journey (Acts 20:15). The island, still called Chios today, was known in antiquity for its wine and later for the mastic resin harvested from its trees.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chisleu
entries.dictNote: Chisleu, also spelled Kislev, is not a person but the name of the ninth month of the Hebrew religious calendar, roughly corresponding to late November and December, adopted from the Babylonians after the exile (Nehemiah 1:1; Zechariah 7:1). It marks the season in which Nehemiah heard the report of Jerusalem's broken walls and Zechariah received several of his visions. The later festival of Hanukkah also falls in this month, though it is not mentioned in these particular passages.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chislon
entries.dictNote: Chislon was the father of Elidad, the leader from the tribe of Benjamin chosen to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:21). Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chisloth-tabor
entries.dictNote: Chisloth-tabor, "the loins of Tabor," marked a point on Zebulun's boundary near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:12). It is usually identified with the village of Iksal, about two and a half miles west of the mountain, and may be the same town called Chesulloth a few verses later in the description of Issachar's territory.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chittim
entries.summary: a Kittite or Cypriote; hence, an islander in general, i.e. the Greeks or Romans on the shores opposite Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kittim was a son of Javan, and the name became a general biblical term for the peoples and islands of the eastern Mediterranean, particularly Cyprus, used in prophecy for distant maritime nations.

Moab and from the children of Ammon, those who were hired, one thousand chosen men, and from Philistia, one thousand chosen men of war, and from Edom  and from the Horites one thousand chosen fighting men, and from the Kittim  mighty men of war.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Chiun
entries.summary: properly, a statue, i.e. idol; but used (by euphemism) for some heathen deity (perhaps corresponding to Priapus or Baal-peor)
entries.dictNote: Chiun was an astral deity, likely identifying the planet Saturn, whose image the prophet Amos says the Israelites carried and worshipped during the wilderness period (Amos 5:26). The Septuagint rendered the name as Rephan or Remphan, the form Stephen uses when quoting the verse in Acts 7:43. Star worship of this kind was widespread across the ancient Near East, and Assyrian astrological texts record Saturn's association with an underworld deity under a related name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chloe
entries.dictNote: Chloe was a Christian woman, probably of Corinth or Ephesus, whose household members reported to Paul the factional disputes dividing the Corinthian church (1 Corinthians 1:11). Nothing further is known about her.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chorashan
entries.dictNote: Chorashan, one of the towns to which David sent gifts from the plunder he took after rescuing the captives of Ziklag from the Amalekites (1 Sam. 30:30). It is generally identified with Ashan, a town of Simeon in the Negev of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chorazin
entries.dictNote: Chorazin was one of the towns around the Sea of Galilee where Jesus performed many of his miracles, yet he pronounced a woe against it for failing to repent, grouping it with Bethsaida and Capernaum (Matt. 11:21; Luke 10:13). It is identified with Khirbet Karazeh, about two miles north of Capernaum, where archaeologists have excavated an ancient synagogue built of black basalt, standing on a site of much older settlement.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Choseba
entries.dictNote: Choseba, also spelled Cozeba, appears in a brief and difficult genealogical note in 1 Chronicles about men of Judah's line who lived long before and reportedly had authority in Moab (1 Chron. 4:22). It may be the same place as Achzib or Chezib in the Shephelah of Judah, birthplace of Judah's son Shelah in Genesis 38:5, though the connection is uncertain given the terse wording of the Chronicles text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Christ
entries.summary: anointed, i.e. the Messiah, an epithet of Jesus
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, Jude, Revelation
entries.dictNote: Christ is not a surname but a title, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning anointed one, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus of Nazareth as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises of a coming anointed king, priest, and deliverer. See the entry for Jesus for his life and ministry.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Chub
entries.dictNote: Chub is not a person but a people named once, in Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt, among the nations allied with Egypt that would fall by the sword (Ezekiel 30:5). Their identity is uncertain; many scholars suspect textual corruption and would read "Lub," meaning Libya, already named in the same list, though the reading is disputed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chun
entries.dictNote: A city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, from which David took bronze later used in Solomon's temple (1 Chr. 18:8). The parallel account in 2 Samuel 8:8 calls it Berothai, likely the same town as Berothah in Ezekiel 47:16, somewhere in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon.

entries.dictNote: Cush was Ham's eldest son, and his descendants are associated with the region south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan and Ethiopia, an area the Old Testament refers to repeatedly as a distant and exotic land.

entries.label: 11 books

entries.title: Chushan-rishathayim
entries.dictNote: Chushan-rishathayim was a king of Aram-naharaim (Mesopotamia) whom God allowed to oppress Israel for eight years during the period of the judges, the first of the foreign oppressions recorded in Judges. Israel cried out to the LORD, who raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman, to defeat him and secure forty years of peace (Judges 3:8-11). His title, which means something like “doubly wicked Cushan,” may be a Hebrew wordplay on his actual name rather than his given name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Chuza
entries.dictNote: Chuza was the household manager, or steward, of Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who ruled Galilee during Jesus' ministry. His wife Joanna was one of the women who had been healed by Jesus and who used their own resources to support him and the disciples, and she was later among the women who discovered the empty tomb (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

entries.title: Cilicia
entries.summary: Cilicia, a region of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Cilicia was a Roman province on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, whose chief city Tarsus was Paul's birthplace and a noted center of Greek philosophy and learning. Jews from Cilicia had their own synagogue in Jerusalem, where members disputed with Stephen before his martyrdom. Paul revisited the region strengthening the churches on his second missionary journey, and the province is also famous for the goat's-hair cloth used in tentmaking, the trade Paul practiced.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Cis
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Kish, father of King Saul, mentioned by Paul in his synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch summarizing Israel's history (Acts 13:21). See Kish for the fuller Old Testament account.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Clauda
entries.dictNote: Clauda, also spelled Cauda, was a small island off the southwest coast of Crete that Paul's ship passed under the shelter of during the storm that eventually wrecked it on Malta (Acts 27:16). Sailors used its lee to haul in the ship's boat and undergird the vessel with ropes before running before the wind. The island is identified with modern Gavdos, the southernmost point of Europe.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Claudia
entries.dictNote: A Christian at Rome whose greetings Paul passes on to Timothy alongside those of Pudens, Linus, and Eubulus (2 Tim. 4:21). Some interpreters have tried to connect her with a Claudia mentioned in the Roman poet Martial's epigrams as the British wife of a soldier named Pudens, but the identification with Paul's Claudia is speculative and rests only on the shared names.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cleopas
entries.dictNote: Cleopas was one of two disciples whom the risen Jesus joined on the road to Emmaus, not recognizing him until he broke bread with them (Luke 24:13-18, 30-31). Some have identified him with the Clopas mentioned in John 19:25 as the husband of one of the women at the cross, but this cannot be confirmed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cleophas
entries.dictNote: Better known as Clopas, named by John as the husband of one of the women named Mary who stood at the cross (John 19:25). Many identify him with the Cleopas of Luke 24:18, one of the two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus, though the Greek spellings Klopas and Kleopas may represent two distinct names, one Aramaic and one Greek, rather than the same man.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cnidus
entries.summary: Cnidus, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: A city and harbor at the southwestern tip of the Cnidian peninsula in Caria, Asia Minor, famous in antiquity for its temple of Aphrodite. Paul's ship passed it with difficulty in adverse winds on the voyage to Rome, just before running for shelter at Crete (Acts 27:7). Extensive ruins of the Greek and Roman city, including a theater and harbor works, have been excavated at the site.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Col-hozeh
entries.dictNote: Col-hozeh was a man of the tribe of Judah whose son Shallun repaired the Fountain Gate and part of Jerusalem's wall during Nehemiah's rebuilding project (Nehemiah 3:15). A descendant, Baruch, is also listed among Jerusalem's returned residents (Nehemiah 11:5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Colosse
entries.summary: Colossæ, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: A city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, on the Lycus River near Laodicea and Hierapolis, and the destination of Paul's letter to the Colossians. Paul had apparently never visited the city himself; its church was founded through Epaphras, a native of Colossae who carried the gospel there (Col. 1:2, 7; 2:1). Archaeological survey has located the unexcavated mound of the ancient city near modern Honaz, Turkey.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Conaniah
entries.summary: Conanjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Conaniah was a Levite entrusted with overseeing the tithes and offerings brought into the temple during Hezekiah's religious reforms.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Coniah
entries.dictNote: Coniah is a shortened form of the name Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon, used by Jeremiah in a prophecy declaring him childless as far as ruling on David's throne was concerned.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Core
entries.dictNote: Core is the Greek form of Korah, the Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron's authority in the wilderness and was destroyed along with his followers when the ground opened beneath them (Numbers 16). Jude 1:11 cites Korah's rebellion as a warning against false teachers who reject authority and pursue gain, grouping him with Cain and Balaam as examples of corrupted faith.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Corinth
entries.dictNote: Corinth was a major commercial city on the isthmus connecting the Peloponnese to mainland Greece, rebuilt by Rome after its earlier destruction, known in the ancient world for its wealth and loose morals. Paul spent eighteen months there founding the church that would receive two of his most substantial letters, and appeared before the Roman proconsul Gallio, whose recorded term of office helps anchor the chronology of Paul's ministry (Acts 18:1-17). A pavement inscription discovered at Corinth naming a civic official called Erastus who paid for it at his own expense is widely thought to refer to the same Erastus, the city treasurer, whom Paul mentions in Romans 16:23.

entries.title: Cornelius
entries.dictNote: Cornelius was a Roman centurion in Caesarea, devout and generous despite not being Jewish, and an angel told him to send for Peter, while a vision simultaneously prepared Peter to accept the invitation despite Jewish law's restrictions on entering a Gentile's home. Cornelius and his household became the first Gentile converts, and the Holy Spirit visibly fell on them the same way it had on the Jewish believers at Pentecost, convincing the Jerusalem church that the gospel extended to Gentiles without requiring them to become Jews first.

Later church tradition, not attested in scripture, associates him with founding churches in Gaul.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Crispus
entries.dictNote: Crispus was the leader of the Jewish synagogue in Corinth who came to believe in Christ under Paul's preaching there (Acts 18:8). Paul later recalled personally baptizing him, one of the few Corinthian converts Paul baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Cushan
entries.dictNote: Cushan appears once, in Habakkuk 3:7, paired poetically with Midian as a nomadic people or territory trembling before the Lord's approach. It most likely refers to a Cushite group in northwest Arabia rather than African Cush, and should not be confused with Cushan-rishathaim, the Mesopotamian king who oppressed Israel for eight years in Judges 3:8-10, despite the similar name. Its precise territory is not established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Cushi
entries.summary: Cushi, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Cushi, meaning “the Cushite” or “Ethiopian,” is applied to at least two men in the Old Testament: the father of Shelemiah, whose son was sent to summon Baruch after Jeremiah's scroll was burned (Jeremiah 36:14), and an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1). The name likely reflects African ancestry or origin somewhere in the family line rather than a single individual, since it recurs at different points in the genealogical record. Some readers connect Zephaniah's own line to royal descent through Hezekiah, named a few generations further back in the same verse.

entries.title: Cuth
entries.summary: Cuth or Cuthah, a province of Assyria
entries.dictNote: Cuth, or Cuthah, was a Babylonian city whose deported inhabitants the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after conquering the northern kingdom; these settlers brought the worship of their god Nergal with them (2 Kings 17:24, 30). The city has been identified with Tell Ibrahim northeast of Babylon, and “Cuthites” became a term Jews later used, often disparagingly, for Samaritans.

entries.title: Cyrene
entries.dictNote: A prominent city in North Africa, in the region later called Libya, founded by Greek colonists around 630 BC; its extensive ruins, including a temple of Apollo and a well-preserved theater, still stand near the modern town of Shahhat in Libya. entries.title: Cyrus
entries.summary: The Persian king Isaiah names by name roughly a century and a half before he was born — 'my shepherd' (Isaiah 44:28) — who then actually issues the decree letting the exiles go home and rebuild the temple. Josephus preserves what he presents as the decree's own wording, the same funding order behind Zerubbabel's return.
entries.dictNote: Cyrus the Great was the Persian king who conquered Babylon and, in a sharp break from earlier imperial policy, allowed the exiled peoples Babylon had deported, including the Jews, to return home and rebuild their temples. Isaiah names Cyrus by name generations before his birth and calls him God's anointed, a shepherd who would carry out God's purposes without even knowing the God he served. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay artifact discovered in Babylon in 1879, independently records Cyrus's policy of returning exiled peoples and restoring their temples, closely matching the biblical account in Ezra.

entries.title: Dabareh
entries.dictNote: Dabareh, also called Daberath, was a town on the border of Zebulun near Mount Tabor (Joshua 19:12) that was later assigned to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 21:28; 1 Chronicles 6:72). It survives in the name of the Arab village Deburiyeh, which still sits at the western foot of Tabor.

entries.title: Dabbesheth
entries.dictNote: Dabbesheth was a town marking part of the border of the tribal allotment of Zebulun (Joshua 19:11). Nothing further is recorded of it, and its exact site has not been identified.

entries.title: Dalaiah
entries.summary: Delajah, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Delaiah was a common postexilic name, including an official who urged King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's prophetic scroll, a plea the king ignored.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Dalmanutha
entries.dictNote: Dalmanutha, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, is named only in Mark's account of Jesus withdrawing there by boat after feeding the four thousand (Mark 8:10). Matthew's parallel account of the same trip names the destination as the region of Magdala instead (Matthew 15:39), suggesting the two names referred to neighboring or overlapping areas rather than two different events. No archaeological site has been confidently matched to the name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dalmatia
entries.dictNote: Dalmatia was the rugged coastal region along the eastern Adriatic, part of the Roman province of Illyricum, corresponding roughly to the coast of modern Croatia and Montenegro. Paul mentions it once, noting that his companion Titus had gone there during Paul's final imprisonment in Rome (2 Timothy 4:10); Paul himself claims earlier to have preached as far as Illyricum (Romans 15:19). Rome fought several wars to subdue the Dalmatian tribes, finally crushing a major revolt under Tiberius in AD 9, decades before Paul's letter.

entries.title: Dalphon
entries.dictNote: Dalphon was the second named of Haman's ten sons, all of whom were killed by the Jews of Susa after Haman's plot against them failed and were afterward hanged on gallows (Esther 9:7-10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Damaris
entries.summary: perhaps gentle; Damaris, an Athenian woman
entries.dictNote: An Athenian woman who became a believer after hearing Paul's speech at the Areopagus (Acts 17:34), one of very few individuals named as converts from that address. She is mentioned alongside Dionysius the Areopagite, though there is no evidence connecting the two beyond their both being named in the same verse.

entries.title: Damascene
entries.summary: a Damascene or inhabitant of Damascus
entries.dictNote: Damascene designates an inhabitant of Damascus, used by Paul when he recalls how the ethnarch under King Aretas guarded the city to arrest him, forcing Paul to escape by being lowered over the wall in a basket. Damascus is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and Aretas IV, the Nabatean king in view, is well attested on coins and inscriptions from the period.

entries.books: Genesis, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Zechariah, Acts, 2 Corinthians, Galatians
entries.dictNote: Damascus sits in a fertile plain northwest of Mount Hermon, watered by the river Barada, which is why a city has stood on this spot without a real break since before the patriarchs. It served as the capital of the Aramean kingdom that fought Israel through the ninth and eighth centuries BC, and centuries later it was on the road into this same city that Saul was converted (Acts 9). The street the New Testament calls Straight was a real colonnaded thoroughfare running through Roman Damascus, and remains of its columns have been found.

entries.title: Dan also
entries.summary: Vedan (or Aden), a place in Arabia
entries.dictNote: A trading partner of Tyre named alongside Javan in Ezekiel's taunt song against the city, supplying wrought iron, cassia, and calamus in exchange for Tyrian goods (Ezek. 27:19). The Hebrew text is difficult at this point, and some scholars read the name as Vedan, an Arabian place, rather than the tribe or territory of Dan.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dan-jaan
entries.dictNote: Dan-jaan, meaning Dan in the forest, is named in the route of Joab's census-taking journey through the tribal territories east and north of Israel, somewhere near the town of Dan by the sources of the Jordan (2 Sam. 24:6). Some ancient translations read the phrase simply as Dan in the forest rather than treating it as a distinct place name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Daniel
entries.summary: Taken to Babylon as a young noble and renamed by his captors (Daniel 1:6-7). Josephus tells the exact same scene — the deportation, the new Babylonian name, Daniel becoming Belteshazzar — as straight political history, no different in kind from any other royal hostage of the era.
entries.dictNote: Two men named Daniel appear in the Old Testament. The one people usually mean is the prophet carried off to Babylon as a young noble of Judah, who rose to high office under three different empires while refusing to compromise his faith, surviving a night in a lion's den for it and receiving visions that stretch to the book's final chapter. The other Daniel was David's second son, born in Hebron to Abigail and also called Chileab, a figure who otherwise disappears from the record entirely.

entries.title: Daniel
entries.summary: Dan, one of the sons of Jacob; also the tribe descended from him, and its territory; likewise a place in Palestine colonized by them
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: This record is Strong's H1835, the Hebrew name Dan, filed here under the spelling “Daniel”; its canonical references are all to Jacob's fifth son and the tribe and city named after him, not to the prophet Daniel (whose own record is Strong's H1840/H1841). Dan was Jacob's son by Rachel's servant Bilhah, and his tribe, finding its original allotment near Philistine territory too cramped, migrated north to conquer the city of Laish, renaming it Dan and making it Israel's northernmost town, the far end of the phrase “from Dan to Beersheba.” Jeroboam I later set up one of his golden calves there. A basalt stele fragment excavated at Tel Dan in 1993, inscribed by a ninth century BC Aramean king, records a victory over the “king of Israel” and the “House of David,” making it one of the earliest confirmed extra-biblical references to David's dynasty.

entries.title: Dannah
entries.dictNote: Dannah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the settlements south of Hebron in Joshua's account of Judah's inheritance (Josh. 15:49). It is sometimes associated with the area near the modern town of Idhna, southwest of Hebron, though the identification is not certain.

entries.title: Dara
entries.dictNote: Dara is likely the same figure as Darda, listed among the sons of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 2:6 and named in 1 Kings 4:31 as one of the wise men, alongside Heman, Chalcol, and Ethan, whose renowned wisdom Solomon's was said to surpass.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Darda
entries.dictNote: One of four men renowned for wisdom before Solomon's time, named as a standard of proverbial wisdom that Solomon was said to exceed (1 Kings 4:31); the same name appears again among the sons of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 2:6.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.title: Darius
entries.summary: Two Persian kings named Darius appear in the Old Testament. Darius the Mede is named in Daniel as ruling Babylon immediately after its fall, the king who reluctantly signed the decree that landed Daniel in the lion's den. Darius the Great, a later and better-attested Persian emperor, authorized the resumption of temple construction in Jerusalem after work had stalled, and his decree is preserved in the book of Ezra.

entries.title: David
entries.summary: Luke opens on the promise of ‘the throne of his father David’ (1:32) and closes the point with Jesus's own riddle about David's son and David's Lord (20:41-44). Josephus, introducing the Bathsheba affair, pauses to say the sin was out of character — the same tension Luke's own ‘son of David’ title leans on without ever mentioning the affair at all.

entries.dictNote: David was Israel's second king and its most consequential one, a shepherd from Bethlehem who killed Goliath as a young man and eventually inherited a kingdom that stretched further than anything before or after it under a single native ruler. He married at least eight women and fathered at least twenty children, among them Solomon, and nearly half the biblical psalms carry his name. For most of the twentieth century critics treated David as a legend with no life outside the text, until a broken Aramaic inscription surfaced at Tel Dan naming the "house of David" as a real dynasty, one an enemy king thought worth boasting about defeating.

entries.summary: Deborah, the name of two Hebrewesses
entries.dictNote: Deborah was a prophetess and the only woman among Israel's judges, and she held court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel where Israelites came to her for judgment. When she summoned the military commander Barak to lead an attack against the Canaanite general Sisera, he refused to go unless she came with him, so she agreed but told him the credit for the victory would go to a woman instead, a prophecy fulfilled when a woman named Jael killed Sisera in her own tent with a tent peg. Deborah is also named as the nurse of Rebekah in Genesis, an earlier figure who has nothing to do with the judge.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Decapolis
entries.summary: the ten-city region; the Decapolis, a district in Syria
entries.dictNote: The Decapolis, Greek for ten cities, was a loose league of Hellenistic cities mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, including Scythopolis, the only one west of the Jordan, along with Gerasa and Philadelphia. Crowds from the region followed Jesus (Matthew 4:25), and the man he freed from a legion of demons near Gerasa went on to proclaim what had happened to him throughout the Decapolis (Mark 5:20). Extensive ruins still stand at cities like Jerash and Beth Shean, among the best preserved Roman-era cities in the region.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dedan
entries.summary: Dedan, the name of two Cushites and of their territory
entries.dictNote: Dedan was a son of Abraham through Keturah and the ancestor of an Arabian trading people associated with caravans and merchandise in the prophetic books.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Dedanim
entries.summary: Dedanites, the descendants or inhabitants of Dedan
entries.dictNote: Dedanim were the descendants of Dedan, an Arabian people whose caravans Isaiah pictures lodging in the desert thickets, and whom Ezekiel later lists among the merchants supplying Tyre with goods. Dedan is generally located at the oasis of al-Ula in northwest Arabia, where excavated inscriptions in the ancient Dedanite and Lihyanite scripts confirm the existence of a real trading kingdom by that name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dehavites
entries.summary: Dahava, a people colonized in Samaria
entries.dictNote: Dehavites were among the foreign peoples the Assyrians settled in Samaria who later wrote to the Persian king opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. Their exact origin is uncertain; some scholars connect them with a nomadic tribe from the region east of the Caspian Sea.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dekar
entries.dictNote: Father of Ben-Dekar, one of Solomon's twelve district officers, responsible for supplying the royal household from the region including Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kings 4:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Delilah
entries.dictNote: Delilah was a Philistine woman Samson loved, and Philistine rulers paid her heavily to discover the secret of his strength. She pressed him repeatedly, and after he lied to her three times with false answers that each failed, she wore him down until he finally admitted his strength depended on his uncut Nazirite hair, and she had it shaved off while he slept, delivering him powerless into his enemies' hands.

witness.excerpt: For he fell in love with a woman that was an harlot among the Philistines: her name was Delilah ; and he lived with her.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Demas
entries.dictNote: Demas was a companion of Paul during his imprisonment who later abandoned him, and Paul writes with evident disappointment that Demas deserted him because he loved this present world.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Demetrius
entries.summary: Demetrius, the name of an Ephesian and of a Christian
entries.dictNote: Demetrius was a silversmith in Ephesus who made shrines of the goddess Artemis, and his fear that Paul's preaching was destroying his trade sparked a citywide riot that lasted two hours of continuous chanting before city officials calmed the crowd.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Derbe
entries.summary: Derbe, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Derbe was a small town in the Lycaonian highlands of Asia Minor, near modern Karaman in Turkey. Paul and Barnabas fled there from Lystra during the first missionary journey after being stoned, and Paul revisited it later; it was the hometown of his traveling companion Gaius. Its exact site was uncertain until 1956, when an inscription dated to AD 157 found at the mound of Kerti Höyük identified it as Derbe, a location now widely accepted by archaeologists.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Deuel
entries.dictNote: Deuel was the father of the tribal leader of Gad during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Diana
entries.summary: prompt; Artemis, the name of a Grecian goddess borrowed by the Asiatics for one of their deities
entries.dictNote: Diana is the Latin name for Artemis, the patron goddess of Ephesus, and a riot broke out there when silversmiths who made her shrines feared Paul's preaching was destroying their trade, chanting for two hours that great is Artemis of the Ephesians.

entries.title: Diblaim
entries.dictNote: Diblaim was the father of Gomer, the woman the prophet Hosea married at God's command as a living symbol of Israel's unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:3). Nothing further is known of Diblaim.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Diblath
entries.dictNote: Diblah is most likely a scribal variant of Riblah, a strategic town on the Orontes River in Syria that served as the Babylonian army's military headquarters during the fall of Jerusalem. Ezekiel 6:14 uses it as one boundary marker in a judgment oracle stretching "from the wilderness to Diblah," meaning the whole length of the land. Nebuchadnezzar's field headquarters at Riblah is where the captured king Zedekiah was blinded after watching his sons executed (2 Kings 25:6-7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dibon. (Also
entries.summary: Dibon, the name of three places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Dibon was a Moabite city Israel captured and later rebuilt, mentioned on the Moabite Stone itself as one of King Mesha's building projects, corroborating the biblical record of the region's contested history.

witness.excerpt: And the seed of them shall perish, from Heshbon even to Dibon.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Dibri
entries.dictNote: A Danite, father of Shelomith, whose son by an Egyptian father was stoned for blasphemy in the wilderness, an episode that prompted the law on blasphemy recorded in Leviticus (Leviticus 24:10-11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Didymus
entries.summary: double, i.e. twin; Didymus, a Christian
entries.dictNote: Didymus is the Greek word for “twin,” used in John's Gospel as a byname for the apostle Thomas (John 11:16; 20:24; 21:2). John likely includes the translation because some readers knew Thomas primarily by this descriptive nickname rather than his Aramaic name. No biblical tradition identifies who his twin sibling was.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Diklah
entries.dictNote: Diklah appears in the table of nations as a son of Joktan, one of the Arabian clans descended from Shem (Genesis 10:27; 1 Chronicles 1:21). Like most of Joktan's other sons, the name almost certainly designates a tribal territory rather than a single historical individual, and its meaning, palm grove, points to a district of Arabia known for date palm cultivation, though its exact location remains uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dilean
entries.dictNote: Dilean was a town in the lowland district, or Shephelah, of Judah's territory, listed among a group of towns that included Migdal-gad and Mizpeh (Josh. 15:38). Its site has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dimnah
entries.dictNote: Dimnah was a town of the tribe of Zebulun assigned to the Levite clan of Merari for their residence (Joshua 21:35). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:77 gives the same town's name as Rimmon instead, suggesting either a scribal variant or a genuine name change. Its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dimon
entries.dictNote: Dimon, the "waters of Dimon," a stream or pool east of the Dead Sea that Isaiah pictures turning to blood in his oracle of judgment against Moab (Isa. 15:9). Many read it as another name for the waters of Dibon, the Moabite capital where the Moabite Stone, King Mesha's own inscription, was later discovered.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dimonah
entries.dictNote: A town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev (Joshua 15:22). It is generally taken as the same place as Dibon mentioned in Nehemiah 11:25 among the towns resettled by Judahites after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dinah
entries.dictNote: Dinah was Jacob and Leah's only daughter, and her rape by a local prince named Shechem triggered one of Genesis's most violent episodes: Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi pretended to negotiate a marriage settlement requiring the men of Shechem's city to be circumcised, then slaughtered the entire incapacitated population while they were recovering, an act of vengeance Jacob condemned on his deathbed as reckless cruelty.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dinaite
entries.summary: a Dinaite or inhabitant of some unknown Assyria province
entries.dictNote: Dinaites were among the peoples the Assyrians had resettled in Samaria who later wrote to the Persian king Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and temple, a complaint that succeeded in halting the work for a time.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dinhaban
entries.dictNote: This entry's name is a data variant of Dinhabah, which is a place, not a person: the capital city of Bela son of Beor, the first king listed in Edom's roster of early rulers (Genesis 36:32; 1 Chronicles 1:43). Its location is unknown, though it lay somewhere in the region later called Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dionysius
entries.dictNote: A member of the Areopagus, the council of Athens, who believed after hearing Paul's speech there and is named as one of the few converts from that address (Acts 17:34).

entries.title: Diotrephes
entries.summary: Jove-nourished; Diotrephes, an opponent of Christianity
entries.dictNote: A leader in a local church rebuked by John for loving to be first, refusing to welcome traveling missionaries, and spreading malicious accusations against John and his coworkers, even expelling members who did welcome them (3 John 1:9-10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dishan
entries.dictNote: Dishan was a Horite chief, the youngest listed among the sons of Seir, whose descendants are counted among Edom's earlier inhabitants.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dishon
entries.summary: Dishon, the name of two Edomites
entries.dictNote: Dishon was a Horite chief listed among the earlier inhabitants of Edom's territory before Esau's descendants settled there.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dizahab
entries.summary: Dizahab, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Dizahab, meaning "place of gold," is named in Deuteronomy 1:1 as one of the wilderness locations near which Moses delivered his final addresses to Israel. It is often identified with modern Dahab on the eastern coast of the Sinai Peninsula, whose name preserves the ancient one, though the identification cannot be proven with certainty.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dodai
entries.dictNote: Dodai was an Ahohite who commanded the army division serving King David during the second month of the year, one of twelve divisions that rotated monthly military duty (1 Chr. 27:4). He may be the father of Eleazar, one of David's three chief warriors (2 Sam. 23:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dodanim
entries.summary: Dodanites, or descendants of a son of Javan
entries.dictNote: One of the peoples descended from Javan in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:4), representing a seafaring group of the eastern Mediterranean rather than a single individual. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:7 spells the name Rodanim, which many connect to Rhodes or to the Dardanians of northwest Asia Minor.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dodavah
entries.dictNote: A man of Mareshah in Judah whose son Eliezer rebuked King Jehoshaphat for allying with the wicked King Ahaziah of Israel in a shipbuilding venture that God then destroyed, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 20:37.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dodo
entries.summary: Dodo, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Dodo was the name of the father or grandfather of two of David's mighty warriors, listed among the elite fighters in his service.

witness.excerpt: After him was Eleazar, the son of Dodo, who was with the king at Arasam.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Doeg
entries.dictNote: Doeg was an Edomite serving as Saul's chief herdsman who reported to Saul that the priest Ahimelech had helped David while David was fleeing, and when Saul's own men refused to kill the priests of Nob for it, Doeg carried out the massacre himself, killing eighty-five priests along with the entire town's population.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Dophkah
entries.summary: Dophkah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Wilderness encampment in the Sinai peninsula, between the desert of Sin and Alush (Num. 33:12-13). Its name, related to a word for smelting or forging, has led some scholars to connect it with ancient Egyptian turquoise and copper mining operations at Serabit el-Khadim, a site in the Sinai with inscriptions documenting mining expeditions from the Egyptian New Kingdom period.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dor
entries.dictNote: Dor was an ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel, a royal Canaanite city whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 11:1-2; 12:23) though its original inhabitants were never fully expelled (Judges 1:27); it was later assigned to one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kings 4:11). Decades of excavation at Tel Dor have made it one of the best sites anywhere for tracing the transition from Bronze Age Canaanite culture to Iron Age Phoenician civilization on the coast.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Dorcas
entries.dictNote: Dorcas, called Tabitha in Aramaic, was a Christian woman at Joppa remembered for her charity; she made clothing for the widows in her care. When she died, the disciples sent for Peter, who raised her back to life, and the miracle led many in Joppa to believe (Acts 9:36-41).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Drusilla
entries.summary: Drusilla, a member of the Herodian family
entries.dictNote: The youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, part of the well documented Herodian dynasty known from Josephus and from coins minted under various family members. Felix, the Roman governor of Judea, persuaded her to leave her first husband, the king of Emesa, and marry him instead, and she was sitting beside Felix when Paul spoke to him of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment (Acts 24:24-25). Josephus reports that she and a son from her marriage to Felix later died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, though some historians question whether he has confused her with another Herodian relative.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Dumah
entries.summary: Dumah, a tribe and region of Arabia
entries.dictNote: Dumah was a son of Ishmael and, by extension, the Arabian tribe and region descended from him (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). The name is generally connected to the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal in northern Arabia, an important caravan stop. Isaiah's brief oracle against Dumah (Isaiah 21:11-12) uses the name, meaning silence, as a play on words, and most read it as directed at Edom or its Arabian neighbors rather than the Ishmaelite region itself.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Dura
entries.dictNote: The plain of Dura, near Babylon, was where Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image that all his officials were summoned to worship, the scene of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego's refusal and their deliverance from the furnace (Daniel 3:1-30). "Dura" likely derives from a common Akkadian word for a walled enclosure, which would make it more a type of place than a single proper name, and several sites near Babylon carried variants of it. No firm identification of this particular plain has been established.

entries.dictNote: This is a region in northern Mesopotamia, distinct from the garden of Eden in Genesis, though the two share a name. entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Edom was the byname given to Esau after he traded his birthright for red stew, and it became the name of the mountainous territory his descendants settled southeast of the Dead Sea, stretching from the Gulf of Aqabah north toward Moab. Its old capital was Bozrah, and its rock cut stronghold Sela, later called Petra by the Greeks, still stands. The Edomites refused Israel passage during the exodus and remained hostile neighbors for centuries, eventually assisting Babylon's sack of Jerusalem, an act the prophets condemned at length. Excavations at the copper smelting site of Khirbet en Nahas and at Busayra, ancient Bozrah, have revealed an organized Edomite kingdom emerging by the tenth and ninth centuries BC, broadly consistent with the biblical timeline for Edom's rise.

entries.dictNote: Ekronite designates an inhabitant of Ekron, the northernmost of the five Philistine lordships. After the ark of the covenant brought plague to Ashdod and Gath, the Philistines sent it on to Ekron, whose people cried out in terror and demanded it be returned to Israel.

entries.title: El-paran
entries.summary: El-Paran, a portion of the district of Paran
entries.dictNote: El-paran was not a person but a place name, "the oak (or terebinth) of Paran," marking a site on the edge of the wilderness bordering the territory of the Horites in the hill country of Seir. It marks the farthest point reached by the invading kings under Chedorlaomer before they turned back toward the Dead Sea cities (Genesis 14:6), and its name incorporates the wilderness of Paran, covered separately, through which Israel later traveled during the exodus.

entries.title: Eladah
entries.dictNote: An Ephraimite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:20, an ancestor of Joshua son of Nun according to the family line given there. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.dictNote: The Valley of Elah, named for the terebinth trees that grew there, lies in the lowlands of Judah and is where the young David killed Goliath while the Israelite and Philistine armies faced off on opposite slopes. The same word names an Edomite chief in Genesis, a son of Caleb, and two kings of Israel: Elah son of Baasha, assassinated while drunk by his own chariot commander Zimri, and Elah father of Hoshea, Israel's last king before Assyria's conquest. Excavations at Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified site overlooking the valley, have uncovered a tenth century BC settlement with one of the earliest known Hebrew inscriptions, physical evidence of an organized kingdom in Judah near the time and place tradition assigns to David.

entries.title: Elamite
entries.summary: an Elamite or inhabitant of Elam
entries.dictNote: Elamites came from Elam, an ancient civilization centered on Susa in what is now southwestern Iran, one of the oldest urban cultures in the Near East and extensively documented in Mesopotamian and Persian records. Ezra lists Elamites among the peoples resettled in Samaria who wrote to oppose the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and Acts names them among the nations represented at Pentecost.

Its site is preserved in the name of the modern Israeli city of Eilat.

entries.title: Eldad
entries.dictNote: Eldad was one of the seventy elders Moses appointed to help bear the burden of leading Israel. entries.title: Elead
entries.dictNote: Elead was an Ephraimite killed by the men of Gath while raiding their livestock, one of several sons of Ephraim who died in the raid and whose loss caused their father Ephraim to mourn for many days (1 Chr. 7:20-22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elealeh
entries.summary: Elale or Elaleh, a place east of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Elealeh was a town in the pastoral plateau east of the Jordan that the tribe of Reuben rebuilt for its herds after the conquest (Numbers 32:3, 37). It reappears centuries later in Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles against Moab, which had reclaimed the region by their time (Isaiah 15:4; 16:9; Jeremiah 48:34). The site survives as the ruin el-Al, just northeast of Heshbon in modern Jordan.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Eliam
entries.dictNote: Eliam appears in two contexts that may describe the same man: as the father of Bathsheba, David's wife (2 Samuel 11:3, where Chronicles gives his name as Ammiel), and as the son of David's counselor Ahithophel and one of David's elite thirty warriors (2 Samuel 23:34). If the two references are the same person, it would mean Bathsheba was Ahithophel's granddaughter, which some read as a motive behind Ahithophel's bitter betrayal of David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15-17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliasaph
entries.summary: Eljasaph, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Eliasaph was a tribal leader of Gad during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives Moses appointed from each tribe.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliashib
entries.summary: Eljashib, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Eliashib was the high priest during Nehemiah's governorship who cooperated with rebuilding Jerusalem's walls but later compromised by giving Nehemiah's political opponent Tobiah a room inside the temple, a decision Nehemiah reversed the moment he discovered it.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Eliathah
entries.dictNote: Eliathah was one of the sons of Heman, a Levite musician in David's court, and headed one of the divisions of temple musicians (1 Chronicles 25:4, 27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elidad
entries.dictNote: Son of Chislon and chief of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribal leaders Moses appointed to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:21).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliel
entries.summary: Eliel, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Eliel was a common Levitical and military name in Chronicles, borne by several temple officials and warriors in David's army.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Elienai
entries.dictNote: Listed among the heads of Benjaminite families living in Jerusalem, recorded in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants (1 Chronicles 8:20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliezer
entries.summary: Eliezer, the name of a Damascene and of ten Israelites
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Luke
entries.dictNote: Eliezer was most likely the name of Abraham's chief servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, though he is named directly only once, when Abraham worried before Isaac's birth that this servant would become his heir instead of a son of his own body. Moses also named his second son Eliezer, meaning my God is my help.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Elihoenai
entries.summary: Eljehoenai or Eljoenai, the name of seven Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elioenai was a common postexilic and royal name, borne by a descendant of David listed in the genealogies of Chronicles and by several returning exiles.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elihoreph
entries.dictNote: One of two scribes serving in Solomon's court alongside his brother Ahijah, part of the administrative staff Solomon organized to run his kingdom (1 Kings 4:3). Their father Shisha may be the same official who served David as scribe under a slightly different spelling of the name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elihu
entries.summary: Elihu, the name of one of Job's friends, and of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elihu was a younger bystander in the book of Job who spoke last among Job's companions, criticizing both Job's self-justification and his three older friends' failure to actually answer him, before God himself finally speaks from the whirlwind.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elijah
entries.summary: Elijah, the name of the famous prophet and of two other Israelites
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Malachi

He fled into the wilderness in despair immediately afterward, convinced he was the last faithful Israelite left, until God met him not in wind or earthquake or fire but in a quiet voice. Elijah never died in the ordinary sense: 2 Kings ends his story with a whirlwind and a chariot of fire that carried him up to heaven while his successor Elisha watched.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Elika
entries.dictNote: Elika was a Harodite listed among David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23:25. He does not appear in the parallel list of mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11, one of several names that differ between the two rosters.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elim
entries.summary: Elim, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Second wilderness campsite reached by Israel after crossing the Red Sea, prized for its twelve springs and seventy palm trees, a welcome contrast to the bitter water they had just left behind at Marah (Exod. 15:27; 16:1; Num. 33:9-10). It is commonly identified with Wadi Gharandal, an oasis on the Sinai peninsula's western coastal route that still supports palm groves.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Elimelech
entries.dictNote: Elimelech was Naomi's husband, and he moved his family from Bethlehem to Moab to escape a famine, only to die there, leaving Naomi a widow along with her two sons, who also died a decade later, setting up the story of Ruth and Naomi's return to Bethlehem.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliphal
entries.dictNote: Eliphal son of Ur was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the roster of elite fighters in 1 Chronicles 11:35. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:34 gives a slightly different name, Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, for what appears to be the same figure.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eliphalet
entries.summary: Eliphelet or Elpelet, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Eliphelet was a common name among David's sons, borne by at least two of them in the lists recorded in 2 Samuel and Chronicles.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Eliphaz
entries.summary: Eliphaz, the name of one of Job's friends, and of a son of Esau
entries.dictNote: Eliphaz was the first and apparently eldest of Job's three friends, a Temanite whose speeches argue that suffering is always the result of personal sin, a position God ultimately rebukes at the book's end for not speaking rightly about him the way Job had.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elipheleh
entries.dictNote: Elipheleh was one of the Levite gatekeepers and musicians appointed to play the harp “on the Sheminith” when David brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 21). The term “Sheminith” likely designates a musical instrument, tuning, or octave register, though its precise meaning is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elisabeth
entries.dictNote: Elizabeth was a priest's wife and a relative of Mary, and she and her husband Zechariah were both old and childless when the angel Gabriel announced she would bear a son who would prepare the way for the Messiah. When the pregnant Mary visited her, Elizabeth's own unborn child, John the Baptist, leapt inside her, and Elizabeth was the first person in the Gospels to call Mary blessed and to recognize by the Spirit that Mary carried her Lord.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elisha
entries.summary: Paired with Elijah in Jesus's own synagogue sermon (4:27) — the same pairing Josephus uses to introduce him: 'Elisha, the son of Shaphat, the disciple of Elijah,' called on by three kings stranded without water in the wilderness.
entries.dictNote: Elisha was a wealthy farmer's son who left his oxen in the field to follow Elijah after the older prophet threw his cloak over him, and he inherited Elijah's ministry, and by his own request a double portion of his spirit, when Elijah was taken up in the whirlwind. He performed roughly twice as many miracles as Elijah, from purifying poisoned water and multiplying a widow's oil to raising a dead boy and healing the Aramean general Naaman of leprosy, and his ministry spanned the reigns of four different kings of Israel. Even his bones kept working after his death: 2 Kings records a corpse tossed into Elisha's tomb coming back to life the moment it touched his remains.

witness.excerpt: One of the servants of Joram said, that he had seen there Elisha, the son of Shaphat, the disciple of Elijah… they asked him, ‘What would become of the army?’

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elishah
entries.dictNote: Elishah was a son of Javan, and his descendants are associated in Ezekiel's prophecy with a source of fine purple dye traded with the Phoenician city of Tyre.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elishama
entries.summary: Elishama, the name of seven Israelites
entries.books: Numbers, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Elishama was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by a tribal leader of Ephraim during the wilderness wanderings and by several other minor figures, including one of David's sons and a royal secretary during Jehoiakim's reign.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Elishaphat
entries.dictNote: Elishaphat was one of the military commanders whom the priest Jehoiada brought into covenant to overthrow the usurping queen Athaliah and restore the boy king Joash to the throne of Judah (2 Chronicles 23:1). The coup he helped carry out ended Athaliah's six-year reign, the only period the Davidic line was interrupted on the throne of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elisheba
entries.dictNote: Daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon the leader of Judah's tribe, and wife of Aaron; she became the mother of Israel's first priestly line through her sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar (Exodus 6:23).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elishua
entries.summary: Elishua, the son of King David
entries.dictNote: Elishua was one of David's sons born to him in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 3:6 lists the same son under the name Elishama.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Eliud
entries.summary: God of majesty; Eliud, an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Eliud appears only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Achim and the father of Eleazar, several generations before Joseph (Matthew 1:14-15). Like many names in this section of the genealogy, he is otherwise unknown outside this list. His inclusion reflects Matthew's concern to trace an unbroken line from Abraham to Jesus through the royal house of David.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elizaphan
entries.dictNote: Elizaphan was a leader of the Kohathite Levites during the wilderness period, tasked with organizing the removal of Nadab and Abihu's bodies after they died offering unauthorized fire.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Elizur
entries.dictNote: Elizur was the tribal leader of Reuben during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elkanah
entries.summary: Elkanah, the name of several Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elkanah was Samuel's father, a Levite with two wives, Hannah and Peninnah, and his deep love for the childless Hannah despite Peninnah's taunting sets up the story of Hannah's prayer for a son and Samuel's eventual birth and dedication to the Lord's service.

witness.excerpt: He also carried Elkanah, the General of the troops of the tribe of Judah, into captivity.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Elkanan
entries.dictNote: Elhanan was a warrior in David's army credited in 2 Samuel with killing Goliath the Gittite, and 1 Chronicles clarifies he killed Goliath's brother Lahmi instead, resolving what would otherwise be a direct contradiction with David's more famous duel.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Elkoshite
entries.summary: an Elkoshite or native of Elkosh
entries.dictNote: Elkoshite identifies the prophet Nahum as being from Elkosh, a town whose location is no longer known, though tradition has variously placed it in Galilee, Judah, and northern Iraq.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ellasar
entries.summary: Ellasar, an early country of Asia
entries.dictNote: Ellasar was not a person but the kingdom ruled by Arioch, one of the four kings who campaigned against Sodom and its allies alongside Chedorlaomer of Elam (Genesis 14:1, 9). Many scholars connect it with Larsa, an ancient Mesopotamian city between Ur and Uruk that has been extensively excavated and whose ruins preserve royal inscriptions from its own line of kings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elmodam
entries.dictNote: Elmodam was the son of Er, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, in the line descended from David's son Nathan (Luke 3:28).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elnaam
entries.dictNote: Father of two of David's mighty men, Jeribai and Joshaviah, named in the expanded roster of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:46.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elnathan
entries.summary: Elnathan, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elnathan was a royal official sent to retrieve the prophet Uriah from Egypt to be executed for prophesying against Jerusalem, and later one of the officials who unsuccessfully urged King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Elon
entries.summary: Elon, the name of a place in Palestine, and also of one Hittite, two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elon, Hebrew for "oak," is applied in the Old Testament to one place and several distinct men. It names a town allotted to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:43); a Hittite whose daughter Basemath married Esau (Genesis 26:34; 36:2); one of the sons of Zebulun who founded the clan of the Elonites (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26); and Elon the Zebulunite, a minor judge who led Israel for ten years and was buried in his own territory (Judges 12:11-12).

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Elon-bethhanan
entries.summary: Elon of Beth-chanan, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Elon-bethhanan was grouped with two towns of Dan to form one of the twelve administrative districts Solomon set up to supply his royal household, this one overseen by Ben-deker (1 Kings 4:9). Nothing more is recorded about it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elonites
entries.summary: an Elonite or descendant (collectively) of Elon
entries.dictNote: Elonites were the clan descended from Elon, a son of Zebulun, counted among the tribe's families in Israel's wilderness census, distinct from the later judge of the same name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elpaal
entries.dictNote: Elpaal was a descendant of Benjamin credited in Chronicles with building several towns, including Ono and Lod.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eltekeh
entries.summary: Eltekeh or Elteke, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Eltekeh was a town allotted to the tribe of Dan and later set apart as a Levitical city for the descendants of Kohath (Josh. 19:44; 21:23). The site is significant beyond the biblical text because Sennacherib's own annals record a battle fought near Eltekeh in 701 BC, in which the Assyrian king defeated an Egyptian and Ethiopian relief force during the same campaign in which he besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eltekon
entries.dictNote: Eltekon was one of eleven towns in the hill country of Judah listed alongside Halhul, Beth-zur, and Gedor in Joshua's allotment to Judah's tribe (Joshua 15:58-59). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eltolad
entries.dictNote: Eltolad was a town in the southern Negev of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to Judah in Joshua 15:30 and then reassigned to Simeon in Joshua 19:4 since Judah's territory was larger than that tribe needed. It appears again as Tolad in 1 Chronicles 4:29, still held by Simeonite families generations later. Its exact site has not been securely identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elul
entries.dictNote: Elul is not a person but the sixth month of the Hebrew religious calendar and twelfth of the civil calendar, falling in August and September. Nehemiah completed Jerusalem's wall on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, a project that took fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eluzai
entries.dictNote: One of the Benjamite warriors who defected to David's side while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag, listed among skilled fighters able to use bow and sling with either hand (1 Chronicles 12:5-6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elymas
entries.dictNote: Elymas, meaning "magician" or "sorcerer," was the surname of the Jewish false prophet Bar-Jesus, who attended the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus on Cyprus and tried to turn him from the faith. Paul struck him with temporary blindness, and the proconsul believed as a result (Acts 13:6-12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Elzabad
entries.summary: Elzabad, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Elzabad was the name of two different men in Chronicles. One was a Gadite warrior who joined David's band at Ziklag before he became king (1 Chronicles 12:8-13), and the other was a son of Shemaiah, a Korahite Levite serving as a gatekeeper of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Emims
entries.summary: Emim, an early Canaanitish (or Maobitish) tribe
entries.dictNote: The Emim were an ancient race of unusually tall people who once lived in Moabite territory before being displaced, remembered in Deuteronomy alongside other giant clans like the Anakim.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Emmanuel
entries.summary: God with us; Emmanuel, a name of Christ
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Immanuel, God with us, the name Matthew applies to Jesus by quoting Isaiah 7:14 to interpret his virgin birth (Matthew 1:23). It functions as a theological title rather than a name Jesus was actually called day to day; see the separate Immanuel entry for the Isaiah oracle it draws on.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Emmaus
entries.dictNote: Emmaus was the village, about seven miles from Jerusalem by Luke's count, where the risen Jesus joined two disciples walking home on Easter Sunday, explaining the Scriptures to them before they recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13-31). Its location has been disputed for centuries: candidates include Amwas/Nicopolis, roughly twenty miles from Jerusalem, which fits an alternate ancient manuscript reading of the distance; el-Qubeibeh, closer to Luke's stated distance but lacking clear first-century remains; and Qaloniyeh, a Roman veteran colony just west of the city. No site has won full scholarly consensus, and the debate remains active in current archaeological literature.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Emmor
entries.dictNote: Emmor is the Greek form of Hamor, the father of Shechem and prince of the Canaanite city of Shechem in Genesis 33-34. Stephen refers to him in Acts 7:16 as the one from whom Abraham purchased a burial site, though Genesis attributes that purchase to Jacob, a detail many read as Stephen collapsing two separate patriarchal land purchases from Genesis 23 and 33 into one for the sake of a concise speech.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-dor
entries.dictNote: En-dor was a town in Issachar's territory, near the site of Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera's army, which Psalm 83 recalls when praying for Israel's enemies to meet the same fate. It is best known as the home of the medium Saul consulted in disguise the night before his final, fatal battle with the Philistines (1 Samuel 28:7). The name survives in the modern village of Endur, southeast of Mount Tabor.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: En-eglaim
entries.dictNote: En-eglaim, "spring of the two calves," is named in Ezekiel's vision of the river flowing from the restored Temple, marking one end of a stretch of Dead Sea shore where fishermen will spread their nets once the water is healed, with En-gedi marking the other (Ezekiel 47:10). Its precise location is unresolved; some place it near the Jordan's mouth at the sea's northern end, others near Ain Feshkha close to En-gedi itself, but no identification has been firmly established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-gannim
entries.dictNote: En-gannim, fountain of gardens, names two separate towns. One lay in the lowlands of Judah, between Zanoah and Tappuah (Joshua 15:34). The other sat on the border of Issachar and was assigned to the Gershonite Levites (Joshua 19:21; 21:29); it is generally identified with the modern city of Jenin, which still preserves the name and its springs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-gedi
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: En-gedi was an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, famous for its vineyards (Song of Solomon 1:14) and fed by a freshwater spring dropping some 600 feet down the cliffs above it. David hid in its caves while fleeing Saul and there spared Saul's life when he crept up on him unseen (1 Samuel 24); excavations at the site have uncovered a Chalcolithic-era temple predating Israel's settlement of Canaan by well over a thousand years.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: En-haddah
entries.dictNote: A town on the border of the tribe of Issachar, named next to Engannim (Joshua 19:21). Its precise site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-hakhore
entries.dictNote: En-hakhore, the spring God opened at Lehi to revive Samson after his victory over the Philistines with a donkey's jawbone, its name meaning "spring of the one who called" (Judg. 15:18-19). The King James Version itself spells the name Enhakkore.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-hazor
entries.dictNote: En-hazor, a fortified town of Naphtali named in Joshua 19:37, distinct from the larger and better known city of Hazor despite the shared element in its name. It appears only once and its precise location has not been recovered.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-mishpat
entries.dictNote: An older name, meaning "spring of judgment," for the place later known as Kadesh, in the wilderness south of Canaan (Genesis 14:7). The coalition of eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer struck this place, along with the Amalekites and the Amorites, in the campaign that later drew Abram into battle to rescue Lot.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-rimmon
entries.dictNote: En-rimmon, "spring of the pomegranate," was one of the towns in the Negev of Judah reoccupied by returning exiles, listed in Nehemiah 11:29. It likely combines two towns named separately in the earlier tribal lists, Ain and Rimmon, among the southernmost cities of Judah and Simeon (Joshua 15:32; 19:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: En-rogel
entries.dictNote: En-rogel was a spring just south of Jerusalem, near where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet, likely used by fullers treading cloth in its waters. Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid there to relay intelligence to David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17:17), and it was the site where David's son Adonijah held a feast to proclaim himself king, a bid for the throne undone when Solomon was anointed at Gihon instead (1 Kings 1:5-53). Many identify it with the deep shaft known as Bir Ayyub, "Job's Well," south of the Pool of Siloam.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: En-tappuah
entries.dictNote: A spring associated with the town of Tappuah, marking a point on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 17:7). The town itself belonged to Ephraim even though it stood on land otherwise allotted to Manasseh, and the spring served as the dividing landmark between the two.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Enaim
entries.summary: Enajim or Enam, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Enaim was the town gate or crossroads where Tamar sat veiled, disguised as a prostitute, and waited for her father-in-law Judah after he had failed to give her his youngest son in marriage (Genesis 38:14, 21). The name means two springs or two eyes, and the site is usually placed somewhere along the road between Adullam and Timnah in the Judean foothills, though it has not been identified with certainty.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Enan
entries.dictNote: Enan was the father of the tribal leader of Naphtali during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Enoch
entries.summary: Named once, in passing, in Luke's genealogy — the same figure who narrates an entire other book. All of 1 Enoch is framed as his own testimony, starting with the Watchers calling him ‘scribe of righteousness’ and sending him to confront the fallen angels.
entries.dictNote: Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam, and Genesis says simply that he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him, the only patriarch in the genealogy who doesn't get a death notice, understood ever since as a bodily removal to heaven without dying. Jude quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch condemning the ungodly, and Enoch became the namesake of an extensive body of later Jewish apocalyptic literature, though that literature was not written by him and dates many centuries after his lifetime. A different Enoch was Cain's son, for whom Cain named the first city built after his exile.

witness.excerpt: Enoch, thou scribe of righteousness, go, declare to the Watchers of the heaven who have left the high heaven, the holy eternal place, and have defiled themselves with women…

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Enos
entries.dictNote: Enosh was Seth's son and Adam's grandson, and Genesis notes that it was in his days that people began to call on the name of the Lord, marking an early point of organized worship in the biblical timeline.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Enshemesh
entries.dictNote: Enshemesh, fountain of the sun, was a spring that served as a boundary marker between the territories of Judah and Benjamin, situated on the road down toward Jericho not far from Bethany (Joshua 15:7; 18:17). It is usually identified with a spring still flowing today along that route.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Epaphras
entries.dictNote: Epaphras was a native of Colossae who likely founded that church and reported its condition to Paul, prompting Paul's letter to the Colossians, and Paul describes him as always wrestling in prayer for the Colossian believers.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Epaphroditus
entries.dictNote: Epaphroditus was a member of the church at Philippi whom the congregation sent to Rome carrying financial support for the imprisoned Paul. He fell seriously ill while there, and Paul, moved by his recovery and homesickness, sent him back to Philippi bearing the letter now known as Philippians, commending him warmly to the church (Philippians 2:25-30; 4:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Epenetus
entries.dictNote: Epenetus was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greeted as his "beloved," calling him the first convert to Christ from the province of Asia (Romans 16:5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephah
entries.summary: Ephah, the name of a son of Midian, and of the region settled by him; also of an Israelite and of an Israelitess
entries.dictNote: Ephah is a name shared by a tribal ancestor and two other individuals. Ephah was a son of Midian and grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whose descendants settled in northern Arabia and gave their name to a region that Isaiah pictures bringing gold and incense to Zion (Genesis 25:4; Isaiah 60:6); the same name belonged to a concubine of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:46) and to a descendant of Judah through Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ephai (from margin)
entries.dictNote: A Netophathite whose sons came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem, part of the remnant of Judean military commanders who initially submitted to Gedaliah's Babylonian-appointed government (Jeremiah 40:7-8). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Epher
entries.summary: Epher, the name of an Arabian and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Epher was a common name, borne by a son of Midian, a descendant of Judah, and a military leader from the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ephes-dammim
entries.dictNote: The site of the Philistine camp in the Valley of Elah when Goliath challenged Israel's army and was killed by David (1 Sam. 17:1). It is also called Pas-dammim in 1 Chronicles 11:13, and is generally located near Socoh in the Shephelah of Judah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephesus
entries.summary: Ephesus, a city of Asia Minor
entries.books: Acts, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Revelation
entries.dictNote: Ephesus was the leading city of Roman Asia and home to the temple of Artemis, one of the ancient world's Seven Wonders, along with a theater that could seat some twenty five thousand spectators. Paul made it the center of his third missionary journey, staying about three years and sparking a riot among silversmiths whose idol trade suffered from his preaching; he later addressed a moving farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus. It is one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, and tradition holds that the apostle John spent his final years and was buried there. Excavations have uncovered much of the ancient city, including the Library of Celsus and the massive theater, still among the best preserved Roman ruins in the eastern Mediterranean.

entries.title: Ephlal
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, listed in a genealogy that traces the family through a servant, Jarha, who married into the household (1 Chronicles 2:34-37).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephod
entries.dictNote: Ephod was the father of Hanniel, the leader chosen from the tribe of Manasseh to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest (Numbers 34:23). Nothing else is recorded of him; his name is distinct from the priestly garment of similar spelling, which is a common word rather than this man's proper name.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ephphatha
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an Aramaic word meaning "be opened," spoken by Jesus when he healed a deaf man with a speech impediment near the Decapolis (Mark 7:34). Mark is noted for preserving several of Jesus's actual Aramaic words in transliterated form, including talitha cumi (Mark 5:41) and his cry from the cross, eloi eloi lama sabachthani (Mark 15:34), details that reflect the eyewitness texture of his gospel.

entries.dictNote: Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, given the greater blessing over his older brother Manasseh when their grandfather Jacob deliberately crossed his hands to bless the younger first. Ephraim's tribe became so dominant in the northern kingdom that Ephraim is often used as a poetic stand-in for the whole northern kingdom of Israel in the prophetic books.

entries.title: Ephraimite
entries.dictNote: Ephraimite designates a member of the tribe of Ephraim. The word is central to one grim episode in Judges 12, where Gilead's forces used the pronunciation of the word "shibboleth" to identify and kill fleeing Ephraimites who could not say the initial sound correctly.

entries.summary: Ephron, the name of a Canaanite and of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ephron was the Hittite from whom Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah as a burial site for Sarah, the first piece of the promised land Abraham actually owned, and it became the family tomb for Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives.

entries.title: Epicurean
entries.summary: an Epicurean or follower of Epicurus
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a follower of the philosophy founded by Epicurus, who taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and disturbance, was the chief good, and that the gods, if they existed, took no active interest in human affairs. Acts 17:18 records Epicurean philosophers debating Paul in Athens alongside Stoics after he preached about Jesus and the resurrection, part of the setting for his address on the Areopagus.
