entries.title: Eran
entries.dictNote: Eran was a son of Shuthelah and grandson of Ephraim, ancestor of the Eranite clan counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:36.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eranites
entries.summary: an Eranite or descendant (collectively) of Eran
entries.dictNote: Eranites were the clan descended from Eran, a grandson of Ephraim through Shuthelah, counted in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Erastus
entries.dictNote: Erastus was a companion of Paul and, according to Romans, held the position of city treasurer of Corinth, a detail confirmed by a first-century inscription found in Corinth naming an Erastus who paid for a public pavement in exchange for an aedileship, a civic office.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Erech
entries.dictNote: One of the cities of Nimrod's kingdom in the plain of Shinar, alongside Babel and Akkad (Gen. 10:10). It is the great Sumerian city of Uruk, modern Warka in Iraq, one of the oldest cities in the world and the probable birthplace of cuneiform writing in the late fourth millennium BC; its excavated temple precincts and monumental architecture remain among the most important archaeological witnesses to early Mesopotamian civilization.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eri
entries.dictNote: Eri was a son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family, and his descendants became the clan of the Erites counted in the wilderness census (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:16).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Erites
entries.summary: an Erite (collectively) or descendants of Eri
entries.dictNote: Erites were the clan descended from Eri, a son of Gad, counted in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Esar-haddon
entries.dictNote: Esarhaddon was the Assyrian king who succeeded Sennacherib after his assassination, and he was the one who took Judah's King Manasseh captive to Babylon, an episode confirmed by Esarhaddon's own inscriptions listing Manasseh among the vassal kings who paid him tribute.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Esau
entries.summary: Esav, a son of Isaac, including his posterity
entries.books: Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Obadiah, Malachi, Romans, Hebrews

Jacob later stole Esau's father's blessing as well, through deception, and Esau's fury forced Jacob to flee for over a decade, though the two brothers reconciled tearfully when Jacob finally returned. Esau, also called Edom, became the ancestor of the Edomites, a nation whose long hostility toward Israel runs through much of the Old Testament.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Esek
entries.dictNote: Esek is not a person but a well that Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar; the name means "contention" or "quarrel," because Philistine herdsmen from Gerar disputed Isaac's claim to the water (Genesis 26:20). It was the first of three wells dug during that dispute, the others being Sitnah and the uncontested Rehoboth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshbaal
entries.summary: Eshbaal (or Ishbosheth), a son of Saul
entries.dictNote: Eshbaal, "man of Baal," was the fourth son of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33; 9:39). He is better known by the name Ish-bosheth, "man of shame" (2 Samuel 2:8), a substitution that reflects later Israelite discomfort with the word "Baal" even inside personal names. After Saul's death, Abner made Eshbaal king over the northern tribes for a brief, troubled reign that ended in his assassination, clearing the way for David to rule over a united Israel (2 Samuel 2-4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshban
entries.dictNote: Eshban was a Horite, one of the four sons of Dishon listed among the clan chiefs of Seir in Edom's genealogy (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Eshcol
entries.summary: Eshcol, the name of an Amorite, also of a valley in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Eshcol is a name shared by a place and a person. Eshcol was an Amorite ally of Abraham who helped rescue Lot from Chedorlaomer's coalition (Genesis 14:13, 24), and the Valley of Eshcol near Hebron, likely named for him or his clan, is where the twelve spies cut the enormous cluster of grapes they carried back as proof of Canaan's fertility (Numbers 13:23-24).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Eshean
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:52). Its site is not securely identified, though some have proposed a location near Dumah, south of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshek
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Saul through Jonathan, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin's royal line (1 Chronicles 8:39).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshkalonites
entries.dictNote: Eshkalonites were the inhabitants of Ashkelon, one of the five Philistine lord-cities listed in Joshua 13:3 among the territory still unconquered when Joshua was old. Ashkelon has been extensively excavated on Israel's Mediterranean coast, uncovering both Canaanite and Philistine occupation layers, including a large Philistine cemetery discovered in the 2010s that has given archaeologists direct skeletal evidence of the Philistine population.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshtaol
entries.dictNote: Eshtaol was a town in the Shephelah of Judah later allotted to Dan (Joshua 15:33; 19:41), remembered chiefly as the place where Samson grew up and where the Spirit of the Lord first began to stir him (Judges 13:25). From here the Danites sent spies north to find territory to settle (Judges 18:2, 8, 11), and Samson was buried nearby, between Zorah and Eshtaol, in his father's tomb (Judges 16:31).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Eshtaulites
entries.summary: an Eshtaolite (collectively) or inhabitant of Eshtaol
entries.dictNote: Eshtaulites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, associated with the town of Eshtaol, the same district from which Samson's parents came and where he was first stirred by the Spirit of the Lord.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eshtemoa
entries.summary: Eshtemoa or Eshtemoh, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Eshtemoa was a priestly town in the hill country of Judah south of Hebron, allotted with its pastureland to the Kohathite priests (Joshua 21:14); David sent part of the plunder from his raid on the Amalekites to its elders as a gift for their friendship during his years as an outlaw (1 Samuel 30:28). It survives as the Palestinian village of es-Samu, where ancient ruins have been found.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Eshton
entries.dictNote: Eshton appears in the genealogy of Judah as a descendant of Chelub, credited with fathering Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash (1 Chronicles 4:11-12). The list preserves little more than these family names, likely tied to towns or clans that no longer survive.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Esli
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, listed as the son of Naggai and father of Nahum, in the line descending through Nathan rather than Solomon (Luke 3:25). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Esrom
entries.dictNote: Esrom is the Greek New Testament form of Hezron, a grandson of Judah through Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33).

witness.excerpt: Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Esther
entries.summary: The orphaned Jewish girl who becomes queen of Persia and saves her people from Haman's plot (Esther 2-9), in a book that famously never names God once. Josephus retells the whole story at length under his own chapter title — the same three names, Esther, Mordecai, Haman, in the same order.
entries.dictNote: Esther was a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai in the Persian capital of Susa who became queen after King Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes, deposed his previous wife. When the king's official Haman plotted to exterminate the Jewish people, Esther risked her life by approaching the king uninvited, and her intervention saved her people and got Haman executed on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The book that bears her name never mentions God directly, but Jews still celebrate the deliverance every year at Purim.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Esther, and Mordecai, and Haman. And how, in the reign of Artaxerxes, the whole nation of the Jews was in danger of perishing.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Etam
entries.dictNote: Etam is the name of two Judean towns. One was a village of Simeon near a rocky refuge where Samson hid in a cleft of rock after slaughtering a group of Philistines (Judges 15:8, 11); the other, near Bethlehem and Tekoa, was fortified by Rehoboam among his network of defensive cities (2 Chronicles 11:6) and sat near the springs that fed Solomon's pools and gardens.

witness.excerpt: Now when Sampson had slain many of the Philistines in the plain countrey, he dwelt at Etam: which is a strong rock of the tribe of Judah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Etham
entries.summary: Etham, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Etham was the third encampment of the Israelites after leaving Egypt, on the edge of the wilderness near the eastern fortification line known as the Wall of Egypt (Exodus 13:20; Numbers 33:6-8). From there God directed Moses to turn back toward Pi-hahiroth, a change of route intended to lure Pharaoh into pursuit (Exodus 14:1-4). Its exact location is unknown, though it lay somewhere near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ethan
entries.summary: Ethan, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ethan was renowned for wisdom in his own right, mentioned in 1 Kings as a standard of comparison Solomon's wisdom exceeded, and Psalm 89 is attributed to an Ethan the Ezrahite, possibly the same man.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ethanim
entries.summary: Ethanim, the name of a month
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the Canaanite name for the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to parts of September and October, used once in 1 Kings 8:2 to date the dedication of Solomon's temple during the feast of Tabernacles. After the Babylonian exile this month came to be called Tishri, the name that stuck in later Jewish usage.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ethbaal
entries.dictNote: King of Sidon and father of Jezebel, whose marriage to Ahab of Israel sealed a political alliance that brought Baal worship into the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:31). Josephus, drawing on the Tyrian historian Menander of Ephesus, identifies him with Ithobalus, a priest of Astarte who seized the throne of Tyre and Sidon after murdering King Pheles and reigned there for over three decades in the early ninth century BC. This Tyrian king list preserved through Josephus is one of the few extrabiblical anchors for the chronology of Phoenician kings in this period.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ether
entries.dictNote: Ether was a town in the lowland district of Judah, first listed among Judah's towns near Lachish (Josh. 15:42) and then again as one of the cities allotted to Simeon within Judah's larger territory (Josh. 19:7). Its exact site has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ethiopian
entries.dictNote: Ethiopian here refers to the treasury official of the Ethiopian queen known as the Candace, an Ethiopian eunuch whom Philip met on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza while he was reading the prophet Isaiah (Acts 8:27). Philip explained that the passage pointed to Jesus, and the official was baptized on the spot, one of the earliest signs in Acts of the gospel reaching beyond Jewish and Samaritan boundaries.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ethnan
entries.dictNote: Ethnan was one of the sons of Helah, a wife of Ashur, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:7. Ashur was the founder of Tekoa, and this brief notice is part of a longer set of family records preserving the descendants of Judah's clans. Nothing else is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ethni
entries.dictNote: Ethni was a Gershonite Levite listed in the genealogy of the musician Asaph in 1 Chronicles 6:41. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eubulus
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whose greetings Paul sends to Timothy near the end of his final letter, alongside Pudens, Linus, and Claudia (2 Timothy 4:21). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eunice
entries.dictNote: Eunice was the mother of Timothy, a Jewish believer married to a Greek man (Acts 16:1). Paul commends her sincere faith and credits her, along with Timothy's grandmother Lois, with raising him in the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Euodias
entries.summary: fine travelling; Euodia, a Christian woman
entries.dictNote: A woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul urges to "be of the same mind" as another woman, Syntyche, indicating the two had fallen into some disagreement (Philippians 4:2). Paul says both women had struggled alongside him in spreading the gospel, evidence that women held visible, active roles in the Philippian church. The King James Version's spelling "Euodias" obscures that the name is feminine in the Greek.

It served as the effective boundary of David's kingdom at its widest extent and later as a symbol of Mesopotamian imperial power, first Assyrian, then Babylonian, threatening Israel and Judah from beyond it.

entries.title: Euroklydon
entries.summary: a storm from the East (or southeast), i.e. (in modern phrase) a Levanter
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the name of the violent wind that drove Paul's ship off course near Crete on the voyage to Rome (Acts 27:14). Many manuscripts instead read Eurakylon, a Greco-Latin hybrid naming a wind roughly equivalent to what modern sailors call a gregale, a fierce northeasterly common in the eastern Mediterranean.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Eutychus
entries.summary: well- fated, i.e. fortunate; Eutychus, a young man
entries.dictNote: Eutychus was a young man at Troas who sat in a third-story window during one of Paul's late-night sermons and, overcome by drowsiness, fell asleep and dropped to the ground below, apparently dead. Paul went down, embraced him, and announced that he was alive, after which the gathering continued and shared a meal before Paul left at daybreak (Acts 20:9-12).

She was deceived by the serpent into eating fruit from the one forbidden tree, and Adam ate as well after she offered it to him, an act that brought sin and death into the world and that Paul later contrasts with the obedience of Christ.

entries.title: Evi
entries.dictNote: Evi was one of five Midianite kings, described elsewhere as princes vassal to the Amorite king Sihon, killed by Israel's forces in the war of vengeance against Midian (Numbers 31:8), and his territory is recalled among the lands allotted afterward (Joshua 13:21). The campaign was ordered in response to Midian's role in luring Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25; 31:1-2). Nothing more is known of Evi individually.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Evil-merodach
entries.dictNote: Evil-merodach, known in Babylonian records as Amel-Marduk, succeeded his father Nebuchadnezzar II as king of Babylon around 562 BC. In the year he began to reign he released the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin from prison, showed him favor, and gave him a regular place at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34). Babylonian sources confirm him as Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, though he reigned only about two years before being overthrown.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezbai
entries.dictNote: Ezbai was the father of Naarai, one of David's mighty men listed in 1 Chronicles 11:37. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezbon
entries.summary: Etsbon, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men are named Ezbon in the genealogies. One was a son of Gad, also called Ozni, who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:16; compare Numbers 26:16). The other was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, listed as a head of a family in that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:7).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezekias
entries.dictNote: Ezekias is the Greek form of Hezekiah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:9-10). Hezekiah was a reforming king of Judah who removed idolatrous shrines and survived the Assyrian king Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC, an episode corroborated outside the Bible by Sennacherib's own Prism, which boasts of shutting Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but stops short of claiming the city itself was captured.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezekiel
entries.summary: The priest-prophet exiled to Babylon whose visions open with the famous wheels-within-wheels (Ezekiel 1:3). Josephus mentions him more briefly than Jeremiah here — the honest gap in this particular chapter — but places him exactly where Scripture does: warning King Zedekiah, unheeded, right before the final fall of Jerusalem.
entries.dictNote: Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles who began prophesying five years into his captivity after a vision of God's throne, described in famously strange imagery of wheels within wheels and four living creatures. He acted out many of his prophecies physically, lying on his side for over a year to symbolize the years of Israel's sin, and his most famous vision is a valley of dry bones brought back to life, a picture of national restoration after exile.

witness.excerpt: This King would not believe what was predicted by Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezel
entries.summary: Ezel, a memorial stone in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ezel was not a person but a stone or landmark near Saul's residence in Gibeah, mentioned only in 1 Samuel 20:19 as the spot where David hid while Jonathan tested his father's intentions toward him. It marks the site of David and Jonathan's last meeting before David fled from Saul for good. The Hebrew name likely means 'departure' or 'separation,' fitting the scene it names.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezer
entries.dictNote: Ezer was a common name, borne by a chieftain of Seir, a son of Ephraim killed raiding cattle from Gath, and one of David's mighty warriors from Gad.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezer
entries.summary: Ezer, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: A different Ezer, distinct from the Seirite chieftain and Ephraimite of the same name, was a Levite who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezion-geber
entries.summary: Etsjon-Geber, a place on the Red Sea
entries.dictNote: Ezion-geber was a port city at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, near Elath, where Solomon built his fleet of ships to trade with Ophir (1 Kings 9:26) and where Jehoshaphat's ships were later wrecked (1 Kings 22:48). Archaeologist Nelson Glueck excavated the mound of Tell el-Kheleifeh in the 1930s and identified it with the site, though later reanalysis of the pottery narrowed its date range and location debates continue.

witness.excerpt: Moreover, the king built many ships in the Egyptian Bay of the Red Sea, in a certain place called Ezion-geber: it is now called Berenice, and is not far from the city Eloth.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ezra
entries.summary: The priest-scribe who leads a second return from exile and reads the Law aloud to a weeping crowd (Ezra 7-8, Nehemiah 8). Josephus's chapter on the Persian king Xerxes' favor toward the Jews is the political backdrop that makes Ezra's whole mission possible in the first place.
entries.dictNote: Two priests named Ezra appear in the Old Testament. The famous one led a second wave of exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem and is remembered as the scribe who restored the law's central place in Jewish worship after the exile, reading it aloud to the assembled people in Nehemiah 8. A different priest by the same name is listed simply among those who returned earlier under Zerubbabel.

witness.excerpt: Upon the death of Darius, Xerxes his son took the Kingdom; who, as he inherited his father's Kingdom, so did he inherit his piety towards God, and honour of him.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezrah
entries.dictNote: Ezrah was a descendant of Judah listed in 1 Chronicles 4:17 as the father of Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon, part of a genealogical unit that also names Mered's wives and descendants, some associated with Egypt. Nothing more is recorded about Ezrah himself beyond this listing of his sons.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ezrahite
entries.summary: an Ezrachite or descendant of Zerach
entries.dictNote: Ezrahite is the title given to Ethan and Heman, two wise men credited as sons of Zerah in Chronicles and named as authors in the headings of Psalms 89 and 88.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ezri
entries.dictNote: The son of Chelub, appointed overseer of the workers who farmed the royal land under David, part of the administrative list of officials Chronicles preserves for David's kingdom (1 Chr. 27:26).

entries.title: Festus
entries.dictNote: Porcius Festus was the Roman governor of Judea who succeeded Felix and held a hearing for the imprisoned Paul, ultimately sending him to Rome after Paul exercised his right as a Roman citizen to appeal directly to Caesar.

entries.title: Fortunatus

entries.title: Gaal
entries.dictNote: Gaal was an agitator who stirred up the citizens of Shechem to rebel against Abimelech's rule, but he was defeated and driven out once Abimelech brought his forces against the city.

entries.title: Gabbai
entries.dictNote: Head of a prominent family of Benjamin living in Jerusalem after the exile, listed in Nehemiah's census of the city's resettled population (Nehemiah 11:8). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gabbatha
entries.summary: the knoll; gabbatha, a vernacular term for the Roman tribunal in Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Gabbatha, an Aramaic word meaning "raised place" or "ridge," was the paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem where he set up the judgment seat and sentenced Jesus (John 19:13). John pairs it with the Greek term lithostroton, describing a mosaic or tiled stone pavement; a paved courtyard at the Antonia Fortress has been proposed as the site, though its dating to Jesus's era remains disputed among archaeologists.

entries.title: Gabriel
entries.summary: The only named archangel in Luke's infancy narrative is also one of the four archangels in Enoch's Watchers narrative — same figure, two very different documents, about two centuries apart.
entries.dictNote: Gabriel is one of only two angels named directly in the Bible, and he appears as God's messenger for major turning points: interpreting Daniel's visions of coming empires in the Old Testament, then announcing the births of both John the Baptist to Zechariah and Jesus to Mary in Luke's Gospel. He introduces himself to Zechariah simply as the one who stands in the presence of God.

entries.label: 12 books

entries.title: Gadarene
entries.summary: a Gadarene or inhabitant of Gadara
entries.dictNote: Gadarene identifies the region around Gadara, one of the cities of the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee, as the setting where Jesus healed a demon-possessed man, or two men in Matthew's account, and sent the spirits into a herd of pigs. Some manuscripts and Gospel parallels instead read Gerasene or Gergesene, reflecting the difficulty of pinning the miracle to one of several towns in the area; Gadara itself, modern Umm Qais in Jordan, preserves an impressive set of excavated Roman ruins.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaddi
entries.dictNote: The man chosen to represent the tribe of Manasseh among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout out Canaan (Numbers 13:10-11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaddiel
entries.dictNote: The representative of the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:10). Along with all his fellow spies except Caleb and Joshua, his name is not mentioned again after the report that discouraged Israel from entering the land.

entries.title: Gadi
entries.dictNote: Gadi was the father of Menahem, a king of Israel who seized the throne by assassinating Shallum and ruled with notable brutality (2 Kings 15:14, 17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gaham
entries.dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gahar
entries.dictNote: Gahar headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:47; Nehemiah 7:49).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gaius
entries.dictNote: Gaius was a common name among Paul's traveling companions and hosts, borne by at least three different men across Acts, Romans, and Paul's letters, making it difficult to know for certain which references describe the same person.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Galal
entries.summary: Galal, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Galal was a common Levitical name among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, listed in the genealogies of Chronicles and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Galatia
entries.dictNote: Galatia was a region and later Roman province in central Asia Minor, named for the Gaulish tribes who settled there after migrating from Europe in the third century BC. Rome annexed it as a province in 25 BC, and Paul addressed one of his sharpest letters to churches there, arguing against teachers who wanted Gentile believers to adopt circumcision and the Jewish law. Peter's first letter and Paul's note that Crescens had departed for Galatia (2 Timothy 4:10) show the region remained a center of early Christian activity.

witness.excerpt: And when he was dead, the people bestowed the high priesthood on Judas; who hearing of the power of the Romans, and that they had conquered in war Galatia, and Iberia, and Carthage, and Libya; and that, besides these, they had subdued Greece, and their kings, Perseus, and Philip, and Antiochus the Great also; he resolved to enter into a league of friendship with them.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Galatian
entries.summary: a Galatian or inhabitant of Galatia
entries.dictNote: Galatian designates an inhabitant of Galatia, a Roman province in central Asia Minor settled centuries earlier by migrating Celtic tribes. Paul rebukes the Galatian churches sharply for turning from the gospel of grace toward a law-based requirement of circumcision.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Galeed
entries.summary: Galed, a memorial cairn East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Galeed was not a person but the name Jacob gave to a heap of stones he and his father-in-law Laban raised in the hill country to mark a covenant of peace between them (Genesis 31:45-48). Laban called the same pile Jegar-sahadutha in Aramaic, while Jacob's Hebrew name, meaning "heap of witness," gave the surrounding region, Gilead, its lasting name.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Gallim
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, home of Palti, the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal after taking her away from David (1 Sam. 25:44). Isaiah names it among the towns thrown into panic as the Assyrian army advances on Jerusalem (Isa. 10:30).

witness.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gallio
entries.dictNote: Gallio was the Roman proconsul of Achaia who dismissed a case Corinthian Jews brought against Paul, ruling it a matter of internal Jewish religious dispute rather than a genuine legal charge. An inscription found at Delphi naming Gallio as proconsul fixes the date of this episode precisely enough to anchor the chronology of Paul's entire ministry.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gamaliel
entries.dictNote: Gamaliel was a highly respected Pharisee and legal scholar who persuaded the Jewish council to release the apostles rather than execute them, arguing that if their movement wasn't from God it would collapse on its own. He was also the teacher under whom the young Saul, later Paul, studied the law.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gammadims
entries.dictNote: The Gammadims were not an individual but a group of soldiers stationed in the towers of Tyre, mentioned alongside the men of Arvad as part of the city's military garrison in Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre (Ezekiel 27:11). Their exact identity is debated: some connect the name to a place called Gammad, while others take it simply as a Hebrew term for valiant or brave warriors.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gamul
entries.dictNote: Gamul headed the twenty-second of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized for rotating temple service (1 Chronicles 24:17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gareb
entries.summary: Gareb, the name of an Israelite, also of a hill near Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Gareb was one of David's mighty warriors, and also the name of a hill near Jerusalem mentioned in Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's future rebuilding.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Garmite
entries.dictNote: Garmite is an epithet attached to Keilah in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:19, in a passage listing descendants connected to the towns of Keilah and Eshtemoa. The meaning of the term itself is uncertain, and it is not explained elsewhere in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gatam
entries.dictNote: Gatam was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau who became one of the clan chiefs, or “dukes,” of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 16; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Like his brothers, he is remembered only as the eponymous head of an Edomite clan in the genealogical lists.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.books: Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Amos, Micah
entries.dictNote: Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities and the hometown of Goliath, whom David killed, though David himself later took refuge there with its king Achish while fleeing Saul. The ark caused disaster among the Philistines after they captured it and brought it to Gath, and David eventually conquered the city outright. It is usually identified with Tell es-Safi, where excavations have uncovered a massive siege system and a potsherd inscribed with two names philologically related to “Goliath,” evidence that such names were genuinely in use at Gath around the era described in Samuel.

entries.title: Gath-kephr
entries.dictNote: Town in Zebulun's territory (Josh. 19:13), better known as Gath-hepher, birthplace of the prophet Jonah (2 Kings 14:25). Local tradition places Jonah's tomb near the site, in the village now called Mashhad next to a hill called Nebi Yunus, close to Nazareth.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gath-rimmon. d
entries.dictNote: Gath-rimmon was a Levitical city in the territory of Dan, given to the Kohathite Levites (Joshua 19:45; 21:24). A second town of the same name appears in the list of Levitical cities within the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 21:25), but the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:70 names the town there as Bileam instead, suggesting a copying error duplicated the Danite town's name into the Manasseh list rather than two identical town names actually existing.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gaza
entries.summary: Gazah (i.e. Azzah), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: One of the five great Philistine cities and a major stop on the coastal trade route between Egypt and the Levant, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It was assigned to Judah but never fully held (Josh. 15:47; Judg. 1:18), and it is remembered as the city where a captured Samson pulled down the temple of Dagon (Judg. 16:21-30); Philip the evangelist later met the Ethiopian official on the desert road leading toward it (Acts 8:26). Egyptian records from the second millennium BC, including the Amarna letters, already name the city as an administrative center under Egyptian control, confirming its antiquity.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gazathite
entries.summary: an Azzathite or inhabitant of Azzah
entries.dictNote: Gazathite designates an inhabitant of Gaza, one of the five Philistine lordships along the coastal plain. Judges uses the term for the men of Gaza who waited at the city gate to kill Samson, only for him to tear the gate from its posts and carry it off.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gazer
entries.dictNote: Gazer is an alternate spelling of Gezer, a Canaanite royal city on the border of Philistia and Israel's central hill country that an Egyptian pharaoh captured and gave to his daughter as a dowry when she married Solomon, after which Solomon fortified it along with Hazor and Megiddo. Excavations there uncovered the Gezer Calendar, a small inscribed tablet from around the tenth century BC listing the agricultural seasons in early Hebrew script, among the oldest known Hebrew inscriptions.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Gazez
entries.summary: Gazez, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gazez is a name that appears twice within a single verse, 1 Chronicles 2:46: first as a son Caleb had by his concubine Ephah, and second as a son of Haran, who was himself Ephah's son, making the second Gazez the first one's nephew. Some read the second occurrence as a scribal repetition of the first rather than a distinct person, but the text as it stands names two.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gazzam
entries.dictNote: Gazzam's descendants, the Bene-Gazzam, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:48; Nehemiah 7:51). Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gebal
entries.dictNote: This Gebal was the great Phoenician port city the Greeks called Byblos, north of Beirut on the Lebanese coast, named in Ezekiel's oracle as the source of skilled craftsmen who caulked Tyre's ships (Ezek. 27:9). Byblos is one of the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and its excavated ruins have produced the Ahiram sarcophagus, inscribed with one of the earliest known examples of the Phoenician alphabet, as well as Bronze Age letters to Egypt in which its king begged Pharaoh for military help against invaders.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gebal
entries.dictNote: This Gebal, distinct from the Phoenician city of the same name, was a mountainous district in Edom south of the Dead Sea, still known by a related Arabic name, Jibal, in later times. It appears in Psalm 83's list of nations allied against Israel (Ps. 83:8), grouped there with Edom, Moab, and the Ishmaelites.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Geber
entries.summary: Geber, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two officials named Geber appear among Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for supplying the royal court: “the son of Geber” was stationed at Ramoth-gilead, and Geber son of Uri administered the region of Gilead itself (1 Kings 4:13, 19). Each governor supplied provisions for one month of the year, and Uri's son's territory corresponded to the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan. It is unclear whether these two references describe one man or two.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gebim
entries.dictNote: Gebim was a village just north of Jerusalem whose people are pictured fleeing as an invading army draws near, in the same poetic list of towns in Isaiah's oracle that includes Madmenah (Isa. 10:31). Its name likely comes from a Hebrew word for cisterns or pits, and it is sometimes located near the modern Jerusalem neighborhood of al-Isawiya.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedaliah
entries.summary: Gedaljah, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gedaliah was appointed governor of Judah by the Babylonians after Jerusalem's destruction, tasked with governing the peasants left behind, and he urged the remaining population to settle down and submit peacefully to Babylonian rule. A royal descendant named Ishmael assassinated him within months, and fearing Babylonian reprisal for the governor's murder, the remaining population fled to Egypt against Jeremiah's direct warning not to go.

witness.excerpt: How Nebuzaradan set Gedaliah over the Jews that were left in Judea : which Gedaliah was a little afterward slain by Ishmael .

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Gedeon
entries.dictNote: Gedeon is the Greek form of Gideon, the judge who delivered Israel from Midianite oppression with a force of three hundred men (Judges 6-8). Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the heroes of faith too numerous to describe in full, alongside Barak, Samson, and Jephthah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Geder
entries.dictNote: Geder, a Canaanite city whose king Joshua defeated during the conquest (Josh. 12:13). It is possibly identified with Gedor or Gederah, other towns in Judah's hill country, though this is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gederah
entries.summary: (with the article) Gederah, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Fortified town in the Shephelah, the lowland region of Judah (Josh. 15:36). A related genealogical note in Chronicles names potters descended from Judah's line who worked at Gederah, apparently a center of pottery production in the king's service (1 Chr. 4:23).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gederathite
entries.summary: a Gederathite, or inhabitant of Gederah
entries.dictNote: Gederathite marks Josabad, one of the Benjaminite warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul, as a native of Gederah in the Judean lowlands.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gederite
entries.summary: a Gederite, or inhabitant of Geder
entries.dictNote: Gederite marks Baal-hanan, the official David placed in charge of the royal olive and sycamore groves in the lowlands, as a native of Geder or Gederah in Judah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gederoth
entries.dictNote: Gederoth was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:41). During the reign of Ahaz it was one of several Judean towns seized by the Philistines while Judah was weakened by war with Israel and Syria (2 Chr. 28:18). Its name, meaning sheepfolds, suggests it began as a pastoral settlement.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gederothaim
entries.dictNote: Gederothaim was a town in the lowland district of Judah, listed immediately after Gederah in Joshua's territorial allotment (Joshua 15:36). The "-ayim" ending is the same dual suffix found in names like Kiriathaim, "double city," which has led some scholars to read it as "the two Gederahs" rather than an independent town, though others take it as its own settlement. Its site, if independent, is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gedor
entries.summary: Gedor, a place in Palestine; also the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gedor is a Hebrew name used for at least two places and a man in the Old Testament. It names a town in the hill country of Judah between Jerusalem and Hebron, whose founding lineage the Chronicler traces through Hur and Ephrathah (Joshua 15:58; 1 Chronicles 4:4, 18), and a second place, likely near Gerar, where a band of Simeonites drove out its peaceful, prosperous residents to make room for their flocks in the days of Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:39-41). The same name also belongs to a man in the genealogy of Benjamin connected to the family of Saul (1 Chronicles 8:31; 9:37).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gehazi
entries.dictNote: Gehazi was Elisha's servant, and after Elisha refused any payment from the healed general Naaman, Gehazi secretly chased Naaman down and lied to get silver and clothing for himself. Elisha, who somehow knew exactly what Gehazi had done even though he wasn't there, transferred Naaman's leprosy onto Gehazi and his descendants forever as punishment for the deception.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Geliloth
entries.dictNote: Geliloth marked a point on the border of the tribal territory of Benjamin, near the Jordan (Joshua 18:17). It is generally taken as another name for Gilgal in the parallel description of Judah's border at Joshua 15:7, though whether it refers to the well-known Gilgal near Jericho or a different site of the same common name (meaning "circles") is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gemalli
entries.dictNote: Father of Ammiel, the representative of the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gemariah
entries.summary: Gemarjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gemariah was a royal scribe in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll of prophecies aloud, and Gemariah's son later tried unsuccessfully to stop King Jehoiakim from burning it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gennesaret
entries.summary: Gennesaret (i.e. Kinnereth), a lake and plain in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Gennesaret refers both to a fertile plain on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and, by extension, to the lake itself, also called the Sea of Galilee or Chinnereth in the Old Testament (Matthew 14:34; Mark 6:53; Luke 5:1). The first-century historian Josephus praised the plain's exceptional fertility, describing it as supporting nearly every kind of tree and crop through most of the year. A first-century fishing boat recovered from the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar on the lakeshore in 1986 has illustrated the fishing economy the Gospels describe in this same area.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gentile
entries.summary: a Hellen (Grecian) or inhabitant of Hellas; by extension a Greek-speaking person, especially a non-Jew
entries.books: John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Colossians
entries.dictNote: Gentile is the English rendering of a Greek word meaning "nation" or "people," used throughout the New Testament for anyone who is not Jewish. Paul's letters make the status of Gentiles central to his gospel, arguing that through Christ they are grafted into God's covenant people alongside Jews without first needing to become Jews themselves, a position defended at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.

entries.title: Genubath
entries.dictNote: Son of the Edomite prince Hadad and an Egyptian princess, sister of Pharaoh's wife Tahpenes; he was raised in Pharaoh's own household alongside the royal children (1 Kings 11:20).

entries.summary: Gera, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gera was a common Benjamite name, the father of both Ehud, the left-handed judge, and Shimei, the man who cursed David during Absalom's rebellion.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Gerar
entries.dictNote: Gerar was a Philistine town and its surrounding district in the Negev, ruled by a king named Abimelech, where both Abraham and later Isaac sojourned and both, in turn, misrepresented their wives as sisters out of fear. Isaac prospered greatly at Gerar, reaping a hundredfold harvest and reopening wells his father had dug, before disputes over water led him to move on toward Beersheba. Excavations at Tel Haror in the western Negev, a leading candidate for the site, have uncovered a substantial Middle Bronze Age fortified city consistent with the patriarchal setting.

entries.title: Gergesene
entries.summary: a Gergesene (i.e. Girgashite) or one of the aborigines of Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Gergesenes, also called Gadarenes, were the inhabitants of a region east of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus cast a legion of demons out of a tormented man and into a herd of pigs that then rushed into the water and drowned.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gerizim
entries.dictNote: Mount Gerizim rises opposite Mount Ebal near Shechem in Samaria, and Moses commanded that after entering Canaan, six tribes should stand on its slopes to pronounce blessings for obedience while six tribes on Ebal pronounced curses, a ceremony Joshua carried out at the site (Deuteronomy 27:12; Joshua 8:33). Centuries later the Samaritans built their own temple on Gerizim as a rival to Jerusalem's, the practice behind the Samaritan woman's question to Jesus about the proper mountain of worship in John 4:20. Archaeological excavations on the summit have uncovered the remains of that Samaritan sacred precinct, including a large temple platform dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, confirming the site's long use as a rival cultic center to Jerusalem.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gershom
entries.summary: Gereshom, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Gershom was Moses's firstborn son, born during Moses's exile in Midian, and his name, meaning a stranger there, reflects Moses's own description of himself as a foreigner in a foreign land.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Gershon
entries.dictNote: Gershon was Levi's eldest son, and his descendants were assigned responsibility for the tabernacle's coverings, curtains, and hangings, transported by cart during Israel's wilderness travels.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Geshan
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Caleb through his son Jahdai, listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:47).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Geshem
entries.dictNote: Geshem was an Arab official who joined Sanballat and Tobiah in opposing and mocking Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Geshur
entries.dictNote: Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of Galilee where Absalom fled and lived for three years after murdering his brother Amnon, protected there by his grandfather, the local king.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Geshuri
entries.summary: a Geshurite (also collectively) or inhabitants of Geshur
entries.dictNote: Geshurites were the people of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. David married Maacah, daughter of Geshur's king Talmai, and their son Absalom fled to his grandfather's court there after murdering his half brother Amnon.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gether
entries.summary: Gether, a son of Aram, and the region settled by him
entries.dictNote: Gether is listed in the Table of Nations as one of the sons of Aram (Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17). As with the other names in this list, it most likely stands for an Aramean clan or tribal group rather than a single ancestor, and no later trace of a people by this name has been identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gethsemane
entries.summary: oil-press; Gethsemane, a garden near Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Gethsemane was not a person but an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, just across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, where Jesus often withdrew with his disciples and where he agonized in prayer the night he was betrayed and arrested (Matthew 26:36-46; John 18:1-2). The garden has been venerated at roughly this location since at least the fourth century, though the olive trees standing there today have been radiocarbon-dated to the medieval period rather than to the first century.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Geuel
entries.dictNote: Son of Machi, chosen to represent the tribe of Gad among the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan (Numbers 13:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gezrites
entries.summary: a Grizite (collectively) or member of a native tribe in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Gezrites, named alongside the Geshurites and Amalekites as targets of David's raids while he lived among the Philistines at Ziklag, are usually read as the Girzites, an otherwise unknown desert tribe in the Negev toward Egypt, rather than the inhabitants of the well-known city of Gezer in central Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Giah
entries.dictNote: Giah is named only to fix the location of the hill of Ammah, near which Joab called off his pursuit of Abner during the civil war between the houses of David and Saul (2 Samuel 2:24-28). Nothing more is known of it beyond this one topographical note, and its site has never been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gibbar
entries.dictNote: Gibbar's descendants numbered ninety-five among the family heads who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:20); the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:25 gives the family name as Gibeon instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gibbethon
entries.dictNote: Gibbethon was a Philistine city in Dan's territory that had been assigned to the Levite family of Kohath (Joshua 19:44; 21:23), though it evidently remained under Philistine control for much of Israel's history. King Nadab of Israel was besieging it when his own officer Baasha assassinated him and seized the throne (1 Kings 15:27), and a generation later King Elah met the same fate while his army was again besieging the city (1 Kings 16:15-17).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gibeah
entries.dictNote: This entity's one canonical reference, 1 Chronicles 2:49, names Gibea as a Judahite clan or settlement founded by a descendant of Caleb, in the genealogical style where Chronicles calls a clan's founder "father of" the town he settled. It should not be confused with the far better known Gibeah of Benjamin, Saul's hometown and later royal residence, site of the outrage against a Levite's concubine that nearly destroyed the tribe of Benjamin (Judges 19-20); that is a different town in a different tribal territory, even though both carry the common Hebrew word for "hill." Nothing more is recorded about this Judahite Gibea, and its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Gibeathite
entries.summary: a Gibathite, or inhabitant of Gibath
entries.dictNote: Gibeathite marks a family of Benjaminite archers and slingers, kinsmen of Saul who nonetheless joined David while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag, as natives of Gibeah, Saul's own hometown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gibeon
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Gibeon was a major Hivite city northwest of Jerusalem whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a peace treaty by posing as distant travelers, a ruse that spared them destruction but bound them to servitude in Israel's sanctuary. The city later hosted the tabernacle for years before Solomon built the temple, and it was there that Solomon offered sacrifices and received his famous dream. It was also the scene of a battle between the forces of David and Ish-bosheth. Excavations at el-Jib uncovered dozens of jar handles stamped with the name “Gibeon” in ancient Hebrew script, confirming the site's identification beyond doubt.

entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Gibeonite
entries.summary: a Gibonite, or inhabitant of Gibon
entries.dictNote: Gibeonites were the inhabitants of Gibeon, a Hivite city that secured a peace treaty with Israel in Joshua 9 by disguising themselves as travelers from a distant land. Centuries later Saul violated that treaty by killing some Gibeonites, and the resulting famine under David was only resolved by handing over seven of Saul's descendants for execution. Excavations at el-Jib, identified with biblical Gibeon, have turned up wine jar handles inscribed with the city's name, confirming the site.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Giddalti
entries.dictNote: Giddalti was one of the sons of Heman, a Levite musician in David's court. He headed one of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians organized under David to lead worship with song and instruments (1 Chronicles 25:4, 29).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Giddel
entries.summary: Giddel, the name of one of the Nethinim, also of one of 'Solomon's servants'
entries.dictNote: Giddel was the head of a family among the temple servants and, separately, among Solomon's servants, listed together among the returning exiles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gideon
entries.dictNote: Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiding Midianites when an angel found him and called him a mighty man of valor, a title Gideon immediately questioned given that his clan was the weakest in Manasseh and he was the least in his father's house. He asked God to prove the call was real with the sign of a fleece left out overnight, wet with dew while the ground stayed dry and then dry while the ground stayed wet, and God still whittled his army down from thirty-two thousand men to three hundred before letting him attack the Midianite camp with torches, trumpets, and empty jars in the middle of the night.

entries.title: Gideoni
entries.dictNote: Gideoni was the father of Abidan, the tribal leader of Benjamin during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gidom
entries.dictNote: Gidom, a site in Benjamite territory named only in Judges 20:45, marking a point along the road where the retreating Benjamite army was cut down during Israel's civil war. Its exact location between Gibeah and the rock of Rimmon is not known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gihon
entries.summary: Gichon, a river of Paradise; also a valley (or pool) near Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Gihon is a name shared by two waters in the Old Testament. It is listed as one of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, encircling the land of Cush (Genesis 2:13), a description scholars have never matched with confidence to a known river. It is also the name of Jerusalem's only natural spring, in the Kidron Valley, whose water Hezekiah rerouted underground into the city ahead of Sennacherib's siege (2 Chronicles 32:30); the resulting tunnel is still walkable today, and the Siloam Inscription carved near its outlet by Hezekiah's workmen is one of the longest surviving inscriptions from ancient Judah.

entries.title: Gilboa
entries.dictNote: Mount Gilboa is a low mountain range bordering the Jezreel Valley where the Philistines defeated Saul's army; three of Saul's sons, including Jonathan, were killed there, and Saul himself, badly wounded, took his own life rather than be captured. David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, "how the mighty have fallen," opens by cursing Gilboa's slopes to remain barren of dew and rain.

entries.dictNote: Gilead was the mountainous region east of the Jordan, bounded by Bashan to the north and Moab and Ammon to the south, split by the Jabbok river into a northern half ruled by Og and a southern half ruled by Sihon before Israel's conquest. It was allotted to Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh, and its rugged terrain made it a natural refuge, most famously for Jacob fleeing Laban and later for David fleeing Absalom. Its forests and pastures were known for balm and spices, giving rise to Jeremiah's question, “Is there no balm in Gilead?”

entries.title: Giloh
entries.dictNote: Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah southwest of Hebron (Josh. 15:51), remembered as the home of Ahithophel, David's counselor who defected to Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam. 15:12). When his advice was rejected in favor of Hushai's, Ahithophel returned to Giloh and hanged himself (2 Sam. 17:23).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Gilonite
entries.summary: a Gilonite or inhabitant of Giloh
entries.dictNote: Gilonite identifies Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor, as being from Giloh, a town in the Judean hill country. Ahithophel defected to Absalom's rebellion and gave him shrewd advice, but when it was rejected in favor of Hushai's counsel, he went home and hanged himself.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gimzo
entries.dictNote: Gimzo was a town in the Judean lowlands noted for its sycamore trees, seized along with its surrounding villages by the Philistines during the reign of the unfaithful King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18). It survives in the name of the modern village Jimzu, southeast of Lydda.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ginath
entries.dictNote: Ginath was the father of Tibni, the man whose supporters contended for the throne of Israel against Omri for four years before Omri prevailed (1 Kings 16:21-22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ginnetho
entries.dictNote: Ginnethoi was a priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, and his family is listed among the priestly houses in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Girgashite
entries.summary: a Girgashite, one of the native tribes of Canaan
entries.dictNote: Girgashites were among the Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan in Genesis 10 and are regularly listed among the nations Israel was to dispossess. Their exact territory is not clearly identified, though they are generally placed somewhere in the central hill country of western Palestine.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Gispa
entries.dictNote: Gispa was, along with Ziha, one of the overseers of the Nethinim, the temple servants who lived on the hill of Ophel in Jerusalem after the return from exile, as recorded in Nehemiah 11:21. The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and are traditionally traced back to Gibeonites and war captives assigned to that service in earlier generations. Nothing more is known of Gispa beyond this administrative role.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gittaim
entries.dictNote: Gittaim was a town, probably in Benjamin, to which the people of Beeroth fled after the assassins of Ish-bosheth were traced there (2 Samuel 4:2-3). Like Beeroth itself, it was resettled by Benjaminite families after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:33).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gittite
entries.summary: a Gittite or inhabitant of Gath
entries.dictNote: Gittite means a native of Gath, one of the five major Philistine cities. Obed-edom the Gittite kept the ark of the covenant in his house before David brought it to Jerusalem, and Ittai the Gittite led a contingent of loyal foreign troops who stood by David when Absalom rebelled.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gittith
entries.dictNote: Gittith is a musical or instrumental term appearing in the superscriptions of three psalms, possibly referring to a tune, instrument, or style associated with the Philistine city of Gath, rather than the name of a person.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gizonite
entries.summary: a Gizonite or inhabitant of Gizoh
entries.dictNote: Gizonite marks Hashem, whose sons appear among David's mighty men, as a native of Gizoh, a place otherwise unknown in the hill country of Judah; the parallel account in 2 Samuel 23:32 lists the same family under the name Jashen.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Goath
entries.dictNote: A place near Jerusalem named only in Jeremiah's vision of the city's future rebuilding, where the measuring line would run out from the hill Gareb to Goath (Jer. 31:39). Its exact location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gob
entries.dictNote: Gob was the site of two battles between David's men and Philistine champions descended from the giants of Gath, in which Sibbecai killed Saph and Elhanan killed a brother of Goliath (2 Sam. 21:18-19). The parallel account in Chronicles calls the location Gezer instead (1 Chr. 20:4), and it is unclear whether this reflects a scribal variation or two nearby sites known by different names.

entries.title: God
entries.summary: (A.S. and Dutch God; Dan. Gud; Ger. Gott), the name of the Divine Being. It is the rendering (1) of the Hebrew ’El, from a word meaning to be strong; (2) of ’Eloah_, plural _’Elohim. The singular form, Eloah, is used only in poetry. The plural form is more commonly used in all parts of the Bible, The Hebrew word Jehovah (q.v.), the only other word generally employed to denote the Supreme Being, is uniformly rendered in the Authorized Version by “LORD,” printed in small capitals. The existence of God is taken for granted in the Bible. There is nowhere any argument to prove it. He who disbelieves this truth is spoken of as one devoid of understanding (Ps. 14:1). The arguments generally adduced by theologians in proof of the being of God are: (1.) The a priori argument, which is the testimony afforded by reason. (2.) The a posteriori argument, by which we proceed logically from the facts of experience to causes. These arguments are, (a) The cosmological, by which it is proved that there must be a First Cause of all things, for every effect must have a cause. (b) The teleological, or the argument from design. We see everywhere the operations of an intelligent Cause in nature. (c) The moral argument, called also the anthropological argument, based on the moral consciousness and the history of mankind, which exhibits a moral order and purpose which can only be explained on the supposition of the existence of God. Conscience and human history testify that “verily there is a God that judgeth in the earth.” The attributes of God are set forth in order by Moses in Ex. 34:6, 7. (see also Deut. 6:4; 10:17; Num. 16:22; Ex. 15:11; 33:19; Isa. 44:6; Hab. 3:6; Ps. 102:26; Job 34:12.) They are also systematically classified in Rev. 5:12 and 7:12. God’s attributes are spoken of by some as absolute, i.e., such as belong to his essence as Jehovah, Jah, etc.; and relative, i.e., such as are ascribed to him with relation to his creatures. Others distinguish them into communicable, i.e., those which can be imparted in degree to his creatures: goodness, holiness, wisdom, etc.; and incommunicable, which cannot be so imparted: independence, immutability, immensity, and eternity. They are by some also divided into natural attributes, eternity, immensity, etc.; and moral, holiness, goodness, etc.

entries.title: Golan
entries.summary: Golan, a place east of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Golan was a city in Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, designated one of Israel's three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, where a person who killed someone accidentally could flee for protection from revenge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8). It was given to the Gershonite Levites and later gave its name to the surrounding region of Gaulanitis, the origin of the modern name Golan Heights. Its precise site has not been conclusively identified.

entries.title: Golgotha
entries.summary: the skull; Golgotha, a knoll near Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Golgotha, meaning “place of a skull” in Aramaic, was the site outside Jerusalem's walls where Jesus was crucified, known by its Latin equivalent, Calvary (Matthew 27:33; Mark 15:22; John 19:17). All four Gospels place it near a public road and close to a garden containing a tomb, yet outside the city gate, details that complicate several traditional identifications of the site. Its exact location remains debated; the traditional site under the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the rocky knoll known as the Garden Tomb both have modern advocates, though neither can be confirmed with certainty.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Goliath
entries.dictNote: Goliath was a Philistine champion from Gath, over nine feet tall by the traditional Hebrew text, though the Dead Sea Scrolls and the earliest Greek translation give a shorter reading of about six foot nine, which is why some modern translations describe him as closer to seven feet. He came from a family of giants that included his brothers Ishbi-benob and Saph, both killed later by David's men. His duel with the young David in the valley of Elah is the single scene that defines him in Scripture, and one later passage even credits a different soldier, Elhanan, with killing him, though Chronicles resolves this by making Elhanan's victim Goliath's brother instead.

entries.title: Gomorrha
entries.summary: Gomorrha (i.e. Amorah), a place near the Dead Sea
entries.dictNote: Gomorrha is the Greek form of Gomorrah, one of the cities of the plain that God destroyed with fire and sulfur alongside Sodom because of their wickedness (Genesis 19:24-25). New Testament writers invoke the memory of its destruction as a warning of certain divine judgment, whether Jesus warning towns that reject his messengers (Matthew 10:15) or Peter and Jude citing it as proof that God punishes the ungodly (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 1:7). Its exact site is unknown, though archaeologists have proposed locations near the southern end of the Dead Sea, including Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira, without any confirmed identification.

entries.title: Goshen
entries.summary: Goshen, the residence of the Israelites in Egypt; also a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Goshen was the fertile district in northeastern Egypt, along the eastern Nile delta, where Joseph settled his father Jacob and the rest of his family, and where the Israelites lived and multiplied until the exodus. Its cities Pithom and Rameses lay within its borders, and it is generally identified with the Wadi Tumilat. Two lesser places in Canaan's south also bore the name Goshen.

entries.dictNote: This form of “Greek” functions as an adjective describing the Greek language itself. It appears in the sign Pilate had placed above Jesus on the cross, written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek (John 19:20), and in the Roman tribune's surprised question to Paul in Acts 21:37 asking whether he could speak Greek, since the tribune had assumed Paul was an Egyptian agitator.

entries.dictNote: This form of the word denotes an ethnic Greek, as distinguished in the New Testament from a “Grecian,” a Greek-speaking Jew of the diaspora. Paul uses it both of Greeks by race and, more broadly, of Gentiles in general as opposed to Jews (Acts 18:17; Romans 1:14; 2:9-10), and John uses it in Revelation to note that the name Apollyon is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Abaddon (Revelation 9:11).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gudgodah
entries.summary: Gudgodah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Gudgodah appears in the wilderness itinerary of Deuteronomy 10:6-7, listed immediately after Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and before Jotbathah. It corresponds to Hor-haggidgad in the fuller itinerary of Numbers 33:32-33, and like most of the stations listed there, its precise location in the Sinai Peninsula has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Guni
entries.summary: Guni, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Guni was a son of Naphtali, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Naphtali's tribe.

witness.excerpt: He had besides by Bilhah, the handmaid of Rachel, Dan and Nephtliali; which last had four sons that followed him - Jesel, Guni, Issari, and Sellim.
And these are the names of the sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shallum, and ‘Îv.  31.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Gunites
entries.summary: a Gunite (collectively with article prefix) or descendants of Guni
entries.dictNote: Gunites were the clan descended from Guni, one of the sons of Naphtali, counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26 taken on the plains of Moab before Israel entered Canaan.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gur
entries.dictNote: An ascent near Ibleam in the Jezreel Valley, the place where the servants of Jehu overtook and mortally wounded King Ahaziah of Judah as he fled (2 Kings 9:27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Gur-baal
entries.dictNote: Gur-baal appears once, in 2 Chronicles 26:7, among the peoples God helped King Uzziah defeat, alongside the Philistines and the Meunites. Its name, "sojourn of Baal," suggests it was an Arabian settlement associated with the worship of Baal, though its exact location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Habaiah
entries.dictNote: Habaiah headed a priestly family that returned from Babylonian exile but could not produce genealogical records proving descent from Aaron. As a result its members were barred from serving as priests and from eating the priests' portion of offerings until the matter could be settled by the high priest using the Urim and Thummim, a resolution the record does not describe as ever occurring (Ezra 2:61-63; Nehemiah 7:63-65).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Habakkuk
entries.dictNote: Habakkuk was a prophet who openly questioned God, asking why he tolerated Judah's injustice and then, when told Babylon would be the instrument of judgment, asking how God could use a nation even more wicked than Judah to punish it. The book records God's answer and ends with Habakkuk choosing to trust and even rejoice in God despite having no resolution to his questions, famously declaring that the righteous will live by faith, a line Paul later builds an entire theology of salvation around.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Habazaniah
entries.dictNote: The grandfather of Jaazaniah, the Rechabite leader whom Jeremiah tested by offering wine to the wine-abstaining Rechabite clan as an object lesson in obedience (Jeremiah 35:3-6). Nothing else is recorded of Habazaniah himself.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Habor
entries.dictNote: River, and the district around it, in Assyrian territory to which the Assyrians deported the population of the northern kingdom of Israel after Samaria fell in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chr. 5:26). It is identified with the Khabur, a major tributary of the Euphrates in what is now northeastern Syria.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hachaliah
entries.dictNote: Hachaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who obtained leave to return to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls (Nehemiah 1:1; 10:1).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hachilah
entries.dictNote: The hill of Hachilah was a wilderness stronghold where David hid from Saul, and it's the site of the episode where David and Abishai snuck into Saul's camp at night and took his spear and water jug rather than kill him while he slept.

witness.excerpt: So he came to them with three thousand armed men: and upon the approach of the night he pitched his camp at a certain place called Hachilah .

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hachmoni
entries.dictNote: Hachmoni, or "the Hachmonite," is named as the father of Jehiel, a court official who attended David's sons, and as the family name behind Jashobeam, one of David's chief mighty warriors, whose immediate father was Zabdiel (1 Chronicles 11:11; 27:32).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadad
entries.summary: Hadad, the name of an idol, and of several kings of Edom
entries.dictNote: Hadad was a common name among Edomite kings and also the name of an Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, later returning as an adversary who troubled Solomon's reign.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadad-rimmon
entries.dictNote: Hadad-rimmon, a place in the plain of Megiddo named for the Syrian storm-deities Hadad and Rimmon. It became proverbial for mourning after King Josiah was fatally wounded near Megiddo and the land lamented him there (2 Chr. 35:22-25); Zechariah draws on that memory to picture Jerusalem's future grief (Zech. 12:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadadezer
entries.dictNote: Hadadezer was a powerful Aramean king David defeated in a series of campaigns that expanded Israel's territory and brought substantial tribute and captured bronze into David's kingdom.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hadar
entries.dictNote: Hadar appears twice in Edom's early history, and both times the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles calls him Hadad instead, suggesting Hadar may simply be a copying variation of that name. The first was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:30), and the second was the last of the Edomite kings listed before Israel had a monarchy, ruling from the city of Pau and married to Mehetabel (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50-51).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadashah
entries.dictNote: Hadashah, a lowland town of Judah in the district that included Lachish, its name meaning "new" (Josh. 15:37). It is not mentioned again in scripture.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadassah
entries.dictNote: Hadassah was the Hebrew name of Esther before she took the Persian name by which she became known as queen to King Ahasuerus. Orphaned young, she was raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa (Esther 2:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadid
entries.dictNote: Hadid was a town in the territory of Benjamin, grouped in the census lists with the nearby towns of Lod and Ono among the places resettled by Jews returning from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37; 11:34). It is identified with the modern site of el-Haditheh, a few miles east of Lydda.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hadlai
entries.dictNote: Hadlai was an Ephraimite and the father of Amasa, one of four Ephraimite chiefs who confronted returning Israelite soldiers and insisted that Judean captives and plunder taken in a war against Ahaz be released and cared for rather than enslaved (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). He is mentioned only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hadoram
entries.summary: Hadoram, a son of Joktan, and the tribe descended from him
entries.dictNote: Hadoram was a son of Joktan in the genealogies of Genesis, and also the name of a Syrian prince sent to congratulate David on a military victory and of Solomon's forced-labor official, stoned to death when the kingdom split under Rehoboam.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hadrach
entries.dictNote: Hadrach was not a person but a region in Syria, named as the opening target of a prophetic oracle in Zechariah 9:1, which continues on to name Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon in the same sweep. The Aramaic Zakkur Stele, an eighth-century BC inscription of King Zakkur of Hamath and Luash found in northern Syria, names his capital city Hazrach, almost certainly the same place, and describes it withstanding a siege by a coalition of Aramean kings, giving real archaeological corroboration to the place name. Its exact borders are no longer certain, but it lay in the region between Hamath and Damascus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hagab
entries.dictNote: Hagab's descendants, the Bene-Hagab, were among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:43-46). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hagaba
entries.summary: Chagaba or Chagabah, one of the Nethinim
entries.dictNote: Hagaba, called Hagabah in Nehemiah's parallel list, was the ancestral head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45; Nehemiah 7:48).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hagar
entries.dictNote: Hagar was Sarah's Egyptian servant, given to Abraham to bear a child when Sarah's own infertility made God's promise seem impossible, and she gave birth to Ishmael. After Isaac's birth, Sarah had Hagar and Ishmael sent away into the wilderness, where God met Hagar directly, promising that Ishmael too would become a great nation, and she is the only person in Genesis recorded giving God a name of her own, calling him the God who sees me.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hagarene
entries.summary: a Hagrite or member of a certain Arabian clan
entries.dictNote: The Hagrites were a nomadic people east of Gilead, likely descended from Hagar's broader family line, defeated by the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in a war recorded in Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Haggai
entries.dictNote: Haggai was a prophet who confronted the returned exiles for rebuilding their own houses while leaving God's temple in ruins, arguing that their economic struggles were a direct result of that misplaced priority. His short book is dated with unusual precision to specific months and days in 520 BC, and his preaching successfully restarted construction on the temple, which the governor Zerubbabel and high priest Joshua completed a few years later.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Haggi
entries.summary: Chaggi, an Israelite; also (patronymically) a Chaggite, or descendant of the same
entries.dictNote: Haggi was the second son of Gad and grandson of Jacob, one of the seventy who went into Egypt with the family (Genesis 46:16). He became the ancestor of the Haggite clan counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:15). Nothing else is recorded of him.

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Haggiah
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Merarite clan, listed in the genealogy of Levi's descendants who served in the temple (1 Chronicles 6:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Haggith
entries.dictNote: Haggith was one of David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, the son who tried to seize the throne while David was dying.
