entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hakkatan
entries.dictNote: Hakkatan was the father of Johanan, a leader of the family of Azgad who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hakupha
entries.dictNote: Hakupha's descendants, the Bene-Hakupha, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). Like most Nethinim family heads, nothing is known of Hakupha beyond this listing. The parallel lists in Ezra and Nehemiah preserve slightly different numbers for the returning families, reflecting the difficulty of transmitting census figures across generations of copying.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Halah
entries.dictNote: Halah was a district in Assyria, likely near Nineveh, to which the Assyrians deported Israelites from both the northern kingdom and the Transjordan tribes after conquering Samaria (2 Kings 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chronicles 5:26). Sargon II's own inscriptions boast of deporting tens of thousands of people from Samaria around 722 BC, independently confirming the mass deportation the Bible describes, even though Halah itself is known mainly from the biblical text and from later geographers who placed a district by a similar name in the same general area.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Halak
entries.dictNote: Mount Halak marked the southernmost point of the territory Joshua conquered, described as the bare mountain that rises toward Seir on the border with Edom (Josh. 11:17; 12:7). It functions in the text purely as a boundary marker, and while various barren ridges south of the Dead Sea have been suggested as its location, none is certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Halhul
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:58). Its ancient name survives almost unchanged in Halhul, a Palestinian town just north of Hebron, making it one of the relatively few biblical place names in the region still in continuous use today.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hali
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Asher, named between Helkath and Beten in the tribal allotment lists (Josh. 19:25).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hallohesh
entries.dictNote: Hallohesh was one of the leaders who set his seal on the covenant Nehemiah drew up, committing the returned exiles to obey God's law (Nehemiah 10:24). His son or descendant Shallum is also named among those who helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 3:12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ham
entries.summary: Cham, a son of Noah; also (as a patronymic) his descendants or their country
entries.dictNote: Ham was Noah's son who saw his father drunk and naked inside his tent and told his brothers instead of covering him discreetly, and when Noah woke and learned what happened, he cursed not Ham himself but Ham's son Canaan to a future of servitude. Ham's other descendants, listed in Genesis 10, became the ancestors of Egypt, Cush, and several other ancient peoples.

The Zuzim are usually identified with the Zamzummim of Deuteronomy 2:20, an earlier people later dispossessed by the Ammonites, which would place Ham somewhere in the region later known as Ammon, east of the Jordan. It is unrelated to Noah's son Ham, despite the identical English spelling.

entries.title: Haman
entries.dictNote: Haman was the Persian king's highest official, and his rage at Mordecai's refusal to bow to him escalated into a plot to exterminate the entire Jewish population of the empire on a single day. Queen Esther's intervention exposed the plot, and Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai, with his ten sons later executed as well.

entries.dictNote: Hamath was the capital of an Aramean kingdom on the Orontes River in Upper Syria, marking the traditional northern boundary of the land promised to Israel. Its king Toi allied with David, and centuries later Assyria conquered the city, deported part of its population to Samaria after Israel's fall, and crushed a revolt there under a rebel named Yahu-bihdi. Excavations at the site, modern Hama, uncovered Hittite hieroglyphic inscriptions carved into building stones, evidence that the city had earlier been under Hittite cultural influence; these “Hamath stones” helped nineteenth century scholars begin deciphering Luwian hieroglyphic script.

entries.label: 13 books

entries.title: Hamath-Dor
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city of Naphtali assigned to the Gershonite clan (Joshua 21:32). It is usually taken as the same town as Hammath, a hot-springs site near the Sea of Galilee close to Tiberias; the parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6:76 gives this town's name as Hammon instead, showing the same site circulating under at least three spellings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamath-Zobah
entries.dictNote: Hamath-zobah is not a person but a fortified city or region that Solomon captured and rebuilt as a store city (2 Chronicles 8:3). Its exact location is disputed; some identify it with Hamath on the Orontes River, while others take it as a separate Aramean stronghold associated with the kingdom of Zobah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamathite
entries.summary: a Chamathite or native of Chamath
entries.dictNote: Hamathites descended from Canaan and were named for Hamath, a major city on the Orontes River in Syria that repeatedly marked Israel's northern border in the Old Testament. Hamath's king Toi sent gifts to congratulate David on defeating a common enemy, and Assyrian records name Hamath's later king Irhuleni as part of the coalition, including Ahab of Israel, that fought Shalmaneser III at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hammath
entries.dictNote: Hammath was one of the fortified towns allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee (Josh. 19:35). Its name means hot springs, and it is identified with the thermal baths still found just south of Tiberias, a site known in Roman times as Hammat Tiberias, where excavations have uncovered an ancient synagogue with an elaborate zodiac mosaic floor.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hammedatha
entries.dictNote: Hammedatha was Haman's father, identified in the book of Esther by the title the Agagite, possibly linking his family to the ancient Amalekite royal line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hammoleketh
entries.dictNote: A woman of the tribe of Manasseh, sister of Gilead and mother of Abiezer, Ishod, and Mahalah, named in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 7:17-18. Her name means "the queen," though nothing further is recorded of any royal role.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hammon
entries.summary: Chammon, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Hammon refers to two separate towns in the Old Testament: one in the territory of Asher near Sidon (Joshua 19:28), likely identified with modern Umm el-Amoud, and a Levitical city assigned to the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chronicles 6:76), probably the same place as Hammath near the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 19:35). The name, meaning “warm” or “hot spring,” likely reflects a nearby thermal spring, a natural feature found along both stretches of coast and lakeshore in the region.

witness.excerpt:

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hamon-gog
entries.summary: the multitude of Gog; the fanciful name of an emblematic place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Symbolic name, meaning "multitude of Gog," for a valley in Ezekiel's apocalyptic vision where the defeated armies of Gog would be buried, so thickly filled with graves that it would take Israel seven months to clear the land of bodies (Ezek. 39:11-15). It represents a future scene of judgment rather than a known geographic site.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamonah
entries.dictNote: Hamonah is not a person but a symbolic name, meaning "multitude," that Ezekiel assigns to the site in Israel where the defeated hordes of Gog would be buried, so numerous that a whole valley would be renamed for them (Ezekiel 39:11-16). The prophecy pictures the burial taking seven months and the valley being renamed the Valley of Hamon-gog, with a nearby city called Hamonah standing as a permanent marker of the event. Like Hamon-gog, the name functions within Ezekiel's vision of judgment rather than naming an actual place already on the map in his day.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamor
entries.dictNote: Hamor was the Canaanite ruler of Shechem whose son raped Jacob's daughter Dinah, and his attempt to negotiate a peaceful marriage settlement ended in a massacre when Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi tricked the city's men into circumcision and slaughtered them while they were incapacitated.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hamuel
entries.dictNote: Hamuel was a Simeonite listed in 1 Chronicles 4:26 among the descendants of Shaul, within the tribal genealogy of Simeon. No other information about him survives.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamul
entries.dictNote: Hamul was a son of Perez, Judah's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted in Judah's tribal genealogy.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hamulites
entries.summary: a Chamulite (collectively) or descendants of Chamul
entries.dictNote: Hamulites were the clan descended from Hamul, a grandson of Judah through Pharez, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hamutal
entries.dictNote: Hamutal was one of King Josiah's wives and the mother of two kings of Judah, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, who both reigned after their father's death.

witness.excerpt: He reigned in Jerusalem: and his mother was Hamutal , of the city Libnah.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hanameel
entries.dictNote: Hanamel was Jeremiah's cousin, and Jeremiah's purchase of Hanamel's field in Anathoth, even as Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem, was a deliberate prophetic sign that Judah would one day be restored and land would again be bought and sold normally.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hananeel
entries.summary: Chananel, probably an Israelite, from whom a tower of Jerusalem was named
entries.dictNote: The Tower of Hananeel was a fortification along Jerusalem's northern wall, mentioned by Nehemiah among the sections rebuilt and by Zechariah and Jeremiah as a landmark in prophecies about the city's future.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hanani
entries.summary: Chanani, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hanani was a common Old Testament name, borne by a prophet who confronted King Asa for relying on a foreign alliance instead of God, and by Nehemiah's own brother, who first brought him the news of Jerusalem's ruined walls that prompted his return.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Hananiah
entries.summary: Chananjah, the name of thirteen Israelites
entries.books: 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Daniel
entries.dictNote: Hananiah was a false prophet who publicly contradicted Jeremiah, breaking a wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck to symbolize Judah's coming freedom from Babylon within two years. Jeremiah returned with a message that God would replace the wooden yoke with an iron one, and predicted Hananiah would die within the year for prophesying rebellion God had not authorized, a prediction fulfilled two months later.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Hanes
entries.dictNote: Hanes was an Egyptian city named in Isaiah's warning against Judah's envoys seeking an alliance with Egypt (Isa. 30:4). It is generally identified with Herakleopolis Magna, known in Egyptian as Henen-nesut, near modern Ihnasiya el-Medina south of Cairo, an ancient regional capital with its own long dynastic history.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hannah
entries.dictNote: Hannah was Elkanah's beloved but childless wife, tormented by her husband's other wife Peninnah for her infertility, and she prayed so fervently and silently at the tabernacle at Shiloh that the priest Eli initially mistook her for drunk. God answered her vow with the birth of Samuel, whom she dedicated to the Lord's service as soon as he was weaned, and her prayer of thanksgiving in 1 Samuel 2 anticipates themes and language that echo later in Mary's song in Luke.

witness.excerpt: Elcanah, a Levite, one of a middle condition among his fellow citizens; and one that dwelt at Ramathaim, a city of the tribe of Ephraim, married two wives, Hannah and Peninnah.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hannathon
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee (Joshua 19:14). It is widely identified with Tell el-Bedeiwiyeh in the Beth-netofa valley, and a town of the same name, Hinnatuna, appears in the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters as a garrison town fought over along a key route through Galilee, giving this minor biblical town a genuine extrabiblical attestation centuries before Joshua's conquest narrative.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hanniel
entries.summary: Channiel, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Hanniel appear in the Pentateuch and Chronicles. One was a chief of the tribe of Manasseh whom Moses appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:23). The other was a chief of the tribe of Asher, listed among mighty warriors and heads of families (1 Chronicles 7:39-40).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hanochites
entries.summary: a Chanokite (collectively) or descendants of Chanok
entries.dictNote: Hanochites were the clan descended from Hanoch, the eldest son of Reuben, counted in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hanun
entries.summary: Chanun, the name of an Ammonite and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hanun was the Ammonite king who humiliated David's envoys of condolence by shaving off half their beards and cutting their garments short, an insult that triggered a full-scale war between Israel and the combined forces of Ammon and its Aramean allies.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Haphraim
entries.dictNote: Haphraim was a town of Issachar named near Shunem in Joshua's allotment list (Joshua 19:19). It is tentatively identified with the village of el-Afuleh in the Jezreel Valley, near ancient Shunem, though the identification rests mainly on geographic fit rather than direct evidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hara
entries.dictNote: A region of Assyria, apparently along the Khabur River between the Tigris and Euphrates, to which the Assyrians deported members of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (1 Chr. 5:26). Assyrian royal annals from Tiglath-pileser III independently record the mass deportation of Israelite populations from Transjordan, corroborating the biblical account of this resettlement policy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Haradah
entries.summary: Charadah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Haradah, meaning fright or fear, was the twenty-fifth stop in Israel's wilderness itinerary, mentioned only in Numbers 33:24-25. Its location is unknown and nothing beyond its name and place in the list has survived.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hararite
entries.summary: Hararite, meaning roughly "the mountaineer," identifies three of David's mighty men, including Shammah son of Agee, remembered for single-handedly defending a field of lentils against a Philistine raiding party.
entries.dictNote: Hararite, meaning roughly "the mountaineer," identifies three of David's mighty men, including Shammah son of Agee, remembered for single-handedly defending a field of lentils against a Philistine raiding party.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Harbona
entries.summary: Charbona or Charbonah, a eunuch of Xerxes
entries.dictNote: Harbona was one of seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus of Persia and was sent to summon Queen Vashti to the king's banquet (Esther 1:10). He reappears at the story's climax, pointing out to the king the gallows Haman had built for Mordecai, which Haman was then hanged on himself (Esther 7:9).

witness.excerpt: 9 [ The eunuch Sabuchadas :] Harbonah, Heb.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hareph
entries.dictNote: Listed in the genealogy of Judah as a son of Hur and "father," meaning founder, of Beth-gader (1 Chr. 2:51). Like most names in this chapter he functions as an eponym marking a town's founding clan rather than a fully narrated individual.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harhaiah
entries.dictNote: Father of Uzziel, one of the goldsmiths who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's wall near the Old Gate under Nehemiah's rebuilding project (Nehemiah 3:8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harhas
entries.dictNote: Harhas was the grandfather of Shallum, keeper of the king's wardrobe, whose wife Huldah the prophetess was consulted after the book of the law was discovered during Josiah's temple repairs (2 Kings 22:14). The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 34:22 spells the name Hasrah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harhur
entries.dictNote: Harhur's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). His name means “fever” or possibly “inflammation.” Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Harim
entries.dictNote: Harim was a common priestly family name in the postexilic period, listed among those who returned from exile and later among those confronted by Ezra for marrying foreign wives against the law.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hariph
entries.summary: Chariph, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hariph was the ancestral head of a family, also called Jorah, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel; his name appears both among the list of returnees and among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:24; 10:19; compare Ezra 2:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harnepher
entries.dictNote: A chief of the tribe of Asher listed among the sons of Zophah in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 7:36. Nothing beyond the name survives; he belongs to the long catalogue of tribal heads Chronicles preserves to anchor Israel's clan structure after the exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harodite
entries.summary: a Charodite, or inhabitant of Charod
entries.dictNote: Harodite identifies Shammah and Elika, two of David's mighty men, as being from Harod, likely the spring near Mount Gilboa where Gideon earlier tested his troops before facing the Midianites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harorite
entries.dictNote: Harorite marks Shammoth among the roll of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:27; the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:25 gives the same warrior's name as Shammah the Harodite, tying him to En-harod, the spring near Mount Gilboa where Gideon had once tested his troops.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harosheth
entries.dictNote: Fortified town on the northern edge of the plain of Jezreel, home base of Sisera, the Canaanite general who commanded Jabin's iron chariots (Judges 4:2). Barak's forces routed Sisera's army at the Kishon River and pursued the survivors back to Harosheth, breaking Canaanite power in the region (Judges 4:13-16). Its exact site is debated, with candidates ranging from a fortress near the Kishon's outlet at the foot of Mount Carmel to a district name covering several Canaanite settlements rather than a single town.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harsha
entries.dictNote: Harsha, whose name means “worker” or possibly “enchanter,” headed a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:52; Nehemiah 7:54). The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and were likely descended from Gibeonites and war captives assigned to that service centuries earlier. Nothing more is recorded of him personally.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Harum
entries.dictNote: Harum was a descendant of Judah named in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:8 as the father of Aharhel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Harumaph
entries.dictNote: The father of Jedaiah, one of the men who helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall opposite his own house after the return from exile (Neh. 3:10). He is named only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Haruphite
entries.summary: a Charuphite or inhabitant of Charuph (or Chariph)
entries.dictNote: Haruphite identifies Shephatiah, a Benjamite archer and slinger, as being from Hariph; he was among the warriors who joined David at Ziklag while David was still hiding from Saul.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Haruz
entries.dictNote: Haruz was the father of Meshullemeth, who became the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of King Amon; he is identified as being from Jotbah (2 Kings 21:19). He is mentioned only in this one royal genealogical notice.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hasadiah
entries.dictNote: Hasadiah was one of the sons of Pedaiah listed in 1 Chronicles 3:20, part of the royal genealogy of David traced through Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. Nothing else about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hasbadana
entries.dictNote: Hasbadana was one of the men who stood beside Ezra on the wooden platform built for the public reading of the law after the return from exile (Nehemiah 8:4). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hasenuah (including the art)
entries.summary: pointed; (used with the article as a proper name) Senuah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hasenuah, whose Hebrew name includes the definite article (“the Senuah”), was an ancestor of a Benjamite family that resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:7; Nehemiah 11:9).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hashabiah
entries.summary: Chashabjah, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hashabiah was a common Levitical name, borne by several temple musicians, officials, and administrators across different generations in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Hashabnah
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders who sealed the covenant of renewed obedience to the law that Nehemiah led the returned exiles to affirm (Nehemiah 10:25-26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hashabniah
entries.summary: Chashabnejah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hashabniah was the name of two men in Nehemiah's time. One was the father of Hattush, who helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 3:10). The other was a Levite who joined in leading Israel's public confession and prayer after the wall's completion (Nehemiah 9:4-5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hashem
entries.dictNote: Hashem was a Gizonite whose sons are named among David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:34. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:32 gives the name differently, as Jashen, reflecting the textual variants common between these two overlapping rosters.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hashmonah
entries.summary: Chasmonah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Hashmonah was one of the stations on Israel's wilderness route, coming shortly before Moseroth in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:29-30), in the general vicinity of Mount Hor. Its name may relate to fruitfulness or fatness, though nothing further is recorded about it and its location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hashub
entries.summary: Chashshub, the name of two or three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hashub was a common postexilic name among those who helped repair sections of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hashubah
entries.dictNote: Hashubah was a descendant of David through Zerubbabel's line, one of several sons listed after Zerubbabel in the royal genealogy compiled after the exile (1 Chr. 3:19-20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hashum
entries.summary: Chashum, the name of two or three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hashum was the head of a family among the returning exiles, listed among those who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hashupha
entries.dictNote: Hashupha, also spelled Hasupha, headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile in the first group led by Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43; Nehemiah 7:46). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hasrah
entries.dictNote: Keeper of the sacred vestments in the temple and husband of Huldah the prophetess, whom King Josiah's officials consulted after the Book of the Law was discovered (2 Chronicles 34:22); the parallel account in 2 Kings 22:14 gives his name as Harhas.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hatach
entries.dictNote: Hathach was a eunuch assigned to attend Queen Esther, and he served as the go-between carrying messages from Esther to Mordecai during the crisis over Haman's plot to destroy the Jews.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hatipha
entries.dictNote: Hatipha headed a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:54; Nehemiah 7:56).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hatita
entries.dictNote: Hatita headed a family of temple gatekeepers whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 7:45).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hattil
entries.dictNote: Hattil headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," temple workers whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:57; Nehemiah 7:59). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hattush
entries.summary: Chattush, the name of four or five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hattush was a descendant of David who returned from Babylonian exile with Ezra, keeping the royal line represented among those who came back to Jerusalem.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hauran
entries.summary: Chavran, a region East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Hauran, cave-land, was the fertile eastern district of Bashan named in Ezekiel's description of Israel's future boundaries (Ezekiel 47:16, 18). The region, known to the Greeks and Romans as Auranitis, is centered on the city of Bosra and is noted for its dense, well-preserved basalt architecture; the Nabateans who controlled the area before Rome annexed it in AD 106 left monumental remains there comparable to those at Petra, confirming the district's long-standing prosperity as a crossroads of Arabian trade routes.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Havilah
entries.summary: Chavilah, the name of two or three eastern regions; also perhaps of two men
entries.dictNote: Havilah is named in Genesis as a land rich in gold near the garden of Eden's rivers, and the name also appears among the descendants of both Cush and Joktan, suggesting it may refer to more than one region.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hazael
entries.dictNote: Hazael was a Syrian official whom the prophet Elijah was told to anoint as the next king of Aram, and Elijah wept when he predicted the atrocities Hazael would commit against Israel. Hazael smothered his own king to death to take the throne and spent decades afterward as one of Israel's most destructive enemies, and an inscription bearing his name has been found at his own capital, Damascus, independently confirming his reign.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Hazaiah
entries.dictNote: Hazaiah was a man of Judah from the Shilonite clan, descended from Shelah, listed among those who settled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:5). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-addar
entries.dictNote: Hazar-addar, a point on Israel's southern boundary in the Negev near Kadesh-barnea, listed among the wilderness border markers of the promised land (Num. 34:4). The same site appears as Addar in Joshua 15:3.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-enan
entries.dictNote: Village named as a landmark on the northeastern frontier of the promised land in Moses' description of Israel's borders (Num. 34:9-10), and again on the northern boundary of Ezekiel's vision of a restored Israel (Ezek. 47:17; 48:1). Its name means "village of springs," and it likely lay somewhere in the Anti-Lebanon range near Damascus, though the exact site has not been identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hazar-enon
entries.dictNote: A landmark village on the northern boundary of Israel's territory, marking the meeting point of the borders of Damascus and Hamath in the tribal boundary lists (Num. 34:9; Ezek. 47:17). Its name means village of springs, but its precise location has not been recovered.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-gaddah
entries.dictNote: Hazar-gaddah was one of the towns in the southernmost district of Judah's tribal allotment, near the border with Edom (Joshua 15:27). Nothing more is recorded of it, and its site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-hatticon
entries.dictNote: Hazar-hatticon, a "middle village" marking part of Israel's future northern boundary in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, located near Hamath toward the region of Hauran (Ezek. 47:16).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-shual
entries.dictNote: Hazar-shual, "village of the jackal," was a town on the southern border of Judah, later included within Simeon's allotment (Joshua 15:28; 19:3). Its residents returned there after the Babylonian exile, according to the settlement list in Nehemiah 11:27. It is commonly identified with a site near Tell es-Sa'weh, between Beersheba and Moladah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Hazar-susah
entries.dictNote: A town on the southern border of Judah assigned to Simeon, its name meaning village of the horse (Josh. 19:5). It is listed among Solomon's chariot cities in 2 Chronicles 1:14, fitting a name tied to horses.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazar-susim
entries.dictNote: A Simeonite town in the Negev whose name means village of horses, listed in the genealogical record of Simeon's clans (1 Chr. 4:31). It corresponds to Hazar-susah in Joshua 19:5.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazarmaveth
entries.dictNote: Hazarmaveth is listed in the Table of Nations as a son of Joktan, part of the Arabian branch of Shem's descendants (Gen. 10:26; 1 Chr. 1:20). The name is preserved almost unchanged in Hadramawt, a region of southern Arabia in modern Yemen, known in antiquity for its role in the frankincense and spice trade routes.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hazelelponi
entries.dictNote: Hazelelponi was a woman named in the genealogy of Judah as the sister of the sons of Etam (1 Chronicles 4:3). Nothing further is recorded about her.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazeroth
entries.dictNote: Hazeroth was the third campsite of the Israelites after leaving Sinai, in the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 33:17-18). It was here that Miriam and Aaron challenged Moses's authority over his marriage to a Cushite woman, and Miriam was struck with a skin disease until Moses interceded for her healing (Numbers 12:1-15).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hazezon-tamar
entries.dictNote: Amorite town by the Dead Sea attacked by the coalition of eastern kings under Chedorlaomer in Abraham's day (Gen. 14:7), later known by the name En-gedi. The older name resurfaces generations later when a coalition of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites invades Judah during Jehoshaphat's reign, approaching from this same location (2 Chr. 20:2).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Haziel
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Gershonite clan, descended through Shimei, listed among those organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 23:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazo
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his wife Milcah, listed among the Aramean clans descended from him (Genesis 22:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hazor
entries.summary: Chatsor, the name (thus simply) of two places in Palestine and of one in Arabia
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Hazor was the largest and most powerful Canaanite city-state in the region, and Joshua's destruction of it, described as the head of all the Canaanite kingdoms, was the decisive victory of the northern campaign. Excavations at the site have uncovered a massive Bronze Age city consistent with the biblical description of its scale.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heber
entries.summary: Cheber, the name of a Kenite and of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Heber was a common Old Testament name, most notably a Kenite whose wife Jael killed the fleeing Canaanite general Sisera in her tent, fulfilling Deborah's prophecy that a woman would receive the credit for his death.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Heberites
entries.summary: a Chebrite (collectively) or descendants of Cheber
entries.dictNote: Heberites were the clan descended from Heber, a grandson of Asher through Beriah, counted in the Numbers 26 census.

entries.summary: Chebron, a place in Palestine, also the name of two Israelites
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Hebron is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, sitting in the hill country south of Jerusalem and known earlier as Kirjath-arba. Abraham camped nearby at Mamre and bought the cave of Machpelah there to bury Sarah, and the site remained associated with the patriarchs; Herod's massive stone enclosure over the traditional tomb still stands as one of the best preserved ancient structures in the region. Joshua assigned the city to Caleb, and centuries later David reigned there for seven years before moving his capital to Jerusalem. The same Hebrew name also belongs to a son of Kohath the Levite and to a descendant of Caleb listed in Chronicles.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hebronites
entries.dictNote: Hebronites were a Kohathite Levitical clan descended from Hebron, one of Kohath's sons, distinct from the city of the same name. Under David they were given administrative duties over Israelite territory west of the Jordan and oversight of temple related treasuries.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hegai
entries.summary: Hege or Hegai, a eunuch of Xerxes
entries.dictNote: Hegai was the eunuch in charge of King Ahasuerus's harem at Susa who managed the young women, including Esther, brought in for the king's consideration (Esther 2:8). He took a particular liking to Esther and gave her preferential treatment, cosmetics, servants, and the best place in the harem, which likely improved her chances of being chosen queen (Esther 2:9, 15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helah
entries.dictNote: Helah was one of two wives of Ashur, the Chronicler's founder of Tekoa, listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:5, 7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helam
entries.summary: Chelam, a place East of Palestine
entries.dictNote: Helam was a location east of the Jordan where David's army, under Joab, decisively defeated the Aramean forces of Hadadezer, commanded by Shobach, ending Aramean support for the Ammonites in that war (2 Samuel 10:15-18). Its exact site has not been identified, though some have proposed a location near the upper Euphrates.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helbah
entries.dictNote: This entry's canonical reference, Ezekiel 27:18, actually names Helbon rather than Helbah: in the prophet's list of Tyre's trading partners, Damascus supplies wine of Helbon along with white wool. Helbon is usually identified with the village of Halbun in the hills northwest of Damascus, a region whose wine, according to the Greek geographer Strabo, was prized enough for the Persian kings to import it. It should not be confused with the Helbah of Asher mentioned in Judges 1:31.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helbah
entries.dictNote: Helbah was a town assigned to the tribe of Asher, one of the Canaanite towns Asher failed to drive its inhabitants out of, according to Judges 1:31. It lay somewhere in the coastal plain of Phoenicia and has not been securely identified with a modern site.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heldai
entries.summary: Cheldai, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men in the Old Testament carry this name. The first, a Netophathite also called Heleb or Heled, was one of David's thirty mighty men and commanded the army division on duty in the twelfth month (2 Samuel 23:29; 1 Chronicles 27:15). The second was one of a group of exiles who returned from Babylon bringing gold and silver, from which the prophet Zechariah was told to make a crown for Joshua the high priest as a sign of the coming Messianic king-priest (Zechariah 6:10-11).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Heleb
entries.dictNote: One of David's thirty mighty men, listed as the son of Baanah the Netophathite (2 Sam. 23:29). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:30 gives his name as Heled; nothing else about him is recorded beyond his place in this roster of elite warriors.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heled
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men, listed among the thirty elite warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:30. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:29 calls him Heleb son of Baanah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helek
entries.dictNote: Helek was a descendant of Manasseh through Gilead, head of the Helekite clan counted in the wilderness census and later allotted land in Gilead (Numbers 26:30; Joshua 17:2). Nothing further is recorded of him individually.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Helem
entries.summary: Helem, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Asher, listed in the tribal genealogy as a great-grandson through the line of Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helem
entries.dictNote: Helem appears in Zechariah's vision as one of the returned exiles whose silver and gold the prophet was told to use for a crown for the high priest Joshua, a sign pointing to the coming messianic "Branch" (Zechariah 6:9-14). Verse 10 calls the same man Heldai, so Helem is likely an alternate form of that name rather than the earlier Asherite of the same name in 1 Chronicles 7:35.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heleph
entries.dictNote: Heleph marked the starting point of Naphtali's tribal boundary in the list recorded at Joshua 19:33. The Hebrew name means exchange or substitution, but the site itself has never been securely identified on the ground, and the text gives no further detail about it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helez
entries.summary: Chelets, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Helez was one of David's mighty warriors, and also, separately, the name of a descendant of Judah in the genealogies of Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Heli
entries.dictNote: Named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Joseph (Luke 3:23), though Matthew's genealogy names Jacob as Joseph's father instead. Since antiquity, readers have proposed that Luke traces Mary's ancestry through Heli while Matthew traces Joseph's, or that the two lists reflect a levirate marriage; the discrepancy is old and remains unresolved. Nothing else concerning Heli is recorded in scripture.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helkai
entries.dictNote: Helkai was the head of a priestly family in the days of the high priest Joiakim, listed in Nehemiah's roster of priests who had returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:15). The list documents the reconstituted priestly courses functioning in the early Second Temple period. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helkath
entries.dictNote: Town allotted to the tribe of Asher and assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh. 19:25; 21:31). A parallel list in Chronicles calls the same town Hukok (1 Chr. 6:75).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helkath-hazzurim
entries.summary: Chelkath Hats-tsurim, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: The site near the pool of Gibeon where twelve of Joab's men and twelve of Abner's men killed each other in mutual single combat, an episode that touched off a larger battle between the forces of David and Saul's son Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:16). The name means roughly "field of daggers" or "field of sword-edges."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helkites
entries.summary: a Chelkite or descendant of Chelek
entries.dictNote: Helkites were the clan descended from Helek, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted among the families that received an inheritance in the land.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Helon
entries.dictNote: Helon was the father of the tribal leader of Zebulun during the wilderness census.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hemam
entries.dictNote: Son of Lotan and grandson of Seir the Horite, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:22), called Homam in the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:39.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heman
entries.summary: Heman, the name of at least two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Heman was a Levite and one of the chief musicians David appointed over temple worship, credited as the author of Psalm 88, one of the darkest and most unresolved laments in the Psalter.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Hemdan
entries.dictNote: Eldest son of Dishon, one of the Horite clan chiefs descended from Seir who inhabited the land before it was taken by Esau's descendants, the Edomites (Genesis 36:20-26). He appears only in this genealogical list; the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:41 gives the name as Hamran.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hen
entries.summary: Chen, a figurative name for an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Hen son of Zephaniah is named in Zechariah 6:14 as one of the men in whose honor a symbolic crown was placed in the temple as a memorial, part of Zechariah's prophetic sign-act pointing to the coming Branch. He is probably the same man called Josiah son of Zephaniah earlier in the same chapter (Zechariah 6:10), though the text does not explain the second name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hena
entries.summary: Hena, a place apparently in Mesopotamia
entries.dictNote: Hena was a city in Mesopotamia that the Assyrian king listed among the places his empire had already conquered when his messenger tried to intimidate Hezekiah into surrendering Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13; Isaiah 37:13). It is usually identified with Anah, a town on the Euphrates not far from Sepharvaim, another city named in the same list.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Henadad
entries.dictNote: Henadad was the head of a Levitical family who helped oversee the rebuilding of both the temple under Zerubbabel and, a generation later, Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hepher
entries.summary: Chepher, a place in Palestine; also the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hepher was a son of Gilead in Manasseh and father of Zelophehad, whose five daughters successfully petitioned Moses for the right to inherit their father's land in the absence of a son, a case that established a lasting principle of inheritance law in Israel. Separately, Hepher was a Canaanite royal city that Joshua conquered; it later gave its name to a district in Solomon's administrative system. The name also belonged to one of Asher's descendants and to one of David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Hepherites
entries.summary: a Chephrite (collectively) or descendants of Chepher
entries.dictNote: Hepherites were the clan descended from Hepher, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted in the Numbers 26 census; his son Zelophehad's five daughters successfully petitioned Moses for a share of the tribal inheritance despite having no brothers.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hephzi-bah
entries.summary: Cheptsi-bah, a fanciful name for Palestine
entries.dictNote: Hephzibah, meaning "my delight is in her," was the wife of King Hezekiah of Judah and mother of his son Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1). Isaiah later uses the same name as a symbolic title for restored Jerusalem, picturing the city as once again the object of God's delight rather than an abandoned wife (Isaiah 62:4).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Heres
entries.dictNote: Heres, meaning sun, names a hill-country location associated with the Amorites, who held Mount Heres along with Aijalon and Shaalbim until the house of Joseph subdued them (Judg. 1:35). The same name recurs as the ascent of Heres, a route Gideon took while returning from his pursuit of the Midianite kings (Judg. 8:13); whether the two references describe the same feature or two different places sharing the name is not certain from the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heresh
entries.dictNote: A Levite listed among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, one of the temple gatekeepers descended from the guild of singers (1 Chronicles 9:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hereth
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a forest in Judah where David hid with his growing band of followers, shortly after he had placed his parents under the protection of the king of Moab and before the prophet Gad advised him to move on (1 Sam. 22:5). Its exact location is unknown today.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hermas
entries.dictNote: A Roman Christian greeted by Paul in Romans 16:14. Later Christian tradition sometimes credited him with writing the second-century work The Shepherd of Hermas, but that book was almost certainly written a generation or more later by a different Hermas.

entries.title: Hermes
entries.summary: Hermes, the name of the messenger of the Greek deities; also of a Christian
entries.dictNote: Hermes, sharing his name with the Greek messenger god, was a Roman Christian Paul greets among a list of believers in Rome at the end of his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:14). entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hermogenes
entries.summary: born of Hermes; Hermogenes, an apostate Christian
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Asia Minor whom Paul names, along with Phygellus, as one who deserted him, part of a wider abandonment Paul laments in 2 Timothy 1:15. He contrasts their desertion with the loyalty of Onesiphorus, mentioned in the very next verse.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hermon
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon
entries.dictNote: Mount Hermon is a prominent peak on Israel's northern border, likely the traditional site of Jesus's transfiguration given its proximity to Caesarea Philippi, and its abundant snowmelt is a recurring image in the Psalms for refreshing dew.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Herod
entries.summary: Luke's Herod (Antipas, the tetrarch who mocks Jesus in 23:7-15) is Herod the Great's son, not the dying king in this passage — but it's the same dynasty, and Josephus's account of the father's final illness is one of the most infamous death scenes in ancient historiography, read by generations as divine judgment on the family.
entries.dictNote: Several different rulers named Herod appear across the New Testament, all from the same Roman-appointed dynasty. Herod the Great, king when Jesus was born, ordered the massacre of infant boys in Bethlehem after failing to trick the magi into revealing the child's location. His son Herod Antipas ruled Galilee during Jesus's ministry, beheaded John the Baptist for condemning his marriage, and briefly interrogated Jesus before his crucifixion. A grandson, Herod Agrippa the First, executed the apostle James and imprisoned Peter, and Agrippa's own son, Herod Agrippa the Second, later heard Paul's defense before his final voyage to Rome. Josephus records the same dynasty in detail outside the Bible, confirming their reigns and building projects, including Herod the Great's expansion of the Jerusalem temple.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Herodians
entries.dictNote: The Herodians were a Jewish political faction supportive of Herod's dynasty and Roman rule, and they occasionally allied with the Pharisees, despite otherwise opposing views, in attempts to trap Jesus, most notably over the question of paying taxes to Caesar.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Herodias
entries.summary: Luke names her only as the reason John rebukes Herod and gets imprisoned for it (3:19) — the marriage itself. Josephus, independent of any Gospel and with no Christian interest at stake, confirms John's death under Herod Antipas and gives his own reason: not the dinner-party beheading of the later Gospel account, but a preemptive political execution, fear of a popular movement Herod couldn't control.
entries.dictNote: Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her first husband to marry his half-brother Herod Antipas, a marriage John the Baptist publicly condemned as unlawful. Her resentment of John's criticism led her to orchestrate his execution, having her daughter dance for Antipas at a banquet and then demand John's head on a platter as the reward, a request Antipas granted reluctantly to avoid breaking an oath made in front of his guests.

witness.excerpt: Herod slew him… who was a good man, and commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, both as to righteousness towards one another, and piety towards God… Herod, who feared lest the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power… to raise rebellion… thought it best, by putting him to death, to prevent any mischief he might cause.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Herodion
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul greets as his "kinsman," likely meaning a fellow Jew rather than a blood relative, near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:11). His name, derived from the Herod family, suggests he may have belonged to the household of a member of the Herodian dynasty.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hesed
entries.dictNote: The father of Ben-hesed, one of twelve district officers Solomon appointed to supply provisions for the royal household, each responsible for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7-10). Ben-hesed's district included Sochoh and the land of Hepher.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heshbon
entries.summary: Cheshbon, a place East of the Jordan
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Heshbon was the capital of Sihon, king of the Amorites, situated east of the Jordan near the northern edge of Moab. Moses captured it and the surrounding territory before Israel entered Canaan, and it later became a Levitical city within the tribe of Reuben. After the Israelite monarchy declined the Moabites reoccupied it, and the prophets accordingly pronounce judgment on Heshbon alongside the rest of Moab. Its ruins, still called Hesban, lie about twenty miles east of the Jordan, and excavations there have traced occupation across many centuries, though matching specific layers to the biblical conquest period remains debated among archaeologists.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Heshmon
entries.dictNote: Heshmon was a town in the Negev district assigned to the tribe of Judah, listed among the southernmost settlements toward the border of Edom (Josh. 15:27). Its location has not been identified with any confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Heth
entries.dictNote: Heth was Canaan's son and the ancestor of the Hittites, the people from whom Abraham purchased a burial cave for Sarah and among whom Uriah, Bathsheba's husband, was numbered generations later.

witness.excerpt: For in patience of spirit he conversed with the children of Heth, to the intent that they should give him a place in which to bury his dead.

And Rebecca went in and said to Isaac: "I loathe my life because of the two daughters of Heth, whom Esau hath taken him as wives; and if Jacob take a wife from among the daughters of the land such as these, for what purpose

do I further live; for the daughters of Canaan are evil."  9.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hethlon
entries.dictNote: Place marking part of the northern boundary of the land in Ezekiel's vision of restored Israel, associated with "the entrance of Hamath" (Ezek. 47:15; 48:1), likely a mountain pass through the Lebanon range leading toward the plain of Hamath.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezeki
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Elpaal in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:17. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezekiah
entries.summary: The reforming king who survives Assyria's siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18-19). Josephus's whole chapter title is basically a recap of the crisis — Sennacherib's threats, Isaiah's reassurance, the army's destruction — confirming the same sequence of events from outside the biblical text.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Micah, Zephaniah
entries.dictNote: Hezekiah was one of Judah's few genuinely good kings, coming to the throne amid the wreckage his father Ahaz had left and immediately reopening the temple, restoring proper worship, and destroying the high places and idols his people had accumulated, even smashing the bronze serpent Moses had made centuries earlier once it became an object of worship in its own right. When the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC after Hezekiah stopped paying tribute, Hezekiah prayed in the temple and the prophet Isaiah promised deliverance, and the siege broke overnight. A royal seal impression reading belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah, found in excavations near the Temple Mount, is the first archaeological find naming a biblical king that was also excavated under controlled conditions rather than bought on the antiquities market, and the tunnel Hezekiah dug to secure Jerusalem's water supply during that same siege still runs beneath the city today.

witness.excerpt: How Sennacherib made an expedition against Hezekiah… How Isaiah the Prophet encouraged him: How Sennacherib, having failed of success in Egypt, returned thence to Jerusalem: and how, upon his finding his army destroyed, he returned home.

entries.label: 11 books

entries.title: Hezion
entries.dictNote: Hezion was an early king of Aram-Damascus, father of Tabrimon and grandfather of Ben-hadad I, the Syrian king whom Asa of Judah paid to attack Israel (1 Kings 15:18). He is sometimes identified with Rezon, who established the Damascene kingdom that opposed Solomon (1 Kings 11:23-25), though the connection is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hezir
entries.summary: Chezir, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Hezir appear in the postexilic records: the head of the seventeenth division of priests organized by David for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:15), and a leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant of reform after the exile (Nehemiah 10:20). Whether the two are related is not stated. A first-century BC tomb in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley, known as the Tomb of the Sons of Hezir, bears an inscription naming a priestly family by this name, showing it remained in use among Jerusalem's priesthood for centuries.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hezro
entries.dictNote: Hezro the Carmelite was one of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters who distinguished themselves in David's service (2 Samuel 23:35; 1 Chronicles 11:37).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hezron
entries.summary: Chetsron, the name of a place in Palestine; also of two Israelites
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Ruth, 1 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Hezron most often names two of Judah's ancestors in Genesis and Chronicles' genealogies, a son of Reuben and, more significantly, the son of Perez through whom the line runs down to David and eventually to Jesus in Matthew's genealogy. The same word also marks a plain on Judah's southern border, west of Kadesh-barnea, listed among the towns on the tribe's frontier in Joshua.

witness.excerpt: 12.  Reuben, the first-born of Israel; and these are the names of his sons: Enoch, and Pallu, and Hezron and Carmi--five.  13.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Hezronites
entries.summary: a Chetsronite or (collectively) descendants of Chetsron
entries.dictNote: Hezronites was the name given to two distinct clans in Israel's wilderness census, both descended from men named Hezron. One family traced to a son of Reuben; the other, listed separately among Judah's descendants, traced to a different Hezron, grandson of Judah through Perez and an ancestor in David's own line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hiddai
entries.dictNote: One of David's elite thirty warriors, from the ravines of Gaash (2 Samuel 23:30). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:32 names him Hurai instead, one of several small spelling variants between the two rosters.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hiddekel
entries.dictNote: Hiddekel is the Hebrew name for the Tigris, one of the four rivers described as flowing out of Eden, said to run east of Assyria (Gen. 2:14). It appears again as the setting for Daniel's final vision, where he stood on its bank (Dan. 10:4). The Tigris rises in the mountains of eastern Turkey and flows more than a thousand miles before joining the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf, its banks home to major Mesopotamian cities including Nineveh and Asshur.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hiel
entries.dictNote: Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho during the reign of Ahab, centuries after Joshua had destroyed the city and pronounced a curse on whoever would rebuild it (Joshua 6:26). The curse was fulfilled literally: 1 Kings 16:34 records that Hiel lost his firstborn son Abiram when he laid the city's foundation and his youngest son Segub when he set up its gates. The episode is presented as proof that the word spoken through Joshua, like the word spoken through Elijah in the surrounding narrative, held true.

witness.excerpt: (4) Upon occasion of this devoting of Jericho to destruction, and the exemplary punishment of Achar, who brake that Cherem or Anathema ; and of the punishment of the future breaker of it, Hiel, 1 Kings 16:34.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hierapolis
entries.summary: holy city; Hierapolis, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Hierapolis was a city in the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, paired with Colossae and Laodicea as one of three churches Paul addresses through his letter to the Colossians, though he had not visited any of them personally; Epaphras is named as the one who worked hard on behalf of all three (Colossians 4:12-13). The city was famous in antiquity, as it still is today, for the white travertine terraces formed by its mineral hot springs, now the site of modern Pamukkale in Turkey. In 2011 archaeologists excavating there identified what they believe are the remains of a martyrium built over the tomb of the apostle Philip, who according to early Christian tradition died in the city.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hilen
entries.dictNote: Hilen was a town of Judah given, along with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite clan descended from Aaron for their residence (1 Chronicles 6:43). The parallel list in Joshua 21:15 gives the same town's name as Holon. Its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillel
entries.dictNote: Hillel was a Pirathonite from the hill country of Ephraim, the father of Abdon, one of the minor judges who governed Israel after Jephthah (Judges 12:13, 15). Nothing more is recorded about him, and he is not related to the later rabbinic sage of the same name who taught in Jerusalem centuries afterward.

witness.excerpt: 1178] Abdon also, the son of Hillel, of the tribe of Ephraim, and born at the city Pyrathon, was ordained their supreme governor after Helon.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hillkiah
entries.summary: Chilhijah, the name of eight Israelites
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Hilkiah was the high priest during King Josiah's reign who discovered a forgotten scroll of the law while the temple was being repaired, a find that triggered Judah's last great religious reform. A different Hilkiah was the father of the prophet Jeremiah.
entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Hirah
entries.dictNote: Hirah was an Adullamite and close friend of Judah, present when Judah married a Canaanite woman and later sent by Judah to deliver a goat to Tamar in payment for what he did not realize was a disguised encounter with his own daughter-in-law (Genesis 38:1, 12, 20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hiram
entries.summary: Chiram or Chirom, the name of two Tyrians
entries.dictNote: Hiram was the king of Tyre who supplied cedar wood, craftsmen, and skilled labor for both David's palace and Solomon's temple, maintaining a friendly trade relationship with Israel across both reigns. A different Hiram, also called Huram-abi, was a master bronzeworker Hiram the king sent to cast the temple's bronze pillars, sea, and other furnishings.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hittite
entries.summary: a Chittite, or descendant of Cheth
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Hittites appear in the Old Testament as one of the peoples native to Canaan, most famously at Hebron, where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site for Sarah, and later as individuals such as Uriah, the Hittite soldier whose wife Bathsheba David took. For a long time critics doubted a Hittite nation ever existed, but nineteenth and twentieth century excavations at Boghazkoy in Turkey uncovered the capital and royal archives of a genuine Hittite Empire, a major Bronze Age power that rivaled Egypt and fought Ramesses II at Kadesh. The biblical Hittites of Canaan were likely a smaller offshoot, or simply a name borrowed loosely from that larger Anatolian people, rather than the imperial Hittites themselves.

entries.label: 15 books

entries.title: Hivite
entries.summary: a Chivvite, one of the aboriginal tribes of Palestine
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Hivites were one of the Canaanite peoples occupying the land before Israel's arrival, associated in Genesis 34 with the city of Shechem, where Hamor the Hivite's son violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, and in Joshua 9 with Gibeon, whose inhabitants tricked Joshua into a treaty by pretending to come from a distant country. That treaty later brought Gibeon under Israelite protection even though the city was never conquered outright.

witness.excerpt: And there they carried off Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, into the house of Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite, the prince of the land, and he lay with her and defiled her, and she was a little girl, a child of twelve years.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Hobab
entries.dictNote: Hobab was Moses' brother-in-law, a Kenite and relative of the Midianite priest Jethro, whose knowledge of the wilderness terrain Moses sought when Israel set out from Sinai, asking him to serve as guide (Numbers 10:29-32). Judges 4:11 uses the same relational term for him as for Moses' father-in-law, an ambiguity in the Hebrew word for in-law that has led some to identify Hobab with Jethro himself rather than as a separate individual. His descendants, the Kenites, settled among the Israelites, first near Jericho and later in the Negev around Arad (Judges 1:16).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hobah
entries.dictNote: Hobah lay north of Damascus and marks the farthest point of Abram's pursuit of the four eastern kings who had captured his nephew Lot, after Abram's night attack routed them near Dan (Genesis 14:15). Nothing else is known of the site, and it has not been identified with any modern location.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hod
entries.dictNote: Hod was a son of Zophah, listed among the descendants of Asher in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:37.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodaiah
entries.dictNote: A descendant of the royal line of Judah listed among the sons of Elioenai in the genealogies following the Babylonian exile (1 Chr. 3:24). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodaviah
entries.summary: Hodavjah, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hodaviah, meaning “praise the LORD,” is the name of several distinct men in the Old Testament genealogies, including a chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:24), a descendant of the royal line of David listed after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:24), and the ancestor of a Levitical family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:40). None of the individuals bearing the name has a recorded narrative beyond their place in these lists.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hodesh
entries.dictNote: A wife of Shaharaim, a Benjamite clan head listed in 1 Chronicles 8:8-9 among the men who bore children in Moab after he had sent away his first two wives, Hushim and Baara. She and Shaharaim's other wives are named only to record the sons who became heads of Benjamite families.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodevah
entries.dictNote: Hodevah is an alternate spelling of Hodaviah, head of a family of Levites who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Neh. 7:43). Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hodijah
entries.summary: Hodijah, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hodijah was a common Levitical name among those who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hoglah
entries.dictNote: Hoglah was one of five daughters of Zelophehad whose successful petition to Moses for the right to inherit their father's land set a new legal precedent for Israel.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hoham
entries.dictNote: The Amorite king of Hebron who joined four other Canaanite kings in besieging Gibeon after it made peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's forced march and the battle in which the sun and moon reportedly stood still (Josh. 10:1-27). He and his allied kings were later found hiding in a cave at Makkedah, captured, and executed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Holon
entries.summary: Cholon, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Holon was a town in the hill country of Judah, later designated as one of the cities given to the Levites.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Homam
entries.dictNote: An Edomite name in the genealogy of Esau's descendants through Seir the Horite; the parallel list in Genesis gives the form Hemam (1 Chronicles 1:39; Genesis 36:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hophni
entries.dictNote: Hophni was one of Eli's two corrupt priestly sons, condemned for abusing his position at the Shiloh tabernacle, and he died alongside his brother Phinehas in the battle where the Philistines captured the Ark of the Covenant.

witness.excerpt: The occasion was this: Eli the High Priest had two sons, Hophni and Phineas.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hor
entries.summary: Hor, the name of a peak in Idumaea and of one in Syria
entries.dictNote: Mount Hor is where Aaron died, stripped of his priestly garments in sight of the people and buried on the mountain, at the edge of the land of Edom near the end of Israel's wilderness wandering.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hor-hagidgad
entries.summary: Chor-hag-Gidgad, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Hor-hagidgad was a desert encampment in Israel's wilderness itinerary, generally taken to be the same place called Gudgodah in Deuteronomy 10:7 (Numbers 33:32-33). Its location among the stations south of Kadesh has not been fixed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Horam
entries.dictNote: King of Gezer at the time of Joshua's southern campaign. He marched to relieve Lachish while Joshua besieged it, but Joshua defeated him and his army, leaving no survivors (Josh. 10:33). Gezer itself remained a Canaanite enclave for generations afterward and was not fully absorbed into Israel until Solomon's reign.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Horeb
entries.summary: Choreb, a (generic) name for the Sinaitic mountains
entries.books: Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, the mountain where Moses first encountered God at the burning bush and later where Israel received the law, and it's also where Elijah later fled and heard God speak in a still, small voice after the fire, earthquake, and wind.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Horem
entries.dictNote: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali, listed in Joshua 19:38 alongside Iron and Migdal-el. Its exact site is unknown; the name means roughly "consecrated" or "sacred place."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hori
entries.summary: Chori, the name of two men
entries.dictNote: Hori was a Horite clan chief in Edom's genealogies, and also the name of the father of the spy who represented the tribe of Simeon.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Horims
entries.dictNote: The Horites were the original inhabitants of the region that became Edom before Esau's descendants displaced them, mentioned in Genesis's genealogical record of the land's earlier population.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hormah
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Hormah, meaning "devoted to destruction," was a town in the Negev originally called Zephath. Israel was first routed there by the Amalekites and Canaanites after presuming to invade Canaan without the Lord's presence following the spies' report. Later, after a Canaanite king attacked and took Israelite captives, Israel vowed to destroy the region's cities in retaliation, a vow finally fulfilled under Joshua, giving the site its lasting name.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Horonaim
entries.dictNote: Horonaim was a Moabite city south of the Arnon River, cited repeatedly in Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles of judgment against Moab as one of the towns that would fall and mourn in the coming disaster (Isaiah 15:5; Jeremiah 48:3, 5, 34). Its name, meaning "two caverns" or "two hollows," suggests it sat in a valley or ravine setting. Its precise location has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Horonite
entries.summary: a Choronite or inhabitant of Choronaim
entries.dictNote: Horonite identifies Sanballat, one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah's project to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, probably from Horonaim in Moab or one of the two towns called Beth-horon. Sanballat's role as governor of Samaria is independently confirmed by the Elephantine papyri, a cache of Jewish letters from Egypt that name him, lending solid historical grounding to Nehemiah's account.

witness.excerpt: (27) Many have here, very weakly, supposed that this Sanballat , under the last Darius, is by Josephus confounded with Sanballat the Horonite in Nehemiah, 13:28.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hosah
entries.summary: Chosah, an Israelite; also a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Hosah is a name shared by a place and a person. It marks a town on the border of Asher near Tyre (Joshua 19:29) and, more prominently, a Levite of the family of Merari whom David appointed as one of the gatekeepers of the sanctuary, a post his family continued to hold (1 Chronicles 16:38; 26:10-16).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hosea
entries.summary: Hoshea, the name of five Israelites
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Hosea
entries.dictNote: Hosea was a prophet to northern Israel whom God commanded to marry a promiscuous woman named Gomer as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God, and Hosea's repeated forgiveness and pursuit of Gomer even after she left him for other men became the book's central metaphor for God's relentless love toward an unfaithful people. He prophesied in the decades leading up to Israel's fall to Assyria, and his book is full of marriage and family imagery, naming his children symbolic names that doubled as warnings to the nation.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Hoshaiah
entries.summary: Hoshajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hoshaiah was the father of a group of Jewish refugees who forced Jeremiah to go with them into Egypt against his warnings, and also the name of a leader who took part in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hoshama
entries.dictNote: Hoshama was a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) of Judah, listed among the royal descendants in 1 Chronicles 3:18, likely born during his father's long imprisonment in Babylon. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hotham
entries.summary: Chotham, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hotham was a chief of the tribe of Asher, son of Heber of the clan of Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:32). A second Hotham, the Aroerite, is listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:44).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hothir
entries.dictNote: Hothir was one of the fourteen sons of Heman, David's seer and a chief Levite musician, and was appointed with his brothers to lead one of the divisions of temple musicians organized by lot (1 Chronicles 25:4, 28).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hukkok
entries.summary: Chukkok or Chukok, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Hukkok was a town near the border of Naphtali and Asher, not far from the Jordan, that appears in the list of Levitical cities given to the Gershonite Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:60). It has been tentatively identified with the village of Yakuk near the Sea of Galilee.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hul
entries.summary: Chul, a son of Aram; also the region settled by him
entries.dictNote: Hul appears in the Table of Nations as one of the sons of Aram and a grandson of Shem (Gen. 10:23; 1 Chr. 1:17). Like other names in this genealogy, it most likely designates an Aramean clan or district rather than a single individual, though its location has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Huldah
entries.dictNote: Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem during King Josiah's reign, and when workers repairing the temple discovered a forgotten scroll of the law, Josiah sent his officials directly to Huldah rather than to any of the male prophets active at the time, and she confirmed the scroll's authority and predicted the coming judgment on Judah, though not within Josiah's own lifetime.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Humtah
entries.dictNote: Humtah was a town in the hill country of Judah, grouped with Hebron in the town list of Joshua 15:54. Nothing further is known of it, and its exact site remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hupham
entries.dictNote: Hupham was a son of Benjamin and founder of the Huphamite clan, counted in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:39. He is also called Huppim in Genesis 46:21 and 1 Chronicles 7:12.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huphamites
entries.summary: a Chuphamite or descendant of Chupham
entries.dictNote: Huphamites were the clan descended from Hupham, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huppah
entries.dictNote: A priest in David's reign, head of the thirteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized for rotating temple service (1 Chr. 24:13).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huppim
entries.dictNote: Huppim was a son of Benjamin, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Benjamin's tribe in Israel's genealogies.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hur
entries.summary: Chur, the name of four Israelites and one Midianite
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah
entries.dictNote: Hur assisted Aaron in holding up Moses's tired arms during the battle against Amalek, a task that kept Israel winning as long as Moses's hands stayed raised, and he was left in charge alongside Aaron while Moses was on Mount Sinai receiving the law.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Hurai
entries.dictNote: Hurai was one of David's thirty mighty warriors, a native of the valley near Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 11:32). The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:30 gives his name as Hiddai.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Huram
entries.summary: Churam, the name of an Israelite and two Syrians
entries.dictNote: Huram is an alternate spelling of Hiram, covered under that entry; it refers to the king of Tyre who supplied materials for Solomon's temple and a skilled bronzeworker of the same name Hiram sent to craft the temple's furnishings.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Huri
entries.dictNote: Huri was a Gadite, father of Abihail, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad that settled in Bashan east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:14). The chapter traces this branch of Gad's descendants down to family heads living in the region during the reigns of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel. Beyond his place in this genealogical chain, nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hushah
entries.dictNote: A name appearing in the genealogies of Judah, associated with the descendants of Ezer (1 Chronicles 4:4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Hushai
entries.dictNote: Hushai was David's loyal friend who stayed behind during Absalom's rebellion specifically to infiltrate Absalom's court and counter Ahithophel's sound military advice with a deliberately worse plan, a deception that bought David crucial time to regroup and ultimately saved his life.
