entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Husham
entries.dictNote: Husham was an early king of Edom, listed among the rulers who governed there before Israel had a king of its own.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hushathite
entries.summary: a Chushathite or descendant of Chushah
entries.dictNote: Hushathite marks two of David's mighty men, Sibbecai and Mebunnai, as coming from Hushah, a town associated with Judah's descendants. Sibbecai is separately credited with killing a Philistine giant during a later battle at Gob.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hushim
entries.summary: Chushim, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Hushim was the name of a son of Dan and also of one of the wives of a Benjamite clan leader listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Dan were Hushim, and Sâmôn, and Asûdî, and ’Îjâka, and Salômôn--six.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Hymenaeus
entries.dictNote: Hymenaeus was a man in the early church, probably at Ephesus, whom Paul names twice as an example of shipwrecked faith. In 1 Timothy 1:20 Paul says he handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan for blasphemy, and in 2 Timothy 2:17-18 he links Hymenaeus with Philetus for teaching that the resurrection had already taken place, a claim Paul says overturned the faith of some believers.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: I-chabod
entries.dictNote: Ichabod was born to the wife of Phinehas, Eli's son, just as she was dying in childbirth after hearing that the ark of the covenant had been captured by the Philistines and that both her husband and father-in-law had been killed in the same battle. She named the child Ichabod, meaning "no glory," saying that Israel's glory had departed since the ark was gone (1 Samuel 4:19-22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ibhar
entries.dictNote: Ibhar was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after he became king.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ibleam
entries.dictNote: Ibleam was a town assigned to Manasseh that lay within Issachar's borders, though the Canaanites there were never fully driven out (Joshua 17:11; Judges 1:27). It is best known as the place where King Ahaziah of Judah was mortally wounded while fleeing Jehu's purge of Ahab's dynasty (2 Kings 9:27). It is generally identified with Khirbet Bel'ameh, near Jenin.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ibneiah
entries.dictNote: Son of Jeroham, a Benjamite listed among the heads of families who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile, named in 1 Chronicles 9:8.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ibnijah
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the family heads who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 9:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ibri
entries.dictNote: Ibri was a Merarite Levite of the family of Jaaziah, listed among the Levitical divisions organized in the time of David (1 Chronicles 24:27). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ibzan
entries.dictNote: Ibzan was the tenth judge of Israel, ruling for seven years from his hometown of Bethlehem (Judges 12:8-10). The text notes that he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, but records nothing else of his rule.

witness.excerpt: 1195] Now when Jephtha was dead, Ibzan took the government; being of the tribe of Judah, and of the city of Bethlehem.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iconium
entries.summary: image-like; Iconium, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Iconium was the capital of ancient Lycaonia in central Asia Minor, modern Konya, visited by Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey after they were expelled from Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51-14:1). A mixed crowd of Jews and Gentiles turned against them there too, forcing them to flee to Lystra and Derbe, though Paul returned to strengthen the young church on his way back (Acts 14:19-21).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Idalah
entries.dictNote: Idalah, a town on the border of the tribe of Zebulun, listed with Bethlehem of Zebulun and Shimron in Joshua 19:15. It is often identified with a site near the Kishon valley, though the location is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Idbash
entries.dictNote: One of three sons of the father of Etam, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah alongside his sister Hazelelponi (1 Chronicles 4:3).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.summary: Iddo (or Iddi), the name of five Israelites

entries.title: Idumaea
entries.summary: Idumæa (i.e. Edom), a region East (and South) of Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Greek and Roman name for Edom, the region south of Judea named for Esau's descendants. By the New Testament era its Idumean population had been forcibly incorporated into Judea under the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus, and it was from this Idumean stock that the family of Herod the Great descended; Mark 3:8 lists Idumea among the regions from which crowds came to Jesus.

entries.title: Igal
entries.summary: Jigal, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Igal was one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, representing the tribe of Issachar, and also the name of one of David's mighty warriors.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Igdaliah
entries.dictNote: Igdaliah was called "the man of God," an otherwise unknown prophet or holy figure whose son Hanan had a chamber in the temple where Jeremiah gathered the Rechabites to test their obedience to their ancestral vow (Jer. 35:1-4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iim
entries.summary: Ijim, a place in the Desert.
entries.dictNote: Iim, meaning ruins, is used of two separate places in the record. The first is a town in the far south of Judah near the Edomite border (Joshua 15:29). The second is one of the late stations in Israel's wilderness itinerary, mentioned just before the arrival at the border of Moab (Numbers 33:45). The two are unrelated beyond sharing a common Hebrew word for heaps of ruins.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ije-abarim
entries.dictNote: Ije-abarim, ruins of Abarim, was a wilderness station on the border of Moab where Israel camped late in the journey from Egypt (Numbers 21:11; 33:44). Its name recalls the Abarim mountain range east of the Jordan, though the precise campsite has not been located.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ijon
entries.dictNote: Ijon was a city in the tribe of Naphtali in Israel's far north, captured by the Aramean king Ben-hadad at Asa's request (1 Kings 15:20; 2 Chronicles 16:4) and later by Assyria's Tiglath-pileser III during Pekah's reign (2 Kings 15:29). Tiglath-pileser's own summary inscriptions list the conquest of this same cluster of Galilean towns, an independent confirmation of the biblical account. It is usually identified with the site of Tell Dibbin in the Marj Ayyun valley.

entries.title: Immanuel
entries.summary: Immanuel, a type name of Isaiah's son
entries.dictNote: Immanuel, meaning "God with us," is not a historical individual but a prophetic name. Isaiah gave it as a sign to King Ahaz, promising that before a child bearing this name grew old enough to know right from wrong, the threat facing Judah would pass (Isaiah 7:14), and used it again as a rallying cry against Judah's enemies (Isaiah 8:8). Matthew's Gospel applies the name to Jesus' birth as its ultimate fulfillment (Matthew 1:23), while the identity of the child originally in view in Isaiah's own day is still debated among interpreters.

It likely refers to the Indus River region rather than the full subcontinent.

entries.dictNote: Ir appears in the genealogy of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 7:12, one of the more textually difficult verses in Chronicles; many read it as a variant or scribal form of Iri, a son of Bela named a few verses earlier (1 Chronicles 7:7). entries.dictNote: Ira was the name of more than one of David's officials, including a priest and one of his elite warriors known as the Ithrite.

entries.title: Irad
entries.dictNote: A grandson of Cain through Enoch, and the father of Mehujael, in the brief genealogy Genesis 4:18 traces from Cain down to Lamech and his children. The list exists mainly to connect Cain's line to the culture-founders named two verses later, Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain.

entries.title: Iram
entries.dictNote: Iram was a clan chief of Edom, listed among the descendants of Esau who headed tribal divisions in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:43; 1 Chronicles 1:54).

entries.title: Iri
entries.dictNote: Son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, head of a family in the tribal genealogies of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 7:7,12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Irijah
entries.dictNote: Irijah was a captain of the guard at Jerusalem's Benjamin Gate who arrested the prophet Jeremiah as he tried to leave the city during a lull in the Babylonian siege, accusing him of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37:13-14). He handed Jeremiah over to the princes, who had him beaten and imprisoned. Jeremiah maintained his innocence, but the episode led to a long and dangerous confinement (Jeremiah 37:15-21).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Irnahash
entries.dictNote: Irnahash, meaning "city of the serpent," a town listed among the descendants of Judah in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 4:12. Nothing else is known of it and its location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iron
entries.dictNote: A fortified town of the tribe of Naphtali in Upper Galilee (Josh. 19:38), distinct from the metal of the same English name. It is generally identified with the modern village of Yarun, which preserves the ancient name, called Yiron in some translations.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Irpeel
entries.dictNote: A town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among its fourteen cities near Gibeon (Josh. 18:27-28). No trace of its site has been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iru
entries.dictNote: Iru was the eldest son of Caleb son of Jephunneh, the faithful spy who received Hebron as an inheritance, listed among Caleb's descendants in 1 Chronicles 4:15. Nothing further is recorded about him.

He married Rebekah through his father's servant's mission back to Mesopotamia, and late in life, blind and dying, he was tricked by his younger son Jacob into giving him the blessing meant for the older twin, Esau. Isaac is the only patriarch who never left the land of Canaan, and the only one recorded marrying just one wife.

entries.dictNote: Isaiah was an eighth-century prophet in Jerusalem, the son of Amoz, who advised four kings of Judah in succession and became the most quoted prophet in the New Testament. He was married to a woman Scripture itself calls a prophetess, and he named his two sons as walking sermons, Shear-jashub, meaning a remnant will return, and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning the spoil speeds, the prey hastens. Isaiah told King Hezekiah that Jerusalem would survive Sennacherib's siege, and Assyria's own record of that campaign, the Taylor Prism, confirms the invasion happened and boasts of shutting Hezekiah up like a caged bird, though notably it never claims Sennacherib actually took the city, matching the Bible's account of a siege that stopped short.

entries.title: Isaiah
entries.summary: Luke opens John the Baptist's ministry by quoting Isaiah (3:4) and has Jesus himself read from the Isaiah scroll in the Nazareth synagogue (4:17) — both times treating the text as self-evidently authoritative. Josephus, writing for outsiders to the faith, argues for that same authority on different grounds: Isaiah never wrote a false word, so his own writings needed no editor to verify them.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans
entries.dictNote: Isaiah was an eighth-century prophet in Jerusalem, the son of Amoz, who advised four kings of Judah in succession and became the most quoted prophet in the New Testament. He was married to a woman Scripture itself calls a prophetess, and he named his two sons as walking sermons, Shear-jashub, meaning a remnant will return, and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning the spoil speeds, the prey hastens. Isaiah told King Hezekiah that Jerusalem would survive Sennacherib's siege, and Assyria's own record of that campaign, the Taylor Prism, confirms the invasion happened and boasts of shutting Hezekiah up like a caged bird, though notably it never claims Sennacherib actually took the city, matching the Bible's account of a siege that stopped short.

witness.excerpt: he was by the confession of all, a divine and wonderful man in speaking truth; and out of the assurance that he had never written what was false, he wrote down all his prophecies.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Iscah
entries.dictNote: Iscah was a daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah and Lot, named in the family record of Terah's household in Ur of the Chaldees (Genesis 11:29). Ancient Jewish tradition sometimes identified her with Sarah, Abraham's wife, though the biblical text does not make this connection explicit.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Iscariot
entries.summary: inhabitant of Kerioth; Iscariotes (i.e. Keriothite), an epithet of Judas the traitor
entries.dictNote: Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles, entrusted with the group's money as its treasurer, and John's Gospel says he regularly stole from the funds even before his greater betrayal. He handed Jesus over to the religious authorities for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in the garden of Gethsemane, and afterward, overcome with remorse, he returned the money and hanged himself, though the accounts in Matthew and Acts describe the specifics of his death somewhat differently.

entries.title: Ish-bosheth
entries.summary: Ish-Bosheth, a son of King Saul
entries.dictNote: Ish-bosheth was Saul's surviving son, installed as a rival king over Israel by Saul's general Abner while David ruled only Judah, and after Abner defected to David's side, two of Ish-bosheth's own captains assassinated him in his bed, bringing his brief and largely powerless reign to an end.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ishbah
entries.dictNote: Ishbah appears in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4 as the father of Eshtemoa, meaning he was reckoned the founder or ancestor of that town's settlers rather than a literal parent. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ishbak
entries.dictNote: Ishbak was a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, traditionally regarded as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, though it cannot be identified with certainty (Genesis 25:2).

entries.title: Ishbi-benob (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of the Rephaim, a Philistine giant who nearly killed David in battle before Abishai intervened and struck him down (2 Samuel 21:16-17). The episode marks the point at which David's men insisted he no longer go out to battle personally.

entries.title: Ishi
entries.summary: Jishi, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Ishi was a common name in the genealogies of Judah and Manasseh, and the word itself, meaning my husband, is also used by Hosea as a picture of Israel's restored, tender relationship with God, contrasted with the more formal my master.

entries.title: Ishiah

entries.dictNote: Isshiah was a common Levitical name in Chronicles, borne by several musicians and descendants of Izhar.

entries.title: Ishma
entries.dictNote: Ishma appears in a terse genealogical fragment of the tribe of Judah, grouped with the clans associated with Etam (1 Chr. 4:3). The family relationships in this passage are difficult to reconstruct with certainty.

entries.books: Genesis, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Ishmael was Abraham's first son, born to Sarah's servant Hagar after Sarah, still childless, offered Hagar to Abraham as a way to fulfill God's promise of an heir on their own timetable. After Isaac was born, tension between the two half-brothers led Sarah to insist Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and God promised Hagar that Ishmael would also become the father of a great nation, though not the covenant line. A later Ishmael, generations afterward, assassinated the Babylonian-appointed governor Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall, triggering a fresh wave of Jewish flight into Egypt.

entries.dictNote: Ishmaelites were descendants of Ishmael, Abraham's son by his wife's servant Hagar, and lived as nomadic traders in the region south and east of Canaan. entries.title: Ishmaiah
entries.summary: Jishmajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Ishmaiah appear in Chronicles. One was a Gibeonite warrior who joined David's forces at Ziklag while David was still fleeing Saul, noted as a leading man among the thirty mighty men (1 Chronicles 12:4). entries.title: Ishmerai
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite of the family of Elpaal, listed among the heads of families living in Jerusalem in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:18. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Ishod
entries.dictNote: Ishod was a son of Hammoleketh, of the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, named in the tribal genealogy of Manasseh (1 Chr. 7:18).

entries.dictNote: Ishvah was a son of Asher who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:17; 1 Chronicles 7:30). He is absent from the later clan census of Asher in Numbers 26, which may mean he died without founding a family line.

entries.title: Ismachiah
entries.dictNote: Ismachiah was a Levite appointed as one of the overseers of the freewill offerings, tithes, and dedicated gifts brought into the temple during King Hezekiah's religious reforms, serving alongside Cononiah and Shimei under the high priest Azariah (2 Chr. 31:12-13).

entries.title: Israelitish
entries.summary: a Jisreelitess or female descendant of Jisrael
entries.dictNote: Israelitish is not a personal name but an adjective describing the mother of the man stoned for blasphemy in Leviticus 24:10-11; she is named Shelomith, daughter of Dibri of the tribe of Dan, married to an Egyptian. The passage uses her Israelite identity to raise the legal question of whether the law against blasphemy applied to someone of mixed parentage. God's answer, that one law applies to native and foreigner alike, settles the case.

entries.title: Isri
entries.dictNote: Isri is not a personal name but the gentilic form of Jezer, one of the sons of Naphtali, used in the wilderness census of Numbers 26:49 to identify the clan descended from him: "of Jezer, the family of the Jezerites." The underlying Hebrew word functions the same way as Hamulites or Shuhamites elsewhere in that same census chapter, marking a family group rather than an individual person. Its appearance among personal-name records in older reference works reflects the difficulty early lexicographers had distinguishing Hebrew gentilic adjectives from proper names once transliterated into English.

entries.title: Italy
entries.dictNote: Italy is named several times in the New Testament in connection with the spread of the early church. Aquila and Priscilla had recently come from Italy when Paul met them in Corinth, having been expelled from Rome along with other Jews by an edict of the emperor Claudius, a decree the Roman historian Suetonius later corroborates, noting that Claudius expelled Jews from the city for rioting "at the instigation of Chrestus," likely a garbled reference to disputes over Christ (Acts 18:2). Paul was later transported to Italy as a prisoner, surviving a shipwreck off Malta before finally reaching Rome (Acts 27:1-6; 28:11-16), and the writer of Hebrews closes his letter with greetings from "those from Italy," likely Italian Christians living abroad (Hebrews 13:24).

entries.dictNote: Ittai was a Philistine commander from Gath who insisted on staying loyal to David and fleeing with him during Absalom's rebellion rather than accepting David's offer to release him from any obligation, and David rewarded that loyalty by giving him command of a third of his army.

entries.dictNote: Ithamar was Aaron's fourth and youngest son, and after his two eldest brothers died for offering unauthorized fire and his other brother Eleazar became high priest, Ithamar oversaw the Levites responsible for transporting and maintaining the tabernacle. His descendants held the high priesthood for a period, including Eli, before it returned to Eleazar's line under Zadok.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Ithiel
entries.summary: Ithiel, the name of an Israelite, also of a symbolical person
entries.dictNote: Two different men bear this name in the Bible. One is listed among the Benjamite ancestors of the Jerusalem settlers who returned after the exile (Nehemiah 11:7). The other appears in the opening line of Agur's sayings in Proverbs 30:1, addressed alongside Ucal, though the Hebrew wording there is difficult and some translations read it as a phrase rather than a personal name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ithmah
entries.dictNote: A Moabite counted among the elite warriors of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:46, notable as a foreigner who attained a place of honor in David's inner circle of fighters.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ithnan
entries.dictNote: Ithnan was one of the southernmost towns allotted to Judah, near the border with Edom, listed alongside Kedesh and Hazor in Joshua's territorial record (Joshua 15:23). Nothing else is known of it, and no trace of the site has been found.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ithra
entries.dictNote: Ithra was the father of Amasa, the commander David's son Absalom placed over his rebel army during the revolt against David. He is called an Israelite in 2 Samuel 17:25 but Jether the Ishmaelite in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:17, one of several small textual variants in the record of David's extended family. His wife Abigail was David's sister, making Amasa David's nephew.

witness.excerpt: He appointed Amasa to be captain of all his host, instead of Joab his kinsman: his father was Ithra and his mother Abigail: now she and Zeruiah, the mother of Joab, were David's sisters.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ithran
entries.summary: Jithran, the name of an Edomite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ithran was a Horite clan name listed among Edom's earlier inhabitants, and also the name of a descendant of Asher in the tribal genealogies.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ithream
entries.dictNote: Ithream was the sixth son born to David during his reign in Hebron, his mother being David's wife Eglah (2 Samuel 3:5; 1 Chronicles 3:3). He is not mentioned again in the narrative.

witness.excerpt: iel, by his wife Abigail; the name of the third was Absalom, by Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth he named Adonijah, by his wife Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth he called Ithream, by Eglah.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ithrite
entries.summary: a Jithrite or descendant of Jether
entries.dictNote: Ithrite marks two of David's mighty men, Ira and Gareb, and may connect them to the town of Kiriath-jearim, though the name's exact origin is uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ittahkazin
entries.dictNote: Ittah-kazin was one of the boundary markers listed for the tribal territory of Zebulun in Joshua 19:13, and it is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. Its precise location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ituraea
entries.summary: Ituræa (i.e. Jetur), a region of Palestine
entries.dictNote: A region northeast of Galilee, around Mount Hermon and the Anti-Lebanon range, ruled together with Trachonitis by the tetrarch Philip in Luke's account of John the Baptist's ministry (Luke 3:1). Its inhabitants, the Itureans, were a semi-nomadic Arab people later absorbed into the Roman client kingdom of Chalcis; Roman-era coinage from the region confirms the local dynasts Luke's Gospel situates alongside Herod's sons.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Izeharites
entries.summary: a Jitsharite or descendant of Jitshar
entries.dictNote: Izharites were a Kohathite Levitical family descended from Izhar, son of Kohath. The most notorious member of this clan was Korah, who led a rebellion against the authority of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and was swallowed up by the earth as a result in Numbers 16.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Izhar
entries.dictNote: Izhar was a son of Kohath and the father of Korah, the Levite who led the rebellion against Moses in the wilderness.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Izrahiah
entries.summary: Jizrachjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name. One was a chief of the tribe of Issachar listed in the tribal genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:3). The other was a priest present at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah, generations later (Nehemiah 12:42).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Izrahite
entries.summary: a Jizrach (i.e. Ezrachite or Zarchite) or descendant of Zerach
entries.dictNote: Izrahite identifies Shamhuth, commander of David's military division for the fifth month, an epithet that likely points to descent from Zerah, one of Judah's sons.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaakan
entries.dictNote: Son of Ezer and grandson of Seir the Horite (1 Chronicles 1:42), called Akan in the parallel Edomite genealogy of Genesis 36. His descendants, the Bene-jaakan, gave their name to one of Israel's wilderness campsites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaakobah
entries.dictNote: Jaakobah, a name built from the same root as Jacob, was a descendant of Simeon listed among the clan leaders of that tribe (1 Chronicles 4:36).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaala
entries.summary: Jaala or Jaalah, one of the Nethinim
entries.dictNote: Jaala headed a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:56; Nehemiah 7:58). The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and are traditionally traced back to Gibeonites and war captives assigned to Levitical service.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jaanai
entries.dictNote: A chief among the Gadites who settled in Bashan, named in the tribal record of 1 Chronicles 5:12.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaare-oregim
entries.dictNote: Jaare-oregim was a Bethlehemite named in 2 Samuel 21:19 as the father of Elhanan, the warrior credited there with killing Goliath the Gittite. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 20:5 instead names the father as Jair and specifies that Elhanan killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath, a difference most scholars attribute to a scribal duplication of the word "oregim" (weavers) from the following clause describing the spear shaft. The name itself, meaning "forests of the weavers," likely preserves a trade-guild connection rather than functioning as a simple personal name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaasau
entries.dictNote: One of the Israelites listed in Ezra's record who agreed to separate from the foreign wives they had married during the years Israelites lived among the surrounding nations (Ezra 10:37).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaasiel
entries.dictNote: This name is attached to two men in Chronicles. Jasiel the Mesobaite appears among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:47), while Jaasiel son of Abner served as chief officer over the tribe of Benjamin under David's administrative system (1 Chronicles 27:21). Whether these are the same man is not stated in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaazaniah
entries.summary: Jaazanjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jaazaniah was the name of more than one Old Testament figure, including a man Ezekiel saw in a vision leading elders in secret idol worship inside the temple itself.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jaazer
entries.summary: Jaazer or Jazer, a place East of the Jordan
entries.books: Numbers, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Jazer was an Amorite town east of the Jordan in Gilead, taken by Israel and assigned to Gad, then given to the Levites descended from Merari. It later belonged to a district under a Hebronite overseer in David's administration. Isaiah and Jeremiah both use Jazer's ruined vineyards as an image of Moab's coming devastation.

witness.excerpt: And when he had subdued them, he seized on the city Jazer, and took their wives and their children captives, and burnt the city, and then returned into Judea.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Jaaziah
entries.dictNote: Jaaziah was a descendant of Merari, one of the three Levitical clans, listed among those reorganized into divisions of temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:26-27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jaaziel
entries.dictNote: A Levite musician appointed to play the harp when David brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18-20). He is probably the same Levite called Aziel in the list of harpists two verses later.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jabal
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Cain through Lamech and Adah, remembered in Genesis 4:20 as "the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle," marking him as the traditional originator of a nomadic, herding way of life. His brother Jubal is credited in the same passage with originating instrumental music.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jabbok
entries.summary: Jabbok, a river east of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: The Jabbok is a stream flowing west into the Jordan roughly midway between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea, running through a deep gorge in the Gilead highlands; it formed a boundary between the Ammonites and the kingdom of Og, and later between Reuben and half of Manasseh (Joshua 12:2; Deuteronomy 3:16). Jacob crossed it alone the night before meeting Esau and there wrestled with a divine figure until daybreak, coming away with the name Israel and a permanent limp (Genesis 32:22-31); it is identified today with the Zarqa River in Jordan.

And he passed over the Jabbok  in the ninth month, on the eleventh thereof.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Jabez
entries.summary: Jabets, the name of an Israelite, and also of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Jabez names both a person and a place under one Hebrew word. The person is a descendant of Judah remembered for a short prayer asking God to bless him and enlarge his territory, a prayer the text says God granted (1 Chronicles 4:9-10). Separately, 1 Chronicles 2:55 lists Jabez as a town inhabited by families of scribes connected to the Kenite clans of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jabin
entries.summary: Jabin, the name of two Canaanitish kings
entries.dictNote: Jabin was a title used for at least two different kings of Hazor, one defeated by Joshua during the conquest and a later one whose general Sisera was defeated by Deborah and Barak generations afterward.

And since in the beginning of the next chapter it is said by Josephus, that there was hardly a breathing time for the Israelites before Jabin came and enslaved them; it is highly probable that some of the copies in his time had here only 8 years, instead of 80.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jabneel
entries.summary: Jabneel, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Jabneel is the name of two towns in the conquest narratives, not a person. One marked the northwestern border of Judah near the coast, later known as Jabneh or Jamnia (Joshua 15:11); the other lay on the boundary of Naphtali in the north (Joshua 19:33). The coastal Jabneh later became a notable Jewish town, and its walls were torn down by King Uzziah of Judah (2 Chronicles 26:6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jabneh
entries.dictNote: Jabneh, a Philistine border town whose walls King Uzziah of Judah broke down after defeating the Philistines (2 Chr. 26:6). It is the same town as Jabneel (Josh. 15:11) and later became known as Jamnia, or Yavne, a center of Jewish scholarship after the Second Temple's destruction in 70 AD.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jachan
entries.dictNote: A chief among the Gadite clans who settled in Bashan, listed among the heads of families in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 5:13. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.dictNote: Jachin was the name given to one of the two bronze pillars Solomon set up at the entrance of the temple, meaning he shall establish, paired with a second pillar named Boaz.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Jachinites
entries.summary: a Jakinite (collectively) or descendants of Jakin
entries.dictNote: Jachinites were the clan descended from Jachin, one of the sons of Simeon, listed in the Numbers 26 census of Israel's fighting men.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jacob
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Nahum, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Jacob was Isaac and Rebekah's younger twin, born grasping his brother Esau's heel, and he later bought Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew and stole his father's dying blessing with his mother's help, forcing him to flee for his life to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia. There he worked fourteen years for his two wives, Leah and Rachel, fathered the twelve sons who became the tribes of Israel, and on his way back to Canaan wrestled all night with a mysterious figure who renamed him Israel, meaning he struggles with God. Jacob spent his last seventeen years in Egypt after his son Joseph, whom he had long believed dead, turned out to be the country's second-in-command, and he was buried back in Canaan in the family tomb at Machpelah exactly as he had asked.

entries.title: Jacob
entries.summary: Luke's angel tells Mary that Jesus will reign ‘over the house of Jacob forever’ (1:33) — the same Jacob paired with Abraham and Isaac as founding-father shorthand later (13:28, 20:37). Josephus's version of the Genesis 28 vision at Bethel has God open with almost a pep talk — don't be dejected at your present circumstances — before the land-and-descendants promise Genesis itself records.
entries.books: Matthew, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews
entries.dictNote: Jacob was Isaac and Rebekah's younger twin, born grasping his brother Esau's heel, and he later bought Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew and stole his father's dying blessing with his mother's help, forcing him to flee for his life to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia. There he worked fourteen years for his two wives, Leah and Rachel, fathered the twelve sons who became the tribes of Israel, and on his way back to Canaan wrestled all night with a mysterious figure who renamed him Israel, meaning he struggles with God. Jacob spent his last seventeen years in Egypt after his son Joseph, whom he had long believed dead, turned out to be the country's second-in-command, and he was buried back in Canaan in the family tomb at Machpelah exactly as he had asked.

witness.excerpt: O Jacob, it is not fit for thee, who art the son of a good father, and grandson of one who had obtained a great reputation for his eminent virtue, to be dejected at thy present circumstances, but to hope for better times, for thou shalt have great abundance of all good things, by my assistance…

entries.title: Janoah
entries.dictNote: Janoah names two different towns. One lay on the northeastern border of Ephraim, in the Jordan Valley, identified with the modern village of Yanun southeast of Nablus (Josh. 16:6-7). The other was a town in Naphtali, in the north, captured by Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria along with Galilee and Gilead during his campaign against Israel under King Pekah, an event corroborated by Tiglath-pileser's own royal inscriptions listing his conquests in the Levant (2 Kings 15:29).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Janum (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: Janum, a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, listed among towns such as Beth-tappuah and Aphekah in Joshua 15:53. It is not mentioned again and its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Japha
entries.dictNote: Japho is the Hebrew name for the port city better known by its Greek form, Joppa (modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv). Solomon's cedar for the temple, and later Ezra's timber for the second temple, arrived by sea at Joppa before being hauled up to Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 2:16; Ezra 3:7). It also marked the tribal border of Dan (Joshua 19:46) and was the port Jonah fled through toward Tarshish. Egyptian records from the Amarna archive already mention a guarded gate of Joppa centuries earlier, showing the city's long standing as a coastal gateway.

Genesis 10 traces his descendants to peoples associated with Asia Minor and the regions around the Aegean.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Japhia
entries.summary: Japhia, the name of a Canaanite, an Israelite, and a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Japhia is a name shared by a place and two men. It names a town on the southern border of Zebulun near Nazareth (Joshua 19:12); a king of Lachish who joined the Amorite coalition against Joshua and was defeated and killed (Joshua 10:3, 5); and a son born to David in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Japhlet
entries.dictNote: Japhlet was a descendant of Asher through Beriah and the head of a family clan within the tribe, the Japhletites (1 Chronicles 7:32-33). Nothing else is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Japhleti
entries.summary: a Japhletite or descendant of Japhlet
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a clan or territorial name: "the border of the Japhletite" marks a boundary point in the description of Ephraim and Manasseh's territorial allotment in Joshua 16:3. The Japhletites are otherwise unknown, and the name likely designated a local Canaanite clan whose territory bordered the tribal land.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jarah
entries.dictNote: Jarah was a descendant of Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, the son of Micah in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 9:42. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8:36 lists the same figure as Jehoadah, evidence of scribal variation in transmitting Benjamite names.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jareb
entries.summary: Jareb, a symbolical name for Assyria
entries.dictNote: Jareb is not a personal name but an obscure Hebrew phrase, traditionally rendered “King Jareb,” that appears twice in Hosea describing Israel's futile appeals to Assyria for help (Hosea 5:13; 10:6). Most modern scholars read it as an epithet for the Assyrian king, something like “a king who contends” or “the great king,” rather than a proper name, so it likely refers to Tiglath-pileser III or the Assyrian monarchy in general rather than to a specific named individual.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jared
entries.summary: Jered, the name of an antediluvian, and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Jared was a descendant of Seth in the genealogy leading to Noah, father of Enoch, and Genesis records his lifespan as nine hundred sixty-two years.

entries.title: Jaresiah
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite descendant of Jeroham, listed among the heads of families in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 8:27.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jarha
entries.dictNote: Jarha was an Egyptian servant of Sheshan, a descendant of Judah who had no sons. Sheshan gave Jarha his daughter in marriage to preserve the family line, and their descendants are traced several generations forward in Chronicles, eventually including Zabad, one of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 2:34-35; 11:41).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jarib
entries.summary: Jarib, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jarib was a common name, borne by a leader Ezra sent to recruit Levites for the return journey and by a priest confronted for a foreign marriage.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jarmuth
entries.summary: Jarmuth, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Jarmuth was a Canaanite city whose king joined a coalition against Gibeon after Gibeon made peace with Israel, a coalition Joshua defeated in the battle where the sun stood still.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jaroah
entries.dictNote: A chief of the tribe of Gad listed among the leading families of that tribe settled in the land of Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:14). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jashen
entries.dictNote: Jashen was the father of several warriors in David's elite fighting force, listed among his mighty men (2 Sam. 23:32); he is called Hashem in the parallel list at 1 Chronicles 11:34.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jashobeam
entries.summary: Jashobam, the name of two or three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jashobeam was the chief of David's three mightiest warriors, credited with killing three hundred men in a single encounter.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jashub
entries.summary: Jashub, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jashub was a son of Issachar, and also the name of a man confronted for a foreign marriage under Ezra.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jashubi-lehem
entries.dictNote: A name in the genealogy of Judah's descendants through Shelah, so obscure that older dictionaries debated whether it names a person or records a place, those who returned to Lehem (1 Chronicles 4:22). Modern translations generally treat it as tied to a place or event referenced in that verse rather than as an individual's name.

entries.title: Jashubites
entries.summary: a Jashubite, or descendant of Jashub
entries.dictNote: Jashubites were the clan descended from Jashub, a son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same name appears as Job in the King James rendering of Genesis 46:13.

entries.title: Jathniel
entries.dictNote: A Korahite Levite, the fourth son of Meshelemiah, listed among the gatekeepers assigned to guard the temple's entrances under David (1 Chr. 26:2).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jattir
entries.dictNote: Jattir was a town in the hill country of Judah assigned to the priestly line of Aaron among the Levitical cities (Joshua 15:48; 21:14). David sent part of the plunder taken from the Amalekites to its elders as a gift, one of many towns he cultivated as allies during his fugitive years (1 Samuel 30:27-31). It is identified with the ruin Khirbet Attir, south of Hebron.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Javan
entries.summary: Javan, the name of a son of Joktan, and of the race (Ionians, i.e. Greeks) descended from him, with their territory; also of a place in Arabia
entries.dictNote: In the table of nations, Javan is the fourth son of Japheth, whose descendants the Hebrews identified with the Ionians and, more broadly, the Greek world (Genesis 10:2, 4). The prophets use "Javan" as shorthand for Greece and its merchants (Isaiah 66:19; Ezekiel 27:13, 19), and the name survives in modern Hebrew as the word for Greece itself.

entries.title: Jaziz
entries.dictNote: Jaziz was a Hagrite who oversaw King David's flocks, one of the officials in charge of royal property listed in 1 Chronicles 27:31.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jearim
entries.dictNote: A hill or wooded ridge on the northern border of Judah's territory (Joshua 15:10). Its name, meaning "forests," is preserved in the fuller place name Kirjath-jearim, "city of forests," the town that stood near it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeaterai
entries.dictNote: Jeaterai was a Gershonite Levite, son of Zerah, listed in the Levitical genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6. Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeberechiah
entries.dictNote: Father of a Zechariah whom Isaiah took as a witness when the prophet inscribed a tablet during the reign of King Ahaz (Isaiah 8:2).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jebus
entries.summary: Jebus, the original name of Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Jebus was the pre-conquest name for Jerusalem while it was still held by the Jebusites, before David captured it and made it his capital.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jecholiah
entries.dictNote: Jecholiah was the wife of King Amaziah of Judah and mother of his successor, Uzziah (also called Azariah), who came to the throne at sixteen and reigned for over fifty years (2 Kings 15:2; 2 Chronicles 26:3). Chronicles names her hometown as Jerusalem. Otherwise nothing further is recorded of her.

witness.excerpt: He was born of Jecoliah his mother, who was a citizen of Jerusalem.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jechonias
entries.dictNote: Jechonias is the Greek form of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the young king of Judah exiled to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar after a three-month reign (2 Kings 24:8-15); Matthew's genealogy lists him at the pivotal generation marking the exile (Matthew 1:11-12). Babylonian ration tablets excavated in the city and dated to Nebuchadnezzar's reign list regular food allotments for “Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud” and his sons, confirming that the exiled king was kept alive and provided for at the Babylonian court, exactly as 2 Kings 25:27-30 describes decades later. Jeremiah had pronounced a curse that none of his descendants would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30), a tension Matthew resolves by tracing Jesus' legal, not biological, throne-right through Joseph rather than a reigning bloodline.

entries.title: Jeconiah
entries.dictNote: Jeconiah is an alternate name for Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon and later released to a place of honor at the Babylonian king's table, covered more fully under the entry for Jehoiachin.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jedaiah
entries.summary: Jedajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jedaiah was a common priestly name in the postexilic period, borne by several priests who returned from Babylonian exile and served in the rebuilt temple.

entries.title: Jedaiah
entries.summary: Jedajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jedaiah was a common priestly name in the postexilic period, borne by several priests who returned from Babylonian exile and served in the rebuilt temple.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jediael
entries.summary: Jediael, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jediael was a common name among David's warriors and Benjamite clan leaders listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jedidah
entries.dictNote: Wife of King Amon of Judah and mother of Josiah, remembered as one of Judah's most thoroughgoing religious reformers (2 Kings 22:1).

witness.excerpt: His mother was of the city of Boscath; and her name was Jedidah.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jedidiah
entries.dictNote: The name the prophet Nathan gave to the infant Solomon at God's direction, meaning "beloved of the LORD" (2 Sam. 12:25). It marks God's favor toward Solomon immediately after the account of David's sin with Bathsheba and the death of their first child, though "Solomon" remained the name history remembered him by.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeduthun
entries.dictNote: Jeduthun was one of the three chief musicians David appointed over temple worship, alongside Heman and Asaph, and several psalms carry his name in their superscriptions as a musical or performance notation.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Jeezer
entries.dictNote: Head of the Manassite clan of the Jeezerites counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:30); the same name appears elsewhere as Abiezer, the fuller form from which Gideon's own clan later descended (Judges 6:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jegar-Sahadutha
entries.summary: Jegar-Sahadutha, a cairn East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Jegar-sahadutha is not a person but the Aramaic name Laban gave to the heap of stones he and Jacob raised as a witness to their covenant in Gilead (Genesis 31:47). Jacob gave the same monument a Hebrew name, Galeed, meaning the same thing: "heap of witness."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehalellel
entries.summary: Jehallelel, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehalellel's name means “praise God.” One man of this name appears in the tribe of Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 4:16). A second Jehalellel was a Levite whose sons helped lead the purification of the temple under King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:12).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jehdai
entries.dictNote: Jehdai, also spelled Jahdai, was a descendant of Caleb through the line of Ezrah, listed as the father of six sons in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:47).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehdeiah
entries.summary: Jechdijah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehdeiah's name means “he who rejoices in the LORD.” One Jehdeiah was a Levite descended from Shubael who was assigned to a division of temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:20). A second Jehdeiah, a Meronothite, was in charge of the donkeys used in David and Solomon's royal service (1 Chronicles 27:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehiah
entries.dictNote: Jehiah was one of the doorkeepers appointed to guard the ark of the covenant when David brought it to Jerusalem, along with Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 15:24). The role placed him among the Levites David organized for tabernacle service ahead of Solomon's temple.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehiel
entries.summary: Jechiel (or Jechavel), the name of eight Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehiel was a common Levitical name in Chronicles, borne by several temple musicians and officials serving under David and later kings.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jehiel
entries.summary: Jeuel, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehiel was a common Levitical name in Chronicles, borne by several temple musicians and officials serving under David and later kings.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jehieli
entries.summary: a Jechielite or descendant of Jechiel
entries.dictNote: Jehieli was a Gershonite Levite descended from Ladan, head of a family placed in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD under David (1 Chronicles 26:21-22). He and his brother Zetham administered the dedicated gifts and spoils brought in for the temple's future construction. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehoada
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in Benjamin's genealogy as the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri (1 Chronicles 8:36). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 9:42 calls the same man Jarah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehoaddan
entries.dictNote: Jehoaddan, also called Jehoaddin, was the wife of King Jehoash of Judah and the mother of his successor, King Amaziah; she is identified as a native of Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:2; 2 Chronicles 25:1). Scripture records nothing further about her, typical of the brief, formulaic queen-mother notices given for most kings of Judah.

witness.excerpt: His mothers name was Jehoaddan , who was born at Jerusalem.

entries.summary: Jehoachaz, the name of three Israelites

entries.title: Jehoiachin
entries.dictNote: Jehoiachin was a king of Judah who reigned only three months before surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar's siege and being taken captive to Babylon along with much of Jerusalem's elite. entries.title: Jehoiada
entries.summary: Jehojada, the name of three Israelites
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Jehoiada was the priest who hid the infant king Joash in the temple for six years after Queen Athaliah massacred the rest of the royal family, then staged a coordinated coup that overthrew Athaliah and installed Joash as Judah's rightful king. As long as Jehoiada lived he guided Joash toward faithful reform, and Judah's leadership honored him at his death with burial among the kings, an honor no other priest received.

entries.title: Jehoiakim
entries.dictNote: Jehoiakim was installed as king of Judah by the Egyptian pharaoh Necho and later switched allegiance to Babylon under pressure, and he is remembered mainly for his contempt toward the prophet Jeremiah's warnings: when a scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was read to him, Jehoiakim cut off each section with a knife and burned it in a fire pot as it was read, unmoved even as advisors begged him to stop. Jeremiah had the entire scroll rewritten, with additional judgments added specifically because of what Jehoiakim had done to the first copy.

entries.title: Jehoiarib
entries.summary: Jehojarib, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehoiarib was a priest in Jerusalem who headed the first of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 9:10; 24:7). His course continued after the Babylonian exile, and the priestly family of Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, later traced its descent from this division.

entries.title: Jehoshabeath
entries.dictNote: Daughter of King Jehoram of Judah and sister of King Ahaziah, married to the priest Jehoiada. When the queen mother Athaliah moved to kill off the royal family after Ahaziah's death, Jehoshabeath hid the infant Joash and his nurse in a temple storeroom, preserving the Davidic line (2 Chronicles 22:11). She appears as Jehosheba in the parallel account in 2 Kings 11.

entries.title: Jehoshaphat
entries.summary: Jehoshaphat, the name of six Israelites; also of a valley near Jerusalem
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Joel
entries.dictNote: Jehoshaphat was a king of Judah remembered for his religious reforms, sending officials and Levites throughout the kingdom to teach the law, and for an alliance with the northern kingdom of Israel that repeatedly went badly, including a joint military campaign that nearly got him killed when enemy soldiers mistook him for the wicked king Ahab. His greatest crisis came when Moab, Ammon, and Edom invaded together; rather than fight, Jehoshaphat sent singers ahead of his army to praise God, and the invading coalition turned on itself and destroyed its own forces before Judah ever engaged. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament also share the name.

entries.title: Jehosheba
entries.dictNote: Jehosheba was a daughter of King Jehoram of Judah and, according to 2 Chronicles 22:11, wife of the high priest Jehoiada. When the usurper Athaliah moved to kill the entire royal family after her son Ahaziah's death, Jehosheba hid the infant prince Joash in the temple for six years, preserving the Davidic line (2 Kings 11:2-3). She is called Jehoshabeath in 2 Chronicles 22:11.

His name, meaning Yahweh saves, is the same Hebrew name later rendered Jesus in Greek.

entries.title: Jehu
entries.summary: Jehu, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jehu was a military commander anointed king of Israel by one of Elisha's prophetic students specifically to destroy Ahab's dynasty, and he carried out that mission with notorious thoroughness, killing King Joram, Queen Jezebel, and every remaining descendant of Ahab's house, then tricking Baal's priests into a fake sacrifice so he could slaughter them all at once. An Assyrian relief, the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, depicts Jehu bowing before the Assyrian king and paying tribute, the only known image of an Israelite king in ancient art.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Jehubbah
entries.dictNote: Jehubbah was a descendant of Asher through Beriah, listed in the tribal genealogy of Asher (1 Chr. 7:34). Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehucal
entries.dictNote: Jehucal, also called Jucal, was an official King Zedekiah sent, along with the priest Zephaniah, to ask the prophet Jeremiah to pray for the besieged kingdom during the final Babylonian siege of Jerusalem (Jer. 37:3). He later appears among the officials who had Jeremiah thrown into a cistern for prophesying the city's fall (Jer. 38:1-6).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehud
entries.dictNote: A town allotted to the tribe of Dan, listed between Baalath and Bene-berak in the coastal plain (Josh. 19:45). It survives as the modern Israeli town of Yehud, near Lod.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehudi
entries.dictNote: Jehudi was the official King Jehoiakim sent to retrieve Jeremiah's scroll of prophecies and read it aloud, the same scroll the king then cut apart and burned section by section as it was read.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehudijah
entries.dictNote: Not actually a personal name: the Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 4:18 reads "ha-Yehudiyyah," an epithet meaning "the Jewess," attached to one of the wives of Mered in the genealogy of Judah. Many interpreters identify her with Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, named in the same verse, whose marriage into Judah's line made her "the Jewess" by adoption rather than birth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jehush
entries.summary: Jeush, the name of an Edomite and of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jeush was a common name, borne by a son of Esau, a son of Rehoboam, and several Levites in the genealogies of Chronicles.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jeiel
entries.summary: Jeiel, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jeiel was a common Levitical and military name in Chronicles, borne by several temple musicians, scribes, and officials across different generations.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jekabzeel
entries.dictNote: Jekabzeel is a fuller form of the name Kabzeel, the southernmost town of Judah on the border with Edom, and appears in Nehemiah's list of towns resettled by the people of Judah after the Babylonian exile (Neh. 11:25). Kabzeel was also the hometown of Benaiah, one of David's elite warriors and later commander of his bodyguard.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jekameam
entries.dictNote: Jekameam was a Levite, one of the sons of Hebron in the Kohathite line, listed among the heads of Levitical divisions organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 23:19; 24:23).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jekamiah
entries.summary: Jekamjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Jekamiah appear in the genealogies of Judah. One descended from Sheshan through his daughter's marriage to an Egyptian servant, in the line of Ahlai (1 Chronicles 2:35-41). The other was a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), born to him in captivity in Babylon (1 Chronicles 3:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jekuthiel
entries.dictNote: Listed in the genealogies of Judah as connected to the town of Zanoah, recorded among the descendants attributed to Mered's Egyptian wife Bithiah (1 Chr. 4:18). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jemimah
entries.dictNote: The eldest of Job's three daughters born after God restored his fortunes at the end of the book, alongside her sisters Keziah and Keren-happuch (Job 42:14). Unusually for the Old Testament, the text specifically notes that Job gave his daughters an inheritance alongside their brothers (Job 42:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jemuel
entries.dictNote: Jemuel was the eldest son of Simeon, one of the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:10; Exodus 6:15). He is called Nemuel in the later census list of Simeon's clans (Numbers 26:12).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jephthah
entries.summary: Jiphtach, an Israelite; also a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Jephthah was the son of a prostitute, driven out by his half-brothers and living as a bandit leader until Gilead's elders begged him to lead their fight against the Ammonites. He made a reckless vow that whatever came out of his house first to greet him after victory would be sacrificed to God, and that turned out to be his own daughter, his only child, a story Judges records without endorsing the vow or explaining why Jephthah felt bound to keep it.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Jephunneh
entries.summary: Jephunneh, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jephunneh was Caleb's father, and Caleb is consistently identified throughout the Old Testament as Caleb son of Jephunneh to distinguish him from others sharing the same name.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Jerah
entries.dictNote: Jerah was a son of Joktan, in the line of Shem, and the ancestor of one of the Arabian tribes descended from him (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). His name means "moon" in Hebrew, though little else is known about the tribe he represents.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jerahmeel
entries.summary: Jerachmeel, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jerahmeel was a descendant of Judah through Perez, and his extensive genealogy in 1 Chronicles preserves the lineage of a prominent clan within Judah's tribe.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jerahmeelites
entries.summary: a Jerachmeelite or descendant of Jerachmeel
entries.dictNote: Jerahmeelites were a Judahite clan descended from Jerahmeel, settled in the Negev south of Judah. While based at Ziklag under Philistine protection, David raided their territory along with the Kenites and other southern groups, then later shared plunder from his pursuit of the Amalekites with Jerahmeelite towns as an ally.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeremai
entries.dictNote: One of the men descended from Hashum listed among those who had married foreign wives during the postexilic community and agreed, under Ezra's direction, to separate from them (Ezra 10:33). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeremiah
entries.summary: Jirmejah, the name of eight or nine Israelites
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Matthew
entries.dictNote: Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth called to prophesy as a young man in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, and he spent the next four decades warning Judah of the coming Babylonian conquest while the nation's leaders imprisoned him, threw him in a cistern, and burned his prophecies rather than listen. He watched Jerusalem fall exactly as he had predicted and was forced into exile in Egypt against his will after the city's remaining leadership was assassinated. A clay seal impression reading Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe, found in Jerusalem and dated to Jeremiah's own lifetime, is widely identified with Baruch, the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah's dictated prophecies in Jeremiah 36. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament share the name Jeremiah but have no connection to the prophet.

entries.dictNote: Jericho sat on the west bank of the Jordan, close enough to the cliffs behind it that the site is traditionally linked to Christ's temptation centuries later. Walled and gated, ruled by its own king, it was the first city Israel took after crossing the Jordan, and the plunder found inside it, Babylonian robes and hoarded silver, became the reason Achan was executed for taking what belonged to God. Long before any of that, Jericho had already been standing for millennia: archaeologists have found remains at the site predating the Neolithic period, roughly ten thousand years old, making it one of the oldest continuously occupied settlements ever excavated.

entries.dictNote: Jeroboam was an official under Solomon who led the ten northern tribes in breaking away to form a separate kingdom of Israel after Solomon's son Rehoboam refused to ease his father's harsh labor policies. To keep his new subjects from returning to Jerusalem to worship and possibly switching allegiance back to Judah, Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and installed his own priesthood, a decision the Old Testament treats as the original sin that doomed every king of northern Israel after him. A later king of Israel, Jeroboam the second, ruled generations afterward during a period of unusual prosperity and military success.

entries.summary: Jerubbesheth, a symbolic name for Gideon
entries.dictNote: An alternate name for Gideon used once, in 2 Samuel 11:21, where the scribe replaces the "-baal" element of Jerubbaal with "-besheth" ("shame") to avoid writing the name of the Canaanite god Baal. It reflects the same scribal habit that turned Ishbaal into Ishbosheth and Meribbaal into Mephibosheth elsewhere in Samuel.

entries.dictNote: A wilderness area on the ascent from the Dead Sea toward Jerusalem, near Tekoa, where King Jehoshaphat's army confronted an invading coalition of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites without having to fight, after God caused the invaders to turn on one another (2 Chr. 20:16-24).

entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Psalm, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Zephaniah, Zechariah, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Jerusalem was Israel's capital under David, who captured it from the Jebusites and made it his political and religious center, and Solomon's temple there made it the focal point of Israelite worship for a thousand years, through destruction by Babylon, rebuilding under the returned exiles, and a final destruction by Rome in AD 70. Jesus's death and resurrection took place just outside its walls, and its name became synonymous throughout Scripture with God's dwelling among his people, extended in Revelation into the vision of a new Jerusalem descending from heaven. It remains one of the most excavated cities in the world, and finds ranging from Hezekiah's tunnel to the Pilate-era Pool of Siloam continue to confirm details from the biblical account.

entries.dictNote: Jerusalem was Israel's capital under David and the site of Solomon's temple, the focal point of Jewish worship through the New Testament period, where Jesus was crucified and rose again, and where the church began at Pentecost. See the main Jerusalem entry for its fuller history.

entries.dictNote: Jerusalem was Israel's capital under David and the site of Solomon's temple, the focal point of Jewish worship through the New Testament period, where Jesus was crucified and rose again, and where the church began at Pentecost. See the main Jerusalem entry for its fuller history.

entries.title: Jerusha
entries.dictNote: Jerusha, daughter of Zadok, was the wife of King Uzziah of Judah and mother of his successor Jotham (2 Kings 15:33; 2 Chronicles 27:1). Nothing more is recorded of her beyond this genealogical notice.

witness.excerpt: 759.] Now Jotham, the son of Uzziah, reigned over the tribe of Judah in Jerusalem: being a citizen thereof by his mother, whose name was Jerusha .

entries.title: Jeshanah
entries.dictNote: Jeshanah was a town in the northern kingdom of Israel that King Abijah of Judah captured from Jeroboam, along with Bethel and Ephron, during a battle in which Judah's forces won despite being badly outnumbered (2 Chronicles 13:19). It is generally identified with Burj el-Isaneh, north of Bethel. The Jeshanah gate mentioned in Nehemiah's account of Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 3:6; 12:39) is a separate, unrelated reference to an old gate in the city itself.

entries.title: Jesharelah
entries.dictNote: Jesharelah, elsewhere spelled Asarelah, was a son of Asaph who headed the seventh of the twenty-four divisions of Levitical musicians David organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 25:14; compare 25:2).

entries.dictNote: Jesher was the first of three sons attributed to Caleb and his wife Azubah in the genealogy of Judah, though the same verse's mention of a second woman, Jerioth, leaves the parentage slightly unclear (1 Chronicles 2:18).

entries.dictNote: Jeshoaiah was one of the family heads of the tribe of Simeon listed in 1 Chronicles 4:36, part of a genealogy describing clans that expanded their pastureland by displacing the Hamites and Meunites (1 Chronicles 4:38-41). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

entries.dictNote: Jeshua is a shortened, post-exilic spelling of the name Joshua, “the LORD saves,” and in Ezra-Nehemiah it belongs to several different people as well as to a resettled town. Its most significant bearer is Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, rebuilt the altar and later the temple, and is called Joshua in the prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah, where he stands beside Zerubbabel as a picture of the coming priest-king. The name also belongs to a priestly family head, several Levites who assisted in reforms and worship under Ezra and Nehemiah, and a town in Judah resettled after the exile.

entries.summary: Jeshurun, a symbolic name for Israel
entries.dictNote: Jeshurun is an affectionate poetic name for Israel, meaning the upright one, used a handful of times in Deuteronomy and Isaiah, often in passages that then pointedly contrast that name with Israel's actual unfaithfulness.

entries.dictNote: A leader of a Simeonite clan named in the record of Simeon's expansion of territory, when several of these clan heads drove out the Hamite inhabitants near Gedor and settled there (1 Chronicles 4:36-41).

entries.title: Jesse
entries.summary: David's own father, named right next to Boaz in the genealogy (3:32) — Obed's son, one generation closer to the throne. The same Josephus chapter that tells Boaz and Ruth's story ends by naming exactly this line down to David.
entries.books: Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Matthew, Luke, Acts, Romans
entries.dictNote: Firm, or a gift, a son of Obed, the son of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17, 22; Matt. 1:5, 6; Luke 3:32). He was the father of eight sons, the youngest of whom was David (1 Sam. 17:12). The phrase “stem of Jesse” is used for the family of David (Isa. 11:1), and “root of Jesse” for the Messiah (Isa. 11:10; Rev. 5:5). Jesse was a man apparently of wealth and position at Bethlehem (1 Sam. 17:17, 18, 20; Ps. 78:71). The last reference to him is of David’s procuring for him an asylum with the king of Moab (1 Sam. 22:3).

entries.dictNote: Jesus of Nazareth is the central figure of the New Testament, born in Bethlehem to Mary, a virgin engaged to Joseph, and raised in Nazareth in Galilee. He began a public ministry around age thirty, teaching in parables, gathering twelve core disciples, and performing miracles of healing and provision that the Gospels present as signs of God's kingdom breaking into the present. His growing following and his direct challenges to the religious establishment led to his arrest in Jerusalem during Passover, a rushed trial before the Jewish council and the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and execution by crucifixion, a Roman method of execution independently confirmed by archaeology, including a first-century heel bone found in Jerusalem still pierced by an iron nail. Christian faith rests on the claim that Jesus rose bodily from the tomb three days later, an event his earliest followers testified to at the cost of their own lives, and the New Testament identifies him as the promised Messiah, God's own Son become human.

entries.title: Jezabel
entries.summary: Jezabel (i.e. Jezebel), a Tyrian woman (used as a synonym of a termagant or false teacher)
entries.dictNote: This Jezebel is not the Old Testament queen but a woman in the church at Thyatira whom Christ rebukes in Revelation for calling herself a prophetess and teaching believers to commit sexual immorality and eat food sacrificed to idols (Revelation 2:20). John applies the notorious name as a label for her corrupting influence, deliberately recalling the Old Testament queen who promoted Baal worship in Israel, rather than naming an actual descendant or namesake of hers.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jezaniah
entries.dictNote: Jezaniah, son of Hoshaiah the Maachathite, commanded one of the bands of Judean soldiers who had escaped into the countryside during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. He submitted to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon installed over Judah, but after Gedaliah's assassination he was among the leaders who, against Jeremiah's warning, forced the remaining Judeans to flee to Egypt (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8; 42:1; 43:2).

entries.title: Jezebel
entries.summary: Izebel, the wife of king Ahab
entries.dictNote: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, daughter of the king of Sidon, whom Ahab married to cement a political alliance, and she used her position as queen to aggressively promote Baal worship and hunt down Yahweh's prophets across Israel. When Naboth refused to sell Ahab a vineyard, Jezebel arranged false charges that got Naboth stoned to death so Ahab could take the land, a crime Elijah confronted directly, prophesying that dogs would eat her body. Years later, when Jehu seized the throne in a violent coup, Jezebel put on makeup and dressed her hair before facing him from a window, and Jehu had her thrown down and left for the dogs, exactly as Elijah had said.

entries.title: Jezerite
entries.summary: an Iezrite or descendant of Iezer
entries.dictNote: Jezerite marks the clan descended from Jeezer, also spelled Abiezer, a son of Gilead within the tribe of Manasseh, counted in the Numbers 26 census. This is the same Abiezrite family into which Gideon was born, and Ophrah, his hometown, belonged to this clan.

entries.title: Jezerites
entries.summary: a Jitsrite (collectively) or descendants of Jetser
entries.dictNote: Jezerites here names the fourth division of the Levitical singers organized under Asaph for temple worship, assigned by lot to Izri, also spelled Zeri, in 1 Chronicles 25:11. Twenty-four such divisions of musicians, each serving in rotation, are listed in the chapter.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeziah
entries.dictNote: Jeziah was one of the descendants of Parosh named in Ezra 10:25 among the men who had married foreign wives during the exile and agreed, under Ezra's reform, to put them away. He appears in a long list of names grouped by ancestral family, reflecting the scale of the intermarriage crisis Ezra addressed after the return from Babylon. Nothing beyond this single mention is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jeziel (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: A son of Azmaveth and one of the skilled Benjamite archers, able to sling stones and shoot arrows with either hand, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still hiding from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:1-3). These early recruits from Saul's own tribe were a notable sign of David's growing support.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jezliah
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, listed among the family heads who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:18). Nothing else is recorded of him.

David never forgave him for Absalom's death and left instructions for Solomon to have Joab executed, which Solomon carried out even after Joab fled to the altar for sanctuary.

entries.title: Joanna
entries.dictNote: Joanna was the name of two figures connected to Luke's Gospel. One was an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, apparently the same man Chronicles calls Hananiah, a descendant of Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27; 1 Chronicles 3:19). The other Joanna was the wife of Chuza, a steward of Herod Antipas; she helped support Jesus' ministry financially, and she was among the women who found the empty tomb and reported it to the apostles (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

Joash ordered the temple repaired and reigned well while Jehoiada lived, but after the priest died he abandoned the reforms, and when Jehoiada's own son confronted him for it, Joash had the man stoned to death in the temple courtyard, a betrayal that led to Joash's own assassination not long after.

entries.title: Job
entries.summary: Ijob, the patriarch famous for his patience
entries.dictNote: Job was a wealthy and righteous man from the land of Uz whose story opens with a wager in the divine council: God allows Satan to strip Job of his children, his wealth, and his health to test whether Job's faith depends on his prosperity. Job never curses God, but he does demand an explanation, and most of the book is a long argument between Job and three friends who insist his suffering must be punishment for hidden sin. When God finally answers from a whirlwind, he never actually explains why Job suffered, instead overwhelming Job with the scale of creation, and Job's response is to fall silent and be restored with double what he had before.

entries.dictNote: The patriarch of the Old Testament book that bears his name, held up in James 5:11 as the model of endurance under undeserved suffering. Job lived in the land of Uz, outside the normal covenant line of Israel, and the book built around him wrestles with why a righteous man suffers, answering not with a tidy explanation but with God's own overwhelming appearance and questions from the whirlwind.

entries.title: Jobab
entries.summary: Jobab, the name of two Israelites and of three foreigners
entries.dictNote: Jobab was a common name, borne by a king of Edom, a Canaanite king who joined a coalition against Joshua, and a son of Joktan in the genealogies of Genesis.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jobesh (-Gilead)
entries.summary: Jobesh, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Town in Gilead east of the Jordan, better known as Jabesh-gilead. Its men failed to join Israel's coalition against Benjamin and were nearly wiped out as punishment, until the tribe's survivors were given Jabesh-gilead's surviving virgin daughters as wives to preserve Benjamin's line (Judges 21:8-14). Generations later the Ammonite king Nahash besieged the town, and Saul's rescue of it was his first act as king, one that secured his authority over Israel (1 Sam. 11). After Saul's death in battle, the town's men risked their lives to recover his body from the walls of Beth-shan and gave it honorable burial (1 Sam. 31:11-13; 1 Chr. 10:11-12).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Jochebed
entries.dictNote: Jochebed was the wife of Amram and the mother of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses (Numbers 26:59). She hid the infant Moses for three months and then placed him in a basket on the Nile to save him from Pharaoh's decree, and later nursed him as his hired wet nurse after Pharaoh's daughter drew him from the water (Exodus 2:1-10).

entries.title: Joed
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, in the genealogy tracing Sallu son of Meshullam back through Joed and Pedaiah (Nehemiah 11:7). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joel
entries.summary: Joel, the name of twelve Israelites
entries.books: 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Joel, Acts
entries.dictNote: Joel was a prophet whose short book uses a locust plague that had devastated Judah as a picture of an even more terrible coming day of the Lord, calling the nation to repentance and fasting in response. His prophecy that God would pour out his Spirit on all people, sons and daughters, old and young, slave and free, is quoted directly by Peter in Acts to explain what was happening at Pentecost. Several minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament also share the name.
