entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Joelah
entries.dictNote: One of the Benjamite warriors, kinsmen of Saul's own tribe, who defected to join David while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joezer
entries.dictNote: One of the Korahite warriors who joined David's growing band of fighting men at Ziklag while he was still fleeing from Saul, part of a group of skilled archers and slingers able to fight with either hand (1 Chronicles 12:6-7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jogbehah
entries.summary: Jogbehah, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Jogbehah was one of the towns east of the Jordan that Gad's tribe built and fortified after settling that territory (Numbers 32:35). Gideon later passed by it while pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna along the caravan route east of Nobah (Judges 8:11).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jogli
entries.dictNote: Jogli was the father of Bukki, the leader of the tribe of Dan appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:22). Nothing further is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joha
entries.summary: Jocha, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Joha appear in Chronicles. One was a Benjamite, son of Beriah, listed among the heads of families living in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:16). The other, called the Tizite, was one of David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:45). Nothing else distinguishes them.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Johanan
entries.summary: Jochanan, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Several men named Johanan appear in the Old Testament, most notably a military commander after Jerusalem's fall who warned the newly appointed governor Gedaliah about an assassination plot, a warning Gedaliah dismissed before the plot succeeded.

entries.title: John
entries.summary: Joannes (i.e. Jochanan), the name of four Israelites
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Galatians, Revelation
entries.dictNote: John was a fisherman, the son of Zebedee and younger brother of James, and part of Jesus's innermost circle along with Peter and James, present at moments the other disciples weren't, including the transfiguration and Gethsemane. Tradition identifies him as the disciple whom Jesus loved in the fourth Gospel, and it was John whom Jesus entrusted with the care of his mother Mary from the cross. He went on to become a leading figure in the Jerusalem church, and early Christian tradition credits him with writing the Gospel of John, three New Testament letters, and the book of Revelation while exiled on the island of Patmos.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Joiakim
entries.dictNote: Joiakim was a high priest during the postexilic period, the son of Joshua and father of Eliashib, serving in the generation between the temple's completion and Nehemiah's later reforms.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joiarib
entries.summary: Jojarib, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Joiarib was the head of one of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized for rotating temple service, and descendants bearing his name appear among the postexilic priestly families.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jokdeam
entries.dictNote: A town in the hill country of Judah, listed near Maon and Carmel (Joshua 15:56). Its site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jokim
entries.dictNote: Jokim was a descendant of Shelah, the son of Judah, listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4:22.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jokmeam
entries.dictNote: Levitical town likely located in the Jordan valley near Ephraim's territory, assigned along with its pasturelands to the Kohathite Levites for their support (1 Kings 4:12; 1 Chr. 6:68).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jokneam
entries.dictNote: Jokneam was a Canaanite royal city defeated by Joshua, situated near Mount Carmel by the Kishon River (Joshua 12:22). It fell within Zebulun's territory and was later assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 19:11; 21:34). It is generally identified with Tel Yokneam, a mound about twelve miles southwest of Nazareth that has been excavated and shows occupation across much of the biblical period.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jokshan
entries.dictNote: Jokshan was a son of Abraham through his wife Keturah, and his descendants included Sheba and Dedan, names associated with Arabian trading peoples.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Joktan
entries.dictNote: Joktan was a son of Eber, and Genesis traces an extensive list of Arabian peoples descended from him, distinguishing his line from his brother Peleg's, through whom Abraham eventually descended.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Joktheel
entries.summary: Joktheel, the name of a place in Palestine, and of one in Idumaea
entries.dictNote: Two places carry this name, meaning "subdued by God." One was a town in Judah near Lachish (Josh. 15:38). The other was the new name Amaziah, king of Judah, gave to Sela after conquering Edom and slaughtering its army (2 Kings 14:7); Sela, meaning "rock," is often linked to the Edomite highlands south of the Dead Sea, where a rock outcrop near Bozrah bears a carved relief and inscription of the Babylonian king Nabonidus, evidence that the region's strongholds remained significant for centuries after Amaziah's campaign.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jonadab
entries.summary: Jonadab, the name of an Israelite and of a Rechabite
entries.dictNote: Jonadab was David's nephew, a clever and manipulative advisor who suggested the scheme that let Amnon get his half-sister Tamar alone, setting up Amnon's rape of her and the chain of violence that followed.

witness.excerpt: So Amnon lay down on his bed, and pretended to be sick, as Jonadab had suggested.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jonah
entries.dictNote: Jonah was a prophet ordered to preach repentance to Nineveh, the capital of Israel's enemy Assyria, and he ran the opposite direction by ship instead, prompting the storm and the famous three days inside a great fish that eventually vomited him onto dry land. When he finally preached to Nineveh, the entire city repented and God spared it, which made Jonah furious rather than pleased, and the book ends with God gently confronting Jonah's anger rather than resolving it. A different man named Jonah is listed as the father of the apostle Peter in the Gospels.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jonah
entries.summary: Jesus calls his own coming death and resurrection ‘the sign of Jonah’ (11:29-30) and rates Nineveh's repentance above his own generation's (11:32) — both times treating the whale story as settled history, not metaphor. Josephus tells it the same way a century later, adding a detail Jonah itself never states: which sea he surfaced in.
entries.dictNote: A dove, the son of Amittai of Gath-hepher. He was a prophet of Israel, and predicted the restoration of the ancient boundaries (2 Kings 14:25-27) of the kingdom. He exercised his ministry very early in the reign of Jeroboam II., and thus was contemporary with Hosea and Amos; or possibly he preceded them, and consequently may have been the very oldest of all the prophets whose writings we possess. His personal history is mainly to be gathered from the book which bears his name. It is chiefly interesting from the two-fold character in which he appears, (1) as a missionary to heathen Nineveh, and (2) as a type of the “Son of man.”

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Jonan
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, listed as the son of Eliakim (Luke 3:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jonathan
entries.summary: Jehonathan, the name of four Israelites
entries.books: Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Jonathan was Saul's eldest son and heir to Israel's throne, best remembered for his loyal friendship with David, a friendship sealed with a covenant even though Jonathan knew it meant giving up his own claim to the kingship. Early in his father's reign he single-handedly triggered a rout of the Philistine army by climbing a cliff with only his armor-bearer and trusting that God could win with few as easily as with many. entries.dictNote: Joppa was Judea's principal seaport, a promontory on the Mediterranean coast from which Jonah once boarded a ship to flee his commission to Nineveh, and through which cedar for both Solomon's and Zerubbabel's temples was floated ashore. In Acts, Peter raised Tabitha from the dead at Joppa and, while staying in the house of Simon the tanner there, received the vision that opened the gospel to Gentiles. The city's capture is recorded in an Egyptian tale from the reign of Thutmose III, describing a general smuggling soldiers inside baskets, evidence of Joppa's strategic importance more than a thousand years before Peter's visit.

entries.summary: Jarden, the principal river of Palestine
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
entries.dictNote: The Jordan is the chief river of Palestine, running north to south from the slopes of Mount Hermon through the Sea of Galilee and down the Rift Valley to the Dead Sea, a straight-line distance of about sixty five miles that the river's winding course stretches to roughly two hundred. Its principal sources are the Dan, Banias, and Hasbany springs, all fed by Hermon's snowmelt. The Israelites crossed it on dry ground to enter Canaan under Joshua, Elijah and Elisha each parted its waters, and John the Baptist used it for the baptisms that included Jesus. Excavations at Bethany beyond the Jordan, on the river's east bank, have uncovered Byzantine era churches and baptismal pools marking the traditional site of that baptism.

entries.title: Jorim
entries.dictNote: Jorim was the son of Matthat, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:29), which traces David's line through his son Nathan rather than through Solomon as Matthew's genealogy does. Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jorkeam
entries.dictNote: Jorkeam is named in the genealogy of Caleb as a descendant of Raham (1 Chronicles 2:44). As with other entries in this genealogical list, the name most likely designates a town or clan founded by this family rather than a literal individual. It does not appear elsewhere in the Bible, and its location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Josabad
entries.summary: Jozabad, the name of ten Israelites
entries.dictNote: Jozabad was a common name among Levites and warriors, including one of David's elite soldiers who defected to him while he was still fleeing Saul.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Josaphat
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Jehoshaphat's name used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, referring to the king of Judah remembered for his religious reforms and his troubled alliance with the northern kingdom of Israel (Matthew 1:8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jose
entries.dictNote: A name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, son of Eliezer, listed among the ancestors of Joseph descending from David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon (Luke 3:29-31). Nothing else is known about him.

entries.title: Joseph
entries.summary: Joseph, the name of seven Israelites
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Ezekiel, Amos, Obadiah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Joseph was Jacob's eleventh son and Rachel's firstborn, sold into Egyptian slavery by his jealous brothers after his father's obvious favoritism and his own tactless dreams made him a target. In Egypt he rose from slave to prison to the second-highest office in the land by correctly interpreting Pharaoh's dreams of coming famine, and when that famine drove his brothers to Egypt for grain, he revealed himself and forgave them, reuniting the family that would become the nation of Israel. His deathbed instructions to carry his bones back to Canaan were kept literally, centuries later, during the exodus.

entries.dictNote: A different Joseph, a descendant of David from the town of Nazareth, was engaged to Mary when she was found to be pregnant before their marriage, and an angel convinced him in a dream to go through with the wedding rather than quietly break the engagement. He raised Jesus as his legal father, and Scripture gives no record of him after Jesus's boyhood, which is usually taken to mean he had died before Jesus's public ministry began.

entries.title: Joses
entries.summary: Joses, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Joses was the name of one of Jesus's brothers, and also of Barnabas, whose birth name was Joses before the apostles nicknamed him Barnabas, meaning son of encouragement.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joshah
entries.dictNote: Joshah was a chief of the tribe of Simeon whose family, during Hezekiah's reign, drove out the Hamite and Meunite inhabitants of a fertile valley near Gedor and settled there in their place (1 Chr. 4:34-41).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joshaphat
entries.dictNote: Joshaphat, called "the Mithnite," is listed among David's mighty warriors in the record of his elite fighting men (1 Chronicles 11:43).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joshaviah
entries.dictNote: Son of Elnaam, listed among David's mighty warriors in the roster of his elite fighting men (1 Chronicles 11:46).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Joshbekashah
entries.dictNote: Joshbekashah was a son of Heman, David's seer, and headed the seventeenth of the twenty-four courses of temple musicians David organized for worship (1 Chronicles 25:4, 24).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Josiah
entries.summary: The boy-king whose reforms follow the rediscovery of the Law scroll in the temple (2 Kings 22-23). Josephus's chapter groups him with Huldah the prophetess, the same pairing 2 Kings makes — the king who acts, and the prophetess he consults to be sure the scroll is genuine.
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Josiah became king of Judah at eight years old after his father Amon was assassinated, and in the eighteenth year of his reign workers repairing the temple found a forgotten scroll of the law, whose reading triggered Judah's last great religious reform: Josiah tore down pagan altars across the kingdom, reinstated Passover on a scale not seen since the days of the judges, and executed the priests of the high places he destroyed. He died young, killed in battle at Megiddo trying to block the Egyptian army from reinforcing Assyria, and Judah's slide toward Babylonian exile resumed almost immediately under his successors. The Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform tablet recording the same Egyptian campaign, confirms the military situation that cost Josiah his life.

witness.excerpt: After Amon reigned Josiah. He was both righteous, and religious. As also concerning Huldah the Prophetess.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Josias
entries.dictNote: Josias is the Greek form of Josiah, the reforming king of Judah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10-11). Josiah came to the throne as a boy and later launched a sweeping religious reform after a scroll of the law was discovered during temple repairs, purging idolatrous worship from Judah before his death in battle against Pharaoh Necho.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Josibiah
entries.dictNote: Father of Jehu, one of the Simeonite family heads listed in 1 Chronicles 4:35 among clans that expanded their pasturelands by displacing the Hamite inhabitants of Gedor in Hezekiah's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Josiphiah
entries.dictNote: Josiphiah was the father of Shelomith, who led a company of about 160 men among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra around 459 BC (Ezra 8:10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jotbah
entries.dictNote: Jotbah, the hometown of Meshullemeth, wife of King Manasseh and mother of King Amon of Judah (2 Kings 21:19). Its precise location is not preserved, and it should not be confused with Jotbathah, a wilderness stopping point during the exodus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jotbath
entries.summary: Jotbathah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Jotbathah was one of the stations where the Israelites camped during the wilderness wanderings, between Hor-hagidgad and Ebronah (Numbers 33:33-34). Moses later recalled it in Deuteronomy 10:7 as a land of brooks of water, a notable contrast to the surrounding desert. Its exact location in the Sinai peninsula is not known with certainty.

entries.title: Jozadak
entries.dictNote: Jozadak was a high priest taken into Babylonian exile, and his son Joshua led the priesthood during the return and rebuilding of the temple, covered more fully under the entry for Jehozadak.

entries.title: Jubal
entries.dictNote: Son of Lamech and Adah, in the line of Cain, remembered as the ancestor of all who play the lyre and pipe, making him the Bible's first named musician (Genesis 4:21).

entries.title: Jucal
entries.dictNote: Son of Shelemiah and one of the officials of King Zedekiah who had Jeremiah thrown into a cistern for discouraging the defenders of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 38:1), also named Jehucal earlier in the same crisis (Jeremiah 37:3). entries.title: Juda(-h
entries.summary: Judas (i.e. Jehudah), the name of ten Israelites; also of the posterity of one of them and its region
entries.dictNote: This entry covers the Greek form of Judah used in the New Testament. Judah, son of Jacob and Leah, gave his name to the tribe from which both David and Jesus descended, and the genealogies of Matthew and Luke trace Jesus' ancestry through him; Hebrews notes that Jesus came from this tribe rather than the priestly line of Levi. Revelation draws on Jacob's blessing over Judah to call Jesus "the Lion of the tribe of Judah." The same Greek name also belongs to Jude, the writer of the short New Testament letter that opens by identifying himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, a different man from the patriarch despite sharing the underlying name.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Judaea
entries.summary: the Judæan land (i.e. Judæa), a region of Palestine
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians
entries.dictNote: Judaea was the Roman name for the southern portion of Palestine centered on Jerusalem, corresponding roughly to the old territory of Judah and, in a broader New Testament usage, sometimes standing for the whole of Jewish Palestine. It was governed for much of the New Testament period by client kings of the Herodian dynasty and then directly by Roman procurators such as Pontius Pilate. John the Baptist preached in its wilderness, and it was the setting for the Passion narratives and much of Acts. After the Jewish revolt of AD 66 to 70, Rome commemorated its conquest of the province with coins stamped “Judaea Capta.”

entries.dictNote: Judah was Jacob and Leah's fourth son, and though not the firstborn, he emerges as the de facto leader among his brothers, proposing they sell Joseph into slavery rather than kill him and later offering himself as a hostage in Benjamin's place to protect his father. His tribe became the dominant one in Israel's history, producing David's royal line and giving its name to the southern kingdom of Judah after the nation split, and Jacob's dying blessing over Judah promises that the scepter will not depart from his line until the coming of one to whom obedience belongs.

entries.title: Judith
entries.dictNote: Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, was one of two Hittite wives Esau married at age forty (Genesis 26:34). She is usually identified with Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, in the later list of Esau's wives in Genesis 36:2, though the two genealogies name his Canaanite wives differently and the harmonization has long been debated. Her marriage, like Esau's other foreign marriages, grieved Isaac and Rebekah.

Nothing else about her is recorded beyond this single mention, though her inclusion shows women held recognized places in the earliest Roman house churches.

entries.title: Junias
entries.dictNote: Junias, or Junia, is a name Paul greets alongside Andronicus in Romans 16:7, calling the pair his relatives and fellow prisoners who were 'outstanding among the apostles.' Whether the Greek name is the masculine Junias or the far more common feminine Junia has been debated, and most modern scholars now favor Junia, which would make her a woman recognized in the earliest church in a role connected to the apostles.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Jushab-hesed
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the first group of exiles back from Babylon to rebuild the temple, listed in the royal genealogy of Judah after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Justus
entries.summary: Justus, the name of three Christian
entries.dictNote: Justus was a common secondary name among several early Christians, including a man in Corinth whose house neighbored the synagogue and became a meeting place for Paul, and a Jewish coworker of Paul mentioned in Colossians.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Juttah
entries.summary: Juttah (or Jutah), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Juttah was a town in the hill country of Judah assigned to the Levites descended from Aaron (Josh. 15:55; 21:16). It survives as the modern village of Yatta, a few miles south of Hebron, and a long tradition, based on Luke's description of Zechariah and Elizabeth's home as a city of Juda in the hill country, identifies it as the birthplace of John the Baptist (Luke 1:39).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kabzeel
entries.dictNote: Kabzeel was a town in the extreme south of Judah's territory, near the border with Edom (Joshua 15:21), and the birthplace of Benaiah, one of David's most celebrated warriors and later commander of his bodyguard (2 Samuel 23:20; 1 Chronicles 11:22). After the exile it appears to have been resettled under the related name Jekabzeel (Nehemiah 11:25).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kadesh
entries.summary: Kadesh, a place in the Desert
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalm, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Kadesh, or Kadesh-barnea, was Israel's main encampment in the wilderness of Zin on the southern edge of Canaan, the base from which Moses sent twelve spies into the land and where, decades later, Miriam died and Moses struck the rock in disobedience that cost him entry into Canaan. It is usually identified with the oasis of Ain el-Qudeis or nearby Ain el-Qudeirat, where excavations have uncovered an Israelite period fortress. A different Kadesh, on the Orontes River in Syria, was a Hittite stronghold and the site of a major battle between Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II, an inconclusive clash later settled by one of the oldest surviving peace treaties in history.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Kadeshbarnea
entries.summary: Kadesh-Barnea, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Kadesh-barnea was an oasis in the wilderness of Zin on the southern border of Canaan where Israel camped for much of the wanderings. It was from here that Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan, and the people's fearful response to their report led God to sentence that generation to die in the wilderness. Kadesh-barnea later marked the southern boundary of the promised land in the tribal allotments.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kadmiel
entries.summary: Kadmiel, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Kadmiel was a Levite who led temple worship and helped oversee the reconstruction efforts among the returning exiles under Zerubbabel and later Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kadmonites
entries.summary: Kadmonite (collectively), the name of a tribe in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kadmonites, meaning easterners, were one of the peoples living in Canaan when God promised the land to Abram in Genesis 15:19. They are named alongside better known groups such as the Hittites and Amorites but are not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and their exact territory and identity remain unknown.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kallai
entries.dictNote: A priest in the days of the high priest Joiakim, head of the priestly family of Sallai (Nehemiah 12:20). He appears only in this list of priestly family heads from the generation after the return from exile.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kanah
entries.summary: Kanah, the name of a stream and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kanah names two separate places sharing one word for reedy. One is a stream that formed part of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, running from the hill country to the Mediterranean (Joshua 16:8; 17:9). The other is a town in the northern part of Asher's territory (Joshua 19:28), distinct from the stream and generally located further north toward Tyre.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Karkaa
entries.summary: Karka (with the article prefix), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: A landmark on the southern boundary of Judah's territory, between Adar and Azmon, in the wilderness of Zin toward the Egyptian border (Joshua 15:3). Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Karkor
entries.summary: Karkor, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Karkor lay in the desert country east of the Jordan, beyond Succoth and Penuel, where Gideon finally caught up with the fleeing Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna and routed their remaining forces (Judges 8:10-12). The rout there ended the Midianite oppression that had driven Israel to hide in mountain caves for seven years. Its precise site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kartah
entries.dictNote: Kartah, a town of the tribe of Zebulun given to the Levites of Merari's clan (Josh. 21:34). It is likely the same town called Kattath in the earlier boundary list of Joshua 19:15.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kartan
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city of Naphtali given to the Gershonite clan (Joshua 21:32). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:76 gives the name of this same town as Kirjathaim, "double city," which is likely the fuller form of the name Kartan represents in abbreviated form.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kattath
entries.dictNote: Kattath was a town allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (Josh. 19:15). It may be the same place as Kitron, mentioned in Judges 1:30 as a town Zebulun failed to fully drive its Canaanite inhabitants from, though its exact site remains disputed and older proposals linking it to Cana of Galilee are no longer widely accepted.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kedar
entries.summary: Kedar, a son of Ishmael; also (collectively) Bedouin (as his descendants or representatives)
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Kedar was a son of Ishmael and the ancestor of a nomadic Arabian tribe known for their dark tents and skilled archers, used poetically in the Old Testament as an image of both remote wilderness life and, in Song of Solomon, of striking dark beauty.

witness.excerpt: Of this wife were born to Ishmael twelve sons: Nabaioth, Kedar, Abdeel, Mabsam, Idumas, Masmaos, Massaos, Chodad, Theman, Jetur, Naphesus, Kadmas.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Kedemah
entries.dictNote: Kedemah was the youngest of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed among the tribal chiefs whose descendants became the Ishmaelite peoples of the Arabian desert (Genesis 25:15-16). His name, meaning “eastward,” fits the pattern of Ishmael's sons settling in the region east of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about him individually.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kedemoth
entries.summary: Kedemoth, a place in eastern Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kedemoth was a town in the territory of Reuben, assigned to the Merarite Levites, that gave its name to the surrounding wilderness from which Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, requesting safe passage before Sihon's refusal led to war (Deuteronomy 2:26; Joshua 13:18; 21:37). Its precise site east of the Jordan has not been securely identified.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kedesh
entries.summary: Kedesh, the name of four places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kedesh was a city of refuge in Galilee, one of six towns designated where someone who killed accidentally could flee for protection from vengeance, and also the hometown of Barak, the military commander Deborah summoned.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Kehelathah
entries.summary: Kehelathah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Kehelathah was one of the stations in Israel's wilderness itinerary, listed between Rissah and Mount Shepher (Num. 33:22-23). Its name is related to the Hebrew word for assembly or congregation, though the text gives no further detail and the site cannot be located today.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Keilah
entries.dictNote: Keilah was a walled town in Judah's lowlands that David rescued from a Philistine raid while he was still a fugitive from Saul, only to learn its residents would have handed him over had Saul come for him, prompting David to move on into the wilderness of Ziph.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Kelaiah
entries.dictNote: Kelaiah, also called Kelita, was a Levite among those who had married foreign wives during the postexilic period and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reform (Ezra 10:23). A Levite named Kelita later helped the people understand the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8:7, likely the same man.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kelita
entries.summary: Kelita, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Kelita was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who signed Nehemiah's covenant renewal.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kemuel
entries.summary: Kemuel, the name of a relative of Abraham, and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Kemuel was Abraham's nephew through his brother Nahor, and also the name of a tribal leader of Ephraim appointed to help divide the conquered land under Joshua.

witness.excerpt: Now Nahor had eight sons by Milcha; Uz, and Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Azau, Pheldas, Jadelph, and Bethuel.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kenath
entries.summary: Kenath, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Kenath was a town in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan, captured during Israel's advance into the territory and renamed Nobah after its conqueror (Num. 32:42). It is also listed among towns taken from Geshur and Aram by the descendants of Machir (1 Chr. 2:23). The site is generally identified with Qanawat, an ancient city on the slopes of Jebel Hauran whose Roman-era ruins, including a theater and temple remains, are still visible today.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kenaz
entries.summary: Kenaz, the name of an Edomite and of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Kenaz was Caleb's younger brother and the father of Othniel, Israel's first judge, and his descendants, the Kenizzites, are counted among the Edomite clans in Genesis.

witness.excerpt: 1441]] There was one whose name was Othniel , the son of Kenaz, of the tribe of Judah; an active man, and of great courage.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Kenezite
entries.summary: a Kenizzite or descendant of Kenaz
entries.dictNote: Kenizzites were a clan descended from Kenaz, associated with Edom in Genesis but later absorbed into Judah. Caleb, one of the two faithful spies who entered Canaan, is called a Kenizzite, showing how outsiders could be fully incorporated into an Israelite tribe.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kenite
entries.summary: a Kenite or member of the tribe of Kajin
entries.dictNote: Kenites were a nomadic clan closely tied to Midian, generally friendly to Israel even though they stood outside the twelve tribes. Moses' father in law Jethro was a Kenite priest, and Heber the Kenite's wife Jael killed the fleeing Canaanite general Sisera in the days of the judges.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Keren-happuch
entries.dictNote: Keren-happuch, whose name means "horn of eye paint," was the youngest of Job's three daughters, born to him after God restored his fortunes at the end of his ordeal (Job 42:14). Job gave his daughters an inheritance alongside their brothers, an unusual provision for that culture (Job 42:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kerioth
entries.summary: Kerioth, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kerioth was a Moabite city named in Jeremiah's and Amos's prophecies of judgment against Moab, and possibly the hometown implied in the name Judas Iscariot, meaning man of Kerioth.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Keros
entries.dictNote: Keros was the ancestral head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Keturah
entries.dictNote: Keturah was the wife Abraham married after Sarah's death, and she bore him six sons who became the ancestors of various Arabian and Midianite peoples, though Abraham sent them away from Isaac with gifts to secure Isaac's position as sole heir.

entries.title: Kezia
entries.dictNote: The second of Job's three daughters, born after God restored his fortunes at the end of the book, and one of the daughters given an inheritance alongside their brothers (Job 42:14-15).

entries.title: Keziz
entries.dictNote: Keziz, fuller in Hebrew as Emek-keziz, was one of the towns assigned to the tribe of Benjamin in the eastern district near the Jordan valley (Josh. 18:21). It is grouped in the list with Jericho and Beth-hoglah, but its precise location is unknown.

entries.title: Kibroth-hattaavah
entries.summary: Kibroth-hat-Taavh, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Kibroth-hattaavah, "the graves of craving," marks the wilderness camp where the Israelites, weary of manna, demanded meat and were sent a massive flock of quails by God. Their gluttony brought on a plague that killed many, and the dead were buried there and the place named for their craving (Numbers 11:31-34). It was one of the stations on Israel's route from Sinai toward Canaan, mentioned again in the itinerary of Numbers 33 and in Moses' later rebuke in Deuteronomy 9:22.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kibzaim
entries.dictNote: A Levitical city in the territory of Ephraim, assigned to the Kohathites (Josh. 21:22). The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:68 gives its name as Jokmeam.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kidron
entries.dictNote: The Kidron Valley runs along Jerusalem's eastern edge, between the city and the Mount of Olives, and it served as a dumping ground for the idols and debris of successive religious reforms, as well as the path Jesus and his disciples crossed on the way to Gethsemane the night of his arrest.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Kinah
entries.dictNote: A town in the extreme south of Judah, near the border with Edom, in the arid district south of Beersheba (Josh. 15:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kir
entries.summary: Kir, a place in Assyrian; also one in Moab
entries.dictNote: Two different places share this name. Kir of Moab, one of Moab's two chief cities alongside Ar, appears in Isaiah's oracle against Moab and is usually identified with Kerak, a fortress town east of the Dead Sea (Isa. 15:1). The other Kir was the original homeland of the Arameans; Amos says God brought Aram from Kir just as he brought Israel from Egypt (Amos 9:7), and elsewhere warns that the Arameans of Damascus would be sent back there in judgment (Amos 1:5), a threat fulfilled when Tiglath-pileser III deported Damascus's population after conquering it in 732 BC, an episode recorded in his own Assyrian annals. Isaiah pairs a Kir with Elam in a separate scene of soldiers preparing for battle (Isa. 22:6), though scholars debate whether it is the same place.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kir-haraseth
entries.summary: Kir-Cheres or Kir-Chareseth, a place in Moab
entries.dictNote: Kir-haraseth, also called Kir-heres or Kir-hareseth and identified with modern Kerak in Jordan, was the fortress capital of Moab. When King Mesha of Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab's death, the combined armies of Israel, Judah, and Edom besieged him there, driving him to sacrifice his own son on the city wall in a desperate act that ended the siege (2 Kings 3:25-27). Mesha's own account of his revolt survives on the Moabite Stone, a black basalt inscription discovered in 1868 that corroborates the biblical narrative of Moab's struggle against Israelite rule. Isaiah and Jeremiah both lament the city's fall in their oracles against Moab (Isaiah 16:7-11; Jeremiah 48:31-36).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kiriathaim
entries.summary: Kirjathaim, the name of two placed in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kiriathaim was a Moabite town, originally allotted to the tribe of Reuben, later listed by Jeremiah and Ezekiel among the cities God's judgment on Moab would fall upon.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Kirjath
entries.summary: Kirjath-Jearim or Kirjath-Arim, a place in Palestine
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: This is Kirjath-jearim, a Gibeonite town on the border of Judah and Benjamin also known as Baalah. The ark of the covenant rested there for twenty years after the Philistines returned it, until David had it brought up to Jerusalem. Kirjath-jearim was also the home of the prophet Uriah, whom King Jehoiakim had executed for prophesying against Jerusalem.

entries.title: Kirjath-arba
entries.summary: Kirjath-Arba or Kirjath-ha-Arba, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-arba, "city of Arba," was the earlier name of Hebron, named for a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there, and Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah nearby as a family burial site. Joshua later gave the city to Caleb as his inheritance for his faithful report as one of the twelve spies.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Kirjath-huzoth
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town, "city of streets," where King Balak met and entertained Balaam after summoning him from the Euphrates region to curse Israel (Numbers 22:39). It stood near the high places from which Balaam later viewed the Israelite camp, and is generally placed in the plains of Moab near Kirjathaim.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kirjath-sannah
entries.summary: Kirjath-Sannah or Kirjath-Sepher, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-sannah is an alternate name for the town also called Kirjath-sepher and, after Israel's conquest, Debir, a royal Canaanite city in the hill country southwest of Hebron thought to have been a center of learning among its Canaanite inhabitants (Joshua 15:15-16, 49). Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captured it, a prize claimed by his nephew Othniel, later Israel's first judge (Judges 1:11-13).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Kirjathbaal
entries.dictNote: Kirjath-baal is another name for Kirjath-jearim, listed alongside it as a boundary town of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:60; 18:14). Also called Baalah, it was one of the four Gibeonite league towns and later held the ark of the covenant for about twenty years before David brought it up to Jerusalem.

entries.dictNote: Kish was King Saul's father, a Benjamite of standing whose lost donkeys sent Saul on the search that led him to Samuel and his anointing as Israel's first king.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Kishi
entries.dictNote: Kishi, also called Kushaiah (1 Chronicles 15:17), was a Levite of the Merarite clan and the father of Ethan, one of the three chief musicians David appointed for service before the ark (1 Chronicles 6:44; 15:17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kishion
entries.dictNote: Kishion was a town in Issachar assigned to the Gershonite Levites, listed among their cities in Joshua 19:20 and again, spelled Kishon, in Joshua 21:28. Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kishon
entries.dictNote: The Kishon is a winter stream draining the Jezreel Valley into the Mediterranean at the foot of Mount Carmel, prone to flash flooding. Its swollen waters swept away Sisera's chariots during Deborah and Barak's battle against the Canaanites (Judges 4:7, 13; 5:21), and it was in its valley that Elijah had the prophets of Baal put to death after the contest on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:40).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Kithlish
entries.dictNote: Kithlish was a town in the Judean lowlands, listed among the towns of Judah's inheritance alongside Lahmam and Gederoth (Joshua 15:40). It has traditionally been located near Jelameh, though the identification is not firmly established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Kitron
entries.dictNote: Kitron was a Canaanite town within Zebulun's allotted territory that the tribe failed to drive out, so its inhabitants remained and were put to forced labor instead (Judges 1:30). Joshua 19:15 lists the same town's territory under the name Kattath. Its exact site is unidentified; the older proposal equating it with Cana of Galilee is not widely accepted today.

entries.title: Koa
entries.dictNote: A name occurring only in Ezekiel 23:23, paired with Shoa and Pekod as peoples or territories allied with Babylon against Jerusalem. Many scholars identify it with Gutium, a region and people named repeatedly in Sumerian, Babylonian, and Assyrian records as lying east of the Tigris, rather than a single city.

entries.title: Kohath

entries.title: Kohathites
entries.summary: a Kohathite (collectively) or descendants of Kehath
entries.dictNote: The Kohathites were the descendants of Kohath, one of Levi's three sons, and formed one of the three Levitical divisions responsible for the tabernacle. Their specific charge was the most sacred furnishings, including the ark of the covenant, which they carried on poles rather than in a cart so that no one would touch it directly, a rule broken with fatal results in 2 Samuel 6. In the wilderness camp they pitched south of the tabernacle, and Moses, Aaron, and Samuel all belonged to this line.

entries.title: Kolaiah
entries.summary: Kolajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Kolaiah was the father of the false prophet Ahab, who along with Zedekiah prophesied lies to the exiles in Babylon and was condemned by Jeremiah; Nebuchadnezzar had both men roasted in the fire as a warning (Jeremiah 29:21-22). A separate Kolaiah was a Benjamite ancestor of one of the returned exiles who resettled Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:7).

entries.summary: Korach, the name of two Edomites and three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Korah was a Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron's leadership, joined by over two hundred fifty prominent Israelites who argued the whole community was holy and Moses had no special claim to authority. The ground opened and swallowed Korah and his family alive, and fire consumed the other rebels, a judgment severe enough that Israel complained about it the very next day.

entries.title: Kushaiah

entries.title: Lachish
entries.books: Joshua, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah
entries.dictNote: Lachish was a heavily fortified Canaanite royal city in Judah's lowlands, captured and destroyed by Joshua and later rebuilt into one of Judah's strongest fortresses under Rehoboam. Sennacherib's Assyrian army besieged and captured it in 701 BC, an episode Assyria commemorated in a series of relief carvings, now in the British Museum, depicting the siege ramp, battle, and deportation of captives in detail. Excavations at Tell ed-Duweir, the city's ruins, also uncovered the Lachish Letters, a set of Hebrew ostraca written during the final Babylonian siege of Judah shortly before Jerusalem's fall, a rare firsthand military correspondence from the very end of the kingdom.

entries.title: Lael

entries.title: Lahmam
entries.summary: Lachmam or Lachmas, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Lahmam was a town in the lowland district of Judah, listed alongside Kithlish and Gederoth in Joshua's territorial allotment (Joshua 15:40). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its site is unidentified.

entries.title: Lahmi
entries.summary: Lachmi, an Israelite; or rather probably a brief form
entries.dictNote: Brother of the Philistine giant Goliath, killed by Elhanan son of Jair during a battle between David's men and the Philistines (1 Chronicles 20:5).

entries.title: Laish
entries.summary: Laish, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Laish was a peaceful, isolated Canaanite city that the tribe of Dan conquered and renamed Dan after failing to fully settle their originally assigned territory.

entries.title: Lakum
entries.dictNote: Lakum was one of several places marking the border of the tribal territory of Naphtali, listed alongside Adami and Jabneel in Joshua 19:33. It is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and its site has not been identified.

entries.title: Lamech
entries.summary: One line in Luke's chain of ‘son of.’ In the Book of Noah fragment he's a frightened new father who flees his own son's birth and needs Methuselah and Enoch to talk him down.
entries.dictNote: Two men named Lamech appear in Genesis. One was a descendant of Cain notorious for boasting to his two wives that he had killed a young man for merely wounding him, escalating the violence Cain's own murder had introduced. The other Lamech was Noah's father, from the righteous line through Seth, and he named his son Noah expressing hope that he would bring relief from the painful labor of farming cursed ground.

entries.title: Laodicea
entries.summary: Laodicia, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Laodicea was a wealthy banking and textile city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor, addressed in Revelation as the last and most sharply rebuked of the seven churches (Revelation 3:14-22), and mentioned by Paul alongside Colossae (Colossians 2:1; 4:15-16). The city had no natural water source and piped water in by aqueduct from the hot springs at Hierapolis and the cold springs at Colossae, which arrived lukewarm and mineral-laden; John's rebuke that the church was "neither cold nor hot" plays directly on that well-known local water supply.

entries.summary: a Laodicean, i.e. inhabitant of Laodicia
entries.dictNote: Laodicean designates an inhabitant of Laodicea, a wealthy city in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor near Colossae. Paul instructs the Colossians to exchange letters with the Laodicean church, and Revelation later rebukes that same congregation for being lukewarm, an image that likely plays on the city's famous aqueduct system, which delivered water that arrived neither hot nor cold.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lappidoth
entries.dictNote: The husband of Deborah, the prophetess and judge who led Israel against the Canaanite general Sisera (Judges 4:4). Scripture says nothing about Lappidoth himself beyond identifying him as Deborah's husband; some older interpreters have suggested the name, meaning "torches" or "flashes," was actually an epithet for Deborah's own fiery character rather than her husband's given name, though the plain reading takes it as his name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lasea
entries.dictNote: Lasea was a city on the south coast of Crete, named in Luke's detailed account of Paul's voyage to Rome as lying near the harbor called Fair Havens where the ship sheltered (Acts 27:8). Its ruins were rediscovered in the nineteenth century a few miles east of Fair Havens, confirming the precise geography behind Luke's narrative, a detail often cited as evidence of Luke's care as a historian of the voyage.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lasha
entries.summary: Lesha, a place probably East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Lasha marks the eastern boundary point of Canaanite territory in the Table of Nations, paired with Sidon in the north and the cities of the plain in the south (Genesis 10:19). Jewish tradition identified it with Callirhoe, a resort on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea famous in the Roman period for its hot mineral springs, which Herod the Great reportedly visited during his final illness. If that identification is correct, the name preserves a memory of the region's thermal springs long before Roman writers described them.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lasharon
entries.summary: Sharon, the name of a place in Palestine
entries.books: Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Isaiah
entries.dictNote: Lasharon, meaning "belonging to Sharon," appears once as the name of a Canaanite town or district whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:18), and most of this record's other references actually belong to the famous Sharon plain, the fertile coastal region between Joppa and Mount Carmel. Sharon supplied excellent royal pastureland (1 Chronicles 27:29) and part of the tribe of Gad settled there (1 Chronicles 5:16); its beauty became proverbial, celebrated as "the rose of Sharon" (Song of Solomon 2:1) and pictured by Isaiah blossoming in the age of restoration (Isaiah 35:2).

Its inclusion reflects Rome's administrative presence in Judea.

entries.title: Lebana
entries.summary: Lebana or Lebanah, one of the Nethinim
entries.dictNote: Lebana, also spelled Lebanah, was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45; Nehemiah 7:48). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.title: Lebanon
entries.summary: Lebanon, a mountain range in Palestine
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Lebanon is the mountain range running along Syria's Mediterranean coast, its western ridge, Lebanon proper, and eastern ridge, the Anti-Lebanon culminating in Mount Hermon, enclosing the long Beqaa Valley between them. Its cedar forests supplied timber for Solomon's temple and palace, cut and floated south under an agreement with Hiram of Tyre, and its snow capped peaks and springs made it a recurring image of grandeur and freshness in the Psalms and Song of Solomon. Israel was promised the territory but never fully conquered it. Egyptian records such as the Tale of Wenamun describe the same cedar trade with the Lebanese coast that the Bible attributes to Solomon and Hiram.

entries.label: 16 books

entries.title: Lebaoth
entries.dictNote: Lebaoth, meaning "lionesses," was one of the southernmost towns of Judah's tribal allotment, near the border with Edom (Joshua 15:32). It is probably identical with Beth-lebaoth, assigned to Simeon in Joshua 19:6.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lebonah
entries.dictNote: Lebonah was a town near Shiloh, used in Judges 21:19 as a landmark to describe Shiloh's location relative to the annual festival where the men of Benjamin seized wives from among the dancing women. It lay along the road between Bethel and Shechem and is generally identified with the modern village of Lubban, south of Nablus, which still preserves the ancient name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lecah
entries.dictNote: Lecah is named once, in the genealogy of Judah, among the descendants of Shelah, Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife Bath-shua (1 Chronicles 4:21). As with several other names in this genealogical passage, it likely denotes a clan or the town it founded rather than a single individual. Nothing further is known of it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lehabim
entries.summary: Lehabim, a son of Mizraim, and his descendants
entries.dictNote: Lehabim appears in the Table of Nations as one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). The name is widely connected to the Rebu or Lebu people known from Egyptian inscriptions, generally identified as ancestors of the Libyans, who lived along the North African coast west of Egypt.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Lehi
entries.dictNote: Lehi, meaning jawbone, was a place in Judah where the Philistines gathered to capture Samson after he had been burning their fields, only for him to break free of his ropes and strike down a thousand of them with the jawbone of a donkey (Judges 15:9-15). Samson then named the site Ramath-lehi and, when thirsty afterward, called on God, who split open a hollow place there that became known as En-hakkore, the spring of the caller (Judges 15:17-19).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lemuel
entries.summary: Lemuel or Lemoel, a symbolic name of Solomon
entries.dictNote: Lemuel was a king whose mother's wise instruction is recorded in Proverbs 31:1-9, advice about avoiding wine and defending the poor and needy. Nothing certain is known about which kingdom he ruled, and later Jewish tradition sometimes identified him with Solomon under a symbolic name, though this cannot be confirmed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Leshem
entries.dictNote: Leshem is an older form of the name Laish, the Canaanite city that the tribe of Dan captured and resettled after abandoning their assigned coastal territory, renaming it Dan after their ancestor (Joshua 19:47; compare the fuller account in Judges 18). The site, at Tel Dan in northern Israel, has been extensively excavated and is best known for producing the Tel Dan Stele, a ninth-century BC inscription in which an Aramean king boasts of defeating the "house of David," the earliest extrabiblical reference to David's dynasty.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Letushim
entries.dictNote: Letushim was not an individual but one of three tribal groups, alongside Asshurim and Leummim, descended from Dedan, a grandson of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:3). Like the other two, its plural Hebrew form marks it as the name of a clan or people rather than a single ancestor, and its historical identity is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Leummim
entries.dictNote: Leummim designates a group of Arabian tribes rather than a single ancestor, listed among the descendants of Dedan, grandson of Abraham through Keturah, in the genealogy of Genesis 25:3. The Hebrew word itself means peoples or nations, marking it as a collective term for related clans rather than one man's name. Like the neighboring Asshurim and Letushim named in the same verse, it names a tribal confederation that settled in the Arabian peninsula along routes later associated with Midian and Sheba.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Levi
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Levi was Jacob's third son, and his violent participation in the massacre at Shechem after his sister Dinah's rape earned Jacob's deathbed condemnation alongside his brother Simeon. Levi's descendants nonetheless became Israel's priestly tribe, set apart for temple and tabernacle service instead of receiving a normal territorial inheritance, a role the Levites earned in part by their zeal in punishing the golden calf idolatry at Sinai. A few minor figures in Jesus's genealogy also carry the name Levi.

entries.dictNote: Leviite is an alternate spelling of Levite found in a handful of biblical manuscripts and translations, referring to the same tribe of Levi set apart for tabernacle and temple service.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Levite
entries.summary: a Levite, i.e. descendant of Levi
entries.dictNote: Levites were members of the tribe of Levi set apart to serve in Israel's tabernacle and later temple, assisting the priests, who came from Aaron's branch of the same tribe. Because their work was religious rather than agricultural, they received no tribal land allotment; instead they were given forty eight designated cities scattered among the other tribes and lived on tithes from the rest of Israel. Their duties ranged from carrying and guarding the sacred furnishings during the wilderness journey to serving later as temple musicians, gatekeepers, and teachers of the law.

entries.title: Libertine
entries.dictNote: "Libertine" in Acts 6:9 does not name an individual but describes members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen in Jerusalem, a congregation of Jews or their descendants who had once been enslaved in Rome, likely deported there after Pompey's conquest of Judea in 63 BC, and later manumitted. entries.title: Likhi
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Manasseh through Shemidah, listed among the family heads of that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:19).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Linus
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul names in his greetings to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21). Early church tradition, recorded by Irenaeus, identifies him as the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul, though the New Testament itself says nothing about any church office he held.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lo-ammi
entries.summary: Lo-Ammi, the symbolic name of a son of Hosea
entries.dictNote: Lo-ammi, meaning “not my people,” was the symbolic name God commanded the prophet Hosea to give his second son by Gomer, representing God's coming rejection of the northern kingdom of Israel for its unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:9). The name is deliberately reversed later in the book, where God promises that those once called “not my people” will be called “sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10; 2:23), a reversal Paul later applies to the inclusion of Gentiles among God's people (Romans 9:25-26). Hosea's children's names function as a set of acted prophecies rather than ordinary personal names.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lo-ruhamah
entries.summary: Lo-Ruchamah, the symbolic name of a son of Hosea
entries.dictNote: Lo-ruhamah, meaning “not pitied” or “not loved,” was the symbolic name God commanded the prophet Hosea to give his daughter, signifying that God would no longer show mercy to the northern kingdom of Israel (Hosea 1:6-8). The name's reversal in Hosea 2:23, where God promises to call her “loved,” became a picture of future restoration that Paul later applies to the inclusion of Gentiles (Romans 9:25).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Lod
entries.dictNote: Lod is the Hebrew name for the town known in the New Testament by its Greek name, Lydda. It is listed among the towns of Benjamin resettled by Jews returning from Babylonian exile, its population numbering over seven hundred according to the lists in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 7:37; 11:35). It lay on the coastal plain along the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, and modern Lod, near Tel Aviv's international airport, preserves the ancient name.

entries.title: Lois
entries.dictNote: The grandmother of Timothy, commended by Paul for the sincere faith she passed down through her daughter Eunice to her grandson (2 Timothy 1:5), making her one of the few New Testament figures named specifically for her role in a family's spiritual formation.

entries.title: Lot
entries.summary: Jesus uses him three times in one breath as a warning — eating, drinking, building, right up until the fire fell (17:28-32), ending in the single starkest line in the passage: 'Remember Lot's wife.' Josephus tells the same land-division story Genesis does, the ordinary choice that put Lot next door to Sodom in the first place.
entries.dictNote: Lot was Abraham's nephew who traveled with him from Ur and eventually settled near Sodom, choosing the fertile Jordan valley for himself when he and Abraham split up to avoid conflict between their herdsmen. When God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, angels physically dragged Lot and his family out of the city, and Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt for looking back against their explicit instructions. Lot's two daughters, believing no other men were left alive, later got their father drunk and conceived children by him, and those sons became the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

entries.title: Lycaonia
entries.summary: Lycaonia, a region of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Lycaonia was an inland region of Asia Minor bordered by Cappadocia and Galatia, home to the cities of Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe. Paul and Barnabas preached across the region on Paul's first missionary journey, and Paul revisited it later (Acts 14:6-21; 16:1-6). Luke notes that the crowd at Lystra shouted in "the speech of Lycaonia" when they mistook Paul and Barnabas for Hermes and Zeus (Acts 14:11-12); an inscription discovered near the site of ancient Lystra referring to priests of Hermes alongside a stone image of Zeus shows this pairing of gods was a genuine local cult, giving real background to Luke's account.

entries.title: Lycia
entries.summary: Lycia, a province of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Lycia was not a person but a mountainous region and Roman province on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor, opposite Rhodes. Paul's ship touched its ports of Patara and Myra on voyages to and from Jerusalem (Acts 21:1-2; 27:5), and its cities have yielded substantial Greek and native Lycian-language inscriptions documenting the region's distinct pre-Roman culture.

entries.summary: Lydda (i.e. Lod), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Lydda was a town on the coastal plain about nine miles southeast of Joppa, known in the Old Testament as Lod (1 Chronicles 8:12). Peter healed a paralyzed man named Aeneas there, a miracle that led many in the surrounding plain of Sharon to turn to the Lord (Acts 9:32-35). The Romans later destroyed and rebuilt the city under the name Diospolis; today it is the Israeli city of Lod, home to Ben Gurion Airport.

entries.title: Lystra
entries.summary: Lystra, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Lystra was a Roman colony in the wild, mountainous district of Lycaonia in Asia Minor, established under Augustus and settled with military veterans; it was Timothy's hometown (2 Timothy 3:10-11; Acts 16:1). Paul preached there after being driven from Iconium and healed a man lame from birth, so impressing the crowd that they tried to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus, an episode matched by inscriptions found near Lystra dedicating statues to that same local pairing of gods; the same crowd, stirred up by Paul's opponents, then stoned him and left him for dead (Acts 14:8-19).

entries.title: Maachah
entries.summary: Maakah (or Maakath), the name of a place in Syria, also of a Mesopotamian, of three Israelites, and of four Israelitesses and one Syrian woman
entries.books: Genesis, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles
entries.dictNote: Maachah was a small Aramean kingdom near Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee in the region later called Batanea, mentioned among the peoples Israel failed to fully dispossess in Joshua's day. The same Hebrew name was borne by several people connected to the royal court: Maacah daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, became one of David's wives and the mother of Absalom, while another Maacah, also called Michaiah, a granddaughter of Absalom, married Rehoboam and later served as queen mother until her grandson Asa removed her for promoting idol worship. A third Maacah fathered Achish, king of Gath, in Saul's day.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Maachathite
entries.summary: a Maakathite, or inhabitant of Maakah
entries.books: Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Maachathite identifies someone from Maacah, a small Aramean kingdom near Mount Hermon that Israel never fully subdued even after entering the land. One of David's officers, Eliphelet, was a Maachathite.
entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Maadai
entries.dictNote: Maadai was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:34 among those who had married foreign wives after the return from exile and agreed to separate from them as part of Ezra's reform.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maadiah
entries.dictNote: A priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and headed one of the priestly families reorganized under Joiakim; the same family is called Moadiah a few verses later (Nehemiah 12:5, 17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maai
entries.dictNote: One of the priests who took part in the musical procession accompanying Ezra at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh. 12:36), playing instruments associated with David. He appears only in this single ceremonial list.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maarath
entries.dictNote: Maarath was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the settlements near Hebron in Joshua's account of Judah's inheritance (Josh. 15:59). It is often placed near the modern village of Beit Ummar, a few miles north of Hebron, though the identification is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maaseiah
entries.summary: Maasejah, the name of sixteen Israelites
entries.dictNote: Maaseiah was a common priestly and Levitical name in the Old Testament, borne by several different individuals involved in temple service, the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah, and the reading of the law to the returned exiles.

entries.title: Maasiai
entries.dictNote: Maasiai was a priest listed among those who resettled Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, as recorded in the genealogical roll of 1 Chronicles 9. Nothing further is known of him beyond his place in that list.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maath
entries.dictNote: Maath appears only as a name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed among the ancestors between the exile and Joseph (Luke 3:26). Nothing else is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maaz
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah, one of the sons of Ram listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:27, alongside his brothers Jamin and Eker.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maaziah
entries.summary: Maazjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Maaziah headed the twenty-fourth and last of the priestly divisions David organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:18). A priest by the same name later sealed Nehemiah's covenant to keep God's law after the exile (Nehemiah 10:8).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Macedonia
entries.books: Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy

Paul revisited the province at least twice more and later praised the Macedonian churches for their generosity despite their own poverty. Travel through the province followed the Via Egnatia, the Roman road linking the Adriatic to Byzantium, whose paved remains can still be traced in parts of modern Greece and North Macedonia.

entries.summary: Madian (i.e. Midian), a region of Arabia
entries.dictNote: Madian, the Greek form of Midian, the region east of the Gulf of Aqaba where Moses fled after killing an Egyptian and where he lived as a shepherd for his father-in-law until God called him at the burning bush (Acts 7:29-30; see Exod. 2:15-22).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Madmannah
entries.dictNote: Madmannah was a town in the southern Negev of Judah, later held by descendants of Caleb (Joshua 15:31; 1 Chronicles 2:49). Two different modern sites have been proposed for it, one southwest of Gaza and another northeast of Beersheba, and neither identification is certain.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Madmen
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town named in Jeremiah's oracle of judgment against Moab, threatened with destruction by an invading army (Jer. 48:2). The prophet plays on the town's name, which sounds like the Hebrew for be silenced, to declare that Moab itself would be silenced.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Madmenah
entries.dictNote: Madmenah was a town near Jerusalem named in Isaiah's vivid poetic sketch of an invading army's advance, whose inhabitants flee before it reaches the city (Isa. 10:31). It appears in a short list of villages north of Jerusalem, alongside Anathoth and Nob, tracing the imagined approach route of an Assyrian force.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Madon
entries.dictNote: Madon was a Canaanite city in northern Palestine whose king joined the coalition Jabin of Hazor assembled against Joshua at the Waters of Merom; the alliance was defeated and its king killed (Joshua 11:1; 12:19). It has been tentatively located at a ruin near Hattin, west of Tiberias.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Magbish
entries.summary: Magbish, an Israelite, or a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Magbish appears once, in the list of families and towns whose people returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, a group of 156 men identified by it (Ezra 2:30). Whether Magbish names a place or an ancestor is debated, since most of the surrounding entries in that list are towns but a few are clearly clan names. Its location, if a place, has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Magdala
entries.summary: the tower; Magdala (i.e. Migdala), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Magdala, from the Hebrew Migdal meaning tower, sat on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and is remembered chiefly as the hometown of Mary Magdalene. Matthew 15:39 names it as the region Jesus reached after feeding the four thousand; Mark's parallel account calls the same area Dalmanutha. Excavations at the site since 2009 have uncovered a first-century synagogue and the intricately carved "Magdala Stone," one of the earliest known depictions of the Jerusalem Temple's menorah, likely carved by someone who had seen the Temple standing before its destruction in AD 70.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Magdalene
entries.summary: a female Magdalene, i.e. inhabitant of Magdala
entries.dictNote: Magdalene identifies Mary as coming from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee, distinguishing her from the Gospels' other women named Mary. She is best known as a witness to the crucifixion and the first person to see the risen Jesus, and the long standing tradition identifying her with the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7 has no basis in the biblical text itself.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Magdiel
entries.dictNote: Magdiel was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau, listed in the Edomite king-and-chief records of Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54. Nothing else is recorded of him individually; his name marks a clan territory rather than necessarily one ruler.

entries.dictNote: Magog was a son of Japheth and, in Ezekiel's prophecy, the homeland of Gog, the leader of a future coalition invading restored Israel, a name later reused symbolically in Revelation for the nations gathered in final rebellion against God.

entries.title: Magpiash
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders of the people who sealed the covenant of renewed obedience under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 10:20). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name in this list of signatories.

entries.summary: Mahalalel, the name of an antediluvian patriarch and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Mahalalel was a descendant of Seth in the genealogy leading to Noah, four generations before Enoch.

entries.dictNote: Two women named Mahalath appear in the genealogies. One was a daughter of Ishmael whom Esau married, apparently also called Bashemath, in an attempt to please his parents after his earlier marriages to Canaanite women displeased them (Genesis 28:9; 36:3). The other was a granddaughter of David, daughter of Jerimoth, who became one of Rehoboam's wives (2 Chronicles 11:18).

entries.summary: 'Machalath', probably the title (initial word) of a popular song
entries.dictNote: Mahalath here is not a person but a musical or liturgical term in the headings of Psalms 53 and 88, both of which are set "upon Mahalath." Its exact meaning is uncertain; suggestions include a tune name, a wind instrument, or a word related to sickness or suffering fitting the psalms' somber content, but no consensus survives from antiquity.

witness.excerpt: For in the days when Jacob went to Mesopotamia, Esau took to himself a wife Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, and he gathered together all the flocks of his father and his wives, and went up and dwelt on Mount Seir, and left Isaac his father at the Well of the Oath alone.  19.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahanaim
entries.dictNote: Mahanaim, meaning "two camps," was the place near the Jabbok River where Jacob was met by angels of God on his return from Paddan-aram and divided his household into two companies before facing Esau. The town later became a Levitical city and, after Saul's death, served as the capital where Ishbosheth reigned over the northern tribes while David ruled from Hebron. Decades later David himself took refuge at Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion, and it was there he received news of Absalom's death.
