entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Mahaneh-dan
entries.dictNote: Mahaneh-dan, meaning camp of Dan, names the place behind Kirjath-jearim where the Spirit began to stir Samson in his youth (Judg. 13:25) and where, later, six hundred armed Danites camped on their way north to conquer the city of Laish and resettle it as Dan (Judg. 18:12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maharai
entries.dictNote: Maharai was one of David's mighty warriors, from the town of Netophah, and he also commanded one of the monthly military divisions David organized.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mahath
entries.summary: Machath, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mahath was a Levite involved in the religious reforms under both Hezekiah, overseeing dedicated offerings, and generations earlier in the genealogies of the Kohathite line.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mahavite
entries.summary: a Machavite or inhabitant of some place named Machaveh
entries.dictNote: Mahavite identifies Eliel, one of David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahazioth
entries.dictNote: Mahazioth was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman appointed by David to lead temple music, and he headed the twenty-third of the twenty-four courses of musicians who served on a rotating schedule (1 Chronicles 25:4, 30-31). His name means “visions,” fitting a family whose musical service was described as prophesying with instruments (1 Chronicles 25:1). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maher-sha-lal-bash-baz
entries.summary: Maher-Shalal-Chash-Baz; the symbolical name of the son of Isaiah
entries.dictNote: Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil,” was the son of the prophet Isaiah, given this deliberately ominous name as a sign to King Ahaz that Assyria would plunder Damascus and Samaria before the child could say “father” or “mother” (Isaiah 8:1-4). Isaiah had the name publicly recorded on a large tablet before the boy's birth, witnessed by two reliable men, underscoring the prophecy's certainty. The prediction was fulfilled within a few years when Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Damascus and stripped Israel of territory.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahlah
entries.summary: Machlah, the name apparently of two Israelitesses
entries.dictNote: Mahlah was one of five daughters of Zelophehad whose successful petition to Moses for the right to inherit their father's land in the absence of a son set a new legal precedent.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mahli
entries.summary: Machli, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mahli was a son of Merari, Levi's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the Levitical clans responsible for tabernacle duties.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Mahlites
entries.summary: a Machlite or (collectively) descendants of Machli
entries.dictNote: Mahlites were the Levitical clan descended from Mahli, son of Merari, counted alongside the Mushites among the families responsible for the tabernacle's structural components.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahlon
entries.dictNote: Mahlon was Naomi's son and Ruth's first husband, who died in Moab along with his brother and father, leaving Ruth a childless widow before her return to Bethlehem with Naomi and her eventual marriage to Boaz.

witness.excerpt: ine, Elimelech of Bethlehem, which is a city of the tribe of Judah, being not able to support his family under so sore a distress, took with him Naomi his wife, and the children that were born to him by her, Chilion and Mahlon; and removed his habitation into the land of Moab: and upon the happy prosperity of his affairs there, he took for his sons wives of the Moabites, Orpah for Chilion and Ruth for Mahlon.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mahol
entries.dictNote: Mahol was the father of four men, Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, renowned for their wisdom, whom 1 Kings 4:31 says Solomon surpassed. Some read 'sons of Mahol' as a guild or family name rather than a literal father, since these same men appear elsewhere as sons of Zerah of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:6). Either way, the comparison shows how far Solomon's proverbial wisdom was thought to exceed even the most gifted of his contemporaries.

witness.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mainan
entries.dictNote: Mainan appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as an ancestor descended from David's son Nathan, several generations before Mattatha and Melea (Luke 3:31). He is not otherwise mentioned in the Old Testament and nothing beyond his place in the list is known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Makaz
entries.dictNote: Makaz appears once, in the list of twelve district officers who supplied provisions for Solomon's royal household, naming the territory under Ben-deker's charge alongside Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kings 4:9). Nothing else is known of it, and its site has not been discovered.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Makheloth
entries.summary: Makheloth, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel, named only in the travel itinerary of Numbers 33 between Haradah and Tahath (Num. 33:25-26). Nothing further is recorded of it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Makkedah
entries.dictNote: Makkedah was a royal Canaanite city in the Shephelah near a cave where five allied Amorite kings hid after their defeat by Joshua at Gibeon. Joshua had the kings sealed inside the cave until the battle was finished, then had them brought out, executed, and their bodies hung on trees before the city itself was captured and destroyed.

witness.excerpt: Insomuch that Joshua took the Kings, which were hidden in a certain cave at Makkedah, and put them to death.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maktesh
entries.summary: dell; the Maktesh, a place in Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Maktesh, meaning the mortar or hollow, named a district in or near Jerusalem inhabited by merchants and silversmiths, addressed directly in Zephaniah's prophecy of coming judgment on the city's commercial quarter (Zeph. 1:11). It is generally thought to refer to a low-lying market area, possibly within the Tyropoeon Valley, though its exact bounds are not known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malachi
entries.dictNote: Malachi is the last prophetic book in the Old Testament's traditional ordering, and almost nothing is known about the man himself beyond his name, which may even be a title meaning my messenger rather than a personal name. The book confronts a post-exilic Judah that had grown spiritually lazy, priests offering blemished sacrifices and the people withholding tithes, and it closes the Old Testament looking forward to a coming messenger who would prepare the way before the Lord.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malcham
entries.summary: Malcam or Milcom, the national idol of the Ammonites
entries.dictNote: Malcham was a descendant of Benjamin listed among the tribal genealogies of Chronicles, and the name is also an alternate rendering of Milcom, the Ammonite deity elsewhere called Molech.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Malchiah
entries.summary: Malkijah, the name of ten Israelites
entries.dictNote: Malchiah was a common priestly and Levitical name in the postexilic period, borne by several men who helped rebuild sections of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Malchiel
entries.dictNote: Malchiel was a son of Asher, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Asher's tribe in Israel's genealogies.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Malchielite
entries.summary: a Malkielite or descendant of Malkiel
entries.dictNote: Malchielites were the clan descended from Malchiel, a grandson of Asher, counted among the tribe's families in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchiram
entries.dictNote: Malchiram was a son of King Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, born during or after the family's Babylonian captivity (1 Chronicles 3:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malchishua
entries.dictNote: Malchishua was one of Saul's sons, killed alongside his father and brothers in the battle against the Philistines at Mount Gilboa.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Malchus
entries.dictNote: Malchus was the servant of the high priest present when Jesus was arrested in the garden of Gethsemane; Peter drew a sword and cut off his right ear, which Jesus then healed with a touch, the last recorded miracle before the crucifixion (John 18:10; Luke 22:51). John is the only Gospel writer who names him.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maleleel
entries.dictNote: Maleleel is the Greek form of Mahalalel, a descendant of Seth before the flood, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back through Noah to Adam (Luke 3:37; cf. Gen. 5:12-17).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mallothi
entries.dictNote: Mallothi was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Heman appointed by David to the temple music service (1 Chronicles 25:4). He headed the nineteenth of the twenty-four divisions of musicians chosen by lot (25:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Malluch
entries.summary: Malluk, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Malluch was a common postexilic Levitical and priestly name among those who signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mamre
entries.dictNote: Mamre was an Amorite ally of Abraham and the name of the site near Hebron where Abraham settled, built an altar, and received the three visitors who announced Isaac's coming birth.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manaen
entries.dictNote: Manaen was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, listed alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, and Saul, the group that laid hands on Barnabas and Saul to send them out on what became the first missionary journey (Acts 13:1-3). Luke notes that Manaen had been brought up together with Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who executed John the Baptist, a striking contrast between two men raised in the same household who took very different paths.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Manahath
entries.summary: Manachath, the name of an Edomite and of a place in Moab
entries.dictNote: Manahath was a son of Shobal and grandson of Seir the Horite, an Edomite clan chief listed in the genealogies of Genesis and Chronicles (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). The name also appears in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:6), likely referring to the related clan or town of the Manahathites, who elsewhere are connected to Zorah and the family of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:52, 54).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Manasseh
entries.summary: Menashsheh, a grandson of Jacob, also the tribe descended from him, and its territory
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Manasseh was Hezekiah's son and Judah's longest-reigning king, and also its worst: he rebuilt the high places his father had torn down, practiced sorcery, and reportedly sacrificed his own son, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Assyrian records confirm he was taken captive to Babylon at one point, and 2 Chronicles says that captivity broke his pride and he genuinely repented, spending his remaining years trying to undo the damage he had done, though the reforms didn't outlast him. Manasseh is also the name of Joseph's elder son, ancestor of one of Israel's twelve tribes.

entries.label: 14 books

entries.title: Manasses
entries.dictNote: Manasses is the Greek New Testament form of Manasseh and refers to two different things. In Matthew's genealogy it names the notorious king of Judah, ancestor of Jesus, who reigned longer than any other Judean king and led the nation into idolatry (Matthew 1:10). In Revelation it instead names the tribe descended from Joseph's son Manasseh, listed among the twelve tribes sealed by God (Revelation 7:6).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Manoah
entries.dictNote: Manoah was Samson's father, and an angel appeared to him and his previously childless wife to announce Samson's birth and his lifelong Nazirite calling, an encounter so overwhelming that Manoah feared they would die for having seen God.

witness.excerpt: There was one Manoah, a person of such great virtue, that he had few men his equals; and without dispute the principal person of his countrey.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maoch
entries.dictNote: Father of Achish, the Philistine king of Gath who sheltered David from Saul (1 Samuel 27:2). A later king of Gath also named Achish, son of Maacah, appears in Solomon's reign (1 Kings 2:39); whether Maoch and Maacah are the same figure or the name simply recurred in Gath's ruling house is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maon
entries.summary: Maon, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Maon was a hill town in the Judean hill country about seven miles south of Hebron that gave its name to the surrounding wilderness where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:24-25) and where the wealthy Nabal, later married to Abigail, kept his flocks (1 Samuel 25:2). Ruins and cisterns at the site, now called Tell Ma'in, still mark its location.

witness.excerpt: For when David was apprized of the malignant intentions of the men of Ziph, and of the approach of Saul, he left the straits of that countrey; and fled to the great rock that was in the wilderness of Maon.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Mara
entries.summary: Mara, a symbolic name of Naomi
entries.dictNote: Mara, meaning "bitter," was the name Naomi took for herself on returning to Bethlehem from Moab, after the deaths of her husband and two sons left her feeling that God had dealt bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20).

entries.title: Marah
entries.summary: Marah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Marah, meaning bitterness, was the first watering stop the Israelites reached after crossing the sea, three days into the wilderness, where the water was too bitter to drink (Exodus 15:23). Moses threw a piece of wood into the water at the Lord's direction and it became drinkable, after which God gave Israel a statute and tested them there (Exodus 15:25-26). It is often identified with Ain Hawarah, a spring in the Sinai peninsula still known for brackish water.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Maralah
entries.dictNote: Maralah marked a point on the southern boundary of Zebulun's territory (Joshua 19:11). It has been identified with the modern village of Ma'lul, southwest of Nazareth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Maran-atha
entries.summary: maranatha, i.e. an exclamation of the approaching divine judgment
entries.dictNote: Maranatha is not a name but an Aramaic expression, “our Lord, come,” that Paul appends to the close of 1 Corinthians as a solemn invocation (1 Corinthians 16:22). It functioned in the early church as both a prayer for Christ's return and a formula of exclusion pronounced against those who did not love him, showing how quickly Aramaic liturgical phrases entered Greek-speaking congregations.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Marcus
entries.dictNote: Marcus, more commonly known as John Mark, was a companion of Paul and Barnabas on part of their first missionary journey before leaving partway through, a departure that later caused a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas. He was also a close associate of Peter, who calls him his son, and early church tradition credits him with writing the Gospel of Mark based substantially on Peter's own preaching and memories.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Mareshah
entries.summary: Mareshah, the name of two Israelites and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Mareshah was a city in the Shephelah of Judah, fortified by Rehoboam and the site where King Asa defeated a vastly larger invading army under Zerah the Cushite. Micah laments over the city in his oracle of judgment on Judah's towns. Excavations at the site, known today as Tell Sandahanna, have uncovered an extensive Hellenistic-era underground city and the painted Sidonian burial caves, whose walls depict exotic animals in a style showing strong Egyptian and Phoenician influence.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Maroth
entries.dictNote: A town named in Micah's oracle of lament over the towns of the Judean lowlands facing Assyrian invasion (Micah 1:12), where the prophet plays on the similarity between the name Maroth and the Hebrew word for "bitterness." Its exact location is unknown, though it lay somewhere in the same district as the other towns Micah names, such as Lachish and Moresheth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Marsena
entries.dictNote: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media named as royal counselors to Ahasuerus, advisers who had direct access to the king and the highest seats in the kingdom (Esther 1:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Martha
entries.dictNote: Martha was the sister of Mary and Lazarus in Bethany, and she's remembered chiefly for two contrasting moments: being gently corrected by Jesus for being distracted by her many household preparations while her sister simply sat and listened to him, and later making one of the boldest declarations of faith in the Gospels, confessing Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, even while grieving her brother's death just before Jesus raised him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mary
entries.summary: Maria or Mariam (i.e. Mirjam), the name of six Christian females
entries.dictNote: Three different women named Mary appear around Jesus. The most important is his mother, engaged to Joseph when the angel Gabriel told her she would bear the Messiah, who raised Jesus in Nazareth and stood at the foot of the cross when he died. Mary Magdalene was a follower Jesus had healed of seven demons, and she was the first person any Gospel records seeing the risen Jesus, mistaking him for a gardener until he said her name. The third, Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is remembered for sitting at Jesus's feet to listen while Martha worked in the kitchen, and for anointing Jesus's feet with expensive perfume shortly before his death.

witness.excerpt: There was a certain woman that dwelt beyond Jordan, her name was Mary; her father was Eleazar, of the village Bethezob, which signifies the house of Hyssop.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Maschil
entries.dictNote: Maschil is a Hebrew term appearing in the superscriptions of thirteen psalms, likely meaning a contemplative or skillfully composed psalm, and it is a literary or musical designation rather than the name of a person.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mash
entries.summary: Mash, a son of Aram, and the people descended from him
entries.dictNote: Mash was one of the four sons of Aram listed in the Table of Nations, and his name attached to a tribe or region east of Mesopotamia (Genesis 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:17 gives the name as Meshech instead, and some geographers connect his descendants with the Mount Masius range in what is now southeastern Turkey.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mashal
entries.dictNote: Mashal was a Levitical town within the tribal territory of Asher (1 Chronicles 6:74), called Mishal in the parallel list at Joshua 21:30 and Misheal in Asher's original town list at Joshua 19:26. Its exact site is unknown, though it lay somewhere along the Mediterranean coastal plain of Asher's territory.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Masrekah
entries.dictNote: Edomite town, home of Samlah, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a monarchy of its own, according to the parallel genealogical lists in Genesis and Chronicles (Gen. 36:36; 1 Chr. 1:47).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Massa
entries.dictNote: Massa was one of Ishmael's twelve sons, each the head of an Arabian tribal confederation (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Assyrian records from the eighth century BC mention a nomadic Arabian tribe called “Mas'a” in the same general region, which many scholars identify with his descendants. Nothing further is recorded of Massa himself.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Massah
entries.summary: Massah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Massah, meaning "testing," was the name given to the site near Rephidim where the Israelites, thirsty in the wilderness, quarreled with Moses and demanded water, provoking God's testing of their faith even as they tested him (Exodus 17:1-7). The same site was also called Meribah, "quarreling," and Israel's rebellion there became a byword for hardened unbelief, invoked later in Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 as a warning against a hardened heart.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Master
entries.summary: my master, i.e Rabbi, as an official title of honor
entries.dictNote: Master is a title used throughout the Gospels, especially in Luke, as a form of respectful address to Jesus, roughly equivalent to teacher or rabbi, rather than the name of a person.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mathat
entries.summary: Matthat (i.e. Mattithjah), the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Luke's genealogy of Jesus lists two different men named Mathat among the ancestors of Joseph, one closer to Joseph's own generation and another, generations further back, near Levi and Melki (Luke 3:24, 29). Little else is recorded about either beyond their place in the genealogical line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Matred
entries.dictNote: Matred was the daughter of Mezahab and mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (also called Hadad), the last king of Edom named in the Genesis king-list before Israel's own kings arose (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50). She is one of the few women named in these otherwise male genealogical lists. Nothing further is recorded of her.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Matri
entries.dictNote: Matri was the family within the tribe of Benjamin to which Saul belonged, named when Saul was chosen by lot to be Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:21). Nothing further is recorded about this family beyond its role in Saul's selection.

witness.excerpt: When the Hebrews had so done, the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin: and when the lot was cast for the families of this tribe, that which was called Matri was taken: and when the lot was cast for the single persons of that family; Saul the son of Kish was taken, for their King.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattan
entries.summary: Mattan, the name of a priest of Baal, and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Mattan was a priest of Baal killed at his own altar when the people tore down Baal worship in Jerusalem after the coup that overthrew Queen Athaliah.

witness.excerpt: After which they then ran to the house of Baal; which Athaliah and her husband Jehoram had built, to the dishonour of the God of their fathers, and to the honour of Ahab; and demolished it, and slew Mattan, that had his priesthood.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mattanah
entries.summary: Mattanah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Mattanah, a gift, was a wilderness station where Israel camped between the desert and the borders of Moab, mentioned in the same brief itinerary that records the springing up of the well at Beer (Numbers 21:18-19). It is generally placed somewhere in the Wadi Waleh.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattaniah
entries.summary: Mattanjah, the name of ten Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mattaniah was the birth name of Zedekiah, Judah's last king, before Nebuchadnezzar changed his name as a sign of his subjugation to Babylon when he installed him on the throne.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Mattatha
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy as the son of Nathan and grandson of David, part of the line traced through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon (Luke 3:31).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattathah
entries.dictNote: One of the men listed in Ezra 10:33 among those of the tribe of Judah who had married foreign wives during the exile and were required to separate from them under Ezra's covenant reform. The name is likely a shortened form of Mattithiah or Mattathiah, "gift of the LORD."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mattathias
entries.summary: Mattathias (i.e. Mattithjah), an Israelite and a Christian
entries.dictNote: Two men named Mattathias appear consecutively in Luke's genealogy of Jesus: the son of Amos and the son of Semein, both several generations before Joseph (Luke 3:25-26). Neither is otherwise known; the name, meaning “gift of the Lord,” was common enough to later be borne by the priest who launched the Maccabean revolt roughly a century and a half before Jesus, though that Mattathias is a different, unrelated figure.

entries.title: Mattenai
entries.summary: Mattenai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mattenai was a common postexilic name, including a priest listed in Nehemiah's genealogies and a man confronted for a foreign marriage under Ezra.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Matthan
entries.dictNote: Matthan appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Jacob and grandfather of Joseph, Mary's husband (Matthew 1:15-16). Luke's parallel genealogy names a different grandfather of Joseph, Matthat, one of several points where the two genealogies diverge, likely because they trace different lines of descent.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Matthew
entries.summary: Matthæus (i.e. Matthitjah), an Israelite and a Christian
entries.dictNote: Matthew was a tax collector, a profession that made him a social outcast among fellow Jews for working on Rome's behalf, and Jesus called him directly from his tax booth to become one of the twelve apostles. Also called Levi in Mark and Luke's accounts, Matthew hosted a large dinner for Jesus with his fellow tax collectors and other social outcasts, and early church tradition credits him with writing the Gospel that bears his name, aimed especially at showing Jewish readers how Jesus fulfilled the Old Testament.

entries.title: Mattithiah. n
entries.summary: Mattithjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mattithiah was a common Levitical name, borne by several temple musicians and gatekeepers appointed under David.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Me-jarkon
entries.dictNote: Me-jarkon, "waters of yellowness," was a river marking part of the boundary of the tribe of Dan, mentioned alongside Rakkon just before the note that Dan's territory proved too small and the tribe went on to conquer Laish in the north instead (Joshua 19:46-47). It is usually identified with the Yarkon River, which still flows through the coastal plain near modern Tel Aviv and rises from springs at ancient Aphek.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meah
entries.dictNote: Meah, meaning "the hundred," was not a person but a tower on Jerusalem's northern wall, rebuilt by the priests as part of Nehemiah's post-exilic restoration of the city's defenses (Nehemiah 3:1; 12:39). Its name most likely marked either its height in cubits or a measurement tied to the surrounding wall section.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mearah
entries.dictNote: Mearah, meaning the cave, was a site on Israel's northern frontier not yet conquered in Joshua's day, located near Sidon on the Phoenician coast (Josh. 13:4). Suggested identifications include a cave near Jezzine in the Lebanon mountains east of Sidon, though its precise location remains uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mebunnai
entries.dictNote: Mebunnai, elsewhere called Sibbecai or Sibbechai (1 Chronicles 11:29; 27:11), was one of David's elite warriors listed among the Thirty (2 Samuel 23:27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mecherathite
entries.summary: a Mekerathite, or inhabitant of Mekerah
entries.dictNote: Mecherathite identifies Hepher, one of David's mighty men in Chronicles' list; the place is otherwise unknown, and the two Old Testament lists of David's mighty men, in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11, differ in several names at points like this one, a mark of their separate transmission history.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mecholathite
entries.summary: a Mecholathite or inhabitant of Abel-Mecholah
entries.dictNote: Mecholathite identifies Adriel, the man Saul gave his daughter Merab in marriage to instead of David, as being from Abel-meholah. Adriel's five sons by Merab were later handed over to the Gibeonites and executed to end a famine caused by Saul's earlier violence against them.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Medad
entries.dictNote: Medad was one of seventy elders appointed to share the burden of leading Israel with Moses; when the Spirit came upon the group, he and his companion Eldad prophesied in the camp rather than at the tent of meeting with the others (Numbers 11:26-27). Joshua wanted Moses to stop them, but Moses answered that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets (Numbers 11:28-29). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Medan
entries.dictNote: Medan was a son of Abraham by his concubine Keturah and became the ancestor of an Arabian tribe grouped with Midian and other Keturah clans east of Canaan (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32).

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mede
entries.summary: a Madian or native of Madai
entries.dictNote: Mede is not an individual but an ethnic designation for an inhabitant of Media, the ancient kingdom in what is now northwestern Iran. The Medes allied with Babylon to topple Assyria and later merged with Persia under Cyrus to form the Medo-Persian Empire that conquered Babylon; Daniel refers to their laws and kings, and Medes are among the nations represented at Pentecost in Acts 2:9.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Medeba
entries.dictNote: Medeba was an ancient Moabite town assigned to the tribe of Reuben after the conquest (Numbers 21:30; Joshua 13:16). Israel's general Joab defeated a coalition of Ammonites and their Aramean allies near the town during David's reign (1 Chronicles 19:7-15), and the Moabites later regained it, a loss Isaiah laments in his oracle against Moab (Isaiah 15:2). The site survives as modern Madaba in Jordan, famous for its sixth-century Byzantine floor mosaic depicting the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Megiddo
entries.summary: Megiddon or Megiddo, a place in Palestine
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Megiddo was a fortified Canaanite royal city guarding the pass into the Jezreel Valley, later held by Manasseh and rebuilt as one of Solomon's chariot cities. Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera took place in its plain, and centuries later King Josiah was killed there confronting Pharaoh Necho, a death so mourned it became proverbial. The site is exceptionally well documented outside the Bible: Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III's siege of Megiddo around 1457 BC is recorded in detail on the walls of Karnak, making it one of the earliest battles in history with a surviving eyewitness account of troop movements and strategy.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Mehetabeel
entries.summary: Mehetabel, the name of an Edomitish man and woman
entries.dictNote: Mehetabel was the wife of an early Edomite king, and also the name of an ancestor of a man who tried to intimidate Nehemiah into hiding in the temple to discredit him.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mehida
entries.dictNote: Mehida headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:52; Nehemiah 7:54). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mehir
entries.dictNote: A member of the tribe of Judah, listed as the son of Chelub (also called Caleb), the brother of Shuah, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4:11. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mehujael
entries.summary: Mechujael or Mechijael, an antediluvian patriarch
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Cain, son of Irad and father of Methusael, part of the genealogy leading to Lamech and his children in Genesis 4:18.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mehuman
entries.dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs who personally served King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and whom the king ordered to bring Queen Vashti before his banquet guests, an order she refused in the incident that opens the book of Esther (Esth. 1:10-12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mekonah
entries.dictNote: Mekonah was one of the towns in the Negev of Judah that Jewish families resettled after returning from the Babylonian exile, listed alongside Ziklag in Nehemiah 11:28. Its precise site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melatiah
entries.dictNote: A Gibeonite who joined the broad coalition of workers Nehemiah organized to repair the wall of Jerusalem after the exile, working alongside men of Gibeon and Mizpah (Nehemiah 3:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melchi
entries.summary: Melchi (i.e. Malki), the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Melchi is the name of two different ancestors in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, both counted through the line of Mary or Joseph's legal descent rather than Matthew's. One Melchi is the father of Neri and stands roughly at the time of the Babylonian exile (Luke 3:27-28); the other is much closer to Jesus, the father of Levi and son of Janna (Luke 3:24).

witness.excerpt: He had three male children, Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchi-shua; with Merab and Michal his daughters.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melchizedek
entries.summary: Genesis names him once and never explains him — a king and priest with no genealogy, blessing Abraham out of nowhere (14:18-20), which is exactly what later readers found so strange about him (Hebrews 7 leans hard on that silence). Josephus is more matter-of-fact: he glosses the name itself ('the righteous king') and identifies Salem as the city that would become Jerusalem.
entries.dictNote: Melchizedek was the king of Salem and a priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham and received a tenth of his war spoils in Genesis, appearing without any recorded genealogy, birth, or death. The Psalms later describe a coming king who would be a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, and the New Testament book of Hebrews builds an extended argument from that same silence about his origins, using Melchizedek's priesthood, older and greater than Israel's own Levitical priesthood, to explain how Jesus can be a priest despite not being descended from Levi.

witness.excerpt: Melchisedeck, King of the city Salem, received him. That name signifies, The righteous King: and such he was without dispute; insomuch that, on this account, he was made the Priest of God. However, they afterward called Salem Jerusalem.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Meleas
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, placed between Menan and Eliakim in the line descending through Nathan, one of David's sons, rather than through Solomon as in Matthew's genealogy (Luke 3:31). Nothing is known about him beyond this listing.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melech
entries.summary: Melek, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Melech was a great-grandson of Jonathan through his father Micah and grandfather Mephibosheth, listed among the descendants of Saul's house in the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:35; 9:41). He appears only in this genealogical record.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melita
entries.summary: Melita, an island in the Mediterranean
entries.dictNote: Melita is not a person but the ancient name of Malta, the island in the central Mediterranean where Paul's ship ran aground during the storm recorded in Acts 27. Long settled by Phoenicians and later held by Carthage and then Rome, Malta preserves Phoenician and Punic remains, including bilingual inscriptions, from this era. Paul and his companions spent three months on the island before completing the voyage to Rome (Acts 28:1-11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Melzar
entries.summary: the butler or other officer in the Babylonian court
entries.dictNote: Melzar is not a personal name but the title of a Babylonian court official, roughly a steward or chief attendant, who was placed in charge of the diet of Daniel and his three companions (Daniel 1:11, 16). The Hebrew term functions more like an office than an individual's name, which is why some translations render it as 'the guard' or 'the steward' rather than treating it as a proper noun.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Memphis
entries.summary: Moph, the capital of Lower Egypt
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the great capital of Lower Egypt, called Moph in Hosea 9:6 and Noph elsewhere (Isa. 19:13; Jer. 2:16, 46:14; Ezek. 30:13-16), located on the west bank of the Nile near modern Cairo. Founded according to tradition by Menes, Egypt's first king, it served as a major religious and political center for centuries. Its ruins, including a colossal fallen statue of Ramesses II, lie near the village of Mit Rahina and are recognized today, along with the nearby pyramid fields of Saqqara, as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Memucan
entries.summary: Memucan or Momucan, a Persian satrap
entries.dictNote: Memucan was one of the Persian king's advisors who recommended deposing Queen Vashti for refusing his summons, a decision that opened the way for Esther to eventually become queen.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Menahem
entries.dictNote: Menahem seized the throne of northern Israel by assassinating his predecessor and then brutally sacking a city that refused to submit to him. He paid a massive tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser the Third to secure his own throne, a payment independently recorded in Assyrian inscriptions that name Menahem directly.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mene
entries.dictNote: Mene was not a person but the first word of the mysterious writing that appeared on the wall during Belshazzar's feast in Babylon, which Daniel alone could read and interpret (Daniel 5:25-28). Repeated as "Mene, Mene," it meant "numbered," and Daniel explained it as God's declaration that Belshazzar's kingdom had been measured out and brought to an end; Babylon fell that same night.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meonothai
entries.dictNote: Meonothai was a son of Othniel, the judge and younger brother of Caleb, and is listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:14 as the father of Ophrah. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mephaath
entries.summary: Mophaath or Mephaath, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Mephaath was a Levitical city in the tribal territory of Reuben, assigned to the Merarite Levites for their dwelling (Joshua 13:18; 21:37; 1 Chronicles 6:79). Jeremiah later includes it in his oracle against Moab, since the region had come under Moabite control by his time (Jeremiah 48:21). Its precise site east of the Jordan has not been securely identified.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mephibosheth
entries.summary: Mephibosheth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son, crippled in both feet after his nurse dropped him while fleeing news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths, and David sought him out years later to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake, restoring his grandfather Saul's land and giving him a permanent place at the king's own table. During Absalom's rebellion a servant falsely accused Mephibosheth of disloyalty, and though David initially believed the accusation, Mephibosheth's evident grief and his choice not to groom himself during David's exile suggest the charge was unjust.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Merab
entries.dictNote: Merab was the elder of King Saul's two daughters. Saul promised her in marriage to David after his victory over Goliath but then gave her instead to Adriel of Meholah, apparently to avoid honoring the pledge (1 Samuel 18:17-19). She and Adriel had five sons, who were later handed over to the Gibeonites and executed to atone for Saul's earlier slaughter of Gibeonite lives, part of the famine narrative in 2 Samuel 21.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meraiah
entries.dictNote: The head of the priestly family of Seraiah during the high priesthood of Joiakim, listed among the priestly leaders in Nehemiah's record of postexilic priests and Levites (Neh. 12:12). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meraioth
entries.summary: Merajoth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Meraioth was a common priestly name in the high priestly genealogy, appearing in the lineage lists of both Ezra and 1 Chronicles.

entries.title: Merari
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra
entries.dictNote: Merari was Levi's third son, and his descendants were assigned responsibility for the heavier structural components of the tabernacle, the frames, bars, pillars, and bases, transported by cart rather than carried by hand.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Merathaim
entries.dictNote: A name meaning "double rebellion" that Jeremiah applies to a district of Babylon in his oracle of judgment against the empire (Jeremiah 50:21). It plays on an Akkadian term for the marshy region near the head of the Persian Gulf, turned into a taunt rather than used as an ordinary place name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mered
entries.dictNote: Mered was a descendant of Judah through the line of Ezra, listed among the tribe's families in the genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 4:17-18). He is recorded as having married Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh, alongside a wife from the Judahite line called "the Jewess," and various towns and craftsmen were reckoned among his descendants.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meremoth
entries.summary: Meremoth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Meremoth was a priest who helped weigh and account for the gold and silver vessels Ezra brought back from Babylon, and he later helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Meres
entries.dictNote: Meres was one of the seven Persian princes who served as close advisers to King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and had access to his presence; he was consulted after Queen Vashti refused the king's summons (Esther 1:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meri-baal
entries.dictNote: An alternate Hebrew spelling of Merib-baal, the name Chronicles uses for Jonathan's son, known in the books of Samuel as Mephibosheth (1 Chronicles 9:40; compare 2 Samuel 4:4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Merib-baal
entries.summary: quarreller of Baal, Merib-Baal, an epithet of Gideon
entries.dictNote: Merib-baal is the name given in the Chronicles genealogies to Jonathan's son, elsewhere called Mephibosheth in the books of Samuel (1 Chronicles 8:34; 9:40; compare 2 Samuel 4:4). The change from Baal-based names to substitutes like Bosheth, meaning shame, likely reflects later discomfort with the divine title Baal, lord, once used more neutrally in personal names.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meribah
entries.summary: Meribah, the name of two places in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Meribah, meaning quarreling, was the site where Israel complained about lacking water and where Moses struck a rock in frustration instead of speaking to it as instructed, a moment of disobedience that cost him entry into the promised land.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Merodach
entries.dictNote: Merodach is not a person but Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, invoked in Jeremiah's oracle announcing Babylon's fall: "Merodach is broken in pieces" (Jeremiah 50:2). Marduk's supremacy in Babylonian religion is confirmed by extensive cuneiform sources, including the creation epic Enuma Elish and the Cyrus Cylinder, which credits the god with handing Babylon to Cyrus the Persian, the very event this oracle anticipates.

witness.excerpt: But now, after the death of Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach his son succeeded in the Kingdom: who immediately set Jechoniah at liberty, and esteemed him among his most intimate friends.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Merodach-baladan
entries.dictNote: Merodach-baladan, also spelled Berodach-baladan, was a Chaldean chieftain who seized the throne of Babylon and led resistance against Assyrian domination in the late eighth century BC. He sent envoys to congratulate King Hezekiah of Judah on his recovery from illness, ostensibly to form an anti-Assyrian alliance, and Hezekiah unwisely showed them the full contents of his treasury, prompting Isaiah's warning of a coming Babylonian exile (Isaiah 39:1-7; 2 Kings 20:12-19). Assyrian royal inscriptions of Sargon II and Sennacherib independently record his repeated seizures of the Babylonian throne and his eventual defeat, confirming him as a genuine historical figure known outside the Bible as Marduk-apla-iddina II.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Merom
entries.dictNote: Merom was not a person but the waters, likely the marshy lake north of the Sea of Galilee now called Lake Huleh, where Joshua won his climactic victory over the northern Canaanite coalition led by Jabin, king of Hazor (Joshua 11:5-7). Hazor's massive Late Bronze Age destruction layer, one of the best documented in Canaanite archaeology, corresponds to this period, even though the mound itself lies a few miles from the waters.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meronothite
entries.summary: a Meronothite, or inhabitant of some (otherwise unknown) Meronoth.
entries.dictNote: Meronothite identifies a person as being from Meronoth, a town of unknown location. Under David, Jehdeiah the Meronothite oversaw the royal donkeys, and generations later Jadon the Meronothite is named among those who helped repair Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Meroz
entries.dictNote: Meroz appears only in the Song of Deborah, cursed by the angel of the Lord for failing to come to Israel's aid against Sisera's army, in contrast to the tribes praised earlier in the poem for answering the call (Judges 5:23). The town's location is unknown, and no convincing identification has been proposed; some scholars suspect it lay near the battle site in the Jezreel Valley, close enough that its refusal to fight would have been especially damning.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mesech
entries.summary: Meshek, a son of Japheth, and the people descended from him
entries.dictNote: Meshech was a son of Japheth and the ancestor of a people associated in the prophets with the distant north, paired repeatedly with Tubal as a symbol of remote, warlike nations.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Mesha
entries.dictNote: Mesha, a place marking the eastern edge of the territory settled by Joktan's descendants in the Table of Nations, paired with Sephar as boundary points (Gen. 10:30). Its exact location in Arabia is uncertain, and it is not to be confused with the Benjamite clan head or the king of Moab who share the same name elsewhere in scripture.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mesha
entries.dictNote: Eldest son of Caleb, named in the genealogy of Judah as the father of Ziph (1 Chronicles 2:42).

witness.excerpt: 895.] When Joram had taken upon him the Kingdom, he determined to make an expedition against the King of Moab, whose name was Mesha.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mesha
entries.summary: Mesha, a place in Arabia; also an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Despite this record's place tag, Mesha here is a person, not a location: the son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, listed as a Benjamite clan head in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:9. He is distinct from both the Arabian place Mesha in Genesis 10:30 and the king of Moab of the same name recorded in 2 Kings 3.

witness.excerpt: 895.] When Joram had taken upon him the Kingdom, he determined to make an expedition against the King of Moab, whose name was Mesha.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mesha
entries.dictNote: King of Moab in the ninth century BC who paid heavy tribute to Israel until Ahab's death, then rebelled (2 Kings 3:4-5). When the combined armies of Israel, Judah, and Edom nearly overwhelmed him, he sacrificed his own son on the city wall in a desperate act to Chemosh, his god. Mesha's own account of his revolt survives on the Moabite Stone, a black basalt inscription he had carved and which was found at Dibon in 1868; it independently confirms the biblical conflict and even names the "house of Omri."

witness.excerpt: 895.] When Joram had taken upon him the Kingdom, he determined to make an expedition against the King of Moab, whose name was Mesha.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshak
entries.dictNote: Meshach was the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of Daniel's three friends who survived Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace unharmed after refusing to worship his golden image.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshak
entries.dictNote: Meshach was the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of Daniel's three friends who survived Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace unharmed after refusing to worship his golden image.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshelemiah
entries.dictNote: Meshelemiah was the head of a family of temple gatekeepers appointed under David, chosen by lot for the east gate, a position of some honor.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshezabeel
entries.dictNote: Meshezabel was the name of an official who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah and of an ancestor of one of those who signed the covenant renewal.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshillemoth
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name. The first was the father of Berechiah, an Ephraimite chief who, along with other leaders, opposed enslaving Judean captives taken in war and insisted they be fed, clothed, and sent home (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). The second was an ancestor of Amashsai, a priest who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:13).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Meshobab
entries.dictNote: One of several Simeonite family heads listed in 1 Chronicles 4:34-38 whose descendants expanded their pastureland by driving out the Hamites and Meunites near Gedor in the days of Hezekiah. Nothing further is recorded of him individually.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Meshullam
entries.summary: Meshullam, the name of seventeen Israelites
entries.dictNote: Meshullam was a common name among priests, Levites, and officials in the postexilic period, borne by several different men involved in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah and in temple administration.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Meshullemeth
entries.dictNote: Wife of King Manasseh of Judah and mother of his successor, King Amon (2 Kings 21:19). She was the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah, one of the few queen mothers of Judah whose father's hometown is specifically recorded.

entries.title: Mesobaite
entries.dictNote: Mesobaite marks Jasiel, one of the last names on the roll of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11:47. The place it refers to, presumably called Mesobah or Zobah, cannot be identified with certainty.

entries.title: Mesopotamia
entries.summary: Mesopotamia (as lying between the Euphrates and the Tigris; compare 0763), a region of Asia
entries.dictNote: Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers, was the Greek and Roman name for the region between the Euphrates and Tigris, called Aram-naharaim or Padan-aram in the Old Testament. It was the ancestral home of Abraham's family before his migration to Canaan, and Stephen recalls this origin in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:2), while Jewish pilgrims from the region were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Cuneiform archives recovered from sites such as Mari and Nuzi, elsewhere in this same region, have supplied scholars with detailed pictures of second-millennium BC social and legal customs, adoption, inheritance, and marriage contracts among them, that closely parallel practices described in the patriarchal narratives of Genesis.

entries.title: Messias
entries.dictNote: Messias is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew and Aramaic “Messiah,” meaning “anointed one,” used only twice in the New Testament: by Andrew telling his brother Simon Peter that he had found the Messiah (John 1:41), and by the Samaritan woman at the well telling Jesus she knew Messiah was coming (John 4:25). John immediately glosses the term for his Greek-speaking readers as “the Christ,” since “Christos” is the Greek equivalent. Both scenes mark the term's first appearance on the lips of ordinary people recognizing Jesus rather than in prophetic or narrative description.

entries.title: Metheg-ammah
entries.dictNote: Metheg-ammah was not a person but a figurative name, meaning roughly 'bridle of the mother city,' that 2 Samuel 8:1 uses for the leading Philistine city David subdued, generally identified with Gath. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 18:1 states the fact plainly: David took Gath and its surrounding towns from the Philistines, breaking their regional dominance.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Methusael
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Cain in the genealogy of Genesis 4, father of Lamech and grandfather of Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain, credited respectively as ancestors of nomadic herders, musicians, and metalworkers (Genesis 4:18-22). His name closely resembles Methuselah, from the separate line of Seth recorded later in Genesis 5, but the two figures are not the same person.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Methuselah
entries.dictNote: Methuselah was Enoch's son and Noah's grandfather, and Genesis records his age at death as nine hundred sixty-nine years, the longest lifespan of anyone in the Bible, giving rise to the phrase old as Methuselah. By the traditional genealogical chronology in Genesis 5, Methuselah's death lines up with the same year as the flood, though the text itself draws no explicit connection between the two.

entries.dictNote: Mibzar, meaning “fortress,” was listed among the chiefs, or “dukes,” of Edom descended from Esau (Genesis 36:42; 1 Chronicles 1:53). entries.title: Micah
entries.summary: Micajah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Micah's name means “who is like the LORD.” The most significant bearer is the eighth-century BC prophet of Judah, a contemporary of Isaiah, whose short book condemns Israel and Judah's social injustice and predicts Bethlehem as the birthplace of a future ruler (Micah 5:2), a line later cited in Matthew's nativity account. A different Micah, an Ephraimite in Judges 17-18, built a private shrine with an idol and hired a wandering Levite as his priest, an episode illustrating the lawlessness before Israel had a king; his household gods were later stolen by the migrating tribe of Dan. Several minor figures share the name as well: a son of Mephibosheth (1 Chronicles 8:34-35), the chief of a Kohathite priestly family (1 Chronicles 23:20), and a Reubenite listed in the tribal genealogies (1 Chronicles 5:5).

entries.title: Michaiah
entries.summary: Mikajah, the name of an Israelite and an Israelitess
entries.dictNote: The name Michaiah is applied to several distinct people in the Old Testament: the mother of King Abijah of Judah, likely the same woman elsewhere called Maacah (2 Chronicles 13:2); one of the officials Jehoshaphat sent throughout Judah to teach the law (2 Chronicles 17:7); a man present when the high priest Hilkiah reported discovery of the law book to King Josiah's officials (2 Kings 22:12); the son of Gemariah, who reported Jeremiah's warnings to the royal court after hearing Baruch read the scroll aloud (Jeremiah 36:11-13); and a Levite and a priest, both involved in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:35, 41). The recurrence of the name across these different roles and generations shows it was common rather than tied to one notable figure.

entries.dictNote: Michmethath was a landmark on the boundary between the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh, located near Shechem (Josh. 16:6; 17:7). It served purely as a boundary reference point in Joshua's territorial descriptions, and its precise site remains unidentified.

entries.title: Migdal-eder
entries.dictNote: Migdal-eder, tower of the flock, was a place near Bethlehem where Jacob pitched his tent after Rachel's death and burial on the road there (Genesis 35:19-21). Micah later uses the same name figuratively for Jerusalem's stronghold, promising that dominion and former glory would return to the daughter of Zion (Micah 4:8). Later Jewish tradition associated the watchtower with a site where shepherds guarded flocks destined for temple sacrifice, though the Bible itself gives no more than the name and its two occurrences.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Migdal-el
entries.dictNote: Migdal-el, tower of God, was a fortified town of Naphtali listed in Joshua 19:38. Some scholars have identified it with Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, the town associated with Mary Magdalene in the Gospels, though the connection is not certain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Migdal-gad
entries.dictNote: Migdal-gad, "tower of Gad," was a town in the lowland district (Shephelah) of Judah's tribal allotment (Joshua 15:37). It is generally identified with the site of el-Mejdel near Ashkelon, whose name preserves the biblical "migdal," meaning tower.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Migdol
entries.dictNote: Migdol, meaning "tower," names a fortified point on Egypt's northeastern frontier. One Migdol is mentioned in the route of Israel's crossing of the Red Sea in Exodus and Numbers, near the sea's northern end. A Migdol is also named by Jeremiah among the places where Jewish refugees settled after fleeing to Egypt, and Ezekiel uses "from Migdol to Syene" as a way of describing the whole length of Egypt in his oracles of judgment.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Migron
entries.dictNote: Migron names two locations near the Benjamite hill country. One lay near Gibeah, where Saul was camped under a pomegranate tree with about six hundred men before Jonathan's raid on the Philistine garrison at Michmash (1 Sam. 14:2). The other, apparently a different site of the same name, appears in Isaiah's description of an invading army's march route toward Jerusalem, positioned near Aiath and Michmash (Isa. 10:28).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mikloth
entries.summary: Mikloth, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Mikloth is not a place but a name shared by two men in Chronicles. One Mikloth belonged to the Benjamite family that settled in Gibeon, appearing in the genealogy leading to King Saul as the father of Shimeah (1 Chronicles 8:32; 9:37-38). A different Mikloth served as a military officer under Dodai, commanding one of David's monthly divisions of twenty-four thousand troops (1 Chronicles 27:4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mikmas
entries.summary: Mikmas or Mikmash, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Michmash was a town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem where the Philistines mustered against Saul's army; it was the site of Jonathan's daring raid with his armor-bearer against a Philistine garrison across a rocky ravine, which triggered a rout that Saul's forces exploited. Isaiah pictures an invading Assyrian army storing its baggage at Michmash on its march toward Jerusalem, and families from the town were among those who returned from Babylonian exile.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Mikneiah
entries.dictNote: Mikneiah was a Levite of the second rank whom David appointed as a gatekeeper and musician, playing the harp in the choir that accompanied the ark's procession to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 21).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Milalai
entries.dictNote: Milalai was a Levite musician, probably a descendant of Asaph, who took part in the procession of singers and instrumentalists at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:36). The event followed the return from Babylonian exile and marked the completion of one of Nehemiah's major building projects.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Milcah
entries.summary: Milcah, the name of a Hebrewess and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Milcah was Nahor's wife and Abraham's niece, and her descendants through her granddaughter Rebekah connect Abraham's extended family in Mesopotamia directly back into the patriarchal line through Isaac's marriage.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Miletus
entries.summary: Miletus, a city of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Ionian port city about thirty-five miles south of Ephesus. Sailing past Ephesus to save time before Pentecost, Paul summoned that city's elders to Miletus and delivered his farewell address, warning them of false teachers to come (Acts 20:15-38); he later left his sick companion Trophimus there (2 Tim. 4:20). Once a leading Greek city, Miletus was already fading by the Roman period as silt from the Meander River pushed its harbor away from the coast, a well-documented process that has left its ancient theater stranded several miles inland today.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Miniamin
entries.summary: Minjamin, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Miniamin was a common priestly name among those who served in the temple during the postexilic period and took part in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Minni
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a kingdom in the mountains east of Assyria, in what is now northwestern Iran, generally identified with Mannea, known from Assyrian royal annals as a frequent target of campaigns. Jeremiah 51:27 summons Minni along with Ararat and Ashkenaz as nations to muster against Babylon, part of the prophet's oracle announcing Babylon's coming fall.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Minnith
entries.summary: Minnith, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Minnith was an Ammonite town that marked the extent of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites (Judges 11:33) and later appears in Ezekiel's list of goods Judah traded with Tyre, exporting wheat from the district around Minnith (Ezekiel 27:17). It lay somewhere in the tableland east of the Jordan, in the general vicinity of Heshbon and Rabbah.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Miphkad
entries.summary: Miphkad, the name of a gate in Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Miphkad is not a person but one of the gates of Jerusalem, called "the gate Miphkad" or the Muster Gate, repaired during Nehemiah's rebuilding of the city wall (Nehemiah 3:31). Its exact location is uncertain, though it likely stood near the northeast corner of the temple area.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Miriam
entries.summary: Mirjam, the name of two Israelitesses
entries.dictNote: Scripture names two women Miriam. The one nearly everyone means is Moses and Aaron's older sister, a prophetess herself, who watched over the infant Moses in the Nile reeds and later led Israel's women in song after the crossing of the sea. A second, much more obscure Miriam turns up once in a genealogy of Judah, a daughter of Mered and Bithiah with no story attached to her at all.

entries.title: Mirma
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite chief, son of Shaharaim, born to him in Moab according to the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:10, a detail suggesting some Benjamites relocated there for a time, perhaps during a period of regional instability.

entries.summary: Mishael, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Mishael was one of Daniel's three friends, renamed Meshach in Babylon, who survived Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace after refusing to worship his golden image.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mishal
entries.dictNote: Coastal town of Asher assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh. 21:30; 1 Chr. 6:74), likely located near Mount Carmel along the Mediterranean coast.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Misham
entries.dictNote: Misham was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, listed in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mishma
entries.summary: Mishma, the name of a son of Ishmael, and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Mishma was a son of Ishmael, and his descendants are counted among the twelve tribal leaders that came from Ishmael's line, paralleling Israel's own twelve tribes.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mishmannah
entries.dictNote: One of the Gadite warriors, described as having faces like lions and being as swift as gazelles on the mountains, who defected to David's camp at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:8-13). These men are singled out among David's early supporters for their skill with shield and spear.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mishraites
entries.summary: a Mishraite, or inhabitant (collectively) of Mishra
entries.dictNote: Mishraites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, named in 1 Chronicles 2:53 alongside the Ithrites, Puhites, and Shumathites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mispereth
entries.dictNote: Mispereth was one of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, named in the roster of returnees in Nehemiah 7:7. The parallel list in Ezra 2:2 gives the name as Mizpar, a variant spelling of the same person.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Misrephoth-mayim
entries.dictNote: Misrephoth-mayim marked the western limit of Joshua's pursuit of the northern Canaanite coalition after their defeat at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:8) and is later listed among territory still unconquered in Joshua's old age (Joshua 13:6). The name, usually rendered burnings of water, may refer to hot springs or to lime-burning kilns near the coast, and the site is generally placed somewhere near the Mediterranean north of Acco, though it has not been identified with confidence.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mithcah
entries.summary: Mithkah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Mithcah appears only in the wilderness itinerary of Numbers 33:28-29, one of the unidentified stations Israel passed through late in the forty years of wandering. Its Hebrew name means sweetness, but nothing in the text explains why it was so called, and its exact location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mithnite
entries.summary: a Mithnite, or inhabitant of Methen
entries.dictNote: Mithnite identifies Joshaphat, one of David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mithredath
entries.summary: Mithredath, the name of two Persians
entries.dictNote: Mithredath, a Hebrew form of the Persian name Mithridates meaning “given by Mithra,” was the royal treasurer of Cyrus who, at the king's command, returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had looted from Jerusalem to the returning exiles (Ezra 1:8). A different Mithredath was a Persian official in Samaria who joined other local officials in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mitspah
entries.summary: Mitspah, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Mizpah was a common town name in Israel, most notably a site where Israel gathered for covenant renewal under Samuel and where Jacob and Laban set up a boundary stone, giving the word Mizpah its familiar meaning as a watchpost between separated parties.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mitylene
entries.summary: Mitylene (or Mytilene), a town on the island of Lesbos
entries.dictNote: Mitylene was the chief city of the island of Lesbos in the Aegean Sea, famous in the classical world as the home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus. Paul's ship anchored there for a night during his third missionary journey as he hurried toward Jerusalem before Pentecost (Acts 20:14-16).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mizar
entries.dictNote: Mizar was not a person but a hill or lesser summit somewhere near Mount Hermon, in the region beyond the Jordan, recalled by the psalmist in Psalm 42:6 while far from Jerusalem and longing to return. Its exact location is no longer known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mizpar
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, counted in the roll of returnees in Ezra 2:2; the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:7 gives the name as Mispereth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mizpeh
entries.summary: Mitspeh, the name of five places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Mizpeh is an alternate spelling of Mizpah, a common watchpost name for several sites in Israel, covered more fully under that entry.

witness.excerpt: So Samuel gathered them together, to a certain city called Mizpeh; which signifies in the Hebrew tongue a watch tower.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mizzah
entries.dictNote: Mizzah was an Edomite clan chief listed among the descendants of Esau.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mnason
entries.dictNote: A Christian from Cyprus, described as an "early disciple," meaning he had been a believer since the earliest days of the Jerusalem church; Paul and his companions stayed at his house in Jerusalem near the end of the third missionary journey (Acts 21:16).

entries.label: 21 books

entries.title: Moadiah
entries.dictNote: A priestly family head in the postexilic community, named Moadiah in Nehemiah 12:17 and Maadiah in the parallel list of Nehemiah 12:5. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moladah
entries.dictNote: Moladah was a town in the Negev originally allotted to Judah and then reassigned to Simeon, whose inheritance lay within Judah's larger territory (Joshua 15:26; 19:2). Its people resettled there after the Babylonian exile, according to the list in Nehemiah 11:26. It is often identified with Tel Malhata, east of Beersheba, a site with excavated Iron Age remains.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Molech
entries.summary: Molek (i.e. king), the chief deity of the Ammonites
entries.dictNote: Molech was a Canaanite and Ammonite deity associated with child sacrifice, and the Old Testament repeatedly and explicitly forbids Israelites from giving their children to Molech, a practice several kings, including Ahaz and Manasseh, were condemned for adopting anyway.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Molid
entries.dictNote: Molid was a son of Abishur and his wife Abihail, descended from Jerahmeel in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:29).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moloch
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the national god of the Ammonites, worshiped with child sacrifice by fire, also called Molech, Milcom, and Malcham in various Old Testament passages (Lev. 18:21, 20:2-5; 1 Kings 11:5, 33; Zeph. 1:5). Solomon built a high place for Moloch on the Mount of Olives to please his foreign wives, and the cult persisted intermittently until Josiah's reforms destroyed it (1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:10, 13). Stephen references the exile-era rebuke of Moloch worship in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:43, quoting Amos 5:26); archaeologists have found child burial sites called tophets at Carthage and other Phoenician colonies that many scholars connect to related West Semitic child-sacrifice cults, though the practice's exact nature remains debated.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Morashthite
entries.summary: a Morashtite or inhabitant of Moresheth-Gath
entries.dictNote: Morashthite identifies the prophet Micah as being from Moresheth, a town in the Judean lowlands near Gath. Jeremiah's elders quote Micah's prophecy against Jerusalem by this epithet nearly a century after he spoke it, citing his unpunished warning as precedent to spare Jeremiah's own life.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Mordecai
entries.summary: Esther's cousin and guardian, the one who refuses to bow to Haman and sets the whole plot in motion (Esther 2:5, 3:2). Josephus's retelling of the book keeps him right where Scripture does — second billing to Esther, first cause of everything that happens to her.
entries.dictNote: Mordecai was a Benjamite in the Persian capital of Susa who raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter and later uncovered a plot to assassinate King Ahasuerus, a service the king had forgotten until a sleepless night sent him back through the royal records. That rediscovery reversed Mordecai's fortunes overnight: the same day his enemy Haman had built a gallows for him, Mordecai was paraded through the city in the king's own robes, and he was later elevated to the second-highest position in the empire.

witness.excerpt: Concerning Esther, and Mordecai, and Haman. And how, in the reign of Artaxerxes, the whole nation of the Jews was in danger of perishing.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Moreh
entries.summary: Moreh, a Canaanite; also a hill (perhaps named from him)
entries.dictNote: The hill of Moreh was where the Midianite camp lay before Gideon's small force of three hundred routed them at night, and a different site called the oak of Moreh near Shechem is where Abraham first built an altar upon entering Canaan.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Moresheth-gath
entries.dictNote: The hometown of the prophet Micah, who is called the Morasthite in Jeremiah 26:18, located in the Shephelah lowlands near Gath (Mic. 1:14). It probably lay at or near the site now called Tell el-Judeideh.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moriah
entries.dictNote: Moriah is not a person but the name of a mountain in Jerusalem, the site where Solomon later built the temple on what had been the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1). Genesis 22:2 identifies 'the land of Moriah' as the place where Abraham was told to offer Isaac, and Jewish tradition has long linked the two locations as the same ridge, generally understood as part of the same hill as Mount Zion.

entries.title: Mosera
entries.summary: Moserah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Mosera, a wilderness campsite near Mount Hor where, according to Deuteronomy's summary, Aaron died and was buried (Deut. 10:6). Numbers 33:38 places his death at Mount Hor itself and lists Moseroth as a nearby stage of the journey; the two accounts are usually read as describing the same general area.

entries.title: Moses
entries.books: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Micah, Malachi
entries.dictNote: Moses was born a Hebrew slave in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's own household, only to flee into the desert after killing an Egyptian overseer and spend the next forty years as a shepherd in Midian. God called him back through the burning bush to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of slavery, and Moses spent the rest of his life shaping that liberated people into a nation, delivering the law at Sinai and leading them through forty years in the wilderness before dying within sight of the promised land at a hundred and twenty. He is named more often than anyone else in the Old Testament, and archaeology confirms plenty of the world he moved through, the store cities, the Egyptian court, the route through Sinai, without ever turning up a record of Moses himself.

entries.title: Moses
entries.summary: Stands beside Elijah at the Transfiguration (9:30) and anchors the risen Jesus's own Bible study on the Emmaus road (24:27, 24:44). Josephus has Moses announce his own death at 120 in his own voice — matching Deuteronomy 34:7's age note exactly, three centuries later. Philo devoted an entire two-volume biography to him alone — it opens on the same infancy-narrative beat Exodus 2 does, an unusually beautiful baby, but reads it as the first sign of what he'd become.

entries.dictNote: Moses was born a Hebrew slave in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's own household, only to flee into the desert after killing an Egyptian overseer and spend the next forty years as a shepherd in Midian. God called him back through the burning bush to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of slavery, and Moses spent the rest of his life shaping that liberated people into a nation, delivering the law at Sinai and leading them through forty years in the wilderness before dying within sight of the promised land at a hundred and twenty. He is named more often than anyone else in the Old Testament, and archaeology confirms plenty of the world he moved through, the store cities, the Egyptian court, the route through Sinai, without ever turning up a record of Moses himself.
