entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Moza
entries.summary: Motsa, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Moza was a common name in the genealogies of Judah and Benjamin, borne by a descendant of Caleb and by a descendant of Saul.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mozah
entries.dictNote: Mozah, a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh. 18:26), commonly identified with Tel Moza just west of Jerusalem. Excavations there have uncovered a large Iron Age temple and grain-storage complex, among the more significant recent archaeological finds in the Jerusalem region.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Muppim
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Benjamin who went to Egypt with Jacob's household, listed in Genesis 46:21; the parallel census in Numbers 26:39 gives the name as Shupham, head of the Shuphamite clan.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mushi
entries.dictNote: Mushi was a son of Merari, Levi's grandson, and his descendants formed one of the Levitical clans assigned to tabernacle service.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Mushites
entries.summary: a Mushite (collectively) or descendants of Mushi
entries.dictNote: Mushites were the Levitical clan descended from Mushi, son of Merari, one of the families charged with caring for the tabernacle's frames, bars, pillars, and other structural furnishings.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Myra
entries.summary: Myra, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Myra was a leading city of the Lycian coast in southwestern Asia Minor, where the centurion guarding Paul transferred him and the other prisoners onto an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy, the same ship later wrecked off Malta (Acts 27:5). The site preserves an impressive Roman theater and a cluster of rock-cut tombs carved into the cliffside above the ancient harbor.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Mysia
entries.summary: Mysia, a region of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Mysia was a region in the northwest of the Roman province of Asia. Paul and his companions passed through it without stopping to preach, prevented by the Spirit from turning into the neighboring regions, and continued on to its port city of Troas (Acts 16:7-8), where Paul received the vision of the Macedonian man that redirected the mission into Europe.

entries.title: Naam
entries.dictNote: Naam was one of the sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr. 4:15). He appears only in this single genealogical notice.

entries.title: Naamah
entries.summary: Naamah, the name of an antediluvian woman, of an Ammonitess, and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Naamah names two people and a place in the Old Testament. The first Naamah was the daughter of Lamech and Zillah, a descendant of Cain, and sister of the metalworker Tubal-cain (Genesis 4:22). A second Naamah was an Ammonite woman, one of Solomon's many foreign wives, and the mother of his heir Rehoboam, the only wife of Solomon's named as the mother of a king (1 Kings 14:21, 31; 2 Chronicles 12:13). A town of the same name lay in the lowland plain of Judah, listed among the cities of that region in Joshua 15:41.

entries.title: Naaman
entries.summary: Naaman, the name of an Israelite and of a Damascene
entries.dictNote: Naaman was the commander of the Aramean army, a respected and successful general who also had leprosy, and it was a captured Israelite servant girl who first told him a prophet in Samaria could heal him. Naaman nearly walked away insulted when Elisha simply sent word for him to wash seven times in the Jordan River rather than perform some dramatic ritual in person, but his servants talked him into trying it, and he came out of the water completely healed. He tried to pay Elisha, who refused any reward, and Naaman left declaring his new faith in Israel's God, while Elisha's own servant Gehazi secretly chased Naaman down for a payment and was struck with the leprosy Naaman had just been cured of.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Naamathite
entries.summary: a Naamathite, or inhabitant of Naamah
entries.dictNote: Naamathite designates Zophar, one of Job's three friends, from a place called Naamah whose location, likely somewhere in Arabia, is not otherwise known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naamites
entries.summary: a Naamanite, or descendant of Naaman (collectively)
entries.dictNote: Naamites were the clan descended from Naaman, a grandson of Benjamin through Bela, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naarah
entries.summary: Naarah, the name of an Israelitess, and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: This record's references actually describe a person rather than a place, despite the entry's classification. Naarah was the second wife of Ashur, a descendant of Judah through Hezron, and the mother of several sons whose names are preserved in the tribal genealogy of Chronicles (1 Chr. 4:5-6). A different place called Naarah, or Naarath, near Jericho on Ephraim's border is mentioned separately in Joshua 16:7.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naarai
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:37), called Paarai the Arbite in the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23:35.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naaran
entries.dictNote: A town of Ephraim near the border with Benjamin, associated with Jericho (1 Chronicles 7:28). It is generally taken as the same place as Naarah, listed among Ephraim's towns in Joshua 16:7, and is usually placed a few miles north of Jericho.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naashon
entries.dictNote: Nahshon was a tribal leader of Judah during the wilderness years and the brother-in-law of Aaron, and he became an ancestor of both David and, through Matthew's genealogy, Jesus.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Naasson
entries.dictNote: Naasson is the Greek New Testament form of Nahshon, a prince of the tribe of Judah during Israel's wilderness wanderings and brother-in-law of Aaron through his sister Elisheba. He is listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:32).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nabal
entries.dictNote: Nabal was a wealthy but harsh landowner who rudely refused David's request for provisions after David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds and flocks, and only his wife Abigail's quick intervention with a generous gift stopped David from slaughtering Nabal's entire household in retaliation. Nabal died of what appears to be a stroke ten days after Abigail told him what he'd nearly brought on his family, and David married Abigail soon after.

entries.title: Naboth
entries.dictNote: Naboth was an Israelite who owned a vineyard next to King Ahab's palace and refused to sell it, since Israelite law protected ancestral land from being permanently sold outside the family. Queen Jezebel arranged false charges of blasphemy that got Naboth stoned to death so Ahab could seize the vineyard, a crime the prophet Elijah confronted directly, prophesying doom on Ahab's entire dynasty.

entries.title: Nachon
entries.dictNote: The owner of the threshing floor near Jerusalem where Uzzah reached out to steady the ark of the covenant and was struck dead for touching it (2 Samuel 6:6). entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nachor
entries.dictNote: Nachor is the Greek form, used in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, of the Old Testament name Nahor, grandfather of Abraham (Luke 3:34; compare Genesis 11:24-26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nadab
entries.summary: Nadab, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: At least five people in the Bible and its associated writings are called Nadab. The priest is the one most people mean: Aaron's eldest son, struck dead alongside his brother Abihu for offering unauthorized fire before the Lord. A king by the same name ruled northern Israel for two years before Baasha assassinated him and wiped out his family. A third Nadab was Saul's uncle, a fourth appears only in a genealogy of Judah as the son of Shammai, and a fifth, a relative of the Ahikar of the book of Tobit, belongs to the Second Temple literature rather than the Hebrew Bible.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Nagge
entries.dictNote: Nagge appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as an ancestor in the line through Mary, listed as the father of Esli and son of Maath (Luke 3:25). Nothing else is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahalal
entries.summary: Nahalal or Nahalol, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Nahalal was a town within the tribal territory of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) later assigned, with its pasturelands, to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 21:35). Zebulun failed to drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who instead were put to forced labor (Judges 1:30). Its exact site is uncertain, though it is sometimes linked to Tell en-Nahl near the Kishon River.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nahaliel
entries.summary: Nachaliël, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: One of the encampments of Israel during the wilderness journey, on the border of Moab, named in the travel itinerary of Numbers 21:19. Its name means "torrent" or "valley of God," and it is often identified with the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in east of the Dead Sea, an area known for hot springs.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naham
entries.dictNote: Named in a difficult genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:19 as the brother of the wife of Hodiah, in the tribe of Judah. The verse is one of the more textually obscure entries in Chronicles' genealogies, and translations vary in how they parse its relationships.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nahamani
entries.dictNote: Nahamani was one of the leaders of the Jewish community who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, named in the roster of returnees in Nehemiah 7:7. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naharai
entries.dictNote: Naharai, from Beeroth, served as armor-bearer to Joab, David's army commander, and is listed among David's mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:37; 1 Chronicles 11:39).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nahash
entries.summary: Nachash, the name of two persons apparently non-Israelite
entries.dictNote: Nahash was an Ammonite king whose brutal siege terms against Jabesh-gilead, offering peace only if he could gouge out every resident's right eye, rallied Israel behind newly anointed King Saul for his first military victory.

entries.summary: Nachath, the name of an Edomite and of two Israelites

entries.title: Nathanael
entries.summary: Nathanaël (i.e. Nathanel), an Israelite and Christian
entries.dictNote: Nathanael was one of Jesus's earliest disciples, introduced to Jesus by his friend Philip and famous for his skeptical first reaction, asking whether anything good could come out of Nazareth. Jesus won him over instantly by telling him he had seen Nathanael sitting under a fig tree before Philip ever called him, a small detail that convinced Nathanael he was looking at the Son of God. Many identify Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew, since the Synoptic Gospels never mention a Nathanael and John's Gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, and the two names always appear paired with Philip in their respective lists.

entries.title: Nathanmelech
entries.dictNote: A court official under King Josiah, associated in the account of Josiah's religious reforms with the removal of horses that earlier kings had dedicated to sun worship at the entrance to the temple (2 Kings 23:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Naum
entries.dictNote: Naum, the Greek form of Nahum, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Esli and father of Amos, one link in the chain tracing Christ's ancestry back through David to Adam (Luke 3:25). Nothing is known of him beyond his place in this list. Luke's genealogy differs substantially from Matthew's for the generations after David, most likely because the two evangelists trace descent through different sons of David, Nathan in Luke's case.

entries.title: Nazarene
entries.summary: a Nazoræan, i.e. inhabitant of Nazareth; by extension, a Christian
entries.dictNote: Nazarene marks Jesus as a native of Nazareth, the small Galilean town where he grew up, and by extension became the name for his early followers, who were known in Jerusalem as "the sect of the Nazarenes" in Acts 24:5. Matthew connects the title to Old Testament prophecy, possibly playing on the Hebrew word for "branch" used of the coming Messiah in Isaiah 11. The name is still the standard Arabic and Hebrew word for Christians today.

entries.title: Nazareth
entries.summary: Nazareth or Nazaret, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament and generally held in low regard, which is likely the force of Nathanael's question, "can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" It was the hometown of Joseph and Mary, the place of Gabriel's announcement to Mary, and where Jesus grew up and later launched his ministry, until his neighbors drove him out after he preached in the synagogue there. Its obscurity is itself part of the gospel writers' point: Israel's Messiah came from a place nobody expected.

entries.title: Neapolis
entries.summary: new town; Neapolis, a place in Macedonia
entries.dictNote: Neapolis, "new city," was the port of Philippi on the coast of Macedonia and the first place in Europe where Paul, Silas, Timothy, and Luke set foot, arriving by ship from Troas at the start of Paul's second missionary journey (Acts 16:11). From there the party took the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway linking the Adriatic to the Aegean, about ten miles inland to Philippi. Neapolis survives today as Kavala, Greece, whose harbor and hillside old town still overlook the same strait Paul's ship would have crossed.

A separate town called Nebo in Benjamin gave its name to a family among the exiles who returned with Zerubbabel.

entries.title: Nebuchadnezzar
entries.summary: The Babylonian king who besieges Jerusalem three times over a generation, the figure behind both Daniel's exile and 2 Kings' final chapters. Josephus dates his rise the same way Jeremiah does — the fourth year of Jehoiakim — and follows the same campaign against Jerusalem.
entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
entries.dictNote: Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and deported Judah's population, making him the central villain of Israel's exile even as the Bible also portrays him as an instrument God used deliberately to judge his people. The book of Daniel records his dramatic humiliation: driven mad and reduced to living like an animal in the fields for seven years after boasting about his own greatness, until he acknowledged God's sovereignty and was restored to his throne. Nebuchadnezzar's building projects, including the massive city walls and temples of Babylon, are extensively documented in his own inscriptions, which independently confirm the scale of the empire the Bible describes.

His Akkadian name, meaning roughly "Nabu, save me," reflects the standard Babylonian court practice of naming officials after the god Nabu.

entries.title: Nehemiah
entries.summary: The cupbearer-turned-governor who rebuilds Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days despite constant sabotage (Nehemiah 1-6). Josephus's chapter title pairs him directly with Ezra, the same pairing their two books share in most English Bibles.
entries.dictNote: Nehemiah was a Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who used his position of trust to get permission, funding, and safe passage to rebuild Jerusalem's ruined walls, finishing the job in just fifty-two days despite constant opposition and sabotage attempts. He went on to serve as governor of Judah, enforcing debt relief for the poor and confronting the intermarriage and Sabbath violations that had crept back into Jewish practice. Two other men named Nehemiah appear only in passing, one in the list of returning exiles and another among those who repaired a section of the wall.

She and her son were among the Judean elite deported to Babylon in 597 BC, an event corroborated by the Babylonian Chronicle, which records Nebuchadnezzar capturing Jerusalem and installing a king of his own choosing that same year.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Nereus
entries.dictNote: Nereus was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greeted by name, along with his sister, at the close of his letter to the Roman church (Romans 16:15). Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nergal
entries.dictNote: Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of war, plague, and the underworld, worshipped at the city of Cuthah; when Assyria deported Cuthites to resettle Samaria after 722 BC, they brought his cult with them into the mixed religion the transplanted population practiced there (2 Kings 17:24, 30). Mesopotamian temple records confirm his cult center at Cuthah, modern Tell Ibrahim, naming him alongside his consort Ereshkigal.

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nergal-sharezer
entries.summary: Nergal-Sharetser, the name of two Babylonians
entries.dictNote: Nergal-sharezer, named for the Babylonian god Nergal, appears among the officials of Nebuchadnezzar's army at the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and one bearing the additional title “Rab-mag” helped release Jeremiah from prison (Jeremiah 39:3, 13). Scholars generally identify this official with Neriglissar, the Babylonian general who later murdered his brother-in-law Evil-Merodach (Amel-Marduk) and reigned as king from about 560 to 556 BC. Neriglissar's short reign and violent seizure of the throne are independently confirmed by Babylonian chronicles and king lists.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Neri
entries.dictNote: Father of Shealtiel in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:27), part of the line traced through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon as in Matthew's genealogy.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Neriah
entries.dictNote: Neriah was the father of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and also of a royal official, making his family prominent in the administration of Judah's final years before Babylon's conquest.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nethaneel
entries.summary: Nethanel, the name of ten Israelites
entries.dictNote: Nethaneel was a common name in the Old Testament, borne by a tribal leader of Issachar during the wilderness census and by several priests and Levites in later generations.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Nethaniah
entries.summary: Nethanjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Nethaniah was the father of Ishmael, the royal descendant who assassinated Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after Jerusalem's fall.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Nethinims
entries.summary: the Nethinim, or Temple-servants (as given to that duty)
entries.dictNote: The Nethinim were temple servants, likely originally war captives, assigned to assist the Levites with menial temple labor, and groups of them are listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile to serve at the rebuilt temple.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Nethinims
entries.summary: The Nethinim were temple servants, likely originally war captives, assigned to assist the Levites with menial temple labor, and groups of them are listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile to serve at the rebuilt temple.
entries.dictNote: The Nethinim were temple servants, likely originally war captives, assigned to assist the Levites with menial temple labor, and groups of them are listed among those who returned from Babylonian exile to serve at the rebuilt temple.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Netophah
entries.dictNote: Town near Bethlehem in Judah. Some of its residents, called Netophathites, returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:22; Neh. 7:26), and two Netophathites served among David's elite soldiers (2 Sam. 23:28-29; 1 Chr. 27:13, 15). Its name, meaning "dripping" or "distillation," likely refers to a local spring.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Netophathite
entries.summary: a Netophathite, or inhabitant of Netophah
entries.dictNote: Netophathite marks a person as coming from Netophah, a small town near Bethlehem. Several of David's mighty men and, later, Levitical singers appointed to temple service are identified by this name in Chronicles and Ezra.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Neziah
entries.dictNote: Neziah headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:54; Nehemiah 7:56). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nezib
entries.dictNote: A town in the Shephelah lowlands of Judah (Josh. 15:43), identified with the ruin of Khirbet Beit Nasib southwest of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nibhaz
entries.summary: Nibchaz, a deity of the Avites
entries.dictNote: Nibhaz is not a person but an idol the Avite settlers brought to Samaria after the Assyrians deported them there following the fall of the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:31). Ancient tradition describes it as having the form of a dog, though little else is known of this god.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nibshan
entries.dictNote: Nibshan was one of six towns Joshua's allotment places "in the wilderness" of Judah, near the western shore of the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:61-62). It is often located near En-gedi, though no firm identification has been established.
entries.label: 1 book

He later spoke up cautiously in Jesus's defense when the council wanted to arrest him without a hearing, and after the crucifixion he helped Joseph of Arimathea bury Jesus's body, bringing a burial spice mixture heavy enough for a king.

entries.title: Nicolaitane
entries.summary: a Nicolaite, i.e. adherent of Nicolaus
entries.dictNote: The Nicolaitans were a group active in the churches of Ephesus and Pergamum in the late first century, condemned twice by Christ in the letters of Revelation for teaching or practices linked to idolatry and sexual immorality (Revelation 2:6, 15). Some early church writers connected the name to Nicolas, one of the seven men chosen to serve the Jerusalem church in Acts 6:5, though the link is disputed and little else is known of the group's actual teaching.

Later Christian writers linked his name to the Nicolaitans condemned in Revelation 2, though the New Testament itself does not connect him to that group.

entries.title: Nimrah
entries.summary: Nimrah, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Nimrah was a well-watered site east of the Jordan that the tribes of Reuben and Gad requested as pastureland for their large herds because of its suitability for cattle (Numbers 32:1-3). It is usually identified with Beth-nimrah, mentioned a few verses later as one of the towns Gad rebuilt (Numbers 32:36), and its name survives in the modern Wadi Nimrin near the Jordan.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nimrim
entries.summary: Nimrim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: The waters of Nimrim were a stream or spring-fed area in Moabite territory, cited by both Isaiah and Jeremiah in their oracles of judgment against Moab as a once-fertile place reduced to desolation (Isa. 15:6; Jer. 48:34). It is usually located southeast of the Dead Sea, in the plain of Moab proper.

entries.title: Nimrod
entries.dictNote: Nimrod was a great-grandson of Noah through Ham, described in Genesis as a mighty hunter before the Lord and the founder of a series of major Mesopotamian cities including Babel, the site of the later tower and scattered languages. His name became proverbial enough that later Old Testament writers refer to Assyria itself as the land of Nimrod.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nisroch
entries.dictNote: Nisroch was not a person but a god in the Assyrian pantheon, worshiped with the head of an eagle, in whose temple King Sennacherib of Assyria was assassinated by his own sons (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38). The god's name does not correspond cleanly to any deity known from surviving Assyrian records, and it may be a scribal corruption of another god's name such as Nusku. Sennacherib's murder itself is corroborated outside the Bible: the Babylonian Chronicle and later Assyrian records confirm he was killed by one of his own sons in a palace coup.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: No
entries.summary: No (i.e. Thebes), the capital of Upper Egypt
entries.dictNote: No, also called No-amon, is the Hebrew name for the great Egyptian city of Thebes, and the prophet Nahum cites its historical destruction as a warning to Nineveh that no city, however powerful, is beyond God's judgment.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Noadiah
entries.summary: Noadjah, the name of an Israelite, and a false prophetess
entries.dictNote: Noadiah is the name of two different figures. One was a Levite who returned from Babylon with Ezra and helped weigh out the temple treasures (Ezra 8:33). The other was a prophetess who, together with the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, tried to intimidate and discourage Nehemiah while he was rebuilding Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 6:14).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Noah
entries.summary: Noach, the patriarch of the flood
entries.dictNote: Noah was the only righteous man of his generation, chosen to build an ark and preserve his family and pairs of every kind of animal through a catastrophic flood God sent to judge human wickedness. After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah never to destroy the earth by flood again, sealed with the sign of the rainbow, and Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, became the ancestors of all the nations listed in Genesis 10.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Noah
entries.summary: Jesus cites ‘the days of Noah’ twice as the pattern for his own return (Luke 17:26–27) — the same Noah whose birth a separate, non-canonical tradition (the Book of Noah fragment preserved inside 1 Enoch) renders as something closer to a portent than an ordinary delivery.
entries.dictNote: Rest, (Heb. Noah) the grandson of Methuselah (Gen. 5:25-29), who was for two hundred and fifty years contemporary with Adam, and the son of Lamech, who was about fifty years old at the time of Adam’s death. This patriarch is rightly regarded as the connecting link between the old and the new world. He is the second great progenitor of the human family. The words of his father Lamech at his birth (Gen. 5:29) have been regarded as in a sense prophetical, designating Noah as a type of Him who is the true “rest and comfort” of men under the burden of life (Matt. 11:28). He lived five hundred years, and then there were born unto him three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Gen. 5:32). He was a “just man and perfect in his generation,” and “walked with God” (comp. Ezek. 14:14, 20). But now the descendants of Cain and of Seth began to intermarry, and then there sprang up a race distinguished for their ungodliness. Men became more and more corrupt, and God determined to sweep the earth of its wicked population (Gen. 6:7). But with Noah God entered into a covenant, with a promise of deliverance from the threatened deluge (18). He was accordingly commanded to build an ark (6:14-16) for the saving of himself and his house. An interval of one hundred and twenty years elapsed while the ark was being built (6:3), during which Noah bore constant testimony against the unbelief and wickedness of that generation (1 Pet. 3:18-20; 2 Pet. 2:5). When the ark of “gopher-wood” (mentioned only here) was at length completed according to the command of the Lord, the living creatures that were to be preserved entered into it; and then Noah and his wife and sons and daughters-in-law entered it, and the “Lord shut him in” (Gen. 7:16). The judgment-threatened now fell on the guilty world, “the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished” (2 Pet. 3:6). The ark floated on the waters for one hundred and fifty days, and then rested on the mountains of Ararat (Gen. 8:3, 4); but not for a considerable time after this was divine permission given him to leave the ark, so that he and his family were a whole year shut up within it (Gen. 6-14). On leaving the ark Noah’s first act was to erect an altar, the first of which there is any mention, and offer the sacrifices of adoring thanks and praise to God, who entered into a covenant with him, the first covenant between God and man, granting him possession of the earth by a new and special charter, which remains in force to the present time (Gen. 8:21-9:17). As a sign and witness of this covenant, the rainbow was adopted and set apart by God, as a sure pledge that never again would the earth be destroyed by a flood. But, alas! Noah after this fell into grievous sin (Gen. 9:21); and the conduct of Ham on this sad occasion led to the memorable prediction regarding his three sons and their descendants. Noah “lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years, and he died” (28:29). (See DELUGE). Noah, motion, (Heb. No’ah) one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11; Josh. 17:3).

entries.title: Nob
entries.dictNote: Nob was a city of priests near Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood during part of Samuel and Saul's era. David, fleeing from Saul, came to the priest Ahimelech there and received the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword, an act Saul's informant Doeg the Edomite reported back to the king (1 Samuel 21:1-9). In retaliation, Saul had Doeg slaughter Nob's entire priestly population, eighty-five priests along with the town's other inhabitants, one of the darkest episodes of his reign (1 Samuel 22:9-19). Isaiah later references Nob's proximity to Jerusalem in his description of an invading army's approach (Isaiah 10:32).

entries.title: Nobah
entries.summary: Nobach, the name of an Israelite, and of a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Nobah was the name a Manassite warrior gave to the Amorite town of Kenath after he captured it during Israel's advance east of the Jordan (Num. 32:42). The renamed town reappears as a landmark on the route Gideon took while pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna (Judg. 8:11), suggesting the new name endured at least into the period of the judges.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Nod
entries.dictNote: Nod, "wandering," was the land east of Eden where Cain settled after murdering his brother Abel and being driven from the ground he had farmed (Genesis 4:16). The name plays on the sentence God had just pronounced over him, that he would be "a fugitive and a wanderer" for the rest of his life (Genesis 4:12). No geographic identification is intended or possible; the name functions as commentary on Cain's condition rather than a real place on any map.

entries.title: Nodab
entries.dictNote: Nodab is not an individual but the name of a tribal group descended from Ishmael, listed in 1 Chronicles 5:19 among the peoples the trans-Jordanic tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh went to war against, along with Jetur and Naphish. The Ishmaelite tribes named there correspond broadly to Arab groups listed in Genesis 25:15. No further information about this particular clan survives outside this one battle notice.

entries.title: Nogah
entries.dictNote: Nogah was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after David became king there, listed among his children by unnamed wives (1 Chronicles 3:7; 14:6).

entries.title: Nohah
entries.dictNote: The fourth son of Benjamin listed in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:2. He does not appear in the earlier lists of Benjamin's sons in Genesis or Numbers, and nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.dictNote: Noph is the Hebrew name for the Egyptian city of Memphis, mentioned by several prophets as a city that would share in Egypt's coming judgment.

entries.title: Nophah
entries.dictNote: A Moabite town captured by the Amorite king Sihon and mentioned in an ancient victory song quoted in Numbers 21:27-30, celebrating Sihon's conquest of Moabite territory before Israel in turn defeated Sihon.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Nymphas
entries.dictNote: A believer, probably in or near Laodicea, whose house served as a meeting place for a local church, greeted by Paul in Colossians 4:15. Ancient manuscripts differ on whether the name is masculine, Nymphas, or feminine, Nympha, a point still debated by textual critics.

entries.summary: Obadjah, the name of thirteen Israelites
entries.books: 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Obadiah

entries.dictNote: Obal was a son of Joktan listed in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:28, one of thirteen sons whose descendants populated Arabia. entries.summary: Obed-Edom, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Obed-edom was a Levite in whose house the ark of the covenant stayed for three months after Uzzah's death, and rather than bringing disaster the way it had for the Philistines, the ark brought blessing to Obed-edom's entire household, encouraging David to finally bring it the rest of the way to Jerusalem.

entries.summary: Oboth, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Oboth was a wilderness campsite of the Israelites, the first stop after they left the site where Moses raised the bronze serpent to heal those bitten by venomous snakes (Numbers 21:9-10; 33:43-44). Its precise location along the route east of Edom is unknown.

entries.title: Ocran
entries.dictNote: Ocran was the father of the tribal leader of Asher during the wilderness census.

entries.title: Oded
entries.summary: Oded, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Oded was the father of the prophet Azariah, who encouraged King Asa's religious reforms, and a different Oded was a prophet who successfully persuaded northern Israel's army to release Judean captives taken in battle rather than enslave them.

entries.title: Og
entries.books: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Kings, Nehemiah, Psalm
entries.dictNote: Og was the king of Bashan, remembered in Deuteronomy as the last of the Rephaim, a race of giants, with a bed reportedly over thirteen feet long. Israel defeated him and took his entire kingdom without losing a man, and his conquest became a standing example, repeated throughout the Old Testament, of God's power to defeat overwhelming odds.

entries.title: Ohel
entries.dictNote: Ohel was one of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the returning exiles and rebuilt the Jerusalem temple, listed among his children in 1 Chronicles 3:20. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Olivet
entries.summary: an olive-orchard, i.e. (specially) the Mount of Olives
entries.dictNote: Olivet, or the Mount of Olives, is the ridge east of Jerusalem where Jesus taught his disciples privately about the future, wept over the city, prayed the night of his arrest in the garden of Gethsemane at its base, and ascended into heaven after his resurrection.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Olympas
entries.dictNote: Olympas was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greets by name at the close of his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:15). Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Omar
entries.dictNote: Omar was a grandson of Esau and an Edomite clan chief listed in Genesis's genealogies.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Omega
entries.summary: the last letter of the Greek alphabet, i.e. (figuratively) the finality
entries.dictNote: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, paired with Alpha, the first letter, in the divine self-description “I am Alpha and Omega,” found three times in Revelation (1:8; 21:6; 22:13). The phrase functions as a title, not a name, declaring God, and in 22:13 Christ, as the beginning and end of all things, encompassing everything in between. The imagery draws on a common ancient rhetorical device of using the first and last letters of an alphabet to signify totality.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Omri
entries.dictNote: Omri was a military commander who seized the throne of northern Israel after a civil war and founded a dynasty significant enough that Assyrian records refer to Israel as the House of Omri for generations after his death, even though the Bible itself gives his reign only a brief summary, noting mainly that he built the city of Samaria as his new capital and did more evil than all who were before him.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: On
entries.dictNote: On was a major Egyptian city on the east bank of the Nile near modern Cairo, the center of Egyptian sun worship and known to the Greeks as Heliopolis. Joseph married Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On (Genesis 41:45, 50; 46:20), tying Egypt's highest religious office to Joseph's own household. A granite obelisk raised by the pharaoh Senusret I still stands at the site today, the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt and one of the few visible remains of the ancient temple complex.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: On
entries.dictNote: A Reubenite, son of Peleth, named as one of the men who joined Dathan and Abiram in the rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1). He disappears from the story immediately after this verse; Jewish tradition holds that his wife talked him out of taking part before judgment fell on the rest of the conspirators, though the biblical text itself says nothing more about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Onam
entries.summary: Onam, the name of an Edomite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Onam was a Horite clan name in Edom's genealogies and also the name of a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel's line.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Onan
entries.dictNote: Onan was Judah's second son, and when custom required him to father a child with his deceased brother's widow Tamar to preserve his brother's line, he deliberately avoided completing the act, a refusal God put him to death for.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Onesimus
entries.dictNote: Onesimus was a runaway slave who ended up with Paul during one of Paul's imprisonments and became a Christian there, and Paul sent him back to his owner Philemon along with a personal letter, tactfully asking Philemon to receive Onesimus back not as a slave but as a beloved brother.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Onespiphorus
entries.dictNote: This entry's name appears to be a misspelling of Onesiphorus in the source data; the person intended is Onesiphorus, a believer from Ephesus who sought Paul out and ministered to him during Paul's Roman imprisonment, unashamed of his chains (2 Timothy 1:16-18). Paul later sends greetings to Onesiphorus's household and recalls his service at Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:19).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ono
entries.dictNote: Ono was a town of Benjamin in a fertile plain northwest of Jerusalem, resettled by returning exiles (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 11:35). Nehemiah's enemies Sanballat and Tobiah tried four times to lure him to a meeting in the plain of Ono, intending to harm him while he rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, but he refused each invitation (Nehemiah 6:2-4).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ophel
entries.dictNote: The Ophel was a fortified section of Jerusalem between the temple mount and the city of David, and Nehemiah records temple servants living there during the wall-rebuilding project.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ophir
entries.summary: Ophir, the name of a son of Joktan, and of a gold region in the East
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah
entries.dictNote: Ophir was a region, likely in southern Arabia or along the Red Sea, famed throughout the ancient world for its fine gold. Solomon's ships, sailing in partnership with Hiram of Tyre, brought back large quantities of gold, precious stones, and rare wood from Ophir, and later biblical poetry uses "gold of Ophir" as shorthand for the finest wealth imaginable. The name also belonged to a son of Joktan in the table of nations, likely the ancestor of a people associated with the region.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Ophni
entries.summary: an Ophnite (collectively) or inhabitants of Ophen
entries.dictNote: Ophni is not actually a clan or people group but a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Joshua 18:24 alongside Geba and other Benjaminite settlements north of Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain, though some identify it with the later village of Gophna mentioned by Josephus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ophrah
entries.summary: Ophrah, the name of an Israelite and of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ophrah was Gideon's hometown, where the angel of the Lord first appeared to him and where he later set up a golden ephod that became, ironically, an object of idolatrous worship for Israel.

witness.excerpt: And when Gideon was come to his own countrey of Ophrah, he slew the Kings of the Midianites.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Oreb
entries.summary: Oreb, the name of a Midianite and of the cliff near the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Oreb was one of two Midianite commanders killed by the men of Ephraim during Gideon's rout of the Midianite army, and the rock where he died was afterward named for him.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Oren
entries.dictNote: Oren was one of the sons of Jerahmeel, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:25. Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ornan
entries.dictNote: Ornan, also called Araunah, was the Jebusite who owned the threshing floor David purchased to build an altar and stop a plague, a site that later became the location of Solomon's temple. Ornan offered to give David the land for free, but David insisted on paying full price, unwilling to offer God a sacrifice that cost him nothing.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Orpah
entries.dictNote: Orpah was a Moabite woman married to Chilion, one of Naomi's sons, and sister-in-law to Ruth. When Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem after her husband and sons died, Orpah wept and, after Naomi's urging, chose to stay in Moab with her own people, unlike Ruth who famously clung to Naomi (Ruth 1:4-14).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Osee
entries.dictNote: Osee is the Greek form of the prophet Hosea's name as it appears in the King James rendering of Romans 9:25, where Paul quotes Hosea's prophecy that God would call a people not his own "my people." The reference points to the same eighth-century BC prophet known from the book of Hosea, not a separate individual.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Othni
entries.dictNote: Son of Shemaiah, a temple gatekeeper of notable ability during David's reign (1 Chronicles 26:6-7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Othniel
entries.dictNote: Othniel was Caleb's younger relative, who won Caleb's daughter Achsah in marriage by capturing a Canaanite city, and he later became Israel's first judge, delivering the nation from eight years of oppression under a Mesopotamian king.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Ozem
entries.summary: Otsem, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name. One was David's older brother, the sixth of Jesse's sons (1 Chronicles 2:15). The other belonged to a different branch of Judah's genealogy, a son of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:25).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ozias
entries.dictNote: Ozias is the Greek New Testament spelling of Uzziah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8-9), where he is listed as the son of Joram and ancestor of Christ. In the Old Testament, Uzziah reigned as king of Judah for over fifty years and was struck with leprosy after presumptuously burning incense in the temple, a priestly duty reserved for Aaron's line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ozni
entries.summary: Ozni, an Israelite; also an Oznite (collectively), his descendant
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad and ancestor of the Oznite clan counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:16). The earlier genealogy in Genesis 46:16 gives his name as Ezbon.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paarai
entries.dictNote: Paarai the Arbite was one of David's thirty mighty men, listed among the elite warriors in 2 Samuel 23:35. The parallel roster in 1 Chronicles 11:37 gives his name as Naarai son of Ezbai, one of several small spelling differences between the two lists of David's champions. Beyond his inclusion in this honor roll, nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Padan
entries.summary: Paddan or Paddan-Aram, a region of Syria
entries.dictNote: Padan is a shortened form of Paddan-aram, the region of upper Mesopotamia around Haran where Abraham's brother Nahor settled. It was from Paddan-aram that Isaac's wife Rebekah came, and Jacob fled there to escape Esau's anger, working for his uncle Laban and marrying Leah and Rachel before returning to Canaan with his large family.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Padon
entries.dictNote: Padon headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pagiel
entries.dictNote: Pagiel was the tribal leader of Asher during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pahathmoab
entries.dictNote: Pahath-moab was the name of a prominent family among the returning exiles, large enough to be listed by household in both Ezra and Nehemiah's records.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pai
entries.summary: Pau or Pai, a place in Edom
entries.dictNote: Pai, also spelled Pau, was the royal city of Hadar, also called Hadad, the last king listed in the genealogy of Edom's early rulers before Israel had a monarchy of its own (Gen. 36:39; 1 Chr. 1:50). Its location within Edom is not otherwise specified in the text and has not been identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Palal
entries.dictNote: A son of Uzai who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, rebuilding the section opposite the corner and the tower projecting from the upper palace near the court of the guard (Nehemiah 3:25). He is one of dozens of otherwise unknown Jerusalemites Nehemiah names by the stretch of wall each repaired.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Palestina
entries.dictNote: Palestina is the King James rendering of the Hebrew word for Philistia, the coastal territory of the Philistines along the southeastern Mediterranean. The term became attached to the wider region over the following centuries and is the ultimate source of the modern name Palestine, though in its Old Testament occurrences it refers specifically to Philistine land, which the prophets warn will share in judgment alongside Israel's other neighbors.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Pallu
entries.dictNote: Pallu was a son of Reuben, and his descendants, the Palluites, are listed among the clans counted in Israel's wilderness census.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Palluites
entries.summary: a Palluite (collectively) or descendants of Pallu
entries.dictNote: Palluites were the clan descended from Pallu, a son of Reuben, counted in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Palti
entries.summary: Palti, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Palti was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, representing the tribe of Benjamin (Numbers 13:9). A different man named Palti, son of Laish, was the husband Saul gave Michal after David fled the court; when David later reclaimed her as his wife, Palti followed her weeping until Abner ordered him back home (1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:14-16).

witness.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Paltiel
entries.summary: Paltiel, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Paltiel appear in the Old Testament: the prince of the tribe of Issachar appointed to help divide the promised land among the tribes (Numbers 34:26), and Paltiel son of Laish, to whom King Saul gave his daughter Michal after taking her from David; when Abner later returned Michal to David, Paltiel followed her weeping until Abner ordered him home (2 Samuel 3:15-16). The two references belong to entirely different periods and are unrelated apart from the shared name, also written “Palti” in 1 Samuel 25:44.

witness.excerpt: So Abner took Michal from Phaltiel, who was then her husband, and sent her to David, Ishbosheth himself affording him his assistance, for David had written to him that of right he ought to have this his wife restored to him.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Paltite
entries.summary: a Paltite or descendant of Palti
entries.dictNote: Paltite identifies Helez, one of David's thirty mighty men, as being from Beth-pelet in Judah's Negev. The parallel list in Chronicles calls him the Pelonite instead, likely a variant spelling of the same epithet.

It was here that John Mark left the mission and turned back to Jerusalem, a decision that later caused Paul and Barnabas to part ways (Acts 15:38).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pannag
entries.dictNote: Pannag is not a person but a term for a trade commodity listed among the goods Judah and Israel exchanged with Tyre in Ezekiel's oracle against that city (Ezekiel 27:17), alongside wheat, honey, oil, and balm. Its exact meaning is uncertain: some take it as a type of confection or pastry, others as the name of a place whose products carried that name, similar to how other goods in the list are identified by their region of origin. The word appears only this once in the Hebrew Bible, which is part of why its meaning remains disputed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paphos
entries.dictNote: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus and residence of its governor when Paul and Barnabas visited during their first missionary journey and confronted the sorcerer Elymas before the proconsul Sergius Paulus (Acts 13:6-13). An inscription found on Cyprus names a proconsul Paulus in office around the same period Luke describes, corroborating the office and roughly the timeframe Acts assigns to Sergius Paulus's governorship.

entries.title: Parah
entries.dictNote: Parah, meaning heifer, was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh. 18:23). It is commonly identified with the ruins at Ain Fara, about six miles northeast of Jerusalem in the Wadi Qelt watershed, a spring-fed site still bearing a version of the ancient name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paran
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Habakkuk
entries.dictNote: Paran was a wilderness region in the Sinai peninsula where Israel camped during part of their wilderness wandering, and where Ishmael later settled and grew up after being sent away with Hagar.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Parbar
entries.summary: Parbar or Parvar, a quarter of Jerusalem
entries.dictNote: Parbar is not a person but a structure or precinct on the west side of the temple complex, apparently a colonnade or open court, mentioned in connection with gatekeepers assigned there (1 Chronicles 26:18) and possibly the same area where wicked King Manasseh had placed horses dedicated to the sun (2 Kings 23:11).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Parmasta
entries.dictNote: Parmashta was one of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa in self-defense on the day appointed for their destruction (Esther 9:9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parmenas
entries.dictNote: One of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, freeing the apostles to focus on prayer and preaching (Acts 6:5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parnach
entries.dictNote: Parnach was the father of Elizaphan, the leader from the tribe of Zebulun appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:25). He is mentioned only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parosh
entries.summary: Parosh, the name of our Israelite
entries.dictNote: Parosh was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, prominent enough to be listed first among the lay families in Ezra's genealogical record.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Parshandatha
entries.dictNote: The eldest of Haman's ten sons, killed by the Jews of Susa along with his brothers when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned (Esther 9:7-10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parthian
entries.summary: a Parthian, i.e. inhabitant of Parthia
entries.dictNote: Parthians were Jews of the diaspora living within the Parthian empire, Rome's great eastern rival centered in Persia and Mesopotamia, and they are named first among the many nationalities gathered in Jerusalem to hear the apostles speak in their own languages at Pentecost.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paruah
entries.dictNote: Paruah was the father of Jehoshaphat, one of the twelve officers Solomon appointed over Israel's administrative districts to supply provisions for the royal court, with Jehoshaphat's district covering Issachar (1 Kings 4:17). He is mentioned only to identify his son.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Parvaim
entries.dictNote: A region of uncertain location from which Solomon obtained gold for overlaying the temple (2 Chronicles 3:6). Suggested locations range from Arabia to India, and some scholars think the word may simply be a general term for "eastern lands" rather than a specific place name, similar to the uncertainty surrounding the gold-source Ophir elsewhere in the Old Testament.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pas-dammim
entries.dictNote: Pas-dammim, called Ephes-dammim in 1 Samuel 17:1, lay between Socoh and Azekah in the Valley of Elah, the same district where David killed Goliath. In 1 Chronicles 11:13 it is the site where Eleazar son of Dodo held his ground against the Philistines when the rest of Israel's army fled, one of the feats that earned him a place among David's three mightiest warriors.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pasach
entries.dictNote: A son of Japhlet in the tribal genealogy of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:33). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paseah
entries.summary: Paseach, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Paseah was the head of a family among the temple servants who returned from Babylonian exile.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pashur
entries.summary: Pashchur, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Pashur was a temple official who had the prophet Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks overnight for his prophecies of coming judgment, and Jeremiah responded the next day by renaming him Magor-missabib, meaning terror on every side, and predicting Pashur would die in exile in Babylon.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Patara
entries.summary: Patara, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Patara was a major port city on the Lycian coast of southwestern Asia Minor where Paul changed ships on his way back from his third missionary journey, boarding a larger vessel bound across the open sea for Phoenicia (Acts 21:1). Excavations at the site have uncovered an extensive Roman city, including a lighthouse built under Nero in the first century AD, among the oldest lighthouses known from the ancient world.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pathros
entries.dictNote: Pathros refers to Upper Egypt, and the prophets mention it as one of the regions Jewish refugees fled to and where God promised a future regathering of his exiled people.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pathrusim
entries.summary: a Pathrusite, or inhabitant of Pathros
entries.dictNote: Pathrusim were a people descended from Mizraim named for Pathros, the region of Upper Egypt along the Nile south of Memphis. Later prophets name Pathros among the places Israelites were scattered to, and where God promises to eventually regather his exiled people.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Patmos
entries.summary: Patmus, an islet in the Mediterranean
entries.dictNote: A small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, part of the Sporades group off the coast of Asia Minor, where the apostle John was in exile when he received the visions recorded in the book of Revelation (Revelation 1:9). Roman authorities used islands like Patmos as places of banishment, and John says he was there "for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ." The island still bears the name Patmos today, and a cave traditionally associated with John's vision remains a pilgrimage site.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Patrobas
entries.dictNote: A Christian in Rome to whom Paul sends greetings, grouped with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, and Hermas near the close of his letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:14). Nothing further about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Paul
entries.summary: (little; but remotely from a derivative of G3973 (παύω), meaning the same); Paulus, the name of a Roman and of an apostle
entries.books: Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, 2 Peter
entries.dictNote: Paul was born Saul, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Roman citizen from Tarsus, trained as a Pharisee under the respected teacher Gamaliel and an active persecutor of the early church until a blinding vision of the risen Christ on the road to Damascus turned him into its most influential missionary. He planted churches across the eastern Mediterranean on three long journeys, wrote roughly half the New Testament in letters to those churches, and was eventually imprisoned and executed in Rome. A Roman inscription found at Delphi naming the proconsul Gallio fixes the date of Paul's time in Corinth precisely enough that it anchors the chronology of his entire ministry.

entries.label: 15 books

entries.title: Pavement
entries.summary: stone-strewed, i.e. a tessellated mosaic on which the Roman tribunal was placed
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an elevated, stone-paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem, called Gabbatha in Aramaic, where Roman governors set up the judgment seat to hear cases in public (John 19:13). It was here that Pilate presented Jesus to the crowd and formally handed him over for crucifixion. Its precise location within ancient Jerusalem has not been conclusively identified, though several sites near the Temple Mount have been proposed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pedahel
entries.dictNote: Pedahel son of Ammihud was the prince of the tribe of Naphtali whom Moses appointed to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:28). His name means "God has redeemed." Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pedahzur
entries.dictNote: Pedahzur was the father of the tribal leader of Manasseh during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pedaiah
entries.summary: Pedajah, the name of six Israelites
entries.dictNote: Pedaiah was a common postexilic and royal name, borne by Zerubbabel's uncle and by several officials involved in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pekah
entries.dictNote: Pekah seized the throne of northern Israel by assassinating his predecessor and allied with Syria against Assyria, an alliance that included invading Judah and trying to force King Ahaz into joining them. Assyria's king Tiglath-pileser the Third responded by conquering large parts of Israel's territory and deporting the population, a devastating blow from which the northern kingdom never recovered, and Pekah himself was assassinated soon after by his successor.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pekahiah
entries.dictNote: Pekahiah was a king of northern Israel who reigned only two years before his own military officer Pekah assassinated him and seized the throne.

witness.excerpt: How Zachariah , Shallum , Menahem , Pekahiah , and Pekah took the government over the Israelites ; and how Pul , and Tiglath-Pileser made an expedition against the Israelites .

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pekod
entries.summary: Pekod, a symbolic name for Babylon
entries.dictNote: Pekod is not a person but a tribal or regional name in southern Babylonia, corresponding to the Puqudu people known from Assyrian and Babylonian records. Jeremiah and Ezekiel both invoke it in judgment oracles against Babylon, likely playing on its similarity to the Hebrew word for “punishment” (Jeremiah 50:21; Ezekiel 23:23).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pelaiah
entries.summary: Pelajah, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Pelaiah's name means “the LORD has distinguished.” One man of this name appears in the royal genealogy as a descendant of David after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:24). A second Pelaiah was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:7) and later signed Nehemiah's covenant (Nehemiah 10:10).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pelaliah
entries.dictNote: Pelaliah was a priest named in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:12). He appears only in this list of returned priestly families.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pelatiah
entries.summary: Pelatjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Pelatiah was a corrupt official Ezekiel saw in a vision advising Jerusalem's leaders toward false security, and he dropped dead during the vision itself, a shock that made Ezekiel cry out in fear for the rest of the people.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Peleg
entries.dictNote: Peleg was a descendant of Shem, and Genesis notes that in his days the earth was divided, generally understood as a reference to the scattering of languages and peoples at Babel occurring around his lifetime.

entries.title: Pelet
entries.summary: Pelet, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Pelet appear in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles: a descendant of Judah through Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and a Benjamite warrior, skilled with bow and sling, who joined David's growing band of fighters at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:2-3). The two belong to different tribes and are unrelated.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peleth
entries.summary: Peleth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Peleth appear in the Old Testament: a Reubenite whose son On joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1), and a son of Jonathan in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:33). The two belong to different tribes and different eras and are otherwise unrelated.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Pelethites
entries.dictNote: Pelethites, always mentioned alongside the Cherethites, formed part of David's personal bodyguard under the command of Benaiah. Their foreign sounding names suggest they were mercenaries of Philistine or Aegean background rather than native Israelites, which made them useful as troops loyal to the king rather than to any Israelite tribe.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pelonite
entries.summary: a Pelonite or inhabitant of an unknown Palon
entries.dictNote: Pelonite marks two of David's mighty men, Helez and Ahijah, whose exact place of origin is unclear; some scholars think the word is simply a variant spelling of "Paltite."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peniel
entries.summary: Penuel or Peniel, a place East of Jordan; also (as Penuel) the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Peniel, also spelled Penuel, was the place near the Jabbok River where Jacob wrestled through the night with a mysterious figure identified as God, emerging with a new name, Israel, and a permanent limp. Jacob named the place "face of God" because, he said, he had seen God face to face and survived. The town there was later destroyed by Gideon for refusing to aid his pursuit of Midian, and Jeroboam I fortified it after Israel's kingdom split.

witness.excerpt: He also built him another at Penuel, a city so called.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Peninnah
entries.dictNote: Peninnah was one of Elkanah's two wives and the mother of several children, while his other wife, Hannah, remained childless for years (1 Samuel 1:2). Peninnah taunted Hannah over her barrenness, provoking the grief that led Hannah to pray for a son at Shiloh, a prayer answered with the birth of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:4-7).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Peor
entries.summary: Peör, a mountain East of Jordan; Baal Peor, (for a deity worshipped there
entries.dictNote: Peor was a mountain peak in Moab from which Balak brought Balaam for one last attempt to curse Israel, only to hear him pronounce a blessing instead, including the famous prophecy of a star and a scepter rising out of Israel (Numbers 23:28; 24:2-17). The name is also attached to a local Moabite and Midianite deity worshiped there, known as Baal-peor, whose fertility rites drew Israelite men into idolatry and immorality at Shittim, provoking a plague that killed twenty-four thousand people (Numbers 25:1-9).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Perazim
entries.dictNote: Mount Perazim appears once, in Isaiah 28:21, where the prophet warns that the Lord will rise against his own people as unexpectedly as he once rose against the Philistines there. That earlier victory is almost certainly the battle of Baal-perazim, where David broke through the Philistine lines in the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem and named the site "the Lord who breaks through" (2 Samuel 5:20). Isaiah's point is that God's coming judgment on Judah will feel just as sudden and decisive, an alien work compared to his usual saving acts.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peresh
entries.dictNote: A son of Machir by his wife Maachah, listed in the genealogy of Manasseh alongside his brother Sheresh (1 Chronicles 7:16). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Perez
entries.summary: Perets, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Perez was Judah's son by Tamar, born pushing ahead of his twin brother Zerah in a delivery marked by a scarlet thread meant to identify the true firstborn, and Perez's line runs directly through Boaz to David and, in Matthew's genealogy, to Jesus.

Judah and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Shela, and Perez, and Zerah--four.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Perezuzza
entries.dictNote: Perez-uzzah, meaning the breach of Uzzah, was the name David gave to the threshing floor where Uzzah was struck dead for touching the ark of the covenant to steady it during its transport toward Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6:6-8; 1 Chr. 13:9-11). The episode led David to leave the ark at the house of Obed-edom for three months before resuming the journey.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Perga
entries.summary: a tower; Perga, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Capital of Pamphylia on Asia Minor's southern coast, on the Cestrus River a few miles inland from the sea. Paul and Barnabas landed there on their first missionary journey, and it was from Perga that John Mark turned back and returned to Jerusalem, a decision that later caused Paul and Barnabas to part ways (Acts 13:13; 15:36-39). Paul preached there again on his way home (Acts 14:25). Excavations at the site, now called Perge in Turkey, have uncovered a Hellenistic city gate, a large Roman theater and stadium, and a temple to Artemis of Perga, confirming its importance as a regional center in Paul's day.

witness.excerpt: 72, 73): Alexander removed from Phaselis, he sent some part his army over the mountains to Perga; which road the Thracians showed him.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pergamos
entries.summary: fortified; Pergamus, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Capital of the Roman province of Asia, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation, commended for holding fast to Christ's name even where Revelation calls "Satan's seat," likely a reference to the city's massive altar to Zeus or its role as a center of emperor worship (Rev. 2:12-17). Its acropolis library was famed in antiquity as second only to Alexandria's, and the city gave its name to parchment, pergamene, a writing material its scribes are credited with popularizing after Egypt restricted papyrus exports.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Perida
entries.summary: Peruda or Perida, one of 'Solomon's servants'
entries.dictNote: Perida, also spelled Peruda, headed a family of servants of Solomon whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Perizzite
entries.summary: a Perizzite, one of the Canaanitish tribes
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah
entries.dictNote: Perizzites are listed among the peoples inhabiting Canaan before Israel's conquest, almost always paired with the Canaanites in the recurring phrase describing the land's population. Unlike most of the other named peoples, they are not listed among Canaan's sons in Genesis 10, and their name may simply describe village or open country dwellers rather than a single ethnic clan.

entries.title: Persia
entries.summary: Paras (i.e. Persia), an Eastern country, including its inhabitants
entries.dictNote: Persia was the empire that conquered Babylon under Cyrus and, in a major policy shift from earlier empires, allowed the exiled Jews to return home and rebuild their temple, a decree preserved in the book of Ezra and independently corroborated by the Cyrus Cylinder.

entries.title: Persis
entries.summary: a Persian woman; Persis, a Christian female
entries.dictNote: Persis was a Christian woman at Rome whom Paul greets in Romans 16:12, describing her as "beloved" and noting that she "labored much in the Lord," language he uses elsewhere for active ministry rather than mere friendship. She is one of several women Paul names by name and commends for their work in that closing chapter.

entries.title: Peter
entries.summary: a (piece of) rock (larger than G3037 (λίθος)); as a name, Petrus, an apostle
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Galatians, 1 Peter, 2 Peter
entries.dictNote: Peter was a Galilean fisherman named Simon before Jesus renamed him Cephas, or Peter, meaning rock, and he became the most prominent of the twelve apostles, the first to confess Jesus as the Messiah and the one Jesus promised to build his church on. He also denied knowing Jesus three times the night of the crucifixion, exactly as Jesus had predicted, and was restored to leadership afterward in a pointed three-part exchange on the shore of Galilee. Peter preached the first Christian sermon at Pentecost, took the gospel to the first Gentile convert, and tradition holds he was crucified in Rome under Nero, upside down at his own request because he considered himself unworthy to die the same way as Jesus.

entries.title: Pethakiah
entries.summary: Pethachjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Pethahiah was a common postexilic name, including the head of one of the priestly divisions and a Levite who helped lead public confession and prayer after Ezra's reading of the law.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pethor
entries.dictNote: Pethor was the hometown of Balaam, the diviner hired by Balak of Moab to curse Israel, located by the Euphrates river in northern Mesopotamia (Deut. 23:5; Num. 22:5). It is generally identified with Pitru, a town on the Sajur river near Carchemish known from Assyrian royal inscriptions, and Balaam himself is independently attested outside the Bible in a plaster inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan naming Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods, dated to roughly the eighth century BC.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pethuel
entries.dictNote: Pethuel was the father of the prophet Joel, named in the opening verse of the book of Joel (Joel 1:1). Nothing else about him is known, and even the dating of Joel's ministry remains uncertain among scholars.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Peulthai
entries.dictNote: Peulthai was one of the sons of Obed-edom, a family of Levite gatekeepers noted in 1 Chronicles 26:5 as particularly capable men. His father's household had been blessed after the ark of the covenant rested there for three months under David (2 Samuel 6:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Phalec
entries.dictNote: Phalec is the Greek form of Peleg, an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:35). Genesis 10:25 explains the Hebrew name's meaning, 'division,' noting that in Peleg's days the earth was divided, generally understood as a reference to the dispersal of peoples after Babel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Phanuel
entries.dictNote: The father of Anna, the elderly prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus in the Jerusalem temple (Luke 2:36). Nothing else is recorded about him; he is named only to establish his daughter's lineage from the tribe of Asher.

entries.title: Pharaoh
entries.summary: Paroh, a general title of Egyptian kings
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Acts, Romans, Hebrews
entries.dictNote: Pharaoh is the Egyptian royal title used throughout the Old Testament for a series of different, usually unnamed, kings, not one individual, spanning from the pharaoh who made Joseph second-in-command to the pharaoh who enslaved the Israelites centuries later and the pharaoh Moses confronted during the exodus. Egyptian records independently confirm many of the events and periods these unnamed pharaohs presided over, even though Egyptian royal inscriptions, understandably, never record embarrassing defeats like the exodus plagues.

entries.title: Pharaoh-hophra
entries.dictNote: Pharaoh Hophra, known to history as Apries, ruled Egypt from about 589 to 570 BC and briefly supported King Zedekiah of Judah's revolt against Babylon before withdrawing, leaving Jerusalem to fall in 586 BC. Jeremiah predicted that Hophra, like Zedekiah, would be handed over to his enemies (Jeremiah 44:30); Egyptian records confirm he was overthrown in a civil war led by his general Amasis and later killed, a case where a specific biblical prophecy about a named foreign king's downfall is corroborated by that king's own country's records.

entries.title: Phares
entries.dictNote: Phares is the Greek form of Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogies of both Matthew (1:3) and Luke (3:33). He was the son of Judah and Tamar, born in the unusual circumstances recounted in Genesis 38, and became the founder of one of Judah's leading clans; Boaz and eventually David descended from him (Ruth 4:18-22). His prominent place in two independent genealogies of Jesus underlines how central the Judah-Tamar line was reckoned in Israel's royal ancestry.

entries.title: Philippi

Paul, guided there by a vision of a Macedonian man, planted the first Christian church on European soil in the city, converting the merchant Lydia and casting a spirit of divination out of a slave girl before he and Silas were beaten and imprisoned (Acts 16:9-40). Archaeologists have excavated its well-preserved forum and theater, along with a prison traditionally associated with Paul's imprisonment, and Paul later wrote his letter to the Philippians to the congregation he founded there.

entries.dictNote: The Philistines were a seafaring people who settled the coastal plain between Gezer and Gaza, most likely arriving from Caphtor, which the Old Testament elsewhere identifies as Crete. Unlike Israel's other neighbors, they never had a single king; five cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, each answered to its own lord, and together those cities gave Israel its most persistent military rival from the judges through the united monarchy. Excavations at Gezer, Lachish, and Ashkelon, along with the Amarna Letters, confirm a settled population in this same region going back to the time of Moses and Joshua, and Egyptian temple reliefs from a century later show the Philistines arriving as part of the larger wave the Egyptians called the Sea Peoples.

entries.title: Phygellus
entries.dictNote: Phygellus was a Christian in the Roman province of Asia named by Paul as one who turned away from him during his final imprisonment in Rome, alongside a man named Hermogenes (2 Tim. 1:15). entries.title: Pi-beseth
entries.dictNote: Pi-beseth, called Bubastis by the Greeks, was an Egyptian city in the eastern Nile Delta and the center of worship for the cat goddess Bastet. Ezekiel 30:17 pairs it with On (Heliopolis) in a prophecy that its young men would fall by the sword and the city go into captivity, part of a broader oracle against Egypt. Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, described Bubastis's annual festival as the most popular in all Egypt, and the site, now called Tell Basta, has been excavated since the nineteenth century, uncovering the remains of Bastet's temple that he described.

entries.title: Pi-hahiroth
entries.dictNote: Pi-hahiroth was the campsite in Egypt where the Israelites, having doubled back from Etham, made camp beside the sea with Pharaoh's pursuing army closing in behind them (Exodus 14:1-9). It was there that Moses stretched out his hand and God parted the sea, letting Israel cross on dry ground before the waters closed over the pursuing Egyptian chariots (Exodus 14:21-28). Its exact location is disputed, since shifting Nile sediment has reshaped the Isthmus of Suez considerably since ancient times.

entries.title: Pilate
entries.summary: Luke's trial narrative (23:1-25) shows a Pilate who tries three times to release Jesus. Josephus's Pilate — who sneaks Caesar's images into Jerusalem by night and later slaughters Samaritans, the incident that gets him recalled to Rome — is a harder, more provocative administrator, the reputation Luke's crowd would have already known him by. Philo tells a separate incident — gilded shields in Herod's old palace, no images, just an inscription — that Tiberius himself ordered taken down after Jewish protest, a second, independent witness to the same abrasive governorship.
entries.books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, 1 Timothy
entries.dictNote: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who presided over Jesus's trial and, despite declaring three times that he found no guilt in Jesus, gave in to pressure from the crowd and religious leaders and had him crucified, a decision he tried to distance himself from by publicly washing his hands. A limestone block found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961, inscribed with Pilate's name and title, is the only archaeological confirmation of his existence outside literary sources, and it settled a long debate over his exact Roman rank.
