entries.title: Piltai
entries.dictNote: Piltai was head of the priestly family of Moadiah in the days of the high priest Joiakim, in the generation after the return from Babylonian exile, as recorded in the priestly and Levitical family lists of Nehemiah 12. Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Pinon
entries.dictNote: Pinon appears among the chiefs, or 'dukes,' of Edom in the genealogical lists of Genesis 36:41 and 1 Chronicles 1:52, where each name marks the head of a clan or territory. Many scholars think Pinon is the same as Punon, an Edomite way station named in Numbers 33:42-43, associated with the copper mining region of Feinan in the Jordan valley, where archaeologists have uncovered extensive ancient smelting sites.

entries.title: Piram
entries.dictNote: The Amorite king of Jarmuth, one of five Canaanite kings who besieged Gibeon and were defeated by Joshua in the battle remembered for the sun standing still (Josh. 10:3, 23). He was captured with his allies hiding in a cave at Makkedah and put to death.

entries.title: Pirathon
entries.dictNote: Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim, home to Abdon, one of the minor judges of Israel, who was buried there (Judges 12:13-15). It also gave its name to Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:30), and is generally identified with the modern village of Far'ata, about six miles southwest of Shechem.

entries.title: Pirathonite
entries.summary: a Pirathonite or inhabitant of Pirathon
entries.dictNote: Pirathonite names two separate figures in the Bible from the town of Pirathon in Ephraim. The first is Abdon son of Hillel, a minor judge who led Israel for eight years and is remembered mainly for his many sons and grandsons who rode donkeys in Judges 12. The second is Benaiah, one of David's thirty elite warriors, distinct from the better known Benaiah son of Jehoiada who commanded David's bodyguard.

entries.title: Pisgah
entries.summary: Pisgah, a Mountain East of Jordan
entries.dictNote: Pisgah was a mountain ridge in Moab, part of the range known as Abarim, from which Balak brought Balaam to view and curse Israel's camp, and from whose summit Moses looked out over the promised land before his death. Its height, Mount Nebo, is usually identified with modern Jebel Siyagha near the northeastern shore of the Dead Sea.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Pisidia
entries.summary: Pisidia, a region of Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Pisidia was a rugged district of Asia Minor north of Pamphylia, crossed by the Taurus mountains, that Paul and Barnabas passed through on their first missionary journey, preaching at Antioch of Pisidia on both the outward and return legs (Acts 13:14; 14:24). Excavations at Pisidian Antioch uncovered dozens of fragments of a Latin copy of the Res Gestae, Augustus's own account of his achievements, inscribed near the city's monumental gate, evidence of how thoroughly Rome had absorbed the district by Paul's time.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pison
entries.dictNote: Pishon was one of four rivers said to branch from the river watering the garden of Eden, described as encircling the land of Havilah, a region rich in gold, bdellium, and onyx (Genesis 2:11-12). Its location has never been convincingly fixed; proposals over the centuries have ranged from the Nile to rivers in Arabia and India, including a now-vanished paleochannel across northern Arabia detected in satellite radar imagery, but none commands consensus. Genesis pairs it with the Tigris and Euphrates, both real and identifiable rivers, which is part of why the search for the other two continues rather than being dismissed outright.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pispah
entries.dictNote: A son of Jether, listed among the leading warriors and family heads of the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:38-40). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Pithom
entries.dictNote: One of the store-cities the Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh in Egypt before the exodus (Exodus 1:11), its name deriving from the Egyptian "Per-Atum," house of the sun-god Atum. Excavations by Édouard Naville in 1883 at Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat uncovered large storage-chamber remains and brickwork consistent with the biblical account, though some Egyptologists now argue the site lay instead a little further west, at Tell er-Retabeh; either way, the identification rests on real excavated store-city ruins in the eastern Nile Delta.

entries.dictNote: Roman province along the southern coast of the Black Sea in northern Asia Minor. Jews from Pontus were present in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Peter addressed part of his first letter to believers scattered across the province (1 Pet. 1:1); Paul's coworker Aquila was a native of Pontus (Acts 18:2). The region had earlier been the heartland of King Mithridates VI, whose decades-long wars against Rome in the first century BC are extensively documented in Greek and Roman historical sources.

entries.title: Priscilla
entries.summary: Priscilla (i.e. little Prisca), a Christian woman
entries.dictNote: Priscilla, usually named alongside her husband Aquila, was a tentmaker and early Christian leader who hosted a church in her home and helped Paul in his ministry across several cities. She and Aquila together took the eloquent but incompletely taught preacher Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately, and Paul consistently names her, unusually for the period, before her husband.

entries.summary: before the dance; Prochorus, a Christian
entries.dictNote: One of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, freeing the apostles to focus on prayer and teaching (Acts 6:5). He is named third, right after Stephen and Philip, the two best known of the seven.

entries.title: Ptolemais
entries.dictNote: Ptolemais was the Greek name given to the ancient port city of Acco after one of the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt took control of the Syrian coast, and it is the name Luke uses for the stop where Paul greeted the local believers on his final journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7). Excavations at Tel Akko, the older mound east of the modern city, and at Hellenistic-era harbor works on the coast have traced the site's occupation back to the early Bronze Age and confirmed it as one of the largest ports on the Levantine coast in the Hellenistic period.

entries.title: Punon
entries.summary: Punon, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Punon was a wilderness station on Israel's route, between Zalmonah and Oboth (Num. 33:42-43). It is identified with Phaeno, mentioned by early Christian writers as a site of Roman-era copper mines, and modern excavations at Khirbet Feinan in southern Jordan have confirmed intensive copper mining and smelting there going back millennia before the Roman period, making it one of the largest ancient metal-production sites in the region.

entries.summary: Ramah, the name of a grandson of Ham, and of a place (perhaps founded by him)
entries.dictNote: Raamah was a son of Cush and, through his sons Sheba and Dedan, the ancestor of Arabian trading peoples (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). Ezekiel lists Raamah's merchants among those who supplied Tyre with spices, precious stones, and gold (Ezekiel 27:22). Most scholars connect the name to a city called Ragmatum known from South Arabian inscriptions in the old Sabaean kingdom of Yemen, matching the trading-nation identity the Bible gives it.

entries.title: Raamses
entries.summary: Rameses or Raamses, a place in Egypt
entries.dictNote: Raamses, also spelled Rameses, was one of the store cities the enslaved Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh in the eastern Nile Delta, alongside Pithom (Exodus 1:11). It also served as Israel's staging point at the start of the exodus, from which the people set out toward Succoth (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:3, 5). Most scholars identify the site with Pi-Ramesse, the Delta capital built by Ramesses II, whose extensive remains, including monumental gateways and colossal statuary, have been excavated at Qantir.

entries.title: Raca
entries.summary: O empty one, i.e. thou worthless (as a term of utter vilification)

entries.title: Rahab
entries.dictNote: Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who hid the two Israelite spies Joshua sent ahead of the conquest, and in exchange for her help and her declared faith in Israel's God she and her family were spared when the city fell. She went on to marry into Israel and became an ancestor of David and, through Matthew's genealogy, of Jesus himself, one of only a handful of women named there. The New Testament holds her up twice as an example of faith demonstrated through action.

entries.title: Rahab
entries.dictNote: This Greek form “Rhaab” refers to Rahab, the Canaanite woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies and was spared when the city fell (Joshua 2, 6). The New Testament cites her twice as an example of faith expressed through action: Hebrews 11:31 credits her rescue to faith, and James 2:25 points to her sheltering of the spies as proof that faith without works is dead. She later married Salmon and became an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), one of only a few women named in that genealogy.

entries.summary: Rama (i.e. Ramah), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Rama is the Greek form of Ramah, used in Matthew's Gospel to quote Jeremiah's image of Rachel weeping for her children, a passage Matthew applies to Herod's slaughter of the infant boys of Bethlehem (Matt. 2:18). entries.title: Ramoth-gilead
entries.summary: Ramoth-Gilad, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Ramoth-gilead was a city of refuge east of the Jordan in Gad's territory, strategically important enough to be repeatedly fought over between Israel and Aram. Ahab died there after being wounded while trying to retake it with Jehoshaphat's help, and it was there, years later, that Jehu was anointed king by one of Elisha's disciples while the army was stationed on the frontier. Its exact site is disputed among several candidates on the northern Gilead plateau.

Most of this entry's other references belong instead to a different but related word, the household of the Rechabites in Jeremiah 35, the clan descended from Jonadab son of Rechab who kept their ancestor's vow to live in tents, drink no wine, and avoid settled farming. entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Reeliah
entries.dictNote: Reeliah is listed among the leaders of the Jewish exiles who returned to Judah from Babylon under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:2). The parallel roster of leaders in Nehemiah 7:7 gives a slightly different set of names, a minor variation common between the two overlapping return lists.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Regem
entries.dictNote: Regem was a son of Jahdai, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah through the line of Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:47). Nothing more is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Regem-melech
entries.dictNote: Regem-melech was one of two men, along with Sherezer, sent by the Jewish community at Bethel to Jerusalem in the fourth year of Darius to ask the priests and prophets whether the fasts commemorating the temple's destruction should continue now that the exile had ended (Zechariah 7:2). The question sparked the series of oracles that follow in Zechariah 7 and 8. Nothing else is known of him beyond this diplomatic mission.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehabiah
entries.dictNote: Rehabiah was a descendant of Moses through his son Eliezer, and his own descendants multiplied greatly according to the genealogical note in Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rehob
entries.summary: Rechob, the name of a place in Syria, also of a Syrian and an Israelite
entries.books: Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah
entries.dictNote: Rehob names both places and people in the Old Testament. Beth-rehob was a town in the far north near Dan that marked the limit of the spies' reconnaissance of Canaan and gave its name to a small Aramean kingdom that fought alongside Ammon against David. Two other towns called Rehob belonged to Asher, one assigned to the Levites; a third Asherite town of the name was never fully cleared of its Canaanite inhabitants. The name also belonged to the father of Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah whom David defeated, and to a leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant after the exile.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Rehoboam
entries.dictNote: Rehoboam was Solomon's son and successor, and his reign began with a catastrophic miscalculation: when the northern tribes asked him to lighten the heavy labor Solomon had imposed, he rejected his older advisors' counsel and threatened even harsher treatment, provoking ten of Israel's twelve tribes to break away and form a separate kingdom under Jeroboam. The kingdom he was left with, Judah, was invaded a few years later by the Egyptian pharaoh Shishak, who stripped the temple of its treasures, an episode Shishak also recorded on his own temple wall at Karnak in Egypt.

He also dedicated to God at Jerusalem the golden quivers, the entire armor which the guards of Hadad used to wear; which Shishak, the king of Egypt, took away when he fought with David's grandson, Rehoboam, with a great deal of other wealth which he carried out of Jerusalem.

However, he dwelt in Jerusalem two years, and became the father of three sons, and one daughter; which daughter was of very great beauty, and which Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, took to wife afterward, and had by her a son named Abijah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Rehoboth
entries.summary: Rechoboth, a place in Assyria and one in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Rehoboth, meaning "broad places" or "open spaces," names at least three different locations in the Old Testament. Isaac's servants dug a well by that name in the Negev after two earlier wells provoked disputes with local herdsmen, this one finally left uncontested (Genesis 26:22). A city called "Rehoboth by the river" is listed among the descendants of Esau as the home of an Edomite king (Genesis 36:37; 1 Chronicles 1:48), likely on the Euphrates. Genesis 10:11 also names Rehoboth-Ir among the cities built in Assyria, though many translators instead render the phrase as simply the "city squares" or open spaces of Nineveh rather than a separate place name.

witness.excerpt: At length the King gave him leave to dig a well, without disturbance: he named this well Rehoboth ; which denotes a large space .

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rehum
entries.summary: Rechum, the name of a Persian and of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Rehum was a common postexilic name, borne by a Persian official who wrote a letter opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem and by several Levites and returning exiles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rei
entries.dictNote: One of the men who remained loyal to David and refused to join Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne near the end of David's reign, named alongside Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah in 1 Kings 1:8.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rekem
entries.summary: Rekem, the name of a place in Palestine, also of a Midianite and an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Rekem is a name shared by a place and several men in the Old Testament. It names a town in Benjamin (Joshua 18:27) as well as one of the five Midianite kings killed by Israel in the days of Moses (Numbers 31:8; Joshua 13:21), a son of Hebron in Caleb's line (1 Chronicles 2:43-44), and a descendant of Manasseh through Gilead (1 Chronicles 7:16).

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Remaliah
entries.dictNote: Remaliah was the father of Pekah, a king of northern Israel, and appears in Isaiah's prophecies mainly in the phrase son of Remaliah, used somewhat dismissively to refer to Pekah during his war against Judah.

witness.excerpt: Who followed the barbarity of his father, and so ruled but two years only: after which he was slain with his friends at a feast, by the treachery of one Pekah , the General of his horse, and the son of Remaliah, who laid snares for him.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Remeth
entries.dictNote: Remeth was a town of Issachar named in Joshua's allotment list (Joshua 19:21). It is probably the same town listed elsewhere as Ramoth (1 Chronicles 6:73) and Jarmuth (Joshua 21:29), Levitical cities assigned to the Gershonite clan, the name apparently shifting between these related forms in different texts. Its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Remmon
entries.summary: Rimmon, the name of a Syrian deity, also of five places in Palestine
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Rimmon was the storm god of Aram-Damascus, and the Aramean commander Naaman, after being healed of leprosy by Elisha, asked forgiveness in advance for the times he would still have to bow in Rimmon's temple while assisting his king.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Remphan
entries.dictNote: Remphan is not a person but a pagan star god, likely an alternate name for Saturn or the deity elsewhere called Chiun, whom Stephen accused Israel of worshipping in the wilderness (Acts 7:43, quoting Amos 5:26). Stephen's speech follows the Greek Septuagint's rendering "Rephan" for the Hebrew "Kiyyun" in Amos.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephael
entries.dictNote: Rephael was one of the sons of Shemaiah, a Korahite gatekeeper of the temple, and was noted along with his brothers for their "strength for service" among the divisions of temple gatekeepers David organized (1 Chronicles 26:6-8). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephah
entries.dictNote: A son of Ephraim listed in the tribal genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7, an ancestor in the line that eventually leads down to Joshua son of Nun several generations later. Nothing else is recorded of him beyond his place in this list.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rephaiah
entries.summary: Rephajah, the name of five Israelites
entries.dictNote: Rephaiah was a common name, borne by a descendant of David in the royal genealogy and by a leader who helped repair a section of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rephidim
entries.summary: Rephidim, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Rephidim was a wilderness campsite of the Israelites near Sinai where the people, desperate for water, nearly stoned Moses before he struck the rock at Horeb and water flowed out for them (Exodus 17:1-7). It was also the site of Israel's first battle, a victory over Amalek won as long as Moses held up his hands, supported by Aaron and Hur (Exodus 17:8-13).

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Resen
entries.dictNote: Resen was one of the cities Nimrod is said to have built in Assyria, located between the great cities of Nineveh and Calah (Gen. 10:12). Some read the verse as implying that these separate settlements eventually grew together into the larger city later known simply as Nineveh, though Resen's precise site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Resheph
entries.dictNote: Resheph was a son of Ephraim, listed in the tribal genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:25. His name is shared with a Canaanite deity associated with plague and war, though nothing suggests any connection beyond the shared word. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Reu
entries.dictNote: Reu was a descendant of Shem and an ancestor of Abraham, listed in the genealogy connecting Noah's family to the patriarchs.

Reuben did try, unsuccessfully, to save Joseph's life when his other brothers wanted to kill him, secretly planning to rescue Joseph later, and his tribe eventually settled east of the Jordan River rather than in the heart of Canaan.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Reumah
entries.dictNote: The concubine of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and mother of four sons named in the brief genealogical note of Genesis 22:24: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah. The verse rounds out the family record Genesis provides for Nahor's household alongside his principal wife Milcah's eight sons, one of whom, Bethuel, becomes the father of Rebekah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rezeph
entries.dictNote: Rezeph was an Assyrian-controlled town cited by Sennacherib's field commander as proof of Assyrian military might, one of the places its gods could not save (2 Kings 19:12; Isaiah 37:12). It is usually identified with Rasappa, a city on the middle Euphrates that Assyrian records name as the seat of its own provincial governor from the ninth century BC onward, confirming the biblical picture of a well-established administrative center under Assyrian control.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Rezia
entries.dictNote: An Asherite descendant of Ulla, listed among the heads of families in the tribal record of 1 Chronicles 7:39.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rezin
entries.summary: Retsin, the name of a Syrian and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Rezin was the king of Aram-Damascus who allied with Pekah of Israel against Judah, an alliance so threatening it prompted King Ahaz's fateful decision to seek Assyrian protection instead of trusting Isaiah's assurance that the threat would fail.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Rezon
entries.dictNote: Rezon son of Eliadah was a former officer of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, who fled after David's victory over his master and gathered a band of raiders that eventually seized Damascus and made him king of Syria (1 Kings 11:23-25). He became a persistent adversary to Solomon throughout his reign, one of several troubles God raised up against Solomon for his unfaithfulness, and his kingdom in Damascus remained a rival power to Israel for generations afterward.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rhegium
entries.dictNote: A port city at the southern tip of Italy on the Strait of Messina, modern Reggio Calabria, where Paul's ship stopped briefly on the final leg of his voyage to Rome (Acts 28:13).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rhesa
entries.dictNote: Listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a son of Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27). Some scholars think "Rhesa" preserves not a separate son's name but the Aramaic title "resh," meaning "prince" or "head," attached to Zerubbabel in a source Luke used, which would mean the name does not belong to a distinct individual at all.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rhoda
entries.dictNote: Rhoda was a servant girl in the Jerusalem house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where believers had gathered to pray for Peter's release from prison. When Peter appeared at the gate after his angelic escape, she was so overjoyed that she ran to tell the others without opening the door, and they at first refused to believe her (Acts 12:13-15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rhodes
entries.summary: Rhodus, an island of the Mediterranean
entries.dictNote: Rhodes is not a person but a large island off the southwest coast of Asia Minor, famous in antiquity for the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and for its naval power in the Hellenistic period. Paul's ship stopped there briefly on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ribai
entries.dictNote: Ribai was a Benjamite from Gibeah, the father of Ittai, one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:29; 1 Chronicles 11:31). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Riblah
entries.dictNote: Riblah was a town on the east bank of the Orontes River in the land of Hamath, at a strategic crossroads between Egypt, Palestine, and Babylon. It served twice as a wartime headquarters, first for Pharaoh Necho after his victory over Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:33), then for Nebuchadnezzar during his final siege of Jerusalem, where the Judean king Zedekiah was brought to be blinded after watching his sons executed (2 Kings 25:6-7; Jeremiah 39:5-6; 52:9-11). Its ruins survive at the modern village of Ribleh in Syria.

witness.excerpt: For he abode himself in the city of Riblah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Rimmon-parez
entries.summary: Rimmon-Perets, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Wilderness campsite of Israel between Rithmah and Libnah, named only in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:19-20). Nothing further is recorded of it, and its location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rinnah
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah listed among the sons of Shimon in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:20. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Riphath
entries.summary: Riphath, a grandson of Japheth and his descendants
entries.dictNote: The second son of Gomer in the Table of Nations, grandson of Japheth (Genesis 10:3). Ancient interpreters connected his descendants with peoples of northern Asia Minor, possibly the Paphlagonians, but the identification is uncertain and the name otherwise disappears from the biblical record.

witness.excerpt: So did Riphath found the Ripheans, now called Paphlagonians; and Thrugramma, the Thrugrammeans, who, as the Greeks resolved, were named Phrygians.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rissah
entries.summary: Rissah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Rissah was a stopping place in Israel's wilderness itinerary, between Libnah and Kehelathah (Num. 33:21-22). Its name may mean ruin or dew, but nothing beyond its place in the list has been preserved about it.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rithmah
entries.summary: Rithmah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Rithmah was one of the stations where Israel camped during the wilderness wanderings, listed in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:18-19). Its name comes from the Hebrew word for the broom shrub common in the desert, and the site is generally placed in the vicinity of Kadesh-barnea, though its precise location is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rizpah
entries.dictNote: Rizpah was one of Saul's concubines, and after David handed over seven of Saul's descendants to be executed to end a famine, Rizpah kept a lonely vigil over their exposed bodies for months, driving off birds and animals by day and night until David finally arranged a proper burial, a grief so striking it moved David to action.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Roboam
entries.dictNote: Roboam is the Greek form, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, of Rehoboam, Solomon's son who succeeded him as king and under whom the kingdom split in two (Matthew 1:7; compare 1 Kings 12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rogelim
entries.summary: Rogelim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Rogelim was a town in Gilead, the home of Barzillai, the elderly and wealthy man who supplied David's camp during Absalom's revolt and later declined the king's invitation to move to Jerusalem, sending his servant Chimham in his place (2 Samuel 17:27; 19:31-40). It probably lay near Mahanaim, though its precise site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Rohgah
entries.dictNote: Rohgah was an Asherite, one of the sons of Shamer (also called Shomer) listed in the tribal genealogy of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:30-40. The chapter identifies this branch of Asher's descendants as mighty men of valor and heads of their fathers' houses. Nothing beyond this genealogical listing is recorded of him.

entries.title: Romamti-ezer
entries.dictNote: Romamti-ezer was a son of Heman, David's seer, and was set apart along with his brothers for the ministry of music in the temple. He headed the twenty-fourth of the twenty-four courses assigned to lead worship by casting lots (1 Chronicles 25:4, 31).

entries.dictNote: Rome was the capital of the empire that ruled Judea throughout the New Testament period, and Paul's letter to the Roman church and his eventual voyage there as a prisoner, appealing his case to Caesar, close out the book of Acts.

entries.title: Rosh
entries.summary: Rosh, the name of an Israelite and of a foreign nation
entries.dictNote: Rosh was one of the sons of Benjamin listed among those who went to Egypt with Jacob in Genesis 46:21, though he does not appear in the later, more detailed genealogies of Benjamin's line in Numbers 26 or 1 Chronicles 7-8. The word rosh also occurs in Ezekiel 38:2-3, where it is usually translated "chief," an unrelated term rather than a reference to this same figure or, as older commentators once speculated, to Russia.

witness.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

entries.title: Rufus
entries.dictNote: Rufus was the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha; Mark names him alongside his brother Alexander as someone his original readers would recognize (Mark 15:21). Paul later greets a Rufus in Rome and calls his mother a mother to him as well, which many take to be the same family, since Mark's Gospel is traditionally linked to the Roman church (Romans 16:13).

entries.title: Rumah
entries.dictNote: Rumah appears in the hill-country town lists of Judah (Josh. 15:52) and, in a different context, as the hometown of Pedaiah, whose daughter Zebudah was the mother of King Jehoiakim of Judah (2 Kings 23:36). Its location is uncertain; some link it to Arumah near Shechem, mentioned in the days of the judges, while others place it farther north in Galilee.

witness.excerpt: Now Jehoiakim’s mother was called Zebudah , of the city Rumah.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ruth
entries.dictNote: Ruth was a Moabite woman who chose to stay with her Israelite mother-in-law Naomi after both their husbands died, famously declaring "where you go I will go" rather than return to her own people. In Bethlehem she married Naomi's relative Boaz through the ancient custom of levirate redemption, and their son Obed became the grandfather of David, making a foreign widow one of the four women named in Jesus's genealogy in Matthew.

entries.title: Sabean
entries.summary: a Sebaite, or inhabitant of Seba
entries.dictNote: Sabeans here are the wealthy traders of Sheba in southern Arabia, named in Isaiah 45:14 among the nations whose wealth will one day come to acknowledge Israel's God. Sheba's caravan trade in spices and gold is well attested, and inscriptions from the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Saba, in modern Yemen, confirm its wealth and prominence in the ancient incense trade.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sabean
entries.summary: a Shebaite or descendant of Sheba
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a demonym for the people of Sheba, the trading kingdom of south Arabia known through the Bible for gold, spices, and long-distance caravan trade. Joel's oracle of judgment (Joel 4:8; Joel 3:8 in most English Bibles) names them as the distant buyers to whom Judah's own captors will one day be sold, a reversal-of-fortune image rather than a reference to any individual. The historical Sabean kingdom, centered in what is now Yemen, is independently attested by its own large corpus of South Arabian inscriptions.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sabta
entries.summary: Sabta or Sabtah, the name of a son of Cush, and the country occupied by his posterity
entries.dictNote: Sabta, also spelled Sabtah, was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham, and became the eponymous ancestor of a people grouped with other early tribes of Arabia or northeast Africa (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sabtecha
entries.summary: Sabteca, the name of a son of Cush, and the region settled by him
entries.dictNote: Sabtecha appears in the table of nations as the fifth son of Cush, grouped with Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, and Raamah among the peoples descended from Ham (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). As with his brothers' names, Sabtecha almost certainly designates a tribal group and its territory rather than one man, generally placed somewhere in southern Arabia or the adjacent African coast, though its exact location has never been fixed.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sacar
entries.summary: Sakar, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men carry this name among David's fighting men. One was the father of Ahiam, listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:35). The other was a Korahite gatekeeper of the temple, a son of Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:4).

entries.title: Sadducee
entries.summary: a Sadducæan (i.e. Tsadokian), or follower of a certain heretical Israelite
entries.dictNote: The Sadducees were a Jewish religious and political party drawn mainly from the priestly aristocracy, distinguished from the Pharisees by their rejection of oral tradition, their denial of bodily resurrection, and their closer cooperation with Roman authority, and Jesus directly challenged their denial of resurrection using an argument from the Torah they themselves accepted.

entries.title: Sadoc
entries.dictNote: Listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of descent between Zerubbabel's family and Joseph (Matt. 1:14). Nothing further about him is recorded in scripture.

entries.title: Sala
entries.dictNote: Sala, also spelled Shelah, appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Arphaxad and ancestor of Abraham, matching the postdiluvian Shelah of Genesis 11:12-15 and 1 Chronicles 1:18, 24.

entries.title: Salamis
entries.dictNote: Salamis was a major port city on the eastern coast of Cyprus, the first stop for Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey, where they preached in the Jewish synagogues of the city (Acts 13:5). Extensive Roman-era ruins have been excavated at the site, including a large gymnasium, a theater, and a forum, testifying to the city's importance in the period of Paul's visit.

entries.title: Salathiel
entries.dictNote: Salathiel, also called Shealtiel, was the son of the exiled king Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) and the father, or in some genealogical lines the uncle, of Zerubbabel, who led the return from Babylonian exile. He appears in both genealogies of Jesus, in Matthew through David's royal line and in Luke through Nathan (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27).

entries.title: Salcah
entries.summary: Salcah, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Salcah was a city of Bashan on the eastern edge of Israelite settlement, assigned to the half tribe of Manasseh after Og, king of Bashan, was defeated (Deuteronomy 3:10; Joshua 12:5; 13:11). It marked the furthest eastern boundary of Israelite territory in several biblical descriptions. It is identified with modern Salkhad in southern Syria, a town built around a prominent volcanic hill still crowned by a medieval citadel.

entries.title: Salim
entries.dictNote: A place near Aenon, west of the Jordan, where John the Baptist was baptizing because water was plentiful there (John 3:23). Its exact location is debated among scholars; some place it in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean, others further south near ancient Shechem.

entries.title: Sallai
entries.summary: Sallu or Sallai, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Sallai was a common postexilic name among the returning exiles and priestly families listed in Nehemiah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Salma
entries.summary: Salma, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Salma, also spelled Salmon, was the son of Nahshon, a leader of the tribe of Judah, and the father of Boaz through his marriage to Rahab of Jericho, according to the genealogies in Ruth 4:20-21 and Matthew 1:5. Chronicles also remembers him as the ancestor, or founding patriarch, of Bethlehem and several related Judahite clans (1 Chronicles 2:11, 51, 54). Through Boaz and Ruth, his line runs directly to David and, in Matthew's genealogy, to Jesus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Salmon
entries.dictNote: Salmon appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Boaz by Rahab, the Canaanite woman who sheltered Israel's spies at Jericho (Matthew 1:4-5). He is the same man the book of Ruth calls Salmon or Salma, an ancestor of David through the line that runs from Judah's son Perez down to Jesse (Ruth 4:20-21).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Salmon
entries.dictNote: Son of Nahshon, the leader of Judah's tribe under Moses, Salmon married Rahab of Jericho and became the father of Boaz, placing him in the ancestral line of David and, through Matthew's genealogy, of Jesus (Ruth 4:20-21; Matthew 1:4-5). He also appears as Salma in the fuller Chronicles genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:11, 51).

entries.title: Salmon
entries.dictNote: A Hebrew strong-number variant tied to the same verse pair as the entry above; refers to the same man, son of Nahshon, father of Boaz by Rahab, and ancestor of David and of Jesus through Matthew's genealogy (Ruth 4:20-21; Matthew 1:4-5).

entries.title: Salmone
entries.dictNote: A cape at the eastern tip of Crete, rounded by the ship carrying Paul toward Rome after it ran into contrary winds (Acts 27:7). It is generally identified with the modern Cape Sidero.

entries.title: Salome
entries.dictNote: Salome was the wife of Zebedee and mother of the apostles James and John. She followed Jesus and ministered to him in Galilee, stood among the women watching the crucifixion, and came to the tomb on the first day of the week with spices to anoint his body, becoming one of the first witnesses of the empty tomb (Mark 15:40; 16:1; compare Matthew 27:56).

entries.title: Samaria
entries.books: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Micah
entries.dictNote: Samaria was built by Omri, king of Israel, on a hill purchased from a man named Shemer, becoming the northern kingdom's capital in place of Tirzah. Ahab and later kings ruled from its fortified summit, and the city withstood two Syrian sieges before finally falling to Assyria after a three year siege under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II in 722 BC, when much of its population was deported. Excavations there uncovered a cache of inscribed potsherds, the Samaria Ostraca, recording shipments of wine and oil to the royal court and preserving personal names that match the biblical record. Herod the Great later rebuilt the city and renamed it Sebaste in honor of Augustus; in the New Testament, Philip preached there after the persecution that followed Stephen's death.

entries.title: Samaria
entries.summary: Samaria (i.e. Shomeron), a city and region of Palestine
entries.dictNote: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, built by King Omri on a hill he purchased and named after its former owner Shemer. It withstood repeated Syrian sieges under Ahab and Jehoram before finally falling to Assyria after a three-year siege under Shalmaneser and Sargon II, who deported much of its population. By New Testament times the surrounding region gave its name to the Samaritans, and Philip's preaching there in Acts 8 marked one of the first expansions of the gospel beyond Judea. Excavations at the site uncovered hundreds of carved ivory furniture inlays dated to Ahab's era, matching Amos's condemnation of Samaria's "houses of ivory."

entries.dictNote: This Aramaic spelling of Samaria appears in the Aramaic-language section of Ezra, in a letter that officials based in the city sent to the Persian king opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:10, 17). It refers to the same city that served as capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, built by Omri and later captured by Assyria, and here shows Samaria functioning as the administrative center of the Persian province governing the region after the exile.

entries.dictNote: Samaritans were the mixed population that settled the territory of the former northern kingdom after the Assyrians deported most of Israel's population in 722 BC and resettled the land with people from Babylon, Cuthah, and other conquered regions. Over time these settlers blended Yahweh worship with their own traditions, and by the postexilic period the returning Jews rejected their claim to a share in rebuilding the Jerusalem temple, a rift that hardened into the open hostility reflected in Jesus' encounter with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4 and the parable of the good Samaritan. The Samaritans built their own temple on Mount Gerizim, and archaeological excavation there has uncovered its remains along with a large fortified precinct; a small Samaritan community, numbering several hundred, still lives near Mount Gerizim and in Holon, Israel, preserving its own version of the Pentateuch.

entries.title: Samothracia
entries.summary: Samo-thrace (Samos of Thrace), an island in the Mediterranean
entries.dictNote: Samothracia was not a person but a mountainous island in the northern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Thrace, whose height made it a landmark and overnight anchorage for ships crossing to Europe. Paul's ship stopped there on the voyage from Troas to Neapolis at the start of his first mission on the European mainland (Acts 16:11).

entries.title: Samson
entries.dictNote: Samson was a judge set apart from birth as a Nazirite, forbidden to cut his hair or drink wine, and he possessed superhuman strength as long as he kept that vow, using it to kill a lion barehanded, slaughter Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, and carry off the gates of a city on his shoulders. His fatal weakness was Philistine women, and Delilah, bribed by Philistine rulers, wore him down until he revealed that his strength was tied to his uncut hair; once shaved, he was captured, blinded, and enslaved. In his final act, Samson prayed for strength one last time and pulled down the pillars of a Philistine temple, killing more people in his death than in his entire life.

entries.title: Samuel
entries.summary: The last judge and the prophet who anoints both of Israel's first two kings (1 Samuel 1:20). Josephus picks up his story as a general leading Israel against the Philistines — prophet and military leader in one, the same combination that makes his later confrontations with Saul so charged.
entries.books: Numbers, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Jeremiah, Acts, Hebrews
entries.dictNote: Samuel was the last of Israel's judges and its first great prophet, born to Elkanah and Hannah after Hannah prayed for a son and dedicated him to the Lord's service before he was even conceived. He anointed Israel's first two kings, Saul and then David, and spent his final years as the nation's conscience, rebuking Saul for disobedience so sharply that the two men never met again. He had two sons of his own, Joel and Abijah, whose corruption as judges is what pushed Israel to demand a king in the first place.

entries.title: Saraph
entries.dictNote: Saraph is listed among the descendants of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:22, in a genealogy that also notes some of these men once ruled in Moab, a detail otherwise unexplained. Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sardis
entries.summary: Sardis, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Sardis was the wealthy capital of ancient Lydia in western Asia Minor, famous in earlier centuries as the seat of King Croesus and a center of gold refining. It received one of the seven letters in Revelation, rebuked for having a reputation for life while being spiritually dead (Revelation 3:1-6). Decades of excavation at the site have uncovered one of the largest ancient synagogues known and a massive temple of Artemis, confirming the city's real prominence in the Roman period.

entries.title: Sarepta
entries.summary: Sarepta (i.e. Tsarephath), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Sarepta is the Greek form of Zarephath, the Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon where the prophet Elijah lodged with a widow during a famine, miraculously sustaining her flour and oil and later restoring her son to life (1 Kings 17:9-24). Jesus cites the episode in his synagogue sermon at Nazareth as an example of God's mercy extended to a Gentile outsider when many widows in Israel were passed over, a comparison that provoked his hometown to try to kill him (Luke 4:25-29).

witness.excerpt: Now the famine had seized upon the whole country, and there was a great want of what was necessary for sustenance, insomuch that it was after the recovery of the widow's son of Sarepta, God sent not only men that wanted it, but the earth itself also, which did not produce enough for the horse and the other beasts of what was useful for them to feed on, by reason of the drought.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sargon
entries.dictNote: Sargon II seized the Assyrian throne after Shalmaneser V's death around 722 BC and completed the conquest of Samaria, deporting the northern kingdom's population, as his own royal annals from his palace at Khorsabad record. He is named directly in the Bible only once, in connection with his general's siege of Ashdod (Isaiah 20:1), and he later drove the Babylonian rebel Merodach-baladan out of Babylon before being killed by one of his own soldiers and succeeded by his son Sennacherib. For years scholars doubted a king named Sargon had even existed, since he appeared nowhere outside Isaiah 20:1; the nineteenth-century excavation of his inscriptions at Khorsabad confirmed both his reign and his Samaria campaign.

entries.title: Sarid
entries.dictNote: Boundary landmark of the tribe of Zebulun, lying west of Chisloth-tabor (Josh. 19:10, 12). Its exact site is unidentified, though several ruins in the eastern Jezreel valley have been proposed.

entries.title: Saron
entries.summary: Saron (i.e. Sharon), a district of Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Greek form of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain of Israel stretching between Joppa and Mount Carmel. Luke uses it in Acts 9:35 to describe the region around Lydda whose residents turned to the Lord after seeing the paralyzed Aeneas healed by Peter.

entries.title: Sarsechim
entries.dictNote: One of the Babylonian officials present at the fall of Jerusalem, listed among the officers who sat in the middle gate at Nebuchadnezzar's order after the city's walls were breached (Jeremiah 39:3).

witness.excerpt: The names of these generals who ravaged and subdued Jerusalem, if any one desire to know them, were these; Nergal Sharezer, Samgar Nebo, Rabsaris, Sarsechim, and Rabmag.

entries.title: Saruch
entries.dictNote: Saruch is the Greek form, used in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, of the Old Testament name Serug, the son of Reu and an ancestor of Abraham (Luke 3:35; compare Genesis 11:20-23).

entries.dictNote: Satan, meaning adversary, appears in the Old Testament as a heavenly figure who challenges Job's righteousness before God and accuses the high priest Joshua before the angel of the Lord in Zechariah. The New Testament identifies him more fully as the tempter who tested Jesus in the wilderness, the ruler of this present evil age, and the ultimate enemy of God's people, and Revelation describes his final defeat and eternal judgment.

entries.title: Saul
entries.summary: Israel's first king, introduced in 1 Samuel 9:2 as tall and striking. Josephus opens his own account the same way Scripture does — through his father Kish's lost donkeys, the errand that puts Saul in Samuel's path in the first place.
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah
entries.dictNote: Saul was Israel's first king, chosen almost by accident while searching for his father's lost donkeys and anointed privately by Samuel before Israel's assembled tribes confirmed him publicly. He started well, rallying Israel against the Ammonites and the Philistines, but lost God's favor through repeated disobedience, most decisively when he offered a sacrifice he had no right to offer and later spared an enemy king God had ordered destroyed. His last three decades were consumed by a jealous pursuit of David, the shepherd Samuel had already anointed to replace him, and he died by his own sword on Mount Gilboa after a defeat by the Philistines. An earlier king of Edom, generations before Israel had any king at all, carried the same name.

entries.title: Sceva
entries.dictNote: A Jew at Ephesus called a "chief priest," probably meaning he held high standing among the local Jewish community rather than an actual Jerusalem office, since no high priest of that name appears in contemporary records (Acts 19:13-16). His seven sons tried to imitate Paul's exorcisms by invoking the name of Jesus over a demon-possessed man, and the spirit turned on them instead, an episode Luke uses to contrast magical formulas with real apostolic authority.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Scythian
entries.summary: a Scythene or Scythian, i.e. (by implication) a savage
entries.dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for the nomadic peoples who inhabited the steppes north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, proverbial in the ancient world as distant and uncivilized outsiders. Paul uses the term in Colossians 3:11 to list categories erased by unity in Christ, alongside Greek, Jew, barbarian, slave, and free, making the point that the gospel's reach extends even to peoples considered furthest outside civilized society.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seba
entries.summary: Seba, a son of Cush, and the country settled by him
entries.dictNote: Seba was a son of Cush, and his descendants are associated with a distant African or Arabian kingdom mentioned in the Psalms alongside Sheba as bringing tribute to Israel's king.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Sebat
entries.dictNote: Sebat, also spelled Shevat, was the eleventh month of the Hebrew religious calendar, falling roughly in January and February. Zechariah dates one of his night visions to the twenty-fourth day of this month, in the second year of the Persian king Darius (Zechariah 1:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Secacah
entries.dictNote: One of six towns assigned to Judah in the wilderness district along the western shore of the Dead Sea, grouped with Beth-arabah, Middin, and En-gedi (Josh. 15:61-62). Its precise site is unidentified, though it lay in the general vicinity later occupied by the Qumran community.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sechu
entries.dictNote: A place between Gibeah and Ramah known for its "great well," where Saul asked after Samuel and David while hunting for David (1 Samuel 19:22). Its precise site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Secundus
entries.dictNote: A Christian from Thessalonica who was part of the group accompanying Paul on his return through Macedonia near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4).

entries.title: Segub
entries.summary: Segub, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Segub was the son a man named Hiel lost as the cost of rebuilding Jericho's gates, fulfilling a curse Joshua had pronounced centuries earlier against anyone who rebuilt the city.

entries.title: Seir
entries.summary: Seir, a mountain of Idumaea and its aboriginal occupants, also one in Palestine
entries.books: Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Seir most often refers to the rugged mountain range east of the Arabah, stretching from the southern end of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqabah, originally home to the Horites before the descendants of Esau displaced them and made it the heartland of Edom. The name also belonged to one of the Horite chiefs listed in Genesis, and separately to a lesser known ridge in the territory of Judah, distinct from the Edomite range. Its terrain of narrow valleys and red sandstone cliffs shaped Edom's reputation for natural defenses.

entries.label: 9 books

entries.title: Seirath
entries.dictNote: A place among the hill country of Ephraim, near the border of Benjamin, where the judge Ehud took refuge after assassinating the Moabite king Eglon at Jericho (Judg. 3:26-27). He rallied Israel's forces there before attacking the leaderless Moabites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sela-hammalekoth
entries.dictNote: Sela-hammalekoth, "the rock of divisions" or "rock of escape," was a cliff in the wilderness of Maon where Saul and David's forces circled opposite sides of a mountain, Saul closing in until a messenger arrived warning of a Philistine raid and forced him to break off the chase (1 Samuel 23:24-28). The name commemorates that narrow escape. Its exact location in the rugged country south of Hebron is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seled
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Jerahmeel through Nadab, listed in Judah's genealogy as having died without children (1 Chronicles 2:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seleucia
entries.dictNote: Seleucia was the seaport of Antioch, situated near the mouth of the Orontes River, from which Paul and Barnabas sailed at the start of their first missionary journey (Acts 13:4). It was founded by Seleucus I Nicator, one of Alexander's successors, and later became a free city under Rome. Excavations at the site, now in southern Turkey, have uncovered its ancient harbor works and a massive Roman-era rock-cut tunnel built to divert floodwater away from the port.

entries.title: Semachiah
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Korahite line, son of Shemaiah, appointed as one of the gatekeepers responsible for the tabernacle stores under David (1 Chronicles 26:7).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Semei
entries.dictNote: A name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed among the ancestors between the exile and David's line (Luke 3:26). Nothing is known about him beyond his place in this list.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Senaah
entries.dictNote: Clan or town whose descendants formed one of the largest single groups to return from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, over three thousand strong (Ezra 2:35; Neh. 7:38). Men from Senaah later helped rebuild Jerusalem's Fish Gate under Nehemiah (Neh. 3:3). Its location is unknown, though some place it near Jericho.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Senazar
entries.dictNote: A son of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, listed in the royal genealogy of David's line preserved after the Babylonian captivity (1 Chronicles 3:18).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seneh
entries.dictNote: Seneh was not a person but the rocky cliff on the south side of the pass of Michmash, opposite the crag called Bozez, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed to attack a Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 14:4-5). The narrow gorge of the Wadi es-Suweinit separating the two crags northeast of Jerusalem is still identifiable in the terrain today.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Senir
entries.summary: Shenir or Senir, a summit of Lebanon
entries.books: Deuteronomy, 1 Chronicles, Song of Solomon, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Senir is an alternate Amorite name for Mount Hermon, mentioned in Deuteronomy and in Ezekiel's description of fir trees used to build Tyre's ships.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Seorim
entries.dictNote: A priest in David's reign, head of the fourth of the twenty-four priestly divisions established for rotating temple service (1 Chr. 24:8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sephar
entries.dictNote: Sephar, the eastern limit of the territory settled by Joktan's descendants in the Table of Nations, paired with Mesha as a boundary marker (Gen. 10:30). It is commonly identified with Zafar (Dhofar) on the southern Arabian coast, a region later known for its frankincense trade.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sepharad
entries.dictNote: Sepharad is named once, as a place where Jerusalem's exiles were scattered and from which they would one day return to resettle the towns of the Negev (Obadiah 1:20). Its identity is uncertain: some scholars connect it with Sardis in Lydia, attested in a bilingual Lydian-Aramaic inscription from that city as "Sparda," while later Jewish tradition took it to mean Spain, giving rise to the term "Sephardic" for Jews of Iberian descent. Some ancient interpreters instead read the word simply as "dispersion" or "diaspora."
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sepharvaim
entries.dictNote: Sepharvaim was a city the Assyrians conquered and whose displaced population they resettled in Samaria after deporting Israel's own population, part of the mixed settlement that later became the Samaritans.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sepharvite
entries.summary: a Sepharvite or inhabitant of Sepharvain
entries.dictNote: Sepharvites were people from Sepharvaim, one of the nations the Assyrians transplanted into Samaria after deporting Israel. 2 Kings 17:31 reports that they burned their children as offerings to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech, and the location of Sepharvaim itself remains uncertain, variously identified with a Syrian or Babylonian site.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Seraiah
entries.summary: Serajah, the name of nine Israelites
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Seraiah was a common name among priests and officials in the Old Testament, borne by the chief priest executed by Nebuchadnezzar after Jerusalem's fall and by several others across different generations of priestly and scribal families.

entries.title: Sered
entries.dictNote: Sered was a son of Zebulun who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Seredites (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26).

entries.title: Sergius
entries.dictNote: Sergius Paulus was the Roman proconsul of Cyprus who summoned Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God, then believed after watching Paul strike the sorcerer Elymas blind (Acts 13:6-12). An inscription discovered on Cyprus names a proconsul Sergius Paulus from roughly this period, lending historical support to Luke's precise use of the title "proconsul" for the island's governor.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Serug
entries.dictNote: Serug was a descendant of Shem and Abraham's great-grandfather, listed in the genealogy connecting Noah's family to the patriarchs.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Seth
entries.summary: One more link in the genealogy (3:38). Josephus tells a story about his descendants that never made it into Genesis at all — warned of coming destruction by fire and flood, they inscribed their astronomical discoveries on two pillars, one brick and one stone, so at least one would survive. He claims the stone pillar was still standing in his own day.
entries.dictNote: Seth was Adam and Eve's third son, born after Cain murdered Abel, and Eve named him as a replacement, saying God had appointed her another child in Abel's place. Seth's line is the one Genesis traces forward through ten generations to Noah, and Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through Seth rather than through Cain's line, which disappears from the record after a handful of generations.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Sethur
entries.dictNote: The representative of the tribe of Asher among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:13). Along with ten of the other spies, he returned with a discouraging report that contributed to Israel's forty years of wandering.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaalabbin
entries.summary: Shaalbim or Shaalabbin, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Shaalabbin, also spelled Shaalbim, was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:42) that the Danites failed to fully conquer, leaving Amorites in control until they were put to forced labor (Judges 1:35). Centuries later it fell within one of Solomon's twelve administrative districts responsible for supplying the royal court (1 Kings 4:9). It is usually located near Aijalon, in the northern Shephelah.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shaalbonite
entries.summary: a Shaalbonite or inhabitant of Shaalbin
entries.dictNote: Shaalbonite identifies Eliahba, one of David's thirty mighty men, as being from Shaalbim, a town in the territory allotted to Dan.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shaaph
entries.summary: Shaaph, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shaaph was the name of two men in Caleb's genealogy in Chronicles. One was a son of Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and the other was a son Caleb had by his concubine Maacah, remembered as the founder or ruler of the town of Madmannah (1 Chronicles 2:49).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaaraim
entries.dictNote: Two Judean towns carried this name, which means "two gates." One lay in the Shephelah along the route the Philistines fled after David killed Goliath (1 Sam. 17:52; called Sharaim in Josh. 15:36); the other was a Simeonite town listed among that tribe's settlements (1 Chr. 4:31). Some archaeologists identify the first with Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified Iron Age site in the Elah Valley with two gates, an unusual feature for the period that would match the town's name and location near the Goliath battle site, though the identification remains debated.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shaashgaz
entries.dictNote: Shaashgaz was the eunuch in charge of the king's concubines in the harem of Ahasuerus, responsible for the women, including Esther, after their first night with the king (Esther 2:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shabbethai
entries.summary: Shabbethai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shabbethai was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra's public reading and who was involved in addressing the crisis over foreign marriages.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shachia (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: A son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, born in Moab and listed among the heads of families in Benjamin's genealogy (1 Chronicles 8:8-10).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shadrach
entries.summary: Aku’s command, the Chaldean name given to Hananiah, one of the Hebrew youths whom Nebuchadnezzar carried captive to Babylon (Dan. 1:6, 7; 3:12-30). He and his two companions refused to bow down before the image which Nebuchadnezzar had set up on the plains of Dura. Their conduct filled the king with the greatest fury, and he commanded them to be cast into the burning fiery furnace. Here, amid the fiery flames, they were miraculously preserved from harm. Over them the fire had no power, “neither was a hair of their head singed, neither had the smell of fire passed on them.” Thus Nebuchadnezzar learned the greatness of the God of Israel. (See ABEDNEGO.)

entries.title: Shage
entries.dictNote: Father of Jonathan the Hararite, one of David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:34).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaharaim
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite who divorced two wives, Hushim and Baara, and later fathered children in Moab by his wife Hodesh (1 Chronicles 8:8-11). His descendants are listed among the heads of families back in Benjamite territory.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shahazimah (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: A border town of the tribe of Issachar, its name meaning toward the heights (Josh. 19:22). Its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalim
entries.dictNote: The "land of Shalim," a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's stray donkeys before his anointing as king (1 Samuel 9:4). Its location within the central hill country of Benjamin or Ephraim is uncertain.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalisha
entries.dictNote: Shalisha, a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's lost donkeys (1 Sam. 9:4). Its name, meaning "triple land," and its position in the itinerary suggest it lay in the hill country of Ephraim, in the same general area as the later town of Baal-shalisha (2 Kings 4:42).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalleketh
entries.dictNote: Shalleketh was not a person but the name of a gate on the western side of the Jerusalem temple complex, assigned to the gatekeepers Shuppim and Hosah along the ascending causeway (1 Chronicles 26:16). Its name, from a root meaning 'to cast' or 'throw down,' most likely refers to the raised causeway leading up to it, though the precise sense is debated.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalmai
entries.dictNote: Shalmai was the ancestral head of a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:46). The parallel list in Nehemiah 7:48 gives the name as Salmai.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shalman
entries.summary: Shalman, a king apparently of Assyria
entries.dictNote: Shalman appears in Hosea 10:14 as the perpetrator of a brutal defeat of Beth-arbel, an event the prophet cites as a warning of the judgment coming on Israel. Most interpreters identify him with Shalmaneser V, the Assyrian king whose forces besieged Samaria and brought the northern kingdom to its end around 722 BC (2 Kings 17:3-6). A minority instead connect the name to Salamanu, a king of Moab recorded as a tribute-payer in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III, since the specific battle Hosea references is not otherwise attested for either ruler.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalmaneser
entries.dictNote: Shalmaneser V ruled Assyria from about 727 to 722 BC, succeeding his father Tiglath-Pileser III. When King Hoshea of Israel withheld tribute and sought an alliance with Egypt, Shalmaneser invaded and besieged Samaria; the siege lasted roughly three years before the city fell (2 Kings 17:3-6; 18:9-11). Assyrian records are notably silent on his own account of the conquest, since he died around the time Samaria fell and his successor, Sargon II, claimed credit for the city's capture in his own inscriptions, a discrepancy that has long puzzled historians reconciling the biblical and Assyrian records. The Babylonian Chronicle independently confirms that a king by this name reigned briefly in this period, corroborating the biblical timeframe.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shalthiel
entries.dictNote: Shealtiel was Zerubbabel's father, listed in the genealogies as a descendant of the exiled king Jehoiachin, keeping David's royal line traceable through the Babylonian captivity and into the postexilic period.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shama
entries.dictNote: One of David's mighty men, an Aroerite listed among the roughly thirty warriors named in David's later roster of champions (1 Chronicles 11:44). He is named alongside his brother Jehiel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shamariah
entries.summary: Shemarjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shemariah was a common name, borne by one of David's warriors who defected to him at Ziklag and by a son of King Rehoboam.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shamer
entries.summary: Shemer, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shomer was a common name, borne by a Levite and by the mother of a servant who assassinated King Joash of Judah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shamgar
entries.dictNote: Shamgar, son of Anath, delivered Israel from a Philistine incursion by killing six hundred men with an ox goad, a long, sharp-tipped pole used for driving cattle (Judges 3:31). He is remembered again in the Song of Deborah as a figure from a dangerous era when travel on the main roads had become unsafe (Judges 5:6).

witness.excerpt: After him Shamgar, the son of Anath, was elected for their governour; but died in the first year of his government.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shamhuth
entries.dictNote: Commander of the fifth division of David's army, serving one month each year in the king's rotating military schedule (1 Chronicles 27:8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shamir
entries.summary: Shamir, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Shamir was a town in the hill country of Judah, and also the name of a judge, Tola, whose hometown of the same name is mentioned in Ephraim's territory.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shamma
entries.dictNote: Shamma was a son of Zophar, listed among the leading men of the tribe of Asher in Israel's genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:37). He is distinct from Shammah, son of Agee, one of David's three mightiest warriors; the two names are spelled differently in Hebrew despite their similar English rendering.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shammah
entries.summary: Shammah, the name of an Edomite and four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shammah was one of David's three mightiest warriors, remembered for single-handedly defending a field of lentils against a Philistine raiding party while the rest of Israel's army fled.

witness.excerpt: Of all which Eliab was the eldest: Aminadab the second: Shammah the third: Nathanael the fourth: the fifth was called Rael : and the sixth Asam .

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shammai
entries.summary: Shammai, the name of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shammai was a common name in the genealogies of Judah and among the Jerahmeelite clans listed in 1 Chronicles.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shammua
entries.summary: Shammua, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shammua was a common name, borne by one of the twelve spies, representing the tribe of Reuben, and by one of David's sons.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shamoth
entries.dictNote: One of David's thirty mighty men, called "the Harorite" in 1 Chronicles 11:27. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:25 gives the same warrior's name as Shammoth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shamsherai
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Jeroham in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:26. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shapham
entries.dictNote: A leading man of the tribe of Gad who settled in the region of Bashan east of the Jordan, named second among the tribal heads listed in 1 Chronicles 5:12.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaphat
entries.summary: Shaphat, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shaphat was Elisha's father, and also the name of one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan, representing the tribe of Simeon.

entries.title: Shapper
entries.summary: Shepher, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Mount Shepher was a wilderness station between Kehelathah and Haradah in Israel's itinerary (Num. 33:23-24). Its name means beauty or brightness, but the text gives no other details, and its location among the mountains of the Sinai peninsula has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharai
entries.dictNote: Sharai was one of the men listed in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives during the postexilic period and agreed to separate from them as part of Ezra's covenant reform. He is identified as one of the sons of Bani.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharar
entries.dictNote: Father of Ahiam, one of David's mighty warriors; the parallel list in Chronicles gives the name as Sacar (2 Samuel 23:33; 1 Chronicles 11:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharesh
entries.dictNote: A son of Machir and brother of Peresh, listed in the genealogy of Manasseh through Machir's wife Maachah (1 Chronicles 7:16). Some English versions spell the name Sheresh.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharezer
entries.summary: Sharetser, the name of an Assyrian and an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Sharezer, along with his brother Adrammelech, assassinated their father Sennacherib, king of Assyria, an event recorded briefly in both 2 Kings and Isaiah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Sharonite
entries.summary: a Sharonite or inhabitant of Sharon
entries.dictNote: Sharonite identifies Shitrai, the official David put in charge of the royal herds grazing in the plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal region between Joppa and Mount Carmel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sharuhen
entries.dictNote: Sharuhen, a town allotted to the tribe of Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh. 19:6), called Shaaraim in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 4:31. Egyptian records describe a fortress by this name that the Hyksos held against a lengthy siege by Pharaoh Ahmose after their expulsion from Egypt; the biblical town is commonly identified with Tell el-Far'ah, near the Negev border with Gaza.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shashai
entries.dictNote: One of the descendants of Bani who had married foreign wives and agreed to separate from them as part of Ezra's reforms after the exile (Ezra 10:40).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shashak
entries.dictNote: Shashak was a Benjamite listed among the sons of Beriah in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:14 and 25. He is mentioned only in this record of Benjamin's clans.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaulites
entries.summary: a Shaülite or descendant of Shaul
entries.dictNote: Shaulites were the clan descended from Shaul, a son of Simeon by a Canaanite woman, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaveh
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Shaveh, also called the King's Valley, was where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram after his rescue of Lot and victory over the invading eastern kings (Gen. 14:17). The same valley is named again generations later as the site where Absalom set up a monument to himself (2 Sam. 18:18), though its precise location near Jerusalem is no longer known.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shaveh Kiriathaim
entries.summary: Shaveh-Kirjathajim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Shaveh Kiriathaim was the plain surrounding Kiriathaim, a town east of the Jordan where the eastern coalition of kings defeated the Emim during the campaign described in Genesis 14:5, before Chedorlaomer moved south to strike Sodom and Gomorrah. Kiriathaim later belonged to Moab and is named in the Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), where King Mesha claims credit for rebuilding it alongside other Moabite towns known from the Bible. The exact location of the surrounding plain is not established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shavsha
entries.dictNote: One of David's royal secretaries (1 Chronicles 18:16); the same official appears under the names Seraiah in 2 Samuel 8:17, Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25, and Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3, the variation typical of how court titles and names were transliterated across parallel records.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheal
entries.dictNote: Sheal was one of the sons of Bani listed among the Israelites who had married foreign wives during the exile and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reform (Ezra 10:29). Nothing more is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shealtiel
entries.summary: Asked for of God, father of Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2, 8; Neh. 12:1).
entries.dictNote: Asked for of God, father of Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2, 8; Neh. 12:1).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shear-jashub
entries.summary: Shear-Jashub, the symbolic name of one of Isaiah's sons
entries.dictNote: Shear-jashub, meaning "a remnant shall return," was the symbolic name Isaiah gave to his son, whom the prophet brought along when he confronted King Ahaz of Judah with a message of assurance during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (Isaiah 7:3). The name itself functioned as a walking prophecy, promising that even after judgment a remnant of Israel would survive and return to God.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheariah
entries.dictNote: Sheariah was a descendant of Saul through Jonathan's son Merib-baal, part of the genealogy Chronicles preserves for Saul's line after the family's near destruction (1 Chronicles 8:38; 9:44). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheba
entries.summary: Sheba, the name of three early progenitors of tribes and of an Ethiopian district
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel
entries.dictNote: Two figures named Sheba appear in the Old Testament. The Queen of Sheba traveled a great distance, likely from southern Arabia, to test Solomon's famous wisdom with hard questions, and left declaring the reports she had heard didn't do him justice. A different Sheba, a Benjamite, led a short-lived rebellion against David shortly after Absalom's revolt was crushed.

entries.title: Shebah
entries.dictNote: Not a person but the well Isaac's servants dug that gave the city of Beersheba its name, "well of the oath" or "well of seven," according to Genesis 26:33. The chapter presents it as the third in a sequence of wells contested between Isaac's household and the Philistines of Gerar, resolved this time by a covenant oath between Isaac and Abimelech rather than by further conflict.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shebam
entries.summary: Sebam or Sibmah, a place in Moab
entries.dictNote: Shebam was a pastoral town east of the Jordan, in territory taken from Sihon, requested by and eventually granted to the tribes of Reuben and Gad because of its excellent grazing land (Numbers 32:3-4, 38). It is likely the same place called Sibmah elsewhere, later famous for its vineyards until Moab overran it (Isaiah 16:8-9; Jeremiah 48:32).
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shebaniah
entries.summary: Shebanjah, the name of three or four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shebaniah was a common Levitical name among those who led worship and signed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah after the law was read publicly.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shebarim
entries.dictNote: A place near Ai where the Israelite forces were routed and pursued down a steep descent after their first, failed assault on the city, a defeat later traced to Achan's sin (Josh. 7:5).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheber
entries.dictNote: Sheber was a son Caleb had by his concubine Maacah, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:48).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shebna
entries.dictNote: Shebna was a palace administrator under Hezekiah whom Isaiah condemned for carving himself an extravagant tomb and prophesied he would be removed from office and die in a foreign land instead, replaced by the more faithful Eliakim.

entries.title: Shebuel
entries.summary: Shebuel or Shubael, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shebuel was a descendant of Moses through his son Gershom, appointed to oversee the treasuries of the tabernacle under David's organization of the Levites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shecaniah
entries.summary: Shekanjah, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shecaniah was a common postexilic name, most notably the man who urged Ezra to lead the community in dealing with the problem of intermarriage with foreign wives, offering personal support for reform even though his own family was implicated.
