4 1 And in the south there came upon us a greater war than that in Shechem; and I joined in battle array with my brethren, and pursued a thousand men, and slew of them two hundred men and 2, 3 four kings.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shedeur
entries.dictNote: Shedeur was the father of the tribal leader of Reuben during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shehariah
entries.dictNote: Shehariah was a Benjamite, son of Jeroham, listed among the heads of families in the tribal genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shelah
entries.summary: Shelah, the name of a postdiluvian patriarch and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Shelah was Judah's third son by his Canaanite wife, and Judah withheld him from marrying his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar as custom required, a broken promise that led Tamar to disguise herself and conceive by Judah directly instead.

witness.excerpt: Japheth, and in the fourth year he begat a son, and called his name Shelah;  for he said: "Truly I have been sent."  6.
And Judah said unto Tamar, his daughter-in-law: "Remain in thy father's house as a widow till Shelah my son be grown up, and I shall give thee to him to wife." 7.
She bare me Er, and Onan and Shelah; and two of them the Lord smote: for Shelah lived, and his children are ye.
6 And I wished to give Shelah also to her, but his mother did not permit it; for she wrought evil against Tamar, because she was not of the daughters of Canaan, as she also herself was.
And while I was away she went and took for 4 Shelah a wife from Canaan.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shelanites
entries.summary: a Shelanite (collectively), or descendants of Shelah
entries.dictNote: Shelanites were the clan descended from Shelah, the third son of Judah by his Canaanite wife Bath-shua, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shelemiah
entries.summary: Shelemjah, the name of nine Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shelemiah was a common name among gatekeepers, priests, and officials in the postexilic period, including a temple gatekeeper Nehemiah trusted enough to help oversee the storehouses.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Sheleph
entries.dictNote: Sheleph was a son of Joktan and became the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, one of many Joktanite peoples listed as settling the Arabian peninsula (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shelesh
entries.dictNote: Shelesh was a son of Helem, of the tribe of Asher, named in the tribal genealogy of Asher (1 Chr. 7:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shelomi
entries.dictNote: An Asherite whose son Ahihud was chosen to help apportion the land of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest, named in the list of tribal representatives in Numbers 34:27.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shelomith
entries.summary: Shelomith, the name of five Israelites and three Israelitesses
entries.dictNote: Shelomith was a common name, borne by the mother of a man executed for blasphemy in Leviticus and by several other Israelite women and Levites across the genealogies.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shelomith (from the margin)
entries.summary: Shelomoth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shelomith is a marginal spelling variant, the main text reads “Shelomoth,” attached to two Levites in Chronicles: a leader of a division of the Kohathite family descended from Izhar and Moses (1 Chronicles 24:22) and a Levite in charge of the temple treasuries under David (1 Chronicles 26:25-26). It is uncertain whether these references point to one man or two, since Chronicles' genealogical lists frequently repeat family names across generations.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shelumiel
entries.dictNote: Shelumiel was the tribal leader of Simeon during the wilderness census, one of twelve representatives appointed to assist Moses.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shem
entries.summary: Noah's son, one generation up from Terah in Luke's chain (3:36). Josephus counts out the exact same ten generations from Noah to Abraham that Luke's genealogy implies, just narrated instead of listed.
entries.dictNote: Shem was Noah's oldest son and the ancestor of the Semitic peoples, including Abraham's line, and Genesis 10 traces his descendants through Elam, Asshur, and Arphaxad down to Eber, whose name is the likely source of the word Hebrew. Noah blessed Shem specifically after the flood, setting his line apart even among his brothers.

witness.excerpt: Terah begat Abram in his seventieth year. Nahor begat Haran, when he was one hundred and twenty years old… Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shema
entries.summary: Shema, the name of a place in Palestine and of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shema is a name shared by at least four different men in the genealogical lists of Chronicles and Nehemiah, not a single figure. One Shema was a descendant of Caleb through Hebron, in the tribe of Judah, and fathered Raham (1 Chronicles 2:43-44). A second was an ancestor of Bela, a leading man among the Reubenites who lived on the plateau east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:8). A third was a Benjamite clan leader who helped drive the inhabitants out of Gath (1 Chronicles 8:13), and a fourth stood on the wooden platform beside Ezra when he read the Law aloud to the assembled people at the Water Gate in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shema
entries.dictNote: Shema was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah in the Negev, listed in Joshua 15:26 among the southernmost cities near the border of Edom; it is generally identified with Sheba in the parallel list at Joshua 19:2, and its exact site is unidentified. Easton's dictionary lists three unrelated men also named Shema under the same headword, but this entry, tied to Joshua 15:26, concerns only the town.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shemaah
entries.dictNote: Shemaah was a Benjamite from Gibeah whose sons Ahiezer and Joash were skilled archers and slingers who joined David's band at Ziklag while he was still hiding from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:1-3). Their defection was notable because they came from Saul's own tribe.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shemaiah
entries.summary: Shemajah, the name of twenty-five Israelites
entries.books: 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Shemaiah was a prophet who stopped King Rehoboam from attacking the northern tribes after Israel's split, declaring the division was God's own doing and further bloodshed between brothers would not be blessed.

witness.excerpt: dy to take a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men out of the army, to make an expedition against Jeroboam and his people, that he might force them by war to be his servants; but he was forbidden of God by the prophet [Shemaiah] to go to war, for that it was not just that brethren of the same contry should fight one against another.
But Shemaiah the prophet told them, that God threatened to forsake them, as they had themselves forsaken his worship.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Shemeber
entries.dictNote: Shemeber was king of Zeboiim, another of the five cities of the plain, and one of the local kings who rebelled against Chedorlaomer's overlordship, an act that triggered the invasion described in Genesis 14:2. He was defeated along with his allies, and Zeboiim was later destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shemida
entries.dictNote: Shemida was a son of Manasseh's grandson Gilead, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted among Manasseh's tribe.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shemidaites
entries.summary: a Shemidaite (collectively) or descendants of Shemida
entries.dictNote: Shemidaites were the clan descended from Shemida, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheminith
entries.dictNote: Sheminith, meaning “eighth,” is a musical direction rather than a personal name, appearing in the titles of Psalms 6 and 12 and in the description of Levitical musicians in Chronicles. Its exact meaning is debated; most understand it as an instruction to play or sing in a lower octave or register (1 Chronicles 15:21).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shemiramoth
entries.summary: Shemiramoth, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shemiramoth was a Levite David appointed as a musician for the ark's procession into Jerusalem, playing the harp among the temple musicians.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shen
entries.dictNote: Shen was a landmark, apparently a rock or ridge, between Mizpah and Jeshanah in the hill country of Benjamin. After Israel's victory over the Philistines described in 1 Samuel 7, Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and named it Ebenezer, "stone of help," to commemorate the Lord's aid in battle. Its exact site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shepham
entries.summary: Shepham, a place in or near Palestine
entries.dictNote: A boundary point named in the description of Israel's ideal eastern border in Numbers 34:10-11, lying on the line between Hazar-enan and Riblah. Its exact location, likely somewhere near the headwaters region north and east of the Sea of Galilee, is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shephatiah
entries.summary: Shephatjah, the name of ten Israelites
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Shephatiah was a common Old Testament name, borne by one of David's sons, a royal official who wanted Jeremiah executed for his discouraging prophecies during the siege of Jerusalem, and several postexilic figures.

witness.excerpt: nd he was called Arenon; the second was Daniel, by his wife Abigail; the name of the third was Absalom, by Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth he named Adonijah, by his wife Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth he called Ithream, by Eglah.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Shephi
entries.dictNote: Shephi was a son of Shobal descended from Seir the Horite, listed among Edom's clan chiefs (1 Chronicles 1:40). The parallel genealogy in Genesis 36:23 gives his name as Shepho.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shephuphan
entries.dictNote: Shephuphan was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, ancestor of the clan of the Shuphamites; the name also appears as Shupham, Shuppim, and Muppim in parallel genealogies (Numbers 26:39; 1 Chronicles 8:5).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sherah
entries.dictNote: A daughter of Beriah in Ephraim's genealogy, credited with building the two towns of Beth-horon, later strategically important sites on the road from the coastal plain to Jerusalem, and a third town named after her, Uzzen-sherah (1 Chr. 7:24). She is one of the rare women in Chronicles' genealogies credited directly with a building project.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sherebiah
entries.summary: Sherebjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Sherebiah was a Levite Ezra specifically recruited to accompany the returning exiles to Jerusalem, valued for his skill and standing among the Levitical families.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sheshach
entries.summary: Sheshak, a symbolic name of Babylon
entries.dictNote: Sheshach was not a person but a coded name for Babylon, formed by substituting each Hebrew letter with its counterpart counted from the opposite end of the alphabet, a cipher called atbash. Jeremiah used the name in oracles against Babylon, and its parallel with "Babylon" in the surrounding verses confirms the identification (Jeremiah 25:26; 51:41).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheshai
entries.dictNote: Sheshai was one of the descendants of Anak, the giant clan Caleb personally drove out of Hebron once he finally claimed the land God had promised him decades earlier.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Sheshan
entries.dictNote: Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, and Chronicles records that he gave one of them in marriage to his own Egyptian servant to continue his family line.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheshbazzar
entries.summary: O sun-god, defend the lord! (Ezra 1:8, 11), probably another name for Zerubbabel (q.v.), Ezra 2:2; Hag. 1:12, 14; Zech. 4:6, 10.
entries.dictNote: O sun-god, defend the lord! (Ezra 1:8, 11), probably another name for Zerubbabel (q.v.), Ezra 2:2; Hag. 1:12, 14; Zech. 4:6, 10.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheshbazzar
entries.dictNote: Sheshbazzar was a prince of Judah appointed governor by King Cyrus of Persia, entrusted with the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and commissioned to lead the first group of returning exiles and lay the foundation of the rebuilt temple (Ezra 1:8, 11; 5:14-16). Some scholars identify him with Zerubbabel, though the text treats them as though performing overlapping roles rather than stating they are the same man.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheth
entries.dictNote: Sheth here is not the name of a person but part of a phrase in Balaam's oracle predicting that a coming ruler of Israel will crush all the sons of Sheth (Numbers 24:17). Most modern translations render this sons of tumult rather than treating Sheth as a proper name, understanding it as poetic language for Israel's warlike neighbors, likely Moab. It is unrelated to the antediluvian patriarch Seth, who is recorded separately.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shethar
entries.dictNote: Shethar was one of the seven princes of Media and Persia who had access to King Ahasuerus and advised him at the start of the book of Esther (Esther 1:14).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shetharboznai
entries.dictNote: Shethar-bozenai was a Persian official who, along with Tattenai, questioned the Jews' authority to rebuild the temple, an inquiry that ultimately confirmed Cyrus's original decree and led to official support for the project instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sheva
entries.dictNote: Two men named Sheva appear in the Old Testament: a son of Caleb in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:49), and one of David's royal scribes or secretaries (2 Samuel 20:25), likely the same official called Seraiah or Shisha elsewhere in the parallel lists of David's officials. Nothing more is recorded of either.

witness.excerpt: He made Sheva the scribe, and appointed Zadok and Abiathar the high priests.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shichemites
entries.summary: a Shikmite (collectively), or descendants of Shekem
entries.dictNote: Shichemites were the clan descended from Shechem, a grandson of Manasseh through Gilead, counted among the families of Manasseh in the Numbers 26 census. The clan shares its ancestor's name with the well-known city of Shechem, though the two are only indirectly related.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shicron
entries.summary: drunkenness, Shikkeron, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Shicron marked one of the landmarks along the northern boundary of Judah's territory, situated between Ekron and Jabneel near the Mediterranean coastal plain (Joshua 15:11). Nothing else is recorded of it, and its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shiggaion
entries.summary: properly, aberration, i.e. (technically) a dithyramb or rambling poem
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a Hebrew musical or poetic term found in the title of Psalm 7, and in its plural form, shigionoth, in Habakkuk 3:1, likely describing an irregular, emotionally intense style of composition, possibly connected to a root meaning "to wander" or "to reel." Its precise musical meaning is uncertain, since no other ancient source explains the term.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shihon
entries.dictNote: Shihon, a town within the tribal allotment of Issachar, named only in Joshua 19:19. Its location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shihor
entries.dictNote: Shihor was a stream or waterway on Egypt's northeastern border, used in the Old Testament as a marker for the southwestern edge of the land promised to Israel.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shihor-libnath
entries.dictNote: Shihor-libnath is not a person but a stream marking part of the southern boundary of the tribe of Asher, mentioned in Joshua 19:26. It is generally identified with the Nahr Zarqa, a river that rises in the Carmel range and empties into the Mediterranean just north of Caesarea. The name, meaning roughly "black-white," may reflect the river's changing color, muddy after rain and clear afterward, and crocodiles were still reported in the Zarqa well into the nineteenth century, a detail later travelers connected to ancient Egyptian associations with the area.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shilhi
entries.dictNote: Shilhi was the father of Azubah, who became the wife of King Asa and mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah (1 Kings 22:42; 2 Chronicles 20:31).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shilhim
entries.dictNote: Shilhim was a town in the southern territory of Judah near the border with Simeon (Joshua 15:32), generally identified with Sharuhen in the parallel list at Joshua 19:6. Sharuhen appears in Egyptian sources as the fortress where the Hyksos made their last stand after being driven from Egypt, besieged for three years by Pharaoh Ahmose according to the tomb inscription of his officer Ahmose son of Ebana, one of the clearer points of contact between the biblical Negev towns and independently dated Egyptian history.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shillem
entries.dictNote: Shillem was a son of Naphtali and ancestor of the Shillemite clan, counted among the families of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob and later numbered in the wilderness census; he is also called Shallum in the parallel genealogy of Chronicles (Genesis 46:24; Numbers 26:49; 1 Chronicles 7:13).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shillemites
entries.summary: a Shilemite (collectively) or descendants of Shillem
entries.dictNote: Shillemites were the clan descended from Shillem, a son of Naphtali, counted in the Numbers 26 census; the same man is called Shallum in 1 Chronicles 7:13.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shiloah
entries.dictNote: The "waters of Shiloah," a gently flowing channel carrying water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem, later linked with the pool of Siloam (Isaiah 8:6). Isaiah contrasts its quiet flow with the overwhelming flood of the Euphrates as an image of trusting God rather than seeking help from Assyria. The city's ancient water system that this name refers to is documented archaeologically by Hezekiah's Siloam Tunnel and the Hebrew inscription its diggers left inside it, discovered in 1880.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shiloh
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Psalm, Jeremiah
entries.dictNote: Shiloh was a town in Ephraim, north of Bethel, where the tabernacle stood through most of the period of the judges until the Philistines captured the ark and the sanctuary's importance faded; it was here that young Samuel served under Eli and heard God's call. Centuries after its destruction, Jeremiah cited Shiloh's ruined fate as a warning to Jerusalem. The same word appears in Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:10, where “until Shiloh comes” has traditionally been read as a title for the coming Messiah, though translators have long debated whether the term there is a place name, a title, or a corrupted phrase.

witness.excerpt: So Joshua removed his camp to the mountainous countrey, and placed the tabernacle in the city of Shiloh: for that seemed a fit place for it; because of the beauty of its situation; until such time as their affairs would permit them to build a temple.

So they gathered themselves to Shiloh, out of a prodigious and a just anger; and assembling in a great congregation before the tabernacle, they immediately resolved to take arms, and to treat the inhabitants of Gibeah as enemies.
Now Elcanah came with his wives to the city Shiloh, to sacrifice, for there it was that the tabernacle of God was fixed, as we have formerly said.

When the news of this defeat came to Shiloh, with that of the captivity of the ark: for a certain young man, a Benjamite, who was in the action, came as a messenger thither: the whole city was full of lamentations.
So she did as her husband bade her, and changed her habit, and came to the city Shiloh, for there did Ahijah live.
And we fought with them and routed them; and their allies from Shiloh we slew, and we did not leave 3 them power to come in against us.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Shiloh
entries.summary: Shiloh, an epithet of the Messiah
entries.dictNote: In Jacob's deathbed blessing over Judah, the phrase "until Shiloh comes" is one of the most debated lines in Genesis (Gen. 49:10). Some read "Shiloh" as a title for a coming ruler descended from Judah, a reading Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have long taken as messianic; others, following a different vocalization of the Hebrew, render it "until he comes to Shiloh," pointing instead to the town where the tabernacle was later set up. This entry concerns only that prophetic phrase; the town itself has its own separate record.

And we fought with them and routed them; and their allies from Shiloh we slew, and we did not leave 3 them power to come in against us.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shilonite
entries.summary: a Shilonite or inhabitant of Shiloh
entries.dictNote: Shilonite names the prophet Ahijah, who came from Shiloh and famously tore his cloak into twelve pieces to announce that God would split Solomon's kingdom. The plural form elsewhere describes a Judahite clan descended from Shelah, Judah's youngest son, rather than people from the town of Shiloh.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shilshah
entries.dictNote: A son of Zophah, listed among the descendants of Asher noted in Chronicles as heads of families and mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 7:37-40). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimah
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, son of Jehiel the father of Gibeon, listed among the families that settled in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:32). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 9:38 calls the same man Shimeam.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimath
entries.dictNote: Shimath was an Ammonite woman whose son Jehozabad, along with an accomplice, assassinated King Joash of Judah in his bed, reportedly in revenge for Joash's earlier execution of the prophet Zechariah (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). She is identified only through this connection to her son.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shimea
entries.summary: Shima, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shimea was a common name, borne by one of David's brothers and by one of David's own sons.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah
entries.dictNote: Shimeah was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse, and the father of Jonadab, the shrewd nephew who advised Amnon in his plot against Tamar (2 Samuel 13:3); he is also called Shimea elsewhere. A second, unrelated Shimeah was a Benjamite descended from Gibeon, also known as Shimeam (1 Chronicles 8:32; 9:38).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeah (from the margin)
entries.summary: Shimi, the name of twenty Israelites
entries.books: Exodus, Numbers, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Esther
entries.dictNote: Shimeah, also spelled Shammah, was one of David's older brothers, the third son of Jesse, and the father of Jonadab, the nephew who advised Amnon on how to get Tamar alone.

entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Shimeam
entries.dictNote: Shimeam was a descendant of Jehiel, the founder of Gibeon, listed among the Benjamite families that resettled Jerusalem after the exile in 1 Chronicles 9:38. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8:32 gives the same figure's name as Shimeah, one of several minor spelling variants between the two overlapping lists. Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimeathites
entries.summary: a Shimathite (collectively) or descendants of Shimah
entries.dictNote: Shimeathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, named in 1 Chronicles 2:55 and identified there as Kenites descended from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimon
entries.dictNote: A man of Judah whose four sons appear in a brief, otherwise unexplained genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:20.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimon-meron
entries.dictNote: Shimon-meron was one of the thirty-one Canaanite royal cities whose kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, named only in the summary list of Joshua 12:20. It is generally taken to be the same place as Shimron, listed among the cities of the northern coalition Joshua defeated at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1) and later assigned to Zebulun (Joshua 19:15).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimrath
entries.dictNote: Shimrath was a Benjamite listed among the sons of Shimhi in the tribal genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:21). Nothing further is known about him beyond this single mention.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimri
entries.summary: Shimri, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shimri was a common name among David's warriors and Levitical families listed in Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shimrith
entries.dictNote: Shimrith was a Moabite woman whose son Jehozabad was one of two officials who conspired to assassinate King Joash of Judah in retaliation for the killing of the prophet Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:25-26). The parallel account in 2 Kings 12:21 calls her Shomer instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimron
entries.summary: Shimron, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Shimron is a name shared by a place and a person in the Old Testament. It names a son of Issachar who gave his name to the clan of the Shimronites (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:24; 1 Chronicles 7:1), and, unrelated in origin, a royal Canaanite city whose king joined Jabin of Hazor's coalition against Joshua at the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1-2) before being allotted to Zebulun (Joshua 19:15); the city is generally identified with a site near the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley a few miles west of Nazareth.

witness.excerpt: Issachar and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Tola, and Phûa,  and Jâsûb,  and Shimron--five.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shimronites
entries.summary: a Shimronite (collectively) or descendants of Shimron
entries.dictNote: Shimronites were the clan descended from Shimron, a son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shimshai
entries.dictNote: Shimshai was a Persian scribe who, along with Rehum, wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem, an effort that successfully halted the work for a time.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shinab
entries.dictNote: Shinab was king of Admah, one of the five cities of the plain that included Sodom and Gomorrah, at the time of the invasion by Chedorlaomer and his allied kings described in Genesis 14:2. He and the other city-kings rebelled against Chedorlaomer after twelve years of vassalage and were defeated in the battle that led to Lot's capture and Abraham's rescue. Admah was later destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shinar
entries.dictNote: Shinar is the ancient name for the region of Babylon, the setting for the tower of Babel and later for Nebuchadnezzar's empire, tying the Old Testament's first and last major confrontations with Babylonian pride to the same geography.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Shiphi
entries.dictNote: Shiphi was a Simeonite, father of Ziza, a leader of his tribe during the reign of Hezekiah, a period when the tribe of Simeon expanded into new pastureland near Gedor (1 Chronicles 4:37-41).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shiphmite
entries.summary: a Shiphmite or inhabitant of Shepham
entries.dictNote: Shiphmite marks Zabdi, the official David put in charge of the royal vineyards and their wine stores, as a native of Shepham, a town whose location is now unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shiphrah
entries.dictNote: One of the two Hebrew midwives, alongside Puah, who defied Pharaoh's order to kill Israelite baby boys at birth and were rewarded by God for their courage (Exodus 1:15-21). Their names are among the few individual Israelites recorded before Moses' birth.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shiphtan
entries.dictNote: Shiphtan appears only as the father of Kemuel, the man Moses appointed to represent the tribe of Ephraim on the commission that oversaw the division of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:24). Like most of the fathers named alongside the twelve tribal commissioners listed in that chapter, nothing else about him is recorded in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shisha
entries.dictNote: Father of Elihoreph and Ahijah, the two royal secretaries who served in Solomon's administration (1 Kings 4:3). He is likely the same official called Shavsha under David and Seraiah or Sheva in the parallel lists of 2 Samuel, the name shifting slightly across transliterations, covered in full under Shavsha.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shishak
entries.dictNote: Shishak was the Egyptian pharaoh who invaded Judah during Rehoboam's reign and stripped Solomon's temple of its treasures, an episode Shishak also commemorated on a triumphal relief at the temple of Karnak in Egypt, listing the cities he claimed to have conquered.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shitrai
entries.dictNote: Shitrai was a Sharonite who managed King David's cattle grazing on the plain of Sharon, one of the officials heading David's royal property listed in 1 Chronicles 27:29.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shittim
entries.summary: Shittim, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Shittim was a plain in Moab east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, where Israel made its final camp before crossing into Canaan; there the Israelite men were seduced into idolatry and immorality with Moabite women in the incident of Baal-peor (Numbers 25:1-3), and it was from this camp that Joshua sent the two spies into Jericho (Joshua 2:1). The prophets later look back to Shittim either as a byword for that sin (Micah 6:5) or, in Joel's vision of restoration, as the source of a life-giving stream flowing from the temple (Joel 3:18).
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Shiza
entries.dictNote: Shiza was a Reubenite, the father of Adina, one of David's thirty mighty warriors and a captain among the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 11:42). Nothing further is recorded about Shiza himself.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shoa
entries.dictNote: Not an individual but a people or district named alongside Pekod and Koa in Ezekiel's oracle against Jerusalem, personified there as one of Oholibah's unfaithful lovers who will turn against her (Ezekiel 23:23). Most scholars identify Shoa with the Sutu, a seminomadic people known from Babylonian and Assyrian records who lived east of the Tigris, making the string of names in this verse a pointed reference to Babylon's own allies and vassals.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shobab
entries.summary: Shobab, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shobab was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after he became king, and also the name of one of David's ancestors through the line of Caleb.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shobach
entries.dictNote: Shobach commanded the army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, mustering forces from beyond the Euphrates to fight alongside the Ammonites against David. He was defeated and killed by Joab's forces at Helam, a loss that led the Arameans allied with the Ammonites to make peace with Israel (2 Samuel 10:15-19); he is called Shophach in the parallel account (1 Chronicles 19:16).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shobai
entries.dictNote: Shobai's descendants, gatekeepers of the temple, were among those who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 7:45). His name means “captor” or “captive.” Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shobal
entries.summary: Shobal, the name of an Edomite and two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shobal was a common name, borne by an Edomite clan chief descended from Seir and by a descendant of Judah listed among the founders of Kiriath-jearim.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shobek
entries.dictNote: One of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant of renewed obedience to the law under Nehemiah after the exiles returned to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 10:24-27). Nothing else is recorded of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shobi
entries.dictNote: Son of Nahash the Ammonite king, Shobi supplied David and his men with food and bedding when they fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, despite his family's earlier hostility toward Israel (2 Samuel 17:27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shocho
entries.summary: Sokoh or Soko, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Socoh was a town in Judah near the Valley of Elah, close to where David's battle with Goliath took place.

witness.excerpt: 1106] Now the Philistines gathered themselves together again, no very long time afterward; and having gotten together a great army, they made war against the Israelites: and having seized a place between Shochoh and Azekah, they there pitched their camp.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Shoham
entries.dictNote: A Merarite Levite, son of Jaaziah, listed among the Levitical divisions organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:26-27).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shomer
entries.summary: Shomer, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two people carry this name in the Old Testament. One was the mother of Jehozabad, a royal servant who joined a conspiracy that killed King Joash of Judah; she is called a Moabite and also named Shimrith elsewhere (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). The other was a man of the tribe of Asher, also called Shamer, listed among the heads of his clan (1 Chronicles 7:32, 34).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shophach
entries.dictNote: Shophach, also spelled Shobach in the parallel account, was the general commanding the army of Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, when Ammon hired Aramean mercenaries against David; Joab's forces defeated the coalition and killed Shophach in battle (1 Chronicles 19:16-18; compare 2 Samuel 10:16-18). His death broke Aramean support for Ammon and led several vassal kings to make peace with David. The battle marks the high point of David's wars establishing Israelite dominance over the Aramean states to the north.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shua
entries.dictNote: Shua was a Canaanite man whose daughter, called Bathshua (“daughter of Shua”), became the wife of Judah and bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah (Genesis 38:2-5). Her death is noted later in the same chapter (Genesis 38:12).

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shua
entries.dictNote: Shua was a daughter of Heber, of the tribe of Asher, listed among his children in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:32. She is a different person from the Canaanite woman named Shua whose daughter married Judah in Genesis 38.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuah
entries.dictNote: Two men named Shuah appear in genealogies: one was a son Abraham had by his second wife Keturah, whose descendants settled in Arabia and gave their name to the “Shuhites,” the people of Job's friend Bildad (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32); the other is a much briefer mention in the tribe of Judah's genealogy as father of Chelub (1 Chronicles 4:11). The two are unrelated apart from sharing a name.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shuah
entries.dictNote: This Shuah, distinct from Abraham's son by Keturah of the same name, was a descendant of Judah named as the brother of Chelub in 1 Chronicles 4:11, in a genealogy that also credits Chelub's line with founding the city of Eshton. Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

witness.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shual
entries.summary: Shual, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: The name Shual covers two distinct entities that share a headword. The land of Shual was a district in Benjamin's hill country that Philistine raiders passed through during Saul's reign (1 Samuel 13:17). Shual son of Zophah was an unrelated individual, an Asherite clan head listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:36; his name, which means jackal, was apparently common enough to double as a place name elsewhere in the same territory.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shuham
entries.dictNote: Son of Dan and ancestor of the Shuhamite clan, one of the tribal divisions counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:42-43).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuhamites
entries.dictNote: Shuhamites were the family descended from Shuham, also called Hushim, the son of Dan; they formed Dan's only recorded clan in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuhite
entries.summary: a Shuchite or descendant of Shuach
entries.dictNote: Shuhite designates Bildad, one of Job's three friends, likely marking him as a descendant of Shuah, a son Abraham had by his later wife Keturah, whose descendants settled in the Arabian desert.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shulamite
entries.summary: peaceful (with the article always prefixed, making it a pet name); the Shulammith, an epithet of Solomon's queen
entries.dictNote: Shulamite designates the young woman celebrated throughout the Song of Solomon, an epithet whose meaning is debated; many take it as a feminine form pointing to the town of Shunem, though the underlying Hebrew could also simply mean the peaceful or perfect one.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shumathites
entries.summary: a Shumathite (collectively) or descendants of Shumah
entries.dictNote: Shumathites were one of the families descended from the clans of Kiriath-jearim in Judah's genealogy, named in 1 Chronicles 2:53 alongside the Ithrites, Puhites, and Mishraites.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shunamite
entries.summary: a Shunammitess, or female inhabitant of Shunem
entries.dictNote: Shunamite designates someone from Shunem, a village in the territory of Issachar. Abishag, brought in to care for the aged David, was a Shunammite, and an unnamed Shunammite woman later hosted the prophet Elisha and saw her son restored to life after he raised him from death.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shunem
entries.dictNote: Village in Issachar's territory near Jezreel where the Philistines camped before the battle in which Saul and his sons died on Mount Gilboa (1 Sam. 28:4). It was also home to the woman who built a room for Elisha to stay in whenever he passed through, and whose son the prophet raised from the dead there (2 Kings 4:8-37). The site is preserved in the name of the modern village of Sulam.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shuni
entries.dictNote: Shuni was a son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Shunites (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:15).

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Shunites
entries.summary: a Shunite (collectively) or descendants of Shuni
entries.dictNote: Shunites were the clan descended from Shuni, a son of Gad, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuphamite
entries.summary: a Shuphamite (collectively) or descendants of Shephupham
entries.dictNote: Shuphamites were the clan descended from Shupham, also spelled Shephupham, a son of Benjamin, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuppim
entries.dictNote: Shuppim was a Benjamite clan name, and also the name of a Levitical gatekeeper appointed under David.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shur
entries.summary: Shur, a region of the Desert
entries.dictNote: Shur was a wilderness region on Egypt's northeastern frontier, between Egypt and Philistia, likely named for a defensive wall the Egyptians built there against desert raiders. Hagar fled toward it after being sent away by Sarah (Genesis 16:7), and Israel entered this same wilderness immediately after crossing the Red Sea, only to find no water for three days (Exodus 15:22).

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shushan
entries.dictNote: Shushan, called Susa by Greek and Roman writers, was the winter capital of the Persian Empire, located east of the Tigris in what is now southwestern Iran. It is the setting for most of the book of Esther, Daniel received a vision there, and Nehemiah was serving as cupbearer in its royal citadel when he learned of Jerusalem's ruined walls. French excavations at the site since the nineteenth century have uncovered the audience hall of Darius and Artaxerxes described in Esther, along with a wealth of Persian and earlier Elamite artifacts, including the stele bearing the Babylonian Code of Hammurabi, carried to Susa centuries earlier as war plunder.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Shuthalhites
entries.summary: a Shuthalchite (collectively) or descendants of Shuthelach
entries.dictNote: Shuthalhites were the clan descended from Shuthelah, a son of Ephraim, one of several Ephraimite families listed in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Shuthelah
entries.summary: Shuthelach, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Shuthelah was a son of Ephraim, and his descendants formed one of the clans counted in Israel's wilderness census.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sia
entries.summary: Sia or Siaha, one of the Nethinim
entries.dictNote: Sia headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to serve at the rebuilt temple (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47, where the name appears as Siaha).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sibbecai
entries.dictNote: Sibbecai was one of David's mighty warriors, credited with killing a Philistine giant descended from the same lineage as Goliath.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Sibboleth
entries.dictNote: Not a person but a word: the way men of Ephraim pronounced "shibboleth" ("ear of grain" or "stream"), since their dialect lacked the "sh" sound. After Jephthah's Gileadites defeated Ephraim, they used the word as a password at the fords of the Jordan, killing any fugitive who could only manage "sibboleth" (Judges 12:5-6). The episode is the origin of "shibboleth" as an English word for a telltale marker of group identity.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sibraim
entries.dictNote: A landmark on the northern boundary of the land as Ezekiel describes it in his vision of Israel's restored territory, situated between the borders of Damascus and Hamath (Ezek. 47:16). The site has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Siddim
entries.dictNote: The Vale of Siddim was a valley described as full of tar pits, where the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, and three other cities clashed with the invading coalition led by Chedorlaomer (Genesis 14:3, 8, 10). Genesis identifies it with the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea, suggesting the battle took place in the region later bordered by, or submerged under, that sea. Its precise location remains debated among geographers of the southern Dead Sea basin.

entries.dictNote: Sidon was the older of the two great Phoenician port cities, north of Tyre, and its name is used in some Old Testament passages for Phoenician trade and craftsmanship generally. It was allotted to Asher but never conquered, and it remained an independent trading power through most of the biblical period. Jesus withdrew to its region at least once, and Paul's ship touched there under Julius the centurion's custody on the voyage to Rome. A sarcophagus of Sidon's king Eshmunazar II, inscribed with a long Phoenician royal text, is one of the best preserved records of the city's own royal history.

entries.title: Silas
entries.dictNote: Silas was a leading member of the Jerusalem church chosen to accompany Paul on his second missionary journey after Paul and Barnabas split up, and he is likely the same person Paul calls Silvanus in his letters. He was imprisoned with Paul at Philippi, where the two of them sang hymns at midnight before an earthquake shook the prison doors open, and the jailer and his household were converted as a result. Silas later worked with Peter as well, helping deliver Peter's first letter to churches in Asia Minor.

entries.title: Simeon
entries.summary: Shimon, one of Jacob's sons, also the tribe descended from him
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Ezekiel, Luke, Acts, 2 Peter, Revelation
entries.dictNote: Simeon was Jacob's second son, and along with his brother Levi he carried out the massacre of Shechem's men after their sister Dinah's rape, an act of vengeance their father Jacob condemned on his deathbed. His tribe's territory was eventually absorbed within Judah's rather than remaining independent. A very different Simeon, centuries later, was a devout old man in Jerusalem who had been promised he would not die before seeing the Messiah, and he recognized the infant Jesus the moment Mary and Joseph brought him to the temple.

entries.dictNote: Sina is the Greek form of Sinai used in the New Testament. Stephen recounts God's appearance to Moses at the mountain in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:30, 38), and Paul uses Mount Sinai allegorically in Galatians, contrasting the covenant of law given there, which he associates with slavery, against the freedom of the promise given to Abraham (Galatians 4:24-25).

entries.dictNote: Sinai, also called Horeb, is the mountain where Israel camped for about a year after the exodus and received the law through Moses, its base in the plain of er-Rahah able to hold the whole camp in view of the summit. Tradition since at least the fourth century AD has identified it with Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai peninsula, where the monastery of Saint Catherine now stands, though other locations both within the peninsula and in Arabia have been proposed and the identification cannot be settled with certainty. It was there that Israel entered into covenant as a nation and received instructions for the tabernacle before resuming its journey toward Canaan.

entries.dictNote: Sinim appears once, in Isaiah 49:12, as a distant land from which God promises to gather his scattered people, named there alongside the north and the west. entries.dictNote: Siphmoth was one of the towns in the Negev of Judah to which David sent a share of the plunder recovered from an Amalekite raid, part of a gesture to the elders of Judah who had sheltered him during his years as a fugitive (1 Sam. 30:28). Its location is unknown.

entries.title: Sirah
entries.dictNote: A well north of Hebron from which Joab's men recalled Abner after David had let him leave in peace; Joab then killed Abner in revenge for his brother's death (2 Samuel 3:26). The site is generally identified with a spring still called Ain Sarah.

entries.summary: Smyrna, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Smyrna, an ancient Ionian port city on the western coast of Asia Minor, about forty miles north of Ephesus. Its church was one of the seven addressed in Revelation and received no rebuke, only a warning of coming suffering and a promise of the crown of life (Rev. 2:8-11). Its early bishop Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, was martyred there around 155 AD. The city survives today as Izmir, and excavations of its Roman-era agora have confirmed the prosperity the city already had in the first century.

Jesus himself invoked Sodom's fate as a warning more severe than anything faced by towns that rejected his disciples.

entries.title: Solomon
entries.summary: Jesus invokes him twice as a byword for splendor (12:27, dressed lilies outshine him) and for wisdom outdone (11:31, ‘something greater than Solomon is here’). Josephus has Solomon ask God for exactly the thing Luke's Jesus says he had — understanding, not riches — and get it granted beyond any mortal before or since.
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Psalm, Proverbs, Song of Solomon, Jeremiah, Matthew, Luke, John, Acts
entries.dictNote: Solomon was David and Bathsheba's son and Israel's third king, placed on the throne in a rushed ceremony after his half-brother Adonijah tried to seize it while David lay dying. Early in his reign he asked God for wisdom rather than wealth or long life and received all three anyway, and he used the resulting forty-year reign to build the Jerusalem temple his father had wanted to build, organize the kingdom into administrative districts, and turn Israel into a regional power with a reputation that reportedly reached the Queen of Sheba. Gate structures at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer, the exact three cities 1 Kings names as his building projects, follow a matching architectural plan and have long been attributed to Solomon's construction program, though archaeologists still argue over whether they actually date to his reign or a century later.
entries.dictSource: Source: Tyndale Bible Dictionary; Baker Encyclopedia of the Bible (Logos)

He is probably the same man Paul calls Sosipater, his kinsman, in Romans 16:21.

entries.title: Sophereth
entries.dictNote: Sophereth headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," temple workers whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57). Nothing further is recorded about him.

entries.title: Sorek
entries.dictNote: The Valley of Sorek, a wadi running west from the Judean hill country toward the Mediterranean near Joppa, was home to Delilah, the woman Samson loved who was bribed by the Philistine lords to discover the secret of his strength (Judg. 16:4). The same valley, now called Wadi es-Sarar, later carried the cart bearing the captured Ark of the Covenant back from Philistine territory toward Beth-shemesh.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sosipater
entries.dictNote: Sosipater was a kinsman of Paul who joined him in sending greetings to the church at Rome (Romans 16:21). He is probably the same man as Sopater of Berea, who accompanied Paul from Greece on his return through Macedonia (Acts 20:4).

entries.title: Sosthenes
entries.summary: of safe strength; Sosthenes, a Christian
entries.dictNote: Sosthenes was the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth who was seized and beaten in front of the Roman proconsul Gallio's judgment seat after the Jewish community's case against Paul was dismissed (Acts 18:12-17). Paul later names a Sosthenes as a co-sender of 1 Corinthians, calling him “our brother” (1 Corinthians 1:1), and tradition has long identified him with the same man, now a Christian, though the text does not confirm it.

entries.title: Sotai
entries.dictNote: Sotai headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," a class of temple workers grouped alongside the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Spain
entries.dictNote: Paul mentions his intention to visit Spain on his way from Rome, hoping the Roman church would help him on his journey after he had first delivered the collection for Jerusalem's poor (Rom. 15:24, 28). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain; the book of Acts ends with him under house arrest in Rome without recording the trip, though early Christian tradition holds that he was released and completed the journey before his final imprisonment and execution.

entries.title: Stachys
entries.dictNote: Stachys was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets as 'my beloved' in Romans 16:9, part of the long list of individual believers Paul singles out for personal recognition. Nothing more about him is recorded in the New Testament.

entries.title: Stephanas
entries.dictNote: Stephanas and his household were among the first converts in Corinth, and Paul specifically commends them for devoting themselves to serving the church, describing their visit to him as a source of real refreshment.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Stephen
entries.dictNote: Stephen was one of seven men chosen to oversee food distribution for Greek-speaking widows in the early Jerusalem church, but he quickly became known for miracles and bold public debate rather than administrative work. His defense before the Jewish council, a long recap of Israel's history culminating in an accusation that his hearers had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One just as their ancestors killed the prophets, got him dragged out and stoned to death, making him Christianity's first martyr. A young man named Saul, who would later become Paul, held the coats of the men throwing the stones and approved of the killing.

entries.title: Stoick
entries.summary: a "Stoic" (as occupying a particular porch in Athens), i.e. adherent of a certin philosophy
entries.dictNote: Not a person but an adjective describing followers of Stoicism, the Greek philosophical school founded by Zeno of Citium that taught self-control and rational acceptance of fate as the path to virtue. Acts 17:18 pairs "certain philosophers of the Epicureans and of the Stoics" among those who debated with Paul in the Athens marketplace before he addressed the Areopagus.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Suah
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Asher listed among the sons of Zophah in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:36.

entries.title: Succoth
entries.summary: Succoth, the name of a place in Egypt and of three in Palestine
entries.books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalm
entries.dictNote: Succoth, “booths,” was Israel's first campsite after leaving Egypt, and separately the name of a town east of the Jordan near the Jabbok where Jacob built shelters for his livestock on returning from Paddan-aram. Its leaders refused to help Gideon's exhausted troops during their pursuit of the Midianites, for which Gideon punished them on his return, and the plain around the town later provided clay for casting the bronze furnishings of Solomon's temple.

entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Succothbenoth
entries.summary: booths of (the) daughters; brothels, i.e. idoalatrous tents for impure purpose
entries.dictNote: Succoth-benoth was a deity brought to Samaria by colonists from Babylon whom the Assyrians resettled there after conquering the northern kingdom of Israel, part of a patchwork of foreign gods the new population continued worshiping alongside a token fear of the Lord (2 Kings 17:24-30). Scholars generally identify the name with a garbled Hebrew rendering of Zarpanitu, the Babylonian goddess who was consort to the chief god Marduk.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Suchathite
entries.summary: a Sukathite or descendant of an unknown Israelite named Sukah
entries.dictNote: Suchathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, named in 1 Chronicles 2:55 alongside the Tirathites and Shimeathites and identified there as Kenites descended from Hammath, father of the house of Rechab.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sukkiims
entries.summary: a Sukkite, or inhabitant of some place near Egypt (i.e. hut-dwellers)
entries.dictNote: Sukkiims were a people who marched with Pharaoh Shishak's Egyptian army when it invaded Judah in Rehoboam's fifth year, listed alongside Libyans and Cushites among his troops. The name likely means tent-dwellers, and some ancient translators rendered it as troglodytes, cave-dwelling nomads along the Red Sea coast.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sur
entries.summary: Sur, a gate of the temple
entries.dictNote: Sur is not a person but the name of a gate at the temple or royal palace in Jerusalem, mentioned in 2 Kings 11:6 as one of the posts assigned to the guard during Jehoiada's coup, which placed the young Joash on the throne and removed the usurper Athaliah. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 23:5 calls the same gate "the gate of the foundation," suggesting either an alternate name for the same entrance or a variation between the two accounts. Its appearance in older name lists likely comes from treating the Hebrew phrase "gate of Sur" as though the second word were a personal name.

entries.title: Susanchites
entries.summary: a Shushankite (collectively) or inhabitants of some unknown place in Assyrian
entries.dictNote: Susanchites were people from Shushan, the great city of Susa in Elam that later served as a winter capital of the Persian empire, among the foreign groups settled in Samaria who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple. Susa's excavated ruins include the palace of Darius and Xerxes, and the site also yielded the famous law code stele of Hammurabi, carried there centuries earlier as war plunder.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Susanna
entries.dictNote: One of several women who traveled with Jesus and the twelve disciples and helped support their ministry out of their own means, named alongside Mary Magdalene and Joanna in Luke 8:3. Nothing further is recorded about her.

entries.title: Susi
entries.dictNote: Susi was the father of Gaddi, the representative of the tribe of Manasseh among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:11). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sychar
entries.summary: Sychar (i.e. Shekar), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: A Samaritan town near Jacob's well, where Jesus rested and spoke with a Samaritan woman in John 4. Early Christian tradition, from the Crusader period on, identified it with nearby Shechem, but most modern scholars instead locate it at 'Askar, a village at the base of Mount Ebal about a mile from the well; the well itself has been preserved and venerated continuously enough that its location, unlike many biblical sites, is not seriously disputed.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Sychem
entries.summary: Sychem (i.e. Shekem), the name of a Canaanite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Sychem is the Greek form of Shechem, used in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin when he recounts that the patriarchs were buried in a tomb Abraham had bought there from the sons of Hamor (Acts 7:16). The Genesis narrative actually records two separate transactions, Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite and Jacob's later purchase of land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, and Stephen's speech appears to compress the two; Shechem itself, modern Tell Balata, has been extensively excavated and shows a fortified Bronze Age city consistent with the biblical setting.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Syene
entries.summary: Seven, a place in Upper Egypt
entries.dictNote: Syene was Egypt's southern frontier town, paired with Migdol in the north as the two ends of the land in Ezekiel's oracles against Egypt (Ezekiel 29:10; 30:6). It sits at modern Aswan, opposite the island of Elephantine at the Nile's first cataract, a strategic gateway between Egypt and Nubia that also gave its name to the region's famous red granite, syenite. Thousands of Aramaic papyri recovered from Elephantine document a Jewish military garrison stationed there in the fifth century BC, evidence of a long-standing Judean presence at this same frontier post.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Syntyche
entries.summary: an accident; Syntyche, a Christian female
entries.dictNote: Syntyche was a woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul urges, alongside Euodia, to "agree in the Lord" after some unrecorded disagreement between them (Philippians 4:2-3). Paul calls both women his fellow workers who had "labored side by side" with him in spreading the gospel, showing the dispute was between valued ministry partners, not marginal figures.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Syracuse
entries.dictNote: Syracuse was not a person but a major Greek city on the southeastern coast of Sicily, founded as a Corinthian colony in the eighth century BC. Paul's ship stopped there for three days on the voyage to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 28:12), by which time it had long been a Roman provincial city, famous earlier as the home of Archimedes.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Syria
entries.summary: Syria (i.e. Tsyria or Tyre), a region of Asia
entries.dictNote: Syria, called Aram in the Old Testament, was the broad region northeast of Israel stretching toward the Euphrates, home to a number of small Aramean kingdoms before coming under Assyrian, then Persian, then Greek and Roman control. In the New Testament, Syria's chief city Antioch became the base for the earliest Gentile church and the starting point of Paul's missionary journeys; Luke notes that Jesus was born during a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria, and Paul passed through the province repeatedly on his travels.

entries.label: 6 books

entries.title: Syrophenician
entries.summary: a Syro-phœnician woman, i.e. a female native of Phœnicia in Syria
entries.dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for a Gentile of Phoenician descent from the Roman province of Syria, used in Mark 7:26 to describe the woman whose daughter Jesus healed from a distance near Tyre; Matthew's parallel calls her "a woman of Canaan" (Matt. 15:22). The term distinguished Syrian Phoenicians from the Phoenicians of Libya around Carthage. Her persistent faith, despite Jesus's initial refusal, became a byword for Gentile inclusion in the gospel.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Taanach
entries.summary: Taanak or Tanak, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Taanach was a royal Canaanite city on the southwest edge of the Jezreel Valley, near Megiddo, whose king Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:21); it was later assigned to the Levites of Kohath, though its Canaanite population was never fully driven out (Judges 1:27). It figures in Deborah's victory song as one of the battle sites near "the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19), and excavations at the site have uncovered Canaanite cult objects and fortifications spanning the period these accounts describe.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Taanath-shiloh
entries.dictNote: Taanath-shiloh marked a point on the southern border of the tribal territory of Ephraim, named only in Joshua 16:6. Its name, roughly "approach to Shiloh," suggests it lay along a route travelers used to reach the sanctuary town of Shiloh, and it is commonly identified with the ruin of Ta'na southeast of Shechem.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tabaoth
entries.dictNote: Tabaoth's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43; Nehemiah 7:46). Nothing further is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tabbath
entries.summary: Tabbath, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Tabbath, a site near the Jordan south of Beth-shean, marking the route the Midianite army fled after Gideon's three hundred routed their camp (Judg. 7:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tabeal
entries.summary: Tabeel, the name of a Syrian and of a Persian
entries.dictNote: Tabeal, also spelled Tabeel, is used of two different men. One was the father of a man whom the kings of Syria and Israel plotted to install on Judah's throne in place of Ahaz, a scheme Isaiah confronted with his sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:1-6). The other was a Persian-appointed official in Samaria who joined in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7-8).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Taberah
entries.summary: Taberah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Wilderness site where fire from the Lord broke out among the Israelites after they complained about their hardships, burning the outskirts of the camp until Moses interceded and the fire died down (Num. 11:1-3). Its name, meaning "burning," commemorates the event, and Moses recalls it alongside the nearby Kibroth-hattaavah in his closing review of Israel's wilderness rebellions (Deut. 9:22).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tabitha
entries.summary: the gazelle; Tabitha (i.e. Tabjetha), a Christian female
entries.dictNote: Tabitha was a disciple at Joppa known for her charity and good works, whom Peter raised from the dead after the local believers sent for him following her sudden death (Acts 9:36-42). Luke gives her Aramaic name, Tabitha, alongside its Greek equivalent, Dorcas, both meaning gazelle, since her circle included both Jewish and Greek-speaking believers.

entries.title: Tabor
entries.summary: Tabor, a mountain in Palestine, also a city adjacent
entries.books: Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Psalm, Jeremiah, Hosea
entries.dictNote: Mount Tabor is a distinctive, dome-shaped peak rising from the Jezreel Valley on the border of Zebulun and Issachar. Deborah summoned Barak and Israel's forces there before their victory over Sisera's army, and Gideon later avenged his brothers' deaths at the hands of Midianite kings near the same mountain. The psalmist pairs Tabor with Hermon as poetic emblems of God's creation, and Hosea and Jeremiah both invoke it in oracles of judgment. A separate Levitical town of the same name belonged to Zebulun.

entries.label: 7 books

entries.title: Tabrimmon
entries.dictNote: Tabrimmon was king of Aram-Damascus and the father of Ben-hadad I, mentioned in 1 Kings 15:18 when Asa of Judah sent temple and palace treasure to Ben-hadad to buy his help against King Baasha of Israel. The reference situates Tabrimmon within the succession of Aramean kings at Damascus who repeatedly clashed with and allied against Israel and Judah in the ninth century BC.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tachmonite
entries.dictNote: Tachmonite, also given as Hachmonite in 1 Chronicles 11:11, marks Jashobeam, chief of David's three mightiest warriors, credited in 2 Samuel 23:8 with killing eight hundred men in a single encounter.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tadmor
entries.dictNote: Tadmor was a city Solomon built in the desert northeast of Damascus, positioned to control the caravan routes crossing the Syrian wilderness (1 Kings 9:18; 2 Chr. 8:4). The Greeks and Romans knew it as Palmyra, and under Roman rule it grew into a wealthy caravan city famous for its colonnaded streets and monumental temples, ruins that stood for centuries as one of the ancient world's best-preserved sites before suffering severe damage during the Syrian civil war.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tahan
entries.summary: Tachan, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim and the ancestral head of the Tahanite clan (Numbers 26:35). In the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 7:25, he appears as the son of Telah rather than directly of Ephraim, one of several small discrepancies between the tribal lists.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tahanites
entries.summary: a Tachanite (collectively) or descendants of Tachan
entries.dictNote: Tahanites were the clan descended from Tahan, a son of Ephraim, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahapanes
entries.summary: Tachpanches, Techaphneches or Tachpenes, a place in Egypt
entries.dictNote: Tahpanhes was a fortified Egyptian city near the eastern edge of the Nile delta where a group of Jewish refugees fled after the assassination of Gedaliah, taking the prophet Jeremiah with them against his counsel. Jeremiah prophesied there that Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne over buried stones at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace, a scene of judgment on Egypt. Archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the site, identified as Tell Defenneh, and uncovered a brick platform at a palace entrance that he proposed matched the setting of Jeremiah's prophecy.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tahath
entries.summary: Tachath, the name of a place in the Desert, also of three Israelites
entries.dictNote: Tahath was an unidentified desert campsite of the Israelites during the wilderness wanderings, listed between Makheloth and Terah in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Numbers 33:26-27). The same name also belongs to two separate Levites in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:9, 22) and to a descendant of Ephraim (1 Chronicles 7:20).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tahpenes
entries.dictNote: Tahpenes was an Egyptian queen, the wife of the pharaoh who gave asylum to Hadad the Edomite when he fled Solomon's kingdom. She raised Hadad's son in Pharaoh's own household and gave her sister in marriage to Hadad (1 Kings 11:19-20).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahrea
entries.dictNote: A great-grandson of Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin preserved after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:41); the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 8:35 gives his name as Tarea.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tahtim-hodshi
entries.dictNote: Tahtim-hodshi appears only in the account of Joab's census route east of the Jordan, somewhere north of Gilead (2 Sam. 24:6). The Hebrew text is difficult, and many scholars think the phrase is a corruption of a reference to the Hittites of Kadesh, pointing to the Hittite center on the Orontes river rather than naming a distinct town.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Talmai
entries.summary: Talmai, the name of a Canaanite and a Syrian
entries.dictNote: Talmai was the name of one of the Anakim giants Caleb drove out of Hebron, and also of a king of Geshur whose daughter Maacah married David and became Absalom's mother.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Talmon
entries.dictNote: Talmon was the head of a family of temple gatekeepers among the returning exiles, a hereditary role his descendants continued to serve in.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Tamah
entries.dictNote: Tamah, or Thamah, was the head of a family among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tamar
entries.summary: Tamar, the name of three women and a place
entries.dictNote: Two women named Tamar stand out in the Old Testament. Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar was widowed twice without bearing an heir and, when Judah failed to give her his third son as custom required, disguised herself as a prostitute and conceived twins by Judah himself, a scheme Judah eventually admitted was more righteous than his own failure to provide for her. A different Tamar was David's daughter, raped by her own half-brother Amnon, an assault that went unpunished by David and led directly to Amnon's murder by Tamar's full brother Absalom.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Tammuz
entries.dictNote: Tammuz was the Mesopotamian god of shepherds and vegetation, known to the Sumerians as Dumuzi and identified by later writers with the Greek Adonis. Ezekiel condemns the women of Jerusalem for sitting at the temple's north gate “weeping for Tammuz” (Ezekiel 8:14), a rite mourning the god's yearly death and descent to the underworld. The name was later applied to the fourth month of the Hebrew civil calendar, corresponding to parts of June and July.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tanhumeth
entries.dictNote: Tanhumeth was a Netophathite whose son Seraiah was among the army captains who submitted to Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Taphath
entries.dictNote: A daughter of Solomon who married Ben-abinadab, one of the twelve district officers responsible for supplying provisions to the royal court on a rotating monthly basis (1 Kings 4:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tappuah
entries.summary: Tappuach, the name of two places in Palestine, also of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Tappuah was a town on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh's territories, and also the name of a son of Hebron in the genealogies of Judah.

entries.title: Taralah
entries.dictNote: Taralah was one of the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the settlements in the hill country near Gibeon (Josh. 18:27). No convincing modern identification for the site has been established.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarea
entries.dictNote: Tarea, also spelled Tahrea (1 Chronicles 9:41), was a son of Micah descended from King Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:35).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tarshish
entries.summary: Tarshish, a place on the Mediterranean, hence, the ephithet of a merchant vessel (as if for or from that port); also the name of a Persian and of an Israelite
entries.books: Genesis, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Esther, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Jonah
entries.dictNote: Tarshish appears first as one of the sons of Javan in the table of nations, and later as a distant western port that became proverbial for long ocean voyages and imported wealth; “ships of Tarshish” came to describe any large seagoing vessel regardless of destination. Solomon's navy sailed to a Tarshish for gold and exotic goods, and it was to Tarshish that Jonah tried to flee by ship from Joppa rather than go to Nineveh. Ancient writers and modern scholars have proposed locations ranging from a Phoenician colony in southern Spain, near the mouth of the Guadalquivir, to a port on the Red Sea or Indian coast, and the question remains unsettled.

entries.title: Tarsus
entries.summary: Tarsus, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Tarsus was the capital of the Roman province of Cilicia and the birthplace of the apostle Paul, who called it no mean city (Acts 21:39). It sat on the Cydnus River about twelve miles from the Mediterranean and was known for its schools of philosophy and rhetoric, rivaling Athens and Alexandria in the ancient world. Barnabas brought Paul there from Jerusalem, and excavation at the site's mound of Gözlü Kule has confirmed continuous settlement stretching back to the Bronze Age.

entries.title: Tartak
entries.summary: Tartak, a deity of the Avvites
entries.dictNote: Not a person but one of two gods worshiped by the Avvites, a people the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting Israel's population (2 Kings 17:31). Almost nothing is known about the god's nature or cult beyond this single mention alongside another Avvite god, Nibhaz.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tartan
entries.dictNote: Tartan was not a personal name but an Assyrian military title meaning roughly "commander-in-chief." One tartan served as one of Sennacherib's envoys sent to demand Jerusalem's surrender under Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:17). An earlier tartan led Sargon II's campaign against Ashdod, an operation Sargon's own palace inscriptions at Khorsabad independently record (Isaiah 20:1).

entries.title: Tatnai
entries.dictNote: Tattenai was a Persian provincial governor who questioned the legitimacy of the Jews rebuilding the Jerusalem temple, and his official inquiry to King Darius led to the discovery of Cyrus's original decree, which confirmed the project's authorization and resulted in Tattenai being ordered to support it instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tebah
entries.summary: Tebach, the name of a Mesopotamian and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: The eldest son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tebaliah
entries.dictNote: The third son of Hosah, a Levite gatekeeper from the family of Merari, listed among those assigned by lot to guard duty at the temple in 1 Chronicles 26:11.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tebeth
entries.dictNote: Tebeth was not a person but the tenth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly corresponding to December-January, during which Esther was brought before King Ahasuerus (Esther 2:16). The word is borrowed from Babylonian, where the month Tebetu shares the same name, reflecting the calendar Jews adopted during and after the exile.

entries.title: Tehinnah
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah credited as the founder of Ir-nahash, "city of Nahash," named in the tribal genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:12).

entries.title: Tekoa
entries.dictNote: Tekoa was a fortified hill town in Judah about six miles south of Bethlehem, overlooking the wilderness that bears its name, strengthened by Rehoboam among his defensive cities (2 Chronicles 11:6). Joab used a "wise woman of Tekoa" to persuade David to bring Absalom back from exile (2 Samuel 14:2), and the shepherd Amos, "among the herdmen of Tekoa," was called from there to prophesy against Israel (Amos 1:1).
