entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Tekoite
entries.summary: a Tekoite or inhabitant of Tekoah
entries.dictNote: Tekoite marks someone from Tekoa, a town in Judah's hill country south of Bethlehem. It was the hometown of the prophet Amos, of the wise woman Joab sent to persuade David to reconcile with his exiled son Absalom, and of at least two of David's mighty men.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Tel-abib
entries.dictNote: A settlement of Judean exiles beside the river Chebar in Babylonia, where the prophet Ezekiel lived among his fellow captives (Ezek. 3:15). The name comes from an Akkadian phrase for an ancient ruin-mound; the founders of modern Tel Aviv borrowed it in 1910 for its Hebrew sense of a mound of spring, joining old ruin and new growth in one name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tel-haresha
entries.dictNote: Tel-haresha, hill of the wood, was a place in Babylonia from which a group of exiles returned to Jerusalem after the exile, listed alongside Tel-melah among those who could not prove their Israelite genealogy (Ezra 2:59; Nehemiah 7:61). Its Babylonian location has not been identified.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tel-melah
entries.dictNote: Tel-melah, hill of salt, was a place in Babylonia from which a group of Jewish exiles returned after the captivity, named alongside Tel-haresha among those unable to document their Israelite ancestry (Ezra 2:59; Nehemiah 7:61). Its site in Babylonia is unknown.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Telah
entries.dictNote: Telah appears in the genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7 as an ancestor of Joshua, Moses's successor. Nothing beyond his place in that family line is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Telaim
entries.dictNote: The place where Saul mustered his army before his campaign against the Amalekites, in the Negev of Judah (1 Sam. 15:4). It is probably the same site as Telem, mentioned in Joshua 15:24.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Telassar
entries.dictNote: Telassar is named by the Assyrian king's messenger, alongside Gozan and Haran, as one of the territories already conquered and resettled by the children of Eden before Assyria's assault on Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:12; Isa. 37:12). It lay somewhere in Mesopotamia, and some have proposed identifying it with a site near Sinjar, though the identification remains uncertain.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Telem
entries.summary: Telem, the name of a place in Idumaea, also of a temple doorkeeper
entries.dictNote: Town on Judah's southern border (Josh. 15:24), possibly the same as Telaim, where Saul mustered his army before attacking the Amalekites (1 Sam. 15:4). The same name also belonged to a temple gatekeeper who, after the exile, agreed to send away the foreign wife he had married (Ezra 10:24).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tema
entries.summary: Tema, a son of Ishmael, and the region settled by him
entries.dictNote: Tema was an oasis town in the north Arabian desert on the caravan route between Damascus and the Arabian interior, named for a son of Ishmael whose descendants settled there (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Job's friend Eliphaz compares the failed hope of Job's rescuers to the caravans of Tema (Job 6:19), and a large inscribed stone found at the site records that the Babylonian king Nabonidus made Tema his residence for a decade in the sixth century BC, confirming its importance into the exilic period.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Temani
entries.summary: a Temanite or descendant of Teman
entries.dictNote: Teman was a grandson of Esau and the ancestor of an Edomite clan renowned for wisdom, and Job's friend Eliphaz is identified as a Temanite.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Temeni
entries.dictNote: Temeni was one of the sons of Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:6. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Terah
entries.summary: Abraham's father, named once in the genealogy (3:34). Josephus gives him an actual date — 292 years after the flood — trying to pin Genesis's long lifespans to a real chronology, the same impulse behind Luke's own carefully unbroken chain.
entries.dictNote: Terah was Abraham's father, and Genesis records that he set out from Ur with Abraham, Abraham's wife Sarah, and his grandson Lot, intending to reach Canaan, but the family settled in Haran instead and Terah died there, leaving Abraham to complete the journey after God's call came to him directly.

witness.excerpt: Terah begat Abram in his seventieth year… Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah: and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Teresh
entries.dictNote: Teresh was a eunuch who guarded the entrance to the palace of the Persian king Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I. Along with a fellow guard, Bigthan, he plotted to assassinate the king, but Mordecai learned of the conspiracy and reported it, and the two men were executed. The record of Mordecai's service was later read to the king and became the turning point that led to Mordecai's promotion (Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tertius
entries.dictNote: The scribe who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans as Paul dictated it, and who added his own greeting to the Roman church in his own voice (Romans 16:22), offering a rare glimpse of the ancient practice of using a secretary, or amanuensis, to produce a letter.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tertullus
entries.dictNote: Tertullus was a professional orator hired by the Jewish leadership to present their accusations against Paul before the Roman governor Felix in Caesarea. He flattered Felix at length before charging Paul with stirring up unrest, leading the sect of the Nazarenes, and attempting to profane the temple (Acts 24:1-9).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Thahash
entries.dictNote: A son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants (Genesis 22:24). Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Thamar
entries.dictNote: Thamar is the Greek form of Tamar, the Canaanite woman who disguised herself and conceived twins, Perez and Zerah, by her father-in-law Judah after he had failed to give her his youngest son in marriage (Gen. 38). She is one of only four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:3).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Thebez
entries.dictNote: Thebez was a fortified town northeast of Shechem where Abimelech, Gideon's son who had made himself king, was killed while besieging its central tower; a woman dropped a millstone on his head, and he had his armor-bearer finish him off rather than die at a woman's hand (Judges 9:50-54). Joab later cites the episode as a cautionary example when explaining to David's messenger why the army had kept its distance from a city wall during the siege that got Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11:21).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Theophilus
entries.summary: friend of God; Theophilus, a Christian
entries.dictNote: Theophilus was the person to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel and the book of Acts (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1). Luke addresses him with the same title, 'most excellent,' that he elsewhere uses for the Roman governors Felix and Festus, which has led some to think Theophilus held an official rank, though nothing certain is known about him beyond these two dedications.

entries.title: Thessalonian
entries.summary: a Thessalonican, i.e. inhabitant of Thessalonice
entries.dictNote: Thessalonian designates an inhabitant of Thessalonica, a major port city in Roman Macedonia where Paul founded a church during his second missionary journey after a rocky start that forced him to leave the city quickly. His two letters to this church are among the earliest documents in the New Testament.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Thessalonica
entries.summary: Thessalonice, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port city on the Via Egnatia named for Alexander the Great's half sister. Paul preached in its synagogue on his second missionary journey and planted a church there, though opposition from local Jews forced him to flee to Berea after only a few weeks (Acts 17:1-10). Luke's account calls the city's magistrates "politarchs," an unusual Greek title once doubted by critics until archaeologists found the same word inscribed on a Roman arch from the city, confirming Luke's precision. Paul later wrote two letters to the congregation he founded there, and the city, modern Thessaloniki, remains one of Greece's largest.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Theudas
entries.dictNote: Theudas led a failed uprising against Roman rule, cited by the Pharisee Gamaliel as an example of a movement that collapsed once its leader was killed (Acts 5:36). The Jewish historian Josephus describes a rebel named Theudas active around AD 44, a decade or more after Gamaliel's speech, and scholars have long debated whether this is the same man, a different Theudas, or evidence of a common revolutionary name in the period.

entries.title: Thomas
entries.dictNote: Thomas was one of the twelve apostles, remembered chiefly for refusing to believe the other disciples' report that Jesus had risen until he could see and touch the wounds himself, earning him the label doubting Thomas ever since. When Jesus did appear and offered his hands and side, Thomas's response was the flattest declaration of Jesus's divinity in any Gospel, my Lord and my God, and Jesus's gentle reply blessed everyone who would believe without that kind of proof. Tradition holds Thomas carried the gospel as far as India, where an ancient Christian community still traces its founding to him.

entries.title: Thyatira
entries.summary: Thyatira, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Thyatira was a commercial city in the Roman province of Asia known for its trade guilds, especially dyers who worked with a purple dye extracted from the madder root; inscriptions naming the city's dyers' guild have been found among its ruins. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul converted at Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). It was also home to one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, commended for its love and service but rebuked for tolerating a false prophetess who led believers into idolatry and sexual immorality (Revelation 2:18-29).

entries.dictNote: Tiberias was a city on the Sea of Galilee built by Herod Antipas and named for the Roman emperor Tiberius, and the lake itself is sometimes called the Sea of Tiberias in John's Gospel.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tiberius
entries.summary: The emperor whose fifteenth regnal year dates the start of John's ministry (3:1) — the same verse that names Pilate, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias all at once. Josephus's own account of Tiberius's court, years later, follows the Herodian family Agrippa grew up inside of — the same royal household Luke's chronology is built around.
entries.dictNote: (in full, Tiberius Claudius Nero), the second Roman emperor, successor of Augustus, who began to reign A.D. 14 and reigned until A.D. 37. He was the son of Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, and hence a stepson of Augustus. He was born at Rome on the 18th of November, B.C. 45. He became emperor in his fifty-fifth year, after having distinguished himself as a commander in various wars, and having evinced talents of a high order as an orator and an administrator of civil affairs. He even gained the reputation of possessing the sterner virtues of the Roman character, and was regarded as entirely worthy of the imperial honors to which his birth and supposed personal merits at length opened the way. Yet, on being raised to the supreme power, he suddenly became, or showed himself to be a very different man. His subsequent life was one of inactivity, sloth and self-indulgence. He was despotic in his government, cruel and vindictive in his disposition. He died A.D. 37, at the age of 78, after a reign of twenty-three years. Our Saviour was put to death in the reign of Tiberius.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tibhath
entries.dictNote: A city belonging to Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, from which David took large quantities of bronze after defeating him (1 Chronicles 18:8); the parallel account in 2 Samuel 8:8 calls the same city Betah. Solomon later used bronze from this campaign to make furnishings for the temple.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tibni
entries.dictNote: Tibni son of Ginath was a rival claimant to the throne of Israel after the death of Zimri, backed by roughly half the people for four years while Omri's faction contended against him. Omri eventually prevailed and Tibni died, leaving Omri sole king (1 Kings 16:21-22).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tidal
entries.dictNote: Tidal, called “king of nations” (Hebrew “Goyim”), was one of four eastern kings, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, who campaigned against a coalition of Canaanite cities and carried off Lot before Abraham pursued and defeated them (Genesis 14:1-16). His name corresponds to Tudhaliya, a royal name borne by several Hittite kings, and “Goyim” most likely designates a confederation of peoples east of the Tigris rather than a single nation. The episode is the Bible's earliest recorded military campaign and treats Abraham as a regional power capable of defeating an organized royal coalition.

entries.title: Tiglath-pileser
entries.summary: Tiglath-Pileser or Tilgath-pilneser, an Assyryrian king
entries.dictNote: Tiglath-pileser the Third was an aggressive Assyrian king whose campaigns against Israel and Syria are recorded both in the Bible and extensively in his own royal inscriptions, which independently confirm the tribute payments and territorial conquests described in 2 Kings.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Tikvah
entries.summary: Tikvah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men in the Old Testament carry this name. One was the father of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah, who confirmed the authenticity of the law scroll found during Josiah's temple repairs (2 Kings 22:14). The other was the father of Jahzeiah, one of the few who opposed Ezra's plan to have Israelite men separate from their foreign wives (Ezra 10:15).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tilon (from the margin)
entries.dictNote: One of four sons of Shimon listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr. 4:20). Nothing beyond his name and parentage is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Timaeus
entries.dictNote: The father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar Jesus healed outside Jericho (Mark 10:46). Mark names him only to identify his son; the name Bartimaeus itself means "son of Timaeus." Nothing else about Timaeus is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Timna
entries.summary: Timna, the name of two Edomites
entries.dictNote: Timna was the name of an Edomite clan leader and also of a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, whose own son Amalek became the ancestor of Israel's long-standing enemy.

entries.title: Timnah
entries.summary: Timnah, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Timnah was a Philistine town, the hometown of the woman Samson wanted to marry, whose wedding feast triggered the riddle contest and violence that began Samson's long conflict with the Philistines.

entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Timnath-heres
entries.dictNote: Timnath-heres, portion of the sun, was the town Joshua received as his inheritance in the hill country of Ephraim and where he was buried after his death (Joshua 19:50; 24:30; Judges 2:9). It lay north of the hill of Gaash, roughly ten miles southwest of Shechem. The book of Joshua elsewhere calls the same town Timnath-serah, likely a transposed spelling of the same name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Timnite
entries.summary: a Timnite or inhabitant of Timnah
entries.dictNote: Timnite marks Samson's Philistine father-in-law, whose daughter Samson had married, as a man of Timnah. After Samson's wife was given to another man, the Timnite's household was burned in the retaliation that follows in Judges 15.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Timon
entries.dictNote: Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to administer the daily distribution to widows in Acts 6:5. Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Tipsah
entries.dictNote: Tipsah marked the northeastern limit of Solomon's dominion, a crossing point on the Euphrates identified with the Greek Thapsacus, an important ford on the river's trade routes (1 Kings 5:4). Centuries later it was sacked by Menahem, king of Israel, when he seized the throne, because its people had refused to open their gates to him (2 Kings 15:16).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tiras
entries.dictNote: Tiras was the youngest son of Japheth, listed in the Table of Nations as the ancestor of a people group whose location Genesis does not specify (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Later Jewish tradition, recorded by Josephus, associated his descendants with the Thracians, though the identification cannot be confirmed.

entries.title: Tirathite
entries.summary: a Tirathite or inhabitant of an unknown Tirah
entries.dictNote: Tirathites were one of the families of scribes living at Jabez, listed in 1 Chronicles 2:55 alongside the Shimeathites and Suchathites. The passage identifies them as Kenites descended from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab, linking these scribal clans to the same Kenite family that produced Moses' father-in-law Jethro.

entries.title: Tirhakah
entries.dictNote: Tirhakah, known in Egyptian and Kushite records as Taharqa, ruled Egypt and Kush as pharaoh of the twenty-fifth (Kushite) dynasty in the early seventh century BC. The Bible names him as the Kushite king whose advance against Assyria prompted Sennacherib to send a threatening message to Hezekiah during the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:9; Isaiah 37:9). Assyrian records confirm his historicity in detail: the annals and inscribed prisms of both Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal describe their invasions of Egypt and repeated defeats of Taharqa, who was eventually driven back into Nubia.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tirhanah
entries.dictNote: Tirhanah was a son of Caleb son of Hezron by his concubine Maachah, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:48). Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tiria
entries.dictNote: Tiria was one of the sons of Jehaleleel, listed in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:16. Nothing further is known about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tirshatha
entries.summary: the title of a Persian deputy or governor
entries.dictNote: Tirshatha was a Persian-derived title for the governor of Judah under Persian rule, applied to both Nehemiah and, in some readings, Zerubbabel, rather than being a personal name.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tirzah
entries.summary: Tirtsah, a place in Palestine; also an Israelitess
entries.books: Numbers, Joshua, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Song of Solomon
entries.dictNote: Tirzah was an ancient Canaanite royal city that became, after Samaria's founding, an earlier capital of the northern kingdom under Jeroboam and his successors, admired enough for its beauty to be paired with Jerusalem as a standard of loveliness in the Song of Solomon. It was also the scene of Menahem's violent seizure of Israel's throne. The same name belongs to the youngest of Zelophehad's five daughters, whose case established Israelite inheritance rights for women without brothers. Tirzah is generally identified with Tell el-Far'ah North, where French excavations uncovered a substantial Iron Age royal quarter consistent with a former capital city.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Tishbite
entries.summary: a Tishbite or inhabitant of Tishbeh (in Gilead)
entries.dictNote: Tishbite identifies the prophet Elijah as coming from Tishbe, though the exact location of that town, whether in Gilead or further north in Galilee, is debated because of an ambiguity in the Hebrew text of 1 Kings 17:1.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Titus
entries.dictNote: Titus was a Gentile convert and close associate of Paul, entrusted with some of Paul's most sensitive assignments, including carrying a stern letter to the fractious church at Corinth and reporting back on how it was received. Paul later left Titus in Crete to organize the churches there and appoint elders, and the New Testament letter of Titus preserves Paul's instructions for that task. Paul held Titus up as proof that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised to be fully accepted, refusing to have Titus circumcised even under pressure from other Jewish Christians.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Tizite
entries.summary: a Titsite or descendant or inhabitant of an unknown Tits
entries.dictNote: Tizite identifies Joha, brother of Jediael, among David's mighty men; the place the epithet refers to is otherwise unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Toah
entries.dictNote: Toah was a Kohathite Levite listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6:19-34 as an ancestor of the prophet Samuel and of Heman, the temple musician David appointed. The same family line appears elsewhere in Chronicles and Samuel under the variant spellings Nahath and Tohu, reflecting the normal drift in how genealogical records preserved names across generations of copying. His only role in the text is as a link connecting the priestly and musical branches of the Kohathite family to the house of Elkanah.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tob
entries.summary: Tob, a region apparently East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: The land of Tob lay somewhere east of Gilead, toward the Syrian desert, and became a refuge for Jephthah after his half brothers drove him from home for being the son of a prostitute (Judges 11:1-3). He gathered a band of outlaws there until the elders of Gilead, desperate for a military leader against the Ammonites, came to recruit him back (Judges 11:4-11). Men of Tob later appear as mercenaries hired by the Ammonites against David (2 Samuel 10:6, 8, where they are called "Ish-tob," meaning "the men of Tob").

witness.excerpt: Tob.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tob-adonijah
entries.dictNote: A Levite sent out by King Jehoshaphat, along with priests and other Levites, to travel through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the Book of the Law (2 Chronicles 17:7-8).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tobiah
entries.summary: Tobijah, the name of three Israelites and of one Samaritan
entries.dictNote: Tobiah was an Ammonite official who, along with Sanballat, mocked and actively opposed Nehemiah's project to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, and Nehemiah later discovered Tobiah had been secretly given a room inside the temple complex itself through a compromised priest, a violation Nehemiah threw him and his belongings out for.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Tochen
entries.dictNote: Tochen was a town assigned to the tribe of Simeon, listed among a handful of Simeonite settlements in a genealogical record (1 Chron. 4:32). Nothing more is known about it, and its location has not been identified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Togarmah
entries.summary: Togarmah, a son of Gomer and his posterity
entries.dictNote: Togarmah was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, and his descendants are associated with a people in eastern Asia Minor known in Ezekiel's prophecies for trading horses and mules.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Tohu
entries.dictNote: An ancestor of Samuel in the genealogy of the prophet's Ephraimite Levite family, several generations before Samuel's father Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:1).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Toi
entries.summary: Tou or Toi, a Syrian king
entries.dictNote: Toi was a king of Hamath who sent his son to congratulate David after his victory over their mutual enemy Hadadezer, bringing gifts of gold, silver, and bronze.

entries.title: Tola
entries.summary: Tola, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Tola was a judge of Israel who led the nation for twenty-three years, though Judges records no specific military deliverance associated with him, only that he rose up to save Israel and judged from his hometown.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Tolad
entries.dictNote: Tolad, a town of the tribe of Simeon in the Negev of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:29. It is the same place called Eltolad in the earlier town lists of Joshua (15:30, 19:4).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tolaites
entries.summary: a Tolaïte (collectively) or descendants of Tola
entries.dictNote: Tolaites were the clan descended from Tola, the firstborn son of Issachar, counted in the Numbers 26 census. A later judge of Israel, also named Tola, belonged to this same tribe and is recorded in Judges 10:1-2.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tophel
entries.summary: Tophel, a place near the Desert
entries.dictNote: Tophel is named in Deuteronomy 1:1 as one of the wilderness locations near which Moses addressed Israel before his death. It is generally identified with modern Tafileh, a town on the edge of the Edomite plateau east of the Dead Sea, whose name is thought to preserve the ancient one.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tophet
entries.dictNote: Tophet was a site in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where children were burned as sacrifices to the god Molech, a practice Josiah defiled and abolished during his reforms. Jeremiah repeatedly condemns Tophet and warns that the valley would itself become a place of slaughter and burial in judgment. Its grim associations with fire and destruction contributed to later Jewish imagery of Gehenna as a place of punishment.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tophet
entries.dictNote: Tophet, a site in the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem where children were burned in sacrifice to Molech during the later Judean monarchy, a practice King Josiah defiled the site to end (2 Kings 23:10; Jer. 7:31). Isaiah uses it as an image of a burning place already prepared for judgment (Isa. 30:33). Archaeologists have found comparable "tophet" precincts, burial grounds containing cremated infant remains, at Phoenician colonies such as Carthage, though scholars still debate how directly these reflect the child sacrifice the Hebrew prophets condemn.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Trachonitis
entries.summary: rough district; Trachonitis, a region of Syria
entries.dictNote: Trachonitis, meaning "the rugged region," was a volcanic, boulder-strewn district east of the Sea of Galilee, named among the territories governed by Philip the tetrarch in Luke 3:1, part of the political framework Luke uses to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry. Herod the Great had earlier campaigned against bandits who used its lava-field terrain, still known today as the Lejah, as a natural fortress, an account preserved by the first-century historian Josephus. Inscriptions found across the wider Hauran region independently confirm the area's governance first by the Herodian dynasty and then directly by Rome, matching Luke's political framework.

entries.title: Troas
entries.summary: the Troad (or plain of Troy), i.e. Troas, a place in Asia Minor
entries.dictNote: Troas was a port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor near the site of ancient Troy, a major stop on Roman sea routes to Macedonia. Here Paul received his vision of a Macedonian man pleading, "Come over and help us," which redirected his second missionary journey into Europe (Acts 16:8-11); he later raised Eutychus from the dead during an all-night sermon there (Acts 20:6-12) and, on his final journey, left a cloak and some books with Carpus in the city (2 Timothy 4:13).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Trophimus
entries.dictNote: Trophimus was a Gentile companion of Paul from Ephesus, and it was the mistaken belief that Paul had brought Trophimus into the Jerusalem temple's restricted area that triggered the riot leading to Paul's arrest in Acts.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Tryphena
entries.dictNote: A Christian woman at Rome, greeted by Paul together with Tryphosa as women who labored in the Lord (Romans 16:12). Their similar names, both suggesting delicacy or refinement, have led some to suggest they were sisters, though this is not stated in the text.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tryphosa
entries.dictNote: Tryphosa was a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul greets alongside Tryphena in Romans 16:12, commending both as women who work hard in the Lord. Their similar names suggest they may have been sisters, since such paired names occur among household members and freedwomen in Roman inscriptions of the period. Nothing further is known of her.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tubal
entries.summary: Tubal, a postdiluvian patriarch and his posterity
entries.dictNote: Tubal was a son of Japheth and the ancestor of a people the prophets associate with distant northern trade and warfare, frequently paired with Meshech.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Tubal-cain
entries.dictNote: The son of Lamech and Zillah in the line of Cain, described in Genesis 4:22 as the forger of bronze and iron tools, the first metalworker named in the Bible. He appears in a short list of culture-founders in Genesis 4, alongside his half-brother Jabal, father of nomadic herdsmen, and Jubal, father of musicians, marking early developments in craft and technology outside the covenant line of Seth.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Tychicus
entries.summary: fortuitous, i.e. fortunate; Tychicus, a Christian
entries.dictNote: Tychicus was a trusted companion of Paul who carried several of his letters, including Ephesians and Colossians, to their destinations and delivered news of Paul's situation to the churches in person.
entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Tyrannus
entries.dictNote: The owner or teacher associated with a lecture hall in Ephesus where Paul taught daily for two years after being expelled from the local synagogue (Acts 19:9). Whether Tyrannus was a Jewish teacher whose "school" doubled as a private synagogue, or a Greek rhetorician who simply rented out the space, is not stated.

entries.books: Joshua, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Zechariah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts
entries.dictNote: Tyre was the leading Phoenician port, built partly on a rocky mainland site and partly on an offshore island, and it grew wealthy on maritime trade and its famous purple dye, extracted from murex shellfish along its coast. Its king Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen for David's and Solomon's building projects, but the prophets later condemned Tyre's pride and predicted its fall, which came in stages: first to Nebuchadnezzar after a long siege, finally to Alexander the Great, who built a causeway to the island city and took it after seven months. Jesus visited its region, and Paul stopped there on his way back from his third missionary journey. Excavated murex shell middens along the Phoenician coast confirm the large scale dye industry ancient sources describe.

entries.title: Ucal
entries.dictNote: One of two men, along with Ithiel, named as recipients of Agur's sayings that open Proverbs 30 (Proverbs 30:1). Many modern scholars read the underlying Hebrew not as proper names at all but as a statement of Agur's exhaustion, something closer to "I am weary, God, I am weary and worn out," which makes Ucal's status as a real historical person doubtful.

entries.title: Uel
entries.dictNote: Uel was a member of the family of Bani who had married a foreign wife after the return from Babylonian exile and was required to divorce her under Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:34). He is one of many men named in this list who complied with the covenant.

entries.title: Ulai
entries.summary: the Ulai (or Eulaeus), a river of Persia
entries.dictNote: River near Susa, capital of Elam, where Daniel stood when he received his vision of the ram and the goat, symbols of the coming Medo-Persian and Greek empires (Dan. 8:2, 16). It is identified with the Eulaeus, a channel of the river system near ancient Susa in southwestern Iran, a site whose extensive ruins, including the palace of Darius, have been excavated by archaeologists.

entries.dictNote: Ulam was a common name in the genealogies of Manasseh and Benjamin, including a family noted in Chronicles for producing many skilled archers.

entries.title: Ulla
entries.dictNote: An Asherite, head of a family within his tribe, listed among the descendants of Jether in 1 Chronicles 7:39.

entries.title: Ummah
entries.dictNote: A town on the border of the tribe of Asher, named only in Joshua 19:30. Some manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament read "Acco" here instead, and many scholars favor that reading, since the major Asherite coastal city of Acco, which Judges 1:31 explicitly places within Asher's territory, is otherwise strangely missing from this town list.

entries.title: Unni
entries.summary: Unni, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Unni's name means “afflicted.” One man by this name was a Levite musician David appointed to play the harp when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 20). A second Unni was a Levite who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:9).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Uphaz
entries.dictNote: Uphaz appears in poetic parallel with fine gold, used for idol-overlay and for the girdle of the figure in Daniel's vision (Jer. 10:9; Dan. 10:5). Its exact location is unknown, and many scholars think the name is simply a variant or scribal alteration of Ophir, the better-known source of gold in the biblical world, rather than a separate place.

entries.title: Ur
entries.summary: Ur, a place in Chaldaea; also an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ur was a major Sumerian city near the mouth of the Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, the ancestral home from which Abraham's father Terah set out for Canaan (Genesis 11:28, 31; Nehemiah 9:7). British archaeologist Leonard Woolley's excavations there in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered a royal cemetery of some 2,000 burials from the mid-third millennium BC, filled with gold jewelry and the famous inlaid "Standard of Ur," giving a vivid picture of the wealthy Sumerian civilization Abraham's family left behind.

entries.title: Urias
entries.dictNote: Urias is the Greek form of Uriah, appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where David is said to have fathered Solomon "of her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matthew 1:6), a pointed reference to Bathsheba and to David's sin. The man himself is the same Uriah the Hittite of 2 Samuel 11, one of David's loyal soldiers whom David had killed in battle after committing adultery with his wife. Matthew's choice to name Uriah rather than simply Bathsheba keeps David's wrongdoing visible even within the genealogy leading to the Messiah.

entries.books: 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Isaiah, Hosea, Amos, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Uzziah, also called Azariah, became king of Judah at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years, a long and mostly prosperous rule that rebuilt Judah's military and economy, until success made him proud enough to enter the temple and burn incense himself, a priestly duty no king was allowed to perform. Priests confronted him in the act, and leprosy broke out on his forehead immediately, forcing him to live in isolation for the rest of his life while his son ruled in his place. The prophet Isaiah dates the beginning of his own famous temple vision to the year King Uzziah died.

entries.dictNote: Vashti was the Persian queen deposed by King Ahasuerus after she refused his order to display herself before his banquet guests, a refusal that opened the way for Esther to eventually become queen in her place.

entries.title: Vophsi
entries.dictNote: Vophsi was the father of Nahbi, the representative of the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:14). Nothing else is known of him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zaanan
entries.dictNote: A town addressed in Micah's oracle against the towns of Judah's lowlands (Micah 1:11), where the prophet puns on its name, related to a Hebrew word for "go out," by saying its people "come not forth." It was to this camp that Sisera fled after his army's defeat at the Kishon, only to be killed there by Heber's wife Jael (Judges 4:11, 17-21).

entries.title: Zaavan
entries.dictNote: Zaavan, also called Zavan, was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). Nothing further is recorded of him.

entries.dictNote: Zabulon is the Greek form of Zebulun, used in Matthew's quotation of Isaiah to describe the territory where Jesus began his Galilean ministry after leaving Nazareth for Capernaum (Matthew 4:13, 15). Revelation also lists Zabulon among the twelve tribes sealed from every tribe of Israel (Revelation 7:8). The underlying territory is the same tribal allotment of Zebulun described in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Zacchaeus
entries.dictNote: Zacchaeus was a wealthy chief tax collector in Jericho, a job that made him wealthy by overcharging his fellow Jews on behalf of Rome and made him widely hated for it, and he was too short to see Jesus over the crowd so he climbed a sycamore tree to get a look. Jesus spotted him and invited himself to Zacchaeus's house, scandalizing the crowd, and Zacchaeus responded by pledging to give half his wealth to the poor and repay four times what he had defrauded from anyone.

entries.dictNote: Zaccur was a common name among Levites and returning exiles, including one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, representing the tribe of Reuben.

entries.title: Zadok
entries.summary: Tsadok, the name of eight or nine Israelites
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Ezekiel

Zadok anointed Solomon king and became Israel's sole high priest after Solomon exiled the rival priest Abiathar for backing Adonijah's failed coup, and Zadok's descendants controlled the high priesthood for centuries afterward.

entries.label: 8 books

entries.title: Zaham
entries.dictNote: Zaham was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah by his wife Abihail, listed among Rehoboam's children in 2 Chronicles 11:19. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zair
entries.dictNote: Zair, a site east of the Dead Sea where King Joram of Judah broke through an Edomite force that had surrounded him during Edom's revolt from Judah (2 Kings 8:21). Its exact location is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zalaph
entries.dictNote: Father of Hanun, one of the men who helped rebuild a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 3:30).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zalmon
entries.summary: Tsalmon, the name of a place in Palestine and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Zalmon names both a person and a place. The wooded hill of Zalmon, near Shechem, supplied the brushwood Abimelech's men used to burn down the tower of Shechem (Judges 9:48), and Psalm 68 pictures snow falling on this same dark, shaded mountain. Separately, Zalmon the Ahohite was one of David's mighty warriors, also called Ilai in the parallel list in Chronicles (2 Samuel 23:28; 1 Chronicles 11:29).
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Zalmonah
entries.summary: Tsalmonah, a place in the Desert
entries.dictNote: Zalmonah was a stop in Israel's wilderness journey, coming after Mount Hor in the itinerary of Numbers 33 (Num. 33:41-42). Its name likely relates to shade or darkness, and it is generally placed somewhere in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, on the route toward Edom, though it has not been securely located.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zalmunna
entries.dictNote: Zalmunna was one of two Midianite kings Gideon pursued and captured after they had killed his brothers, and Gideon executed both kings personally once his young son, too frightened to do it himself, couldn't carry out the task.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zamzummim
entries.summary: a Zamzumite, or native tribe of Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Zamzummim were a people of great size and numbers whom the Lord destroyed before the Ammonites so that Ammon could settle their territory east of the Jordan, an episode Moses recalls as evidence that God had cleared land for other nations besides Israel (Deuteronomy 2:20-21). Some identify them with the Zuzim, a similarly obscure people defeated earlier by the coalition of eastern kings in Genesis 14.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zanoah
entries.summary: Zanoach, the name of two places in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Zanoah was a town in Judah, and its residents helped repair a section of Jerusalem's gates under Nehemiah's rebuilding project.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Zaphnath-paaneah
entries.dictNote: Zaphnath-paaneah is not a separate person but the Egyptian title or name Pharaoh gave to Joseph when he made him governor over Egypt (Genesis 41:45). The name is genuinely Egyptian, though scholars disagree on its exact meaning, with proposals ranging from 'God speaks and he lives' to a title connected to Joseph's administrative role.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zaphon
entries.dictNote: Zaphon, meaning "north," was a town assigned to the tribe of Gad in the Jordan Valley (Joshua 13:27). Some scholars connect the same Hebrew word in Judges 12:1, traditionally translated "northward," to this same town, understood there as the mustering point for the Ephraimites who confronted Jephthah. Its precise site remains unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zara
entries.dictNote: Zara is the form used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3) for Zerah, the twin brother of Perez born to Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38:27-30). Matthew lists him only to mark the line continuing through his brother Perez, since Zerah himself is not an ancestor of Jesus.

entries.dictNote: Zerah was Judah's son by Tamar, born as a twin to Perez in a delivery marked by a scarlet thread tied to his hand when he seemed to be arriving first, only for Perez to be born ahead of him after all.

entries.title: Zarchite
entries.summary: a Zarchite or descendant of Zerach
entries.dictNote: Zarchite identifies a descendant of Zerah, a name borne by sons of both Judah and Simeon, and appears mainly in genealogical and census lists in Numbers and Chronicles rather than attaching to any single well known figure.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Zareah
entries.dictNote: Zareah, better known as Zorah, was a town on the border of Judah and Dan and the hometown of Samson. It was there that the angel of the Lord announced his birth to Manoah's wife, and the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him between Zorah and Eshtaol. Danite spies set out from Zorah to scout territory for their tribe's migration north, and Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father's tomb.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Zared
entries.summary: Zered, a brook East of the Dead Sea
entries.dictNote: The Zered was a valley and brook Israel crossed near the end of their wilderness wandering, marking a stage in their journey around Edom and Moab toward the promised land.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zarephath
entries.dictNote: Zarephath, a Phoenician town on the coast road between Tyre and Sidon, is best known as the place where the prophet Elijah lodged with a widow during a three-year famine, multiplying her flour and oil and later restoring her son to life (1 Kings 17:8-24). Obadiah later cites it as a name marking how far north Israelite exiles will one day resettle (Obadiah 1:20). Excavations at the site, ancient Sarepta, directed by James Pritchard in the 1970s, uncovered more than twenty pottery kilns, olive-oil and purple-dye workshops, and an inscribed shrine that confirmed the site's identity, along with continuous occupation through the Iron Age. The New Testament refers to it by its Greek name, Sarepta, when Jesus cites the widow's story (Luke 4:26).

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zareth-shahar
entries.dictNote: Zareth-shahar, "splendor of the dawn," was a town in the territory allotted to Reuben east of the Jordan, situated on a hill overlooking the plain by the Dead Sea (Joshua 13:19). It is usually identified with ruins near the mouth of the Wadi Zarqa Ma'in, close to the ancient hot-spring resort of Callirhoe on the sea's eastern shore. Little survives at the site beyond scattered wall fragments and column pieces.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zarthan
entries.dictNote: Zarthan, also spelled Zaretan, was a place in the Jordan Valley near Succoth, in an area of dense clay soil suited for metalworking. The Jordan's waters are said to have piled up near Zarthan when Israel crossed on dry ground (Joshua 3:16), and centuries later Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in molds in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan (1 Kings 7:46). Its exact site in the plain is uncertain, though it is sometimes linked to Tell es-Sa'idiyeh.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zattu
entries.dictNote: Zattu was the head of a large family among the returning exiles, listed by household count in both Ezra and Nehemiah.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zaza
entries.dictNote: A descendant of Judah in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, listed among the sons of Jonathan (1 Chronicles 2:33). Nothing else is recorded about him.

entries.dictNote: Zebedee was a Galilean fisherman, the father of the apostles James and John, and prosperous enough to employ hired servants alongside his sons, based on the detail Mark includes when the brothers leave the family fishing business to follow Jesus.

entries.title: Zebudah
entries.dictNote: Wife of King Josiah of Judah and mother of his son Jehoiakim, who succeeded to the throne after the brief reign of his brother Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:36).

entries.title: Zebul
entries.dictNote: Zebul was Abimelech's deputy governor over Shechem, and he warned Abimelech of Gaal's rebellion and helped defeat it, staying loyal even as the city around him turned against Abimelech's rule.

entries.title: Zebulonite
entries.summary: a Zebulonite or descendant of Zebulun
entries.dictNote: Zebulonite designates a member of the tribe of Zebulun. In the wilderness census it names the tribe collectively, and in Judges it is applied specifically to Elon, one of the minor judges who led Israel for ten years and was buried in Aijalon within Zebulun's own territory.

entries.title: Zechariah
entries.summary: Luke's Zechariah here (11:51, 'killed between the altar and the house of God') is almost certainly the priest murdered in 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, centuries before Jesus spoke — not the same person as John the Baptist's father, who shares the name earlier in this Gospel. Josephus, decades after the Gospel was written, records a startlingly similar killing: a different man, also named Zacharias, cut down 'in the middle of the temple' during the Jewish War of AD 66-70. Two different men, two different centuries, the same name and the same terrible detail — not the same event, but a real and well-known coincidence scholars still discuss.
entries.dictNote: Zechariah was an extremely common name in the Old Testament and New, and this entry centers on two of its most significant bearers. The prophet Zechariah, active after the exile alongside Haggai, encouraged the rebuilding of the temple through a series of vivid symbolic visions and looked forward to a coming king who would enter Jerusalem humble and riding on a donkey, a prophecy the Gospels connect directly to Jesus's entry into Jerusalem. A different Zechariah, a priest married to Elizabeth, was struck mute after doubting the angel Gabriel's announcement that his elderly wife would bear a son, John the Baptist, and only regained his speech after confirming in writing that the child's name would be John as instructed.

witness.source: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 4.5

entries.title: Zedad

entries.dictNote: Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar after deporting his predecessor, and his reign ended in disaster when he rebelled against Babylon despite Jeremiah's repeated warnings not to. Nebuchadnezzar besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in response, captured Zedekiah trying to flee, executed his sons in front of him, and then blinded him, making the massacre of his sons the last thing he ever saw. A few minor figures elsewhere in the Old Testament, including a false prophet who opposed Jeremiah, also carried the name.

entries.title: Zeker
entries.dictNote: Zeker was a Benjamite listed among the descendants of Jeiel in 1 Chronicles 8:31, part of the genealogy tracing Saul's ancestry. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:37 spells the same name Zecher.

entries.title: Zelah
entries.dictNote: Town in Benjamin (Josh. 18:28), likely Saul's own hometown, where he and his son Jonathan were finally buried in the family tomb of Kish after David had their bones brought back from Jabesh-gilead's earlier rescue at Beth-shan (2 Sam. 21:12-14).

entries.title: Zelek
entries.dictNote: Zelek was an Ammonite who served among David's thirty mighty warriors, an unusual inclusion of a foreigner among David's elite fighting men (2 Samuel 23:37; 1 Chronicles 11:39).

entries.title: Zelotes
entries.summary: a Zealot, i.e. (specially) partisan for Jewish political independence
entries.dictNote: Zelotes, meaning the Zealot, is the epithet attached to the apostle Simon in Luke's lists of the twelve, distinguishing him from Simon Peter (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). It likely reflects either former ties to the Jewish Zealot movement, which sought armed resistance to Roman rule, or simply a zealous temperament; Matthew and Mark instead call him Simon the Canaanite, a Semitic term with the same meaning.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zelzah
entries.dictNote: A place on the border of Benjamin near Rachel's tomb, cited by Samuel as a landmark in the sign he gave Saul confirming his anointing as king (1 Sam. 10:2).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zemaraim
entries.dictNote: Zemaraim names two distinct places in the older sources, and the entity's two canonical references reflect both. The first is a town of Benjamin listed in Joshua 18:22, generally located at a ruin north of Jericho. The second is a hill in the Ephraim highlands where King Abijah of Judah routed Jeroboam's much larger army of Israel, a defeat from which the northern king never fully recovered (2 Chronicles 13:4-20).

witness.excerpt: , he was not affrighted at it, but proved of a courageous temper of mind, superior both to his youth and to the hopes of his enemy; so he chose him an army out of the two tribes, and met Jeroboam at a place called Mount Zemaraim, and pitched his camp near the other, and prepared everything necessary for the fight.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zemarite
entries.summary: a Tsemarite or branch of the Canaanites
entries.dictNote: Zemarites descended from Canaan and were named for Zemar, a Phoenician coastal town at the western foot of the Lebanon range. The city appears as Sumur in the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters, where it served as an Egyptian administrative center in Syria, confirming its existence as a real Late Bronze Age settlement.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zemira
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite, one of the sons of Becher, listed among the heads of families noted for their military strength in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zenan
entries.dictNote: Zenan was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland district of Judah's territory (Joshua 15:37). It is probably the same town Micah calls Zaanan in his taunting oracle against the towns of the Judean foothills, playing on the sound of the name to say its people will not "come out" (Micah 1:11). Its exact site is unidentified.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zenas
entries.dictNote: Zenas was a Christian identified as 'the lawyer,' whom Paul asks Titus to help outfit for a journey, along with Apollos (Titus 3:13). Whether 'lawyer' refers to expertise in Jewish law or Roman law is uncertain, and nothing more about him is recorded.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zephaniah
entries.summary: Tsephanjah, the name of four Israelites
entries.dictNote: Zephaniah prophesied during King Josiah's reign, warning of a coming day of the Lord that would bring judgment not just on Judah's idolatry but on the surrounding nations as well, before the book ends with an unexpected turn toward restoration and God rejoicing over his people with singing. His genealogy is traced back four generations in the opening verse, possibly to identify him as a great-great-grandson of King Hezekiah.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Zephath
entries.dictNote: Zephath was a Canaanite town that the tribes of Judah and Simeon captured and destroyed, renaming it Hormah, "devotion to destruction," after which the name Zephath drops from the biblical record (Judges 1:17). The same city had earlier repelled an unauthorized Israelite attack during the wilderness wandering (Numbers 14:45). Its site is usually placed near Tell es-Seba or Tell el-Meshash in the northern Negev, though the exact identification remains debated among archaeologists.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zephi
entries.dictNote: Zephi, also spelled Zepho, was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Nothing beyond his place in this genealogy is recorded of him.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zephon
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad and head of the clan of the Zephonites counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:15); the earlier list in Genesis 46:16 spells the name Ziphion.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zephonites
entries.summary: a Tsephonite, or (collectively) descendants of Tsephon
entries.dictNote: Zephonites were the clan descended from Zephon, a son of Gad, counted in the Numbers 26 census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zer
entries.dictNote: A fortified town assigned to the tribe of Naphtali, named only once (Joshua 19:35). It was likely near the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, though its exact site is unknown.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zerahiah
entries.summary: Zerachjah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Zerahiah was a priest in the high priestly genealogy, an ancestor of Ezra listed in the line connecting him back to Aaron.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zereda
entries.dictNote: Zereda was a town on the north side of Mount Ephraim, the birthplace of Jeroboam, who later led the ten tribes into revolt against Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:26). It is probably the same place, spelled Zarethan, associated with the clay ground where Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast (2 Chronicles 4:17), and has also been connected with the Zererath of Judges 7:22.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zererath
entries.dictNote: A place named in the account of Gideon's rout of the Midianites, along the line of their flight down the Jordan valley toward Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah (Judges 7:22). Its exact site is unknown, and some scholars connect it with Zeredah or Zarethan further down the valley.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zeresh
entries.dictNote: Zeresh was Haman's wife, and she encouraged him to build the gallows meant for Mordecai, only to warn him later, once his plans began collapsing, that his downfall before a Jew was now certain.

witness.excerpt: So he went home, and called for his wife Zeresh, and his friends; and when they were come, he shewed them what honour he enjoyed not only from the King, but from the Queen also.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zereth
entries.dictNote: A son of Ashhur, the Calebite clan chief remembered as the founder of Tekoa, by his wife Helah (1 Chronicles 4:5-7). He appears only in this genealogical list, alongside his brothers Zohar and Ethnan; Tekoa later became the hometown of the prophet Amos.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zeri
entries.dictNote: One of the sons of Jeduthun appointed by David to prophesy with musical instruments in the temple service, listed in 1 Chronicles 25:3; he is probably the same man called Izri a few verses later in the same chapter's roster of Levitical musicians (1 Chr. 25:11).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zeruah
entries.dictNote: Mother of Jeroboam, who became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the nation split following Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:26).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zerubbabel
entries.dictNote: Zerubbabel was a descendant of David who led the first wave of Jewish exiles back from Babylon to Jerusalem and served as governor of the province, overseeing the rebuilding of the temple's foundation and, with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah's encouragement, its eventual completion. His place in David's line, preserved even in exile, keeps the promise of an eventual Davidic king alive in the postexilic books.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Zetham
entries.dictNote: Zetham was a Levite of the family of Ladan who served among those David put in charge of the temple treasuries (1 Chronicles 23:8; 26:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zethan
entries.dictNote: Zethan was a Benjamite named in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:10.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zethar
entries.dictNote: Zethar was one of the seven eunuchs who attended King Ahasuerus and was sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's guests, a summons she refused, setting off the events that led to Esther's rise (Esther 1:10-12).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zia
entries.dictNote: A head of a family in the tribe of Gad, listed among those settled in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:13).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziba
entries.dictNote: Ziba was a servant of Saul's household whom David put in charge of Mephibosheth's restored land, and Ziba later falsely accused Mephibosheth of disloyalty during Absalom's rebellion, a lie that cost Mephibosheth half his property.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zibeon
entries.dictNote: Zibeon was a Horite chief in Edom's genealogies, ancestor of Esau's wife Oholibamah's family line.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zibia
entries.dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Shaharaim in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:9. Nothing further is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zibiah
entries.dictNote: Zibiah, from Beersheba, was the mother of King Joash of Judah, the boy king who was hidden from the murderous queen Athaliah and later crowned at age seven (2 Kings 12:1; 2 Chronicles 24:1).

witness.excerpt: His mother’s name was Zibiah, of the city Beersheba.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zichri
entries.summary: Zicri, the name of twelve Israelites
entries.dictNote: Zichri was a common Old Testament name, borne by several military officers, Levites, and officials, including an Ephraimite warrior who killed a son of King Ahaz during a war between Israel and Judah.
entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ziddim
entries.summary: Tsiddim (with the article), a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ziddim, a fortified town of Naphtali listed in Joshua 19:35 alongside Hazor, Rakkath, and Kinnereth. It appears only in this one boundary list and its exact site is not known with certainty, though some place it near the Sea of Galilee.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zif
entries.dictNote: Zif is not a person but the name of the second month of the ancient Hebrew calendar, meaning “brightness” or “blossoming,” later called Iyar; it is used only to date the start of Solomon's temple construction, in the fourth year of his reign, and its completion seven years later (1 Kings 6:1, 37). The month falls roughly in April and May.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziha
entries.summary: Tsicha, the name of two Nethinim
entries.dictNote: Ziha was the head of a family of temple servants among the returning exiles, listed in both Ezra and Nehemiah's records.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ziklag
entries.summary: Tsiklag or Tsikelag, a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Ziklag was a town in the Negev assigned to Judah and Simeon that fell under Philistine control; King Achish of Gath gave it to David as a base during his flight from Saul, and David used it as his home for over a year. While David's men were away, Amalekite raiders burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children, prompting David's pursuit and recovery of the captives. It was at Ziklag that David received news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths at Gilboa. Archaeologists led by Yosef Garfinkel have proposed Khirbet a-Ra'i, between Kiryat Gat and Lachish, as the site of Ziklag, based on a destruction layer and finds dated to the time of David, though the identification is contested by other scholars.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Zillah
entries.dictNote: Zillah was one of Lamech's two wives in Cain's genealogical line, and the mother of Tubal-cain, remembered as an early forger of bronze and iron tools.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zilpah
entries.dictNote: Zilpah was Leah's servant, given to Jacob as a secondary wife in the competition between Leah and Rachel to produce sons, and she became the mother of Gad and Asher.

entries.title: Zilthai
entries.summary: Tsillethai, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Zilthai's name means “shadow of the LORD.” One Zilthai was a Benjamite family head (1 Chronicles 8:20). A second Zilthai was a captain from the tribe of Manasseh who defected to join David's forces at Ziklag while David was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:20).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zimmah
entries.summary: Zimmah, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Zimmah was a common Levitical name among the descendants of Gershon listed in the genealogies of Chronicles.
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zimran
entries.summary: Zimran, a son of Abraham by Keturah
entries.dictNote: Zimran was a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, generally taken as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, though the tribe cannot be identified with certainty (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zimri
entries.summary: Zimri, the name of five Israelites, and of an Arabian tribe
entries.dictNote: Zimri assassinated King Elah of Israel and seized the throne, only to reign seven days before the army proclaimed a rival commander king instead; Zimri burned the palace down around himself rather than be captured.

entries.label: 5 books

entries.title: Zin
entries.summary: Tsin, a part of the Desert
entries.dictNote: The Wilderness of Zin was a desert region Israel passed through during their wilderness wanderings, the site of Kadesh, where Miriam died and where Moses struck the rock in anger instead of speaking to it.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Zina
entries.dictNote: Zina was one of the sons of Shimei, a Levite of the Gershonite line, listed among the Levitical family heads David organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 23:10). The next verse calls him Zizah, likely a variant spelling of the same name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zion
entries.summary: Tsijon (as a permanent capital), a mountain of Jerusalem
entries.books: 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Psalm, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Micah, Zephaniah, Zechariah
entries.dictNote: Zion was originally the fortified hill on Jerusalem's southeastern ridge that David captured from the Jebusites and made his capital, building his palace there and giving it the name “the city of David.” Excavations on this ridge have exposed a massive Stepped Stone Structure and an adjoining Large Stone Structure that many archaeologists link to fortifications from David's era, along with tunnels including Warren's Shaft and Hezekiah's Tunnel. Later biblical writers extended the name to cover all of Jerusalem, then Israel as God's chosen people, and New Testament writers apply it to the church and to the heavenly city.

entries.title: Zior
entries.dictNote: Zior, a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, listed in Joshua 15:54. It occurs only this once in scripture and is commonly identified with the modern village of es-Sa'ir northeast of Hebron.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziph
entries.summary: Ziph, the name of a place in Palestine; also of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah southeast of Hebron whose surrounding wilderness gave David refuge while he fled from Saul. The Ziphites twice betrayed David's location to Saul, prompting psalms that reflect on that betrayal. A second, smaller Ziph lay further south in the Negev, and the name also recurs among Judah's genealogies.

entries.label: 4 books

entries.title: Ziphah
entries.dictNote: Ziphah was a son of Jehallelel listed among the descendants of Judah in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:16.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziphim
entries.summary: a Ziphite or inhabitant of Ziph
entries.dictNote: Ziphites were the inhabitants of Ziph, a town in the wilderness of Judah southeast of Hebron. Twice they betrayed David's hiding place to Saul while he was a fugitive, an episode remembered in the heading of Psalm 54.

witness.excerpt: 1097.] There was a man that was a Ziphite, of the city of Maon; who was rich, and had a vast number of cattle: for he fed a flock of three thousand sheep, and another flock of a thousand goats.

entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Ziphion
entries.dictNote: A son of Gad listed among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen. 46:16). The parallel census in Numbers 26:15 gives his name as Zephon, and most translations treat the two forms as the same person.

witness.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziphron
entries.dictNote: Ziphron marked a point on the northern boundary of the land Israel was to inherit, as described in Moses' instructions before entering Canaan, situated southeast of Hamath (Numbers 34:9). Its exact site is unidentified, though the boundary description places it in the general region of the Beqaa Valley or southern Syria.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zippor
entries.dictNote: Zippor was the father of Balak, the Moabite king who hired Balaam to curse the invading Israelites.
entries.label: 3 books

entries.title: Zipporah
entries.dictNote: Zipporah was Moses's wife, a daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro, and in a strange episode on the way back to Egypt she circumcised their son herself and touched Moses with the foreskin to avert what Scripture describes only as the Lord seeking to kill him, an act that saved his life.

witness.excerpt: And Moses took Zipporah his wife, and his children, and pleased himself with his coming.
And he took with him Zipporah, the daughter of Raguel, whom he had married, and the children he had by her, Gersom and Eleazer, and made haste into Egypt.

entries.title: Zithri
entries.dictNote: A Levite of the Kohathite line, son of Uzziel and brother of Mishael and Elzaphan (Exodus 6:22).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziz
entries.dictNote: The ascent of Ziz was a pass near En-gedi on the western shore of the Dead Sea, the route by which a coalition of Moabites and Ammonites advanced against King Jehoshaphat of Judah (2 Chron. 20:16). It is generally identified with a steep track climbing from the Dead Sea shore toward Tekoa, matching the rugged terrain of the En-gedi cliffs.

entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Ziza
entries.summary: Ziza, the name of two Israelites
entries.dictNote: Two men named Ziza appear in Chronicles. The first was a Simeonite prince whose clan drove out the peaceful people of Gedor and settled their land during Hezekiah's reign (1 Chronicles 4:37-43). The second was a son born to King Rehoboam of Judah by his favored wife Maachah (2 Chronicles 11:20-21).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zizah
entries.dictNote: A Gershonite Levite, son of Shimei, listed among the heads of Levitical families organized by David for temple service (1 Chr. 23:11). He is likely the same man called Zina one verse earlier in the same list (1 Chr. 23:10), Zizah apparently being a variant spelling of his name.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zoan
entries.dictNote: Zoan, known to the Greeks as Tanis, was an ancient city in the Nile delta that served for a time as Egypt's capital and is described in Numbers as having been built seven years after Hebron. The psalmist recalls the plagues of the exodus as wonders worked "in the field of Zoan," and Isaiah and Ezekiel both single it out in oracles against Egypt's rulers and counselors. Excavations at Tanis by Pierre Montet in 1939 uncovered the intact royal tombs of several pharaohs, including Psusennes I, a discovery rivaling Tutankhamun's tomb that was overshadowed at the time by the outbreak of the Second World War.

witness.excerpt: 22 Tanis or Zoan.

entries.title: Zoar
entries.summary: Tsoar, a place East of the Jordan
entries.dictNote: Zoar was a small town near the Dead Sea, originally called Bela, to which Lot and his daughters fled for refuge when Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed; Lot had asked that the town be spared because of its small size, and it was. Isaiah and Jeremiah both mention Zoar in oracles concerning Moab, since it lay near the border between Moab and the Dead Sea plain.

entries.title: Zoba
entries.summary: Zoba or Zobah, a region of Syria
entries.dictNote: Zobah was an Aramean kingdom north of Damascus that repeatedly clashed with Israel. Saul fought against it, and David decisively defeated its king Hadadezer, capturing chariots, horsemen, and a large amount of bronze that later went into temple furnishings. Solomon later contended with a rebel from Zobah named Rezon, who established himself as a persistent adversary in Damascus.

entries.title: Zobebah
entries.dictNote: Zobebah was a son of Coz, of the tribe of Judah, listed in the brief genealogical notice of 1 Chronicles 4:8 alongside his brother Anub and the families of Aharhel. The verse is part of a cluster of otherwise unattached Judahite genealogical fragments in that chapter. Nothing further is known of him.

entries.title: Zohar
entries.summary: Tsochar, the name of a Hittite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Zohar was the father of Ephron, the Hittite from whom Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah as a family burial site.

entries.title: Zoheleth
entries.summary: Zocheleth, a boundary stone in. Palestine
entries.dictNote: Zoheleth, meaning "the serpent stone," was a rock near the spring of En-rogel outside Jerusalem where Adonijah, David's son, held a sacrificial feast to have himself proclaimed king while David lay dying, deliberately leaving out Solomon, Nathan, and Solomon's other supporters (1 Kings 1:9-10). The plot collapsed once Nathan and Bathsheba persuaded David to have Solomon publicly anointed instead.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zoheth
entries.dictNote: A son of Ishi listed among the descendants of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:20. Nothing else is recorded about him.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zophah
entries.dictNote: Zophah was a son of Helem and a chief of the tribe of Asher, listed at the head of a family record noted for its many able warriors (1 Chronicles 7:35, 40).
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zophai
entries.summary: Tsuph or Tsophai or Tsiph, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
entries.dictNote: Zophai, also spelled Zuph, was not a place but a Kohathite Levite, an ancestor of the prophet Samuel through Elkanah's line (1 Chronicles 6:26, 35). The region where Elkanah's family lived, in the hill country of Ephraim, was named "the land of Zuph" after him, which is likely why this record was filed as a place rather than a person (1 Samuel 1:1; 9:5).
entries.label: 2 books

entries.title: Zophar
entries.dictNote: Zophar was the third and harshest of Job's three friends, a Naamathite whose brief, blunt speeches insist even more forcefully than his companions that Job's suffering proves hidden sin, a position God later rebukes.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zorites
entries.summary: a Tsorite or Tsorathite, i.e. inhabitants of Tsorah
entries.dictNote: Zorites were the inhabitants of Zorah, a town on the border of Judah and Dan and the birthplace of Samson. In Chronicles they appear as a Judahite clan within the larger genealogical record of Caleb's descendants.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zuar
entries.dictNote: Zuar was the father of the tribal leader of Issachar during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zur
entries.summary: Tsur, the name of a Midianite and of an Israelite
entries.dictNote: Zur was a Midianite chief killed in Israel's war against Midian, and his daughter Cozbi was killed by Phinehas for her role in the idolatry and sexual immorality that had provoked a plague on Israel.

entries.title: Zuriel
entries.dictNote: Zuriel was the chief of the Merarite Levite clan at the time of the exodus, appointed to oversee that family's portion of the tabernacle service (Numbers 3:35). The Merarites camped on the north side of the tabernacle and were responsible for its frames, bars, pillars, and sockets.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zurishaddai
entries.dictNote: Zurishaddai was the father of the tribal leader of Simeon during the wilderness census.
entries.label: 1 book

entries.title: Zuzims
entries.summary: Zuzites, an aboriginal tribe of Palestine
entries.dictNote: The Zuzim were a people living east of the Jordan whom the invading coalition led by Chedorlaomer defeated in the campaign that eventually swept up Lot at Sodom (Genesis 14:5). Some identify them with the Zamzummim, a similarly obscure people the Ammonites are said to have displaced from the same region (Deuteronomy 2:20).
